stem: You are a general practitioner in a regional South Australian practice. Your next patient is Mia Delacruz, a 25-year-old woman, who has presented complaining of excessive nausea and vomiting. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago and she has had a positive home pregnancy test. Antenatal screening bloods have been performed and are normal. She has not had any ultrasound scan.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Perform a physical examination by asking the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Hyperemesis gravidarum with clinical dehydration — ketones 3+, blood glucose normal (5.4). Uterus consistent with 8 weeks, no mass.
plan: Vitals from examiner — BP, postural drop by name, pulse, temp
Open, one acknowledgement, signpost
Characterise vomiting: onset, colour, blood, frequency, dizzy, keep anything down
Five buckets: obstetric · acute abdomen · infection · endocrine · neuro
PEFE ladder (about 3 min): dehydration, weight, abdomen incl. mass, pelvic with consent + chaperone, os, uterine size, dipstick ketones first, BGL
Diagnosis + differentials by group
Management: ED for IV fluids + IV antiemetic, ultrasound regardless, diet, stepwise meds, safety-net
ask: Vital signs before you sit — ask the postural drop by name
What colour is the vomit? (green = obstruction, station over)
Any blood? Frequency? Anything make it better/worse?
Dizzy on standing? Can you keep anything down?
Obstetric: LMP, bleeding, bloods, scan, first pregnancy, twins in family, IVF
Acute abdomen: any abdominal pain at all? bowels, bloating, passing wind, jaundice
Infection: fever, urinary symptoms, headache, photophobia, rash, neck stiffness, travel
Endocrine/neuro if time: heat intolerance, FHx thyroid, polyuria, weakness
Ask her concerns — hidden agenda: friend said vomiting means something is wrong with the baby
pefe: General: alert/drowsy, degree of dehydration, weight vs booking
Postural drop
Abdomen: distension, tenderness, guarding, mass (uterus not palpable until ~12 wk), organomegaly, bowel sounds
Pelvic with consent + chaperone: bleeding/discharge, os, CMT, uterine size, adnexae
Urine dipstick — ketones first — then nitrites, leucocytes, protein, blood
Blood glucose (excludes DKA)
fails: Never asked the colour of the vomit
Never asked about abdominal pain
No urine dipstick / ketones
No ultrasound arranged
No ED referral for intravenous fluids
numbers: Postural drop ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic within 3 min
Uterus palpable abdominally from ~12 wk; fetal heart on TVUS from ~6–7 wk
Referral triggers: ketones · no oral intake · failed oral antiemetics · instability
Meds: pyridoxine + doxylamine → metoclopramide or ondansetron wafer → IV
Variants: green vomit → obstruction; BGL 21 + ketones → DKA; size > dates → twins/molar, urgent scan

setting: Your general practice, rural South Australia.
stem: Lily Fraser, 30, is 36 weeks pregnant and has come for a routine antenatal visit. The pregnancy has been uneventful and all antenatal screening is complete and normal.

Last week she developed swelling of both legs. The baby is kicking well. Today: blood pressure raised on two readings, urine protein 3+. Fundal height 36 cm, fetal heart rate 140, longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Outline your investigations and your management
time: 8 minutes. Two-minute warning.

back.dx: Pre-eclampsia with severe features — BP 150/95, protein 3+, headache and flashes, hyperreflexia and ankle clonus present. Clonus makes it severe regardless of the number.
plan: Vitals
Open question + one-line acknowledgement
The swelling — onset, progression, level, one or both, and present on waking?
Red-flag set by organ group: neuro → hepatic → cardiorespiratory/haematological/renal
Obstetric complications (bleeding, fluid, movements) and background, FHx
Examination request — findings not technique
Diagnosis, reasons, differentials
Investigations (CTG first), management split at 160/110, safety-net repeated back
ask: Is the swelling there when you first wake up in the morning?
How far up does it go? One leg or both?
Headache? Vision — blurring, flashes, spots? Dizziness or confusion?
Pain under the right ribs? Nausea/vomiting? Jaundice?
Chest pain or breathlessness? Rashes or bruising? Passing less urine?
Bleeding, leaking fluid, baby moving as usual?
Past hypertension or kidney disease; family history of hypertension or pre-eclampsia
Confirm the antenatal timeline briefly — do not re-take what the stem gave
pefe: General appearance: alert, rash, bruising, jaundice
Neuro: fundoscopy, reflexes, and specifically ankle clonus — then say out loud that clonus makes this severe
Heart sounds; chest — bibasal crackles
Abdomen: liver tenderness, uterine tenderness, fundal height, FHR
Lower limbs: pitting oedema and level
Urine dipstick
fails: Never asked for ankle clonus by name
Differentials given as causes of leg swelling (DVT, heart failure) instead of hypertensive/multisystem disorders
CTG omitted from investigations
Management not split at 160/110; no target under 135/85
Promising her the baby will be fine; 'try not to worry'
numbers: 140/90 hypertension · 160/110 severe (IV labetalol/hydralazine, monitored area) · target <135/85
20 weeks — the line between chronic and gestational/pre-eclampsia
Oral labetalol first line; methyldopa or nifedipine alternatives; no ACEi/ARB/diuretics
MgSO4 4 g IV over 20 min then 1 g/h; reflexes go first in toxicity
Admit under obstetrics today; birth within days at 36 wk; no steroids at 36 wk (VERIFY)
Aspirin 100–150 mg nightly from 12 wk (before 16) to ~36 wk next pregnancy (VERIFY); BP review 6–12 wk postpartum
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS · TIS 131 450

setting: General practice, shared antenatal care, rural South Australia.
stem: Jenny Mahoney, 28, G1 P0. At 30 weeks everything was normal and her symphysis–fundal height was 29 cm. Today, at 34 weeks, it is 30 cm.
tasks: Take a history
Tell the examiner the investigations you would request
Results are then handed to you. Explain the results
Explain the diagnosis
Tell her the outcome for the baby
time: 8 minutes. Prompt bell at 5:00 — tasks 1 and 2 must be finished before the bell.

back.dx: Small for gestational age; most likely cause fetal growth restriction from placental insufficiency — EFW and abdominal circumference both below the 10th centile, reduced fetal movements.
plan: Part one: open and acknowledge the worry before any question; obstetric spine down the timeline one question at a time; fetal movements (reduced — treat as important)
Part two: pre-eclampsia questions, first pregnancy, then M D I S C — maternal disease · dates · infections · growth · substances · constitutional; leaking/bleeding/pain; small babies in the family
STOP the history whatever is left. Investigations to the examiner: ultrasound AND CTG, Doppler, maternal bloods
Prompt bell; charts handed over. Read them aloud — EFW and AC below the 10th
Diagnosis in four sentences; causes each with a reason; outcome — six words; referral, in-utero transfer, safety-net, summary
ask: Acknowledge: 'I understand why that's worrying, and I'm glad you came in'
Routine bloods? Dating scan? Down syndrome screen? 18–20 wk scan normal? Sweet drink test? Swab?
Is the baby kicking as usual? → respond immediately that it matters
Headaches, blurred vision, swelling, less urine?
High blood pressure? Kidney disease? Diabetes? Clots? Joint pain/rash? Lupus in family?
LMP — sure of the date? cycles regular?
Fever/rash in pregnancy? sick contacts? cat/litter tray? raw meat?
Weight monitored? Smoking, alcohol, drugs, medicines? Small babies in the family?
Leaking fluid? Bleeding or abdominal pain?
pefe: Investigations, not examination: growth ultrasound (AFI, EFW, AC, HC, FL, malformation)
CTG for fetal wellbeing
Umbilical artery Doppler
Mother: BP, dipstick ± PCR, UEC, antiphospholipid antibodies, toxoplasma and CMV serology
Amniocentesis with microarray if structural abnormality
fails: Ultrasound and CTG not both named before the 5:00 bell
Charts read silently — must say EFW and AC aloud
Saying hyperglycaemia (it is hypoglycaemia)
Telling her to stop exercising
Reassuring that reduced movements are common; naming a delivery week
numbers: SFH ≈ weeks ± 3 cm (VERIFY) · SGA <10th centile · FGR <3rd or both EFW and AC <10th · serial growth scans every 2–3 wk (VERIFY)
Oligohydramnios AFI <5 cm or pocket <2 cm; normal AFI 5–24
Outcomes: breathing · help at birth · temperature · low blood sugar · feeding · jaundice
Steroids if birth before ~34–35 wk anticipated (VERIFY); MgSO4 neuroprotection <30 wk (VERIFY)
Constitutionally small is a diagnosis of exclusion — say so
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848

stem: Chloe Bennett, 28, G2 P1, who believes she is about 20 weeks pregnant. The pregnancy was unplanned. She has been travelling with her partner, has had no antenatal screening or check-ups, and has a history of irregular periods. On examination the symphysis–fundal height is well above the gestation.
tasks: Take a focused history
Explain the diagnosis with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
(Older versions) Tell the examiner your investigations
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Large for gestational age — a measurement, not a diagnosis. Fundal height 30 cm at a believed 20 weeks. Most likely wrong dates or macrosomia; scan decides.
plan: Part one: open, name the worry, signpost; planned pregnancy? how has it been? why missed care — once, without judgement
Part two, the obstetric spine: bloods, dating scan, screening, 18–20 wk scan — one baby or more?, sugar test; movements; pre-eclampsia questions; previous pregnancy — was the baby large?
Part three, I M D D: infections · macrosomia · multiple · masses · dates · diabetes; smoking/alcohol/drugs/medicines/allergies

Part four: BP, dipstick, fundal height, FHR from examiner; finding + reason + honesty line; six causes each with a reason; what the scan looks for, OGTT, catch-up bloods; safety-net, follow-up, summary
ask: Was this a planned pregnancy? How has it been going?
Why did you miss your check-ups? — 'I only ask so we can make it easier from here'
Did the 18–20 week scan show one baby or more than one?
Feeling the baby move? Headaches, vision, swelling?
Previous pregnancy — problems, and was the baby large?
Fever/rash, sick contacts, pets/litter tray, raw meat
Big babies in the family? Rapid weight gain?
Very sick early on? Twins in family? IVF?
Ever told you have fibroids? Heavy periods?
LMP — sure? cycles regular? (irregular — dates uncertain)
Thirst, polyuria, diabetes in the family?
Smoking, alcohol, drugs, medicines, allergies
pefe: BP, urine dipstick (protein, glucose), fundal height, uterine contour and tone, FHR
Investigations: ultrasound — AFI, biometry/EFW, number of fetuses, fibroids, structural survey
75 g OGTT; catch-up booking bloods (FBC, group/antibodies, rubella, syphilis, hep B/C, HIV)
CTG in third trimester or with reduced movements
fails: Never asked whether the scan showed one baby or more
Never asked about diabetes — test, symptoms or family history
Fewer than six causes, or causes without reasons
Giving a single diagnosis instead of a finding
Advising bed rest; saying TORCH causes big babies
numbers: SFH ≈ weeks ± 3 cm (VERIFY) · LGA = EFW >90th · macrosomia >4000 g, high-risk >4500 (VERIFY)
Polyhydramnios AFI >24 cm or pocket ≥8 cm
Six causes: wrong dates · macrosomia · polyhydramnios · multiple pregnancy · GDM · fibroid (+ parvovirus/syphilis, fetal GI atresia)
OGTT 75 g at 24–28 wk: fasting 5.1 · 1 h 10.0 · 2 h 8.5 (VERIFY)
Past first trimester the uterus is abdominal — bimanual adds nothing

setting: Emergency department of a South Australian hospital.
stem: Lily Chen, 30, is 36 weeks pregnant and has presented with a headache.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Two-minute warning.

back.dx: Pre-eclampsia (BP 150/90, protein 3+, papilloedema, hyperreflexia, clonus) — then the examiner interrupts: 'Your patient is now having a fit.' After the seizure the diagnosis is eclampsia. Say eclampsia, not pre-eclampsia.
plan: Vitals including temperature by name
Open, acknowledge, signpost
SICORA + the four discriminators
Pre-eclampsia set, then the obstetric block (movements cannot be skipped)
'Other causes I need to rule out': meningitis, focal deficit, migraine/stress/sinus/dental
Examination request — a headache examination, full neuro incl. cranial nerves
Comment on the card → seizure: four priorities to the examiner until stopped
Explain eclampsia to her; headache differentials; delivery plan; summary
ask: Vital signs including temperature
Site, severity /10, character (offer: throbbing, pressure, dull ache), onset, constant, worse, radiation, relievers
Sudden onset over seconds? Worst headache of your life? Worse on cough/strain? Wakes you at night?
Vision changes, dizziness, RUQ pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice, swelling, chest pain/SOB, less urine
Antenatal tests normal? Baby kicking as usual? Bleeding, discharge, fluid?
Previous hypertension in pregnancy; kidney problems
Fever/chills? Rash? Neck stiffness? Photophobia?
Weakness or numbness anywhere?
Family history of migraine; stress; dental/sinus
pefe: General appearance, conscious level, rash, jaundice; BP and temperature
Full neuro: fundoscopy (blurred disc = papilloedema — say it), reflexes, ankle clonus by name, cranial nerves, limb tone/power/sensation, neck stiffness
ENT: sinus tenderness, dental hygiene
Heart sounds; chest — bibasal crackles
Abdomen: liver and uterine tenderness, fundal height, FHR, lie
Lower limbs oedema; urine dipstick for protein
fails: Saying 'pre-eclampsia' after the fit
Hypertension differentials (gestational/chronic HTN, APS) instead of headache differentials
Benzodiazepine before magnesium; no left lateral position
Delivering before resuscitating; running a litre of fluid
Attributing a fever to pre-eclampsia (variant)
numbers: Seizure: call help · DRS ABC, left lateral, high-flow O2, 2 large-bore cannulae · MgSO4 4 g IV/20 min then 1 g/h (benzo if continuing) · BP >160/110 IV labetalol/hydralazine · delivery
Monitor reflexes (lost first), RR, urine output; antidote calcium gluconate; 24 h Mg after birth or last seizure
Postpartum eclampsia — most within 48 h, described to 4 weeks (VERIFY)
Thunderclap → SAH: CT then LP; fever → meningitis: cultures and antibiotics before imaging/LP
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 at the same time as starting magnesium

stem: You are the medical officer in a country emergency department. Jess Tuiono, 26, has come in with vaginal bleeding that started yesterday and is getting worse, together with lower abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago.
A urine pregnancy test has already been done in triage. You will be told the result only if you ask.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain the most likely diagnosis to the patient
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Ectopic pregnancy, right tube — empty normal-sized uterus, os closed, CMT positive, right adnexal tenderness, shoulder-tip pain. The trap: urine pregnancy test NEGATIVE. It changes nothing.
plan: Obs incl. postural drop
Open, acknowledge
Bleeding: onset, worse, tissue, clots, pads. Pain: site, which came first, constant vs waves, severity, shoulder tip, faint
LMP/cycles, pregnancy symptoms
Risk sweep one at a time: previous ectopic, miscarriage/TOP, tubal surgery, contraception/IUD, IVF, STI/PID, smoking, blood group
PEFE in order: pallor → abdomen → os → tissue/bleeding → CMT → uterine size/empty → adnexae → THEN ask the urine test
The trap answer, one sentence, then carry on
Explain to her: name it, reasons, deal with the negative test, why it matters, what happens now; anti-D; escalation advice
ask: Which came first — pain or bleeding?
Passed any tissue? Clots? How many pads, soaked?
Pain constant, or coming in waves?
Any pain at the tip of your shoulder?
Felt faint or dizzy?
LMP and cycle regularity; pregnancy symptoms
Previous ectopic? Miscarriage or termination? Surgery on tubes/womb?
Contraception or a coil? IVF? Ever an STI or PID? (chlamydia — only if asked directly)
Smoking? Blood group?
pefe: General: pale or distressed?
Abdomen: where tender, guarding, rebound
Pelvic with consent + chaperone: os open/closed; tissue or bleeding; cervical lesion
Bimanual: cervical motion tenderness; uterine size and empty/full; adnexal mass/tenderness
Then: 'May I have the result of the urine pregnancy test?'

Reply verbatim: 'That does not change my diagnosis. A negative urine test does not exclude an ectopic at this gestation… I would send a quantitative serum βhCG and arrange an urgent transvaginal ultrasound. My working diagnosis remains an ectopic pregnancy.'
fails: Abandoning ectopic on the negative urine test — or saying nothing about it
Sending her home / outpatient review
Never asking previous ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD or STI
Missing anti-D in a rhesus-negative woman
Managing it yourself (offering methotrexate) instead of urgent gynaecology; refusing the bimanual 'in case it ruptures'
numbers: Urine hCG detects ~20–25 IU/L; serum from ~5 IU/L
TVUS discriminatory zone ~1500–2000 IU/L — guides timing of imaging, never diagnoses alone; βhCG 700 excludes nothing, repeat 48 h
Anti-D 250 IU within 72 h — ectopic is an indication
IV access, FBE, serum βhCG, group & antibody screen; nil by mouth; unstable → theatre not scanner
Retrieval not self-transport: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 / RFDS; SHINE SA for contraception and chlamydia retest

stem: You are a general practitioner in a rural South Australian practice. Mary Whitfield, 27, has come in this morning with vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was eight weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive three weeks ago.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately six minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain the diagnosis and your management to the patient
time: 8 minutes. A one-minute warning is given.

back.dx: Threatened miscarriage with a subchorionic haematoma — os closed, uterus 8 weeks, single intrauterine pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity, a collection of blood behind the developing placenta. Blood group O positive. (Card may say 'retroplacental clot' — correct term at 8 weeks is subchorionic haematoma; management identical.)
plan: Obs incl. postural drop before sitting
Open, acknowledge fear before any question; 'was this a planned pregnancy?'
Bleeding: start, worse/settling, tissue, clots, pads, colour. Pain: site, constant vs waves, shoulder tip, faint
P1–P5: LMP/cycles · symptoms persisting · first pregnancy/IVF/miscarriage/TOP/uterine surgery · relationship/STI · cervical screening; SNAP once; meds/allergies/blood group
PEFE — os first, then bleeding/tissue, cervix, CMT, uterine size, adnexae, then ultrasound
Reassure first, label second, the clot as a bruise, no bed rest, rescan, no anti-D (O pos), safety-net
ask: Was this a planned pregnancy? (never congratulate, never assume grief)
Have you passed any tissue — anything solid?
Is the pain constant, or in waves?
Shoulder-tip pain? Dizzy or faint?
Still getting morning sickness and sore breasts?
First pregnancy? IVF? Previous miscarriage/termination? Uterine surgery?
Stable relationship, any STI? Cervical screening up to date?
Smoking/alcohol/drugs — one question; meds, allergies, blood group
pefe: General: pale or distressed?
Abdomen: tenderness, uterus above symphysis?
Pelvic with consent + chaperone: is the os open or closed? — ASK THIS FIRST
Tissue or active bleeding at the os; cervical or vaginal lesion
Bimanual: CMT, uterine size and tenderness, adnexae
Has she had an ultrasound, and what does it show?
fails: Saying 'threatened miscarriage' before reassuring her — she hears the second word
Prescribing bed rest as treatment
Telling her the pregnancy is at risk when the scan is normal
Never asking whether she passed tissue
Giving anti-D to an O positive woman; ending without a safety net
numbers: Verbatim order: right place, right size, heartbeat, os closed → 'you are not having a miscarriage' → then the name
'A bruise where the pregnancy has attached' — say bruise, not haematoma; never say abruption
Most settle — do not promise; rescan in 1–2 weeks
Progesterone only with bleeding AND ≥1 previous miscarriage — not indicated here
Anti-D not recommended for threatened miscarriage <12 wk even if Rh negative
Serial βhCG adds nothing once cardiac activity seen
Red flags: soaks a pad in an hour, tissue, severe pain, faint, fever, offensive discharge

stem: You are a hospital medical officer in the early pregnancy assessment clinic. Sarah Nguyen, 25, was referred yesterday with light vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was eight weeks ago. She has had an ultrasound this morning and has come back for the result. She is on her own.

Information you have been given: observations BP 112/70, HR 76, T 36.6, she is well. Speculum yesterday: os closed, scant old blood, cervix healthy. Bimanual yesterday: uterus consistent with dates, non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, adnexae normal. Transvaginal ultrasound today: single intrauterine gestational sac, crown–rump length consistent with 8 weeks, no fetal cardiac activity, no adnexal mass, no free fluid. Blood group A negative. Her own words at reception: 'Is everything all right? Nobody would tell me anything.'
tasks: Explain the ultrasound findings to the patient
Counsel her about further management
Answer any questions she has
time: 8 minutes. There is no history to take.

back.dx: Missed miscarriage — CRL of 8 weeks with no cardiac activity (secure on a single scan: CRL ≥7 mm no heartbeat, or MSD ≥25 mm no embryo). Breaking bad news, three management options, anti-D (A negative).
plan: Set up (private; 'is there anyone you'd like me to call?') → 'what do you understand so far?' → normal findings first (os closed, right place) → warning shot 'I'm afraid I don't have good news for you today', pause → one plain sentence 'The scan shows the pregnancy has stopped growing. I'm very sorry — you have had a miscarriage.' → about ten seconds of silence, tissues → empathy, then permission to go on. Volunteer that nothing she did caused it
Three options, each with pros and cons, no steering; decline to choose for her, help her weigh knowing when vs avoiding an anaesthetic
Anti-D within 72 h (A negative), histology, red flags, trying again, recurrence, folic acid, written information, review next week, Sands / Red Nose
ask: Is there anyone you would like me to call to be with you?
Can you tell me what you understand so far about why you came in?
(Volunteer, unasked) There is nothing you did that caused this
Would it be all right if I explain what happens from here?
What matters more to you — knowing when, or avoiding an anaesthetic?
pefe: No examination. Three options: expectant (no drugs/surgery, at home; can't say when; bleeding and cramping) · medical (tablet then second medicine 1–2 days later; avoids anaesthetic; cramping, heavy bleeding, nausea; 15–25% still need surgery) · surgical (day-case under anaesthetic; predictable, least bleeding, tissue to lab; anaesthetic, infection, uterine injury, rarely adhesions)
Anti-D within 72 h if managed medically or surgically (A negative)
Histopathology on any tissue (excludes molar)
Red flags: soaks a pad in an hour, severe pain, fever, offensive discharge
fails: Opening with the diagnosis and no warning shot
Talking over her crying
Leaving without offering all three options
Not saying she did not cause it (or implying she did)
Missing anti-D in a rhesus-negative woman
Saying 'fetal demise', 'products of conception' or 'evacuation' to her face
numbers: Clock: news and silence by 2:30 · options by 5:00 · anti-D, red flags, trying again, follow-up by 7:30
Non-viability: MSD ≥25 mm no embryo, or CRL ≥7 mm no heartbeat; borderline → rescan 7–10 days, don't use the word
Medical management needs surgery in ~15–25% (not 5%); 63-day limit is for TOP, not miscarriage
Try again: no need to wait beyond one normal period; recurrence after one loss ≈ same as anyone; ~1 in 5 pregnancies end this way
Never: 'at least you know you can get pregnant', 'it was for the best'
Sands · Red Nose Grief and Loss · Miscarriage Australia · Country Health Connect · PATS · TIS 131 450

stem: You are the medical officer in the emergency department of a country hospital. Chloe Barrett, 24, has presented with vaginal bleeding that started early this morning and is getting heavier. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately four minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain the diagnosis and your immediate management
time: 8 minutes. The history is short deliberately.

back.dx: Incomplete miscarriage with shock — BP 90/60, HR 110, pale; os OPEN with products of conception at the os, active bleeding, uterus 5 weeks and contracting. Hypovolaemia dominant (tachycardia) plus possible cervical (vagal) shock — remove the tissue NOW. Blood group O negative.
plan: Obs before sitting → 'I'd move her to resus, two large-bore cannulae, bloods incl. cross-match, fluids while I continue' — one sentence
Four-minute history: bleeding start/worse, tissue, clots, pads, pain and waves, faint, shoulder tip, LMP, first pregnancy, fever/offensive discharge, blood group, meds/allergies
PEFE: general → abdomen → os first
'The os is open with products at the os' → IMMEDIATELY: 'I would remove that tissue now with sponge forceps and send it for histopathology'
Continue: bleeding, lesions, bimanual size/tender/contracting, adnexae; repeat obs after removal
Explain plainly; nothing she did; fluids, bloods, cross-match; anti-D; gynae; scan once stable; not going home while bleeding; red flags
back.planNote: only the four-minute history limit is from the source
ask: Observations first — she is shocked; say so out loud
When did it start? Worse or settling?
Have you passed any tissue — anything solid?
Clots? How many pads, soaking through?
Pain — constant or in waves?
Felt faint or dizzy? Shoulder-tip pain?
LMP; first pregnancy; previous miscarriage/TOP
Any fever, or offensive discharge? (septic miscarriage)
Blood group; medications; allergies
pefe: General: pale, distressed, alert?
Abdomen: tenderness, guarding, rebound, uterus palpable?
Pelvic with consent + chaperone: os open or closed? → tissue at os → remove with sponge forceps at that moment
Active bleeding; cervical/vaginal lesion
Bimanual: uterine size, tender, contracting; adnexae (CMT not assessed — tender)
Repeat observations after removal (improvement supports vagal component)
fails: Not removing the tissue, or removing it only as an afterthought in the summary
Not asking for observations before starting
Taking a full eight-minute history from a shocked woman
Discharging her while still bleeding
Missing anti-D in an O negative woman; missing the fever/offensive discharge screen
numbers: Drop when history is four minutes: cervical screening, partner/STI, SNAP, full PMH — 'I'd complete the history once stable'
Cervical shock classically bradycardia; HR 110 = hypovolaemia dominant — name both, removal treats both
Anti-D 250 IU within 72 h
Crystalloid, blood if no response; cross-matched blood, gynae + anaesthetics, theatre for evacuation if unstable — scan follows stability
Uterus 5 wk at 6 wk by dates = part expelled, contracting down
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 / RFDS — retrieval, not transfer by car; know on-site O negative units

stem: You are the medical officer in a country emergency department. Amy Coulthard, 25, has vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago.
tasks: Focused history
Ask for examination findings and investigations
Explain the diagnosis and your management
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Pregnancy of unknown location — serum βhCG 900 with no intrauterine sac, no free fluid, 1.5 cm corpus luteum cyst (a distractor), uterus empty and normal size, no CMT. Three possibilities; ectopic is the must-not-miss; uncertainty IS the diagnosis.
plan: Obs incl. postural drop
Open, acknowledge, planned pregnancy?
Bleeding: worse/settling, tissue, clots. Pain: site, constant vs waves, shoulder tip, dizziness
LMP and cycle length (irregular 28–40 d — matters), ectopic risk sweep: previous ectopic/miscarriage/TOP/tubal surgery, coil, IVF, STI, smoking, blood group
PEFE + TVUS + βhCG from examiner
State the uncertainty first; three possibilities each with its reason; name ectopic as must-not-miss
Plan with dates: βhCG now and 48 h (≥ two-thirds rise), rescan 7–10 days, EPAS referral booked, written red flags and number
ask: Have you passed any tissue? Clots?
Is the pain constant or in waves?
Shoulder-tip pain? Dizziness?
LMP — and are your cycles regular? How long?
Previous ectopic, miscarriage, termination, tubal/uterine surgery?
Coil? IVF? Ever an STI?
Smoking? Blood group?
pefe: Abdomen, speculum (os, blood, tissue), bimanual (CMT, uterine size and empty/full, adnexae)
Transvaginal ultrasound and serum βhCG
Say: 'I have to be honest — the scan hasn't given a clear answer today'

Three possibilities: very early IUP (most likely — 900 is below the discriminatory zone; long cycles) · complete miscarriage (against: no tissue, uterus normal size not contracted) · ectopic (must rule out)
'I'd treat her as an ectopic until proven otherwise'
fails: Committing to 'complete miscarriage'
Saying 'you're not pregnant' or 'it's nothing'
Discharging without serial βhCG and a booked rescan
Failing to name ectopic as the must-not-miss
No written red flags; inventing a straight answer when she demands one
numbers: Urine hCG threshold ~20–25 IU/L · TVUS discriminatory zone 1500–2000 · TA ~6000
Normal 48 h rise ≥ about two-thirds; slow/plateau → ectopic or failing; fall → ended
Sac visible ~5 wk; cardiac activity ~6 wk or CRL ≥7 mm
Corpus luteum cyst = she has ovulated; never the diagnosis; 'no adnexal mass' does not exclude ectopic
Red flags: severe or one-sided pain, shoulder tip, faint/black out, heavy bleeding — do not wait for the blood test
Book the 48 h βhCG with SA Pathology and the rescan before she leaves; EPAS at TQEH/RAH/FMC/WCH; PATS

stem: Nadia Haddad, 25, is eight weeks by dates and has had two days of light vaginal bleeding. She has been scanned and bloods taken.
tasks: Focused history
Explain the findings and the diagnosis
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Viable intrauterine pregnancy today — threatened miscarriage with two concerns: sac measures 6 weeks at 8 by dates (cycles 35 days — possible late ovulation) and embryonic heart rate ~80 bpm (bradycardia; expect 110–160). βhCG 70 000 is normal, not the problem. Rescan 7–10 days. Blood group A positive.
plan: Open; apologise she was left waiting
Short history: bleeding worse/settling, tissue/clots, pain and pattern, LMP and cycle length, symptoms persisting, first pregnancy/previous miscarriage, blood group
Good news first: heartbeat, right place
'I'm not going to tell you everything is fine' — concern 1: size vs dates; concern 2: slow heartbeat
Refuse to promise either way; rescan 7–10 days to compare growth and heart rate
No tablet, no bed rest, nothing she did; red flags; book the scan before she leaves
ask: Bleeding — worse or settling? Tissue or clots?
Pain — constant or coming and going?
LMP — and how long are your cycles?
Still getting pregnancy symptoms?
First pregnancy? Any previous miscarriage?
Blood group?
pefe: Findings to explain: obs normal; os closed, no tissue, uterus non-tender, adnexae normal; βhCG 70 000; TVUS sac ~6 wk, fetal pole, cardiac activity ~80 bpm
Say both: 'there is a heartbeat and it is in the right place' AND 'there are two things I'm not happy about'
Rescan 7–10 days; sooner if anything changes
fails: 'Everything is fine, there's a heartbeat'
'You're going to lose this pregnancy'
No written red flags
Serial βhCG once cardiac activity seen (adds nothing); saying βhCG must be >10 000 to see a heartbeat (no such rule)
numbers: Embryonic HR at 8 wk ~110–160; ~80 = bradycardia, materially higher loss rate
Viability by measurements, not hormone level
Progesterone not indicated (first pregnancy)
No bed rest — 'it just gives people something to blame themselves for'
Red flags: heavy bleeding, tissue, severe pain, faint

stem: You are the medical officer in a country emergency department. Priya Ramanathan, 28, has vaginal bleeding and has been vomiting persistently. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago.
tasks: Focused history
Ask for examination findings
Explain the most likely diagnosis
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Molar pregnancy — uterus 10 weeks at 6 by dates, vomiting 8–10×/day, passed 'little grapes' (only if asked), ultrasound: no fetal pole, cavity filled with heterogeneous mass with multiple cystic spaces, βhCG markedly elevated. Blood group AB negative. Commit on uterine size + hyperemesis; do not wait for the grapes.
plan: Obs — she is dehydrated
Open; quantify the vomiting (times/day, keeping fluids down)
Bleeding: onset, pattern; tissue — anything solid? clots; pain/fullness; LMP
Feel more pregnant than expected? Headache/vision/swelling (early pre-eclampsia)? Tremor/palpitations/heat (hyperthyroid)?
Previous pregnancies; blood group; SNAP
PEFE: abdomen, os, CMT, uterine SIZE, adnexae → 'ten weeks when she is six by dates' → ultrasound + quantitative βhCG
Commit: 'the most likely explanation is a molar pregnancy'; plain words: no baby, never was; STOP and let her react
Reasons; rehydrate; suction curettage not tablets, tissue to lab; βhCG surveillance and why (persistent/malignant, very treatable); contraception; anti-D; future pregnancies normal
ask: How many times a day are you vomiting? Can you keep fluids down?
Have you passed any tissue — anything solid? (grapes, only if asked)
Do you feel more pregnant than you'd expect at six weeks? Very sore breasts?
Headaches, blurred vision, swelling of hands/face?
Tremor, palpitations, feeling unusually hot?
Previous pregnancies, miscarriages; blood group
pefe: Abdomen: fullness
Speculum: os, blood, tissue
Bimanual: CMT, uterine size (the finding), softness, tenderness, adnexae
Ultrasound and quantitative βhCG

Management to examiner: IV fluids + antiemetics; FBE, βhCG, UEC, LFT, TFT, group/antibody/cross-match; BP + urinalysis; baseline CXR; suction curettage under gynae; histology; serial βhCG surveillance, GTD registration; reliable contraception (no IUD until βhCG normal); anti-D (AB neg) — discuss with unit
fails: Diagnosing hyperemesis gravidarum and stopping there
Offering medical management for a molar pregnancy
Not mentioning βhCG surveillance and contraception after evacuation
Missing anti-D in an AB negative woman
numbers: Large for dates at 6 wk: wrong dates · twins · mole — scan separates (twins: two sacs, two hearts)
Very high βhCG → early pre-eclampsia (<20 wk) and biochemical hyperthyroidism (TSH receptor cross-stimulation)
CXR baseline — lung commonest metastatic site
Complete mole no fetal RhD antigen, partial does — give anti-D until histology; VERIFY surveillance duration, SA GTD pathway
Transfer for curettage — not managed in a YNLHN hospital; PATS/MedSTAR; write surveillance into discharge summary and recall

stem: Georgia Falzon, 24, six weeks by dates, has vaginal bleeding that started today, with right-sided lower abdominal pain. She still has pregnancy symptoms.
tasks: Focused history
Ask for examination findings
Explain the diagnosis and your differentials
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Normal intrauterine pregnancy with separate right adnexal pathology (the ectopic decoy) — uterus FULL and exactly 6 weeks, CMT negative, os closed, right adnexal tenderness, no definite mass. Most likely haemorrhagic/ruptured corpus luteum cyst. Blood group O positive.
plan: Obs incl. postural drop
Open; which came first — pain or bleeding? Bleeding amount, tissue, clots
Pain: site, constant vs waves, severity, worse on twisting; nausea/vomiting; shoulder tip; dizziness
Pregnancy symptoms persisting; LMP/cycles; first pregnancy; ectopic risk sweep (ectopic, miscarriage, TOP, surgery, IVF, coil, STI/PID); fever/offensive discharge
PEFE: abdomen, os, CMT, uterine size and empty/full, adnexae
The sentence: 'uterus full and exactly six weeks — in an ectopic the uterus is empty — working diagnosis normal IUP with separate right adnexal pathology'
Ordered differential; explain to her, good news first; TVUS today, bloods incl. βhCG; keep her in; escalation advice
ask: Which came first, the pain or the bleeding?
Is the bleeding heavy? Tissue or clots?
Where is the pain — constant or comes and goes? Worse if you twist?
Nausea or vomiting with it?
Shoulder-tip pain? Dizziness?
Still getting sore breasts and tiredness?
LMP/cycles; first pregnancy; previous ectopic/miscarriage/TOP; IVF; coil; STI/PID
Fever or offensive discharge?
pefe: Abdomen: RIF tenderness, guarding
Speculum: os, blood, tissue
Bimanual: CMT (negative), uterine size — empty or full?, adnexae
TVUS today of uterus and both adnexae (Doppler if torsion suspected); FBE, βhCG, group/antibodies; chlamydia/gonorrhoea if PID possible
Analgesia; gynae review, urgent if torsion possible; keep her in until scanned
fails: Diagnosing ectopic pregnancy
Leading with heterotopic pregnancy
Sending her home before the scan
numbers: Differential in order: haemorrhagic/ruptured ovarian cyst → ovarian torsion → PID (against: CMT negative) → other ovarian mass → appendicitis → heterotopic last (~1 in 30 000 spontaneous)
Torsion: severe colicky pain, vomiting, tender adnexal mass, pain out of proportion — same-day surgical transfer
'I can't exclude an ectopic without a scan; a full uterus of the right size makes it much less likely' — scan still mandatory
Corpus luteum cyst present in every early pregnancy

setting: General practice, Wallaroo, regional South Australia. You are the general practitioner.
stem: Jenny, 21 years old, a primary school teacher. She has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 14. She takes insulin aspart (NovoRapid) before meals and insulin glargine (Lantus) at night.
Recorded today. BMI 24. BP 118/72. HbA1c 9.0% (75 mmol/mol), taken last week. No other medical history, no allergies, non-smoker.
Reason for attending. She and her partner are planning to start a family.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient, exploring the reasons for her poor blood sugar control
Counsel her regarding your management plan — before pregnancy, during pregnancy, at the birth, and after the birth
time: You have 8 minutes.

back.dx: Pre-conception counselling, type 1 diabetes, HbA1c 9%. Hidden reason for poor control: a severe public hypo at school six months ago (ambulance called) so she under-doses her night Lantus; plus lipohypertrophy from injecting the same abdominal site. Discriminating issue: saying 'not yet' — name a target HbA1c, advise postponing conception, offer contraception meanwhile.
plan: WIPE, open question, congratulate and appreciate that she came before conceiving
Diabetes history, five blocks — dig hard at block 3 (why is control poor): missed doses, hypos, injection technique/sites, what gets in the way
Complications screen (eyes, feet, chest, kidneys, hypo awareness, ketone strips), then a fast antenatal sweep: five Ps, medications incl. OTC/supplements, family history, diet and exercise, mood
Summarise back; signpost the four parts of the plan
Before pregnancy — the discriminating issue
During pregnancy
The birth
After the birth — do not run out of time here
Written information, diabetes educator, safety-net, review in four weeks, teach-back
ask: Do not open with the HbA1c
Are there days you miss a dose, or is it fairly consistent?
Have you ever had your sugar drop too low? Tell me about that. → What made you start doing that?
Has anyone gone through the injection technique with you — where you inject, rotating sites?
Is there anything that gets in the way — cost, work, remembering, being sick of it?
Eyes last checked? Numbness/burning feet? Chest pain? Kidney problems/protein? Warning symptoms when low? Ketone strips at home?

LMP/cycles, previous pregnancies, partner, cervical screening, any other medicines at all incl. over-the-counter (ACEi/statin in the harder variant), family history, a normal day's eating, exercise, mood
Respond to the hypo disclosure before moving on: 'that sounds awful… something we can fix properly rather than asking you to try harder'
pefe: No examination. Plan in four parts:

BEFORE: hold off trying — HbA1c under 7% first (organs form in the first weeks); 'this isn't a no, it's let's do this properly'; reliable contraception (implant/device) meanwhile; educator for technique and site rotation, safe descent without hypos (premixed, pump, CGM); complication screen (dilated eye check, kidney bloods/urine, feet, thyroid); folic acid 5 mg and iodine 150 mcg today; routine pre-pregnancy screen and rubella vaccination if not immune; stop ACEi/ARB, statins, non-insulin/metformin agents

DURING: team (high-risk clinic, obstetrician, endocrinologist, educator, dietitian, midwives, GP); BGL 4×/day, HbA1c every 4–6 wk; insulin needs rise; aspirin at night from ~12 wk; dating + morphology + fetal heart scan 22–24 wk + growth scans; eyes each trimester; routine advice
BIRTH: not past the due date; plan 38–39 wk aiming for normal birth; caesarean discussed if very big baby; Adelaide hospital with special care nursery, PATS; hourly sugars and insulin drip in labour

AFTER: insulin needs drop sharply at birth — cut doses immediately, further with breastfeeding; baby's sugar checked early, fed early, breathing and jaundice watched; encourage breastfeeding; contraception again; come before the next pregnancy
fails: Lecturing ('you must take your insulin properly') and never finding the hypo or the injection site
Not naming a target HbA1c and advising postponement
Not offering contraception in the meantime
Running out of time before the after-birth limb (it is in the task)
Promising a normal vaginal birth or a local birth; the complication avalanche
numbers: HbA1c <7% before conception (type 1), <6% (type 2) VERIFY
Folic acid 5 mg daily from 1 month before to 12 weeks · iodine 150 mcg
Aspirin 100–150 mg nocte from 12–16 wk, stopped ~36 wk
BGL targets fasting ≤5.0–5.3, 1 h ≤7.4, 2 h ≤6.7 VERIFY · HbA1c every 4–6 wk · NDSS for strips
Scans: NT 11–13+6 or NIPT · morphology 18–20 wk · fetal echo 22–24 wk · growth 4-weekly from 28 wk
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM ×2, 24 h apart if birth <~35 wk — expect hyperglycaemia VERIFY
Birth 38–39 wk; caesarean discussed at EFW ~4500 g; insulin falls to ~pre-pregnancy dose after birth

Variants: 'sick of injections' → premixed / pump + CGM / metformin; already pregnant at 8 wk → work from here, don't say delay; declines to delay → respect, folic acid today, refer, come straight in if pregnant

setting: General practice, Wallaroo, regional South Australia. You are the general practitioner.
stem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, 12 weeks pregnant, has come to discuss her antenatal screening results. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far.
Recorded today. BP 112/70. Weight 82 kg, height 1.62 m, BMI 31. Urine dipstick negative.

Results available to you: Full blood examination normal. Blood group / antibody screen A positive / negative. Urine MCS no growth. Rubella IgG positive (immune). Syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C negative. Chlamydia PCR negative. 75 g OGTT — fasting 5.6 mmol/L (reference <5.1); 1 hour 7.8 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 6.9 mmol/L (<8.5).
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
(Harder reported version adds) Outline your management plan
time: You have 8 minutes.

back.dx: Gestational diabetes on a 12-week OGTT — fasting 5.6 (one value is enough). Hidden: GDM in the previous pregnancy (diet-controlled, baby 4.1 kg, heel-prick sugars), the postpartum OGTT was never done — so recurrent GDM vs undiagnosed type 2 cannot yet be separated; say so. Discriminating issue: asking why the test was done at 12 weeks, and whether she had the test after the birth.
plan: WIPE, congratulate, check it was a planned pregnancy — do not open with the abnormal result
Current pregnancy: dates, symptoms, how she is feeling, vitamins
Previous pregnancy — the whole station. Five questions one at a time, then 'why was the test done this early?' and 'did you have the test after the birth?'
Diabetes symptoms, PMH, medications, family history, diet and exercise, mood, cervical screening, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander
Summarise back and signpost
Explain: normals first → the test → the number → the name → what it means and does not mean → two forward statements
Management, if the third task is present
Her concerns, written information, referrals, safety-net, review, teach-back
ask: Congratulations. Was this a planned pregnancy, and how have you been feeling?
LMP/cycles, weeks, bleeding/pain/vomiting, keeping food down, pregnancy vitamins
Tell me about that pregnancy → any problems, high BP or high sugar? → ever high sugar before that pregnancy? → what treatment? → how was the birth — long labour, big baby, problems?
Do you know why they arranged the sugar test this early?
After Jack was born, did anyone arrange a repeat sugar test — about six weeks afterwards?

Thirst, polyuria, thrush? Other medical problems (BP, thyroid, PCOS)? Medicines incl. OTC/herbal? Allergies? Family diabetes? Cervical screening? A normal day's eating, activity? Smoking/alcohol? Partner, mood? Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander?
pefe: No examination. Explain in order: normals first; the test (fasting, sugary drink, 1 h, 2 h); 1 h and 2 h normal; fasting 5.6, want <5.1; one reading is enough; 'gestational diabetes again'
Placental hormones stop insulin working — not caused by what she ate, not her fault; more likely with previous GDM, family history, higher weight — she has all three
Does NOT mean the baby will be born with anything wrong (organs formed before this); DOES affect growth (big baby, harder birth) and low sugars after birth — both preventable
Usually settles after birth — prove it with OGTT 6–12 wk postpartum (the missed test); lifelong type 2 risk → sugar check every 1–3 years

Management (task 3): dietitian, ~30 min activity most days, glucose meter + educator, BGL 4×/day; review 1–2 wk; insulin first-line if above target, metformin alternative — 1 in 4 to 1 in 3 need medication VERIFY; NDSS; diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic team; extra growth scans; BP each visit; birth 40–41 wk diet-controlled, 38–39 wk on medication/large baby; heel-prick and early feeding; book the postpartum OGTT before leaving hospital
fails: Leading with 'your sugar test is abnormal'
Never asking why the OGTT was done at 12 weeks
Never asking about the postpartum test
Reciting malformation/miscarriage risk to a woman with gestational diabetes — that belongs to hyperglycaemia at conception
Not booking/promising the 6–12 week postpartum OGTT
numbers: OGTT 75 g: fasting ≥5.1 · 1 h ≥10.0 · 2 h ≥8.5 — any one value

Overt diabetes in pregnancy: fasting ≥7.0 · 2 h/random ≥11.1 · HbA1c ≥6.5% — different diagnosis, different plan (Variant 1: fasting 7.4, HbA1c 7.1 → complication screen, aspirin, fetal echo, care continues after birth)
Screen 24–28 wk; at booking if previous GDM, obesity, strong FHx, higher-risk background — repeat at 24–28 wk if early test normal
Targets fasting ≤5.0–5.3 · 1 h ≤7.4 · 2 h ≤6.7 VERIFY
Postpartum OGTT 6–12 wk; then HbA1c/fasting every 1–3 years for life; OGTT at first visit next pregnancy
Recurrence 30–70%; lifetime type 2 risk ~50% VERIFY
Not used: glucose challenge test; HbA1c to diagnose GDM
SA: WCH / FMC / Lyell McEwin diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic; telehealth via Country Health Connect; PATS; SA Pathology (fast, stay 2 h); ACCHS, Closing the Gap PBS; TIS 131 450

stem: You are a general practitioner in a regional South Australian practice. Your next patient is Mary Coombes, a 26-year-old woman in her first pregnancy, now at 13 weeks gestation. She has attended to discuss the antenatal screening investigations you arranged at her booking visit. The results are available to you and are shown on the card inside the room.

The result card in the room: Full blood examination normal. Blood group and antibody screen A positive, antibodies not detected. HIV serology negative. Syphilis serology negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative. Rubella IgG positive — immune. Varicella IgG positive — immune. Down syndrome screening low risk. Urine microscopy leucocytes present, no red cells, no casts. Urine culture Group B Streptococcus, >10⁵ CFU/mL — sensitive to penicillin, cefalexin, nitrofurantoin.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Explain the investigation results to the patient
Explain the diagnosis and your differential diagnosis
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: You have 8 minutes. A prompt will be given at approximately three minutes to move you on from the history. No physical examination is required.

back.dx: Asymptomatic bacteriuria with Group B Streptococcus at 13 weeks. Differential: cystitis (bladder — burning, frequency) and pyelonephritis (kidney — fever, back pain, vomiting); she has neither. Three key points: treat 5 days nitrofurantoin · test of cure 1–2 weeks after · antibiotics in labour because the organism is GBS.
plan: Introduce, confirm identity, ask permission to take a history before giving results; one exchange of rapport (planned? congratulations)

Five-question focused history: dysuria/frequency/urgency/blood → fever/chills, nausea/vomiting, loin/abdominal pain → previous or recurrent UTI, kidney problems/stones/operations → allergies to medications, particularly antibiotics
Prompt: move on. Explain every normal result first — FBE, blood group, HIV/syphilis/hep B ('negative is the good result'), rubella and varicella immune, Down syndrome screen low risk
The urine: protein fine, significant number of bugs, Group B Streptococcus; defuse immediately; 'because you have no symptoms we call this asymptomatic bacteriuria'; differential in lay terms
Three numbered key points; safety-net for pyelonephritis; written information; check understanding; routine antenatal marks if time
back.planNote: only the three-minute prompt is timed in the source
ask: Would it be alright if I ask a few quick questions first? It will help me explain what the results mean
Was this a planned pregnancy? (one exchange only)
Any pain or burning when you pass urine? Passing urine more often? Sudden urgency? Any blood?
(If more often) Small amounts more often, or uncomfortable? Changed in the last few days? — say aloud that frequency without dysuria/urgency in early pregnancy is physiological
Any fevers or shaking chills? Nausea or vomiting? Pain in your back, loin or tummy?
Urine infections before — repeated? Kidney problems, stones, operations?
Any allergies to any medications, particularly antibiotics? ★ ask before prescribing
Ask her concerns — hidden agenda: cousin's baby had an infection after birth, two weeks in special care
pefe: No examination. Management: KEY POINT 1 nitrofurantoin 5 days — with food, urine may go brownish, finish the course · KEY POINT 2 repeat urine culture 1–2 weeks after finishing · KEY POINT 3 intravenous antibiotics in labour because the organism is GBS — prevents serious neonatal infection; doesn't change mode of delivery; write it in the notes and pregnancy record
If it recurs: low-dose preventive antibiotic to the end of pregnancy
Safety-net: fever, shaking chills, back/side pain, vomiting → same day or ED
If 30 seconds remain: folic acid and iodine, pertussis and influenza vaccination later, weight and BP each visit, review in 4 weeks
fails: Prescribing with no allergy history (single-item fail)
Stopping after key point two — no intrapartum antibiotics for GBS
Giving only the abnormal result instead of the whole panel
Opening with the results because task 2 says so
Calling it 'asymptomatic' without having asked about symptoms
numbers: >10⁵ CFU/mL — significant growth threshold
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly, 5 days VERIFY; cefalexin 500 mg 12-hourly 5 days (third line); cefalexin 250 mg nocte prophylaxis for recurrence VERIFY
Test of cure 1–2 weeks after completing treatment
20–30% progress to pyelonephritis untreated VERIFY
GBS swab 35–37 wk — universal screening in SA; intrapartum antibiotics ideally ≥4 h before birth; avoid nitrofurantoin from ~36 wk

Variants: E. coli → same first two steps, NO intrapartum antibiotics; dysuria + frequency → cystitis, same antibiotic, review 48 h; penicillin allergy → nitrofurantoin fine; labour: cefazolin non-severe, clindamycin if susceptible else vancomycin for immediate hypersensitivity; sister told not to treat → correct outside pregnancy; test of cure still positive → different antibiotic per sensitivities, urine every visit, prophylaxis if recurs

stem: You are a general practitioner in a regional South Australian practice. Your next patient is Lily Marchetti, a 24-year-old woman, who has booked an urgent appointment today. She thinks she is pregnant. She works at a childcare centre. The centre has notified staff that a child attending has a confirmed case of rubella. She has been in contact with that child and is frightened about what this means for her and for the pregnancy.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Arrange the relevant investigations, explaining them to the patient
Counsel the patient
time: You have 8 minutes. No physical examination is required. No investigation results will be provided.

back.dx: Rubella exposure in early pregnancy (about 8 weeks by LMP), significant exposure — indoors, 4–5 h/day all week, symptomatic child, immunity status unknown. Three investigations: beta-hCG, rubella IgM and IgG, dating scan. Repeat serology at 2–3 weeks. MMR after delivery, never now. Any decision is hers.
plan: Open and empathise — one clear empathic statement; the bridge to questions
The exposure: confirmed? where? how long? when? child's symptoms? her vaccination status?
Her symptoms: fever, rash, joint pain, lymph nodes, eyes
The 5 Ps — LMP and cycle regularity first, then the rest
Investigations — beta-hCG, rubella IgM and IgG, dating scan — each with a reason
Counselling: antibodies, CRS, the scenarios, the repeat, termination, MMR after delivery
Close — 'too early to worry', written information, support, follow-up
ask: Do not answer 'is the baby alright?' with 'I'm sure it will be fine' — 'I can't answer that yet, and I'm not going to guess; I can tell you exactly how we'll find out'
Has the child's rubella been confirmed with a blood test, or is it a suspicion?
Indoors in a room, or outside in the yard? How long — minutes or whole sessions? What day? Did the child have a fever or rash?
Are you up to date with your vaccinations — were you checked when you started at the centre?
Any fever? Rash? Aching joints? Swollen glands behind the ears/neck? Red or gritty eyes?
LMP, cycles regular, pregnancy symptoms; partner supportive; first pregnancy? (if previous: was rubella immunity documented?)
When she says 'I feel fine so I must be okay' — say that a quarter to a half of people with rubella never get symptoms
pefe: Investigations, each with a reason: beta-hCG (confirm pregnancy) · rubella serology IgM and IgG (immune? recent infection?) · dating scan ('at eight weeks I'd be worried; at twenty-two weeks I'd be reassuring you — I need to know which conversation we're having')

Counsel in six moves: what antibodies are (IgM recent, IgG immunity) → why we care (congenital rubella syndrome: hearing, eyes, heart) → the two questions the tests answer → every scenario aloud (IgG+/IgM− immune, no risk · IgM+ possible recent infection, false positives, repeat 2–3 wk, rising IgG confirms · both negative still repeat) → if no infection: avoid febrile/rash children, letter to work, MMR after the baby is born (live vaccine) → if confirmed in first 12 weeks: fetal testing (CVS/amniocentesis, own risk), option of termination, entirely her decision, support either way
If she says she would never end a pregnancy: accept immediately, plan surveillance with specialists and hearing/eyes/heart checks after birth
Close: sorry, written information, bring partner for results, ring when results are back
fails: Offering MMR today (live vaccine — single-item fail regardless of everything else)
Not exploring the exposure — confirmed, place, duration, date, symptoms
Agreeing that feeling well means she is fine
Forgetting the dating scan
Falsely reassuring that the baby will be fine; arguing when she refuses termination
numbers: 25–50% of rubella infections are subclinical · incubation 14–21 days
Under 11 weeks: fetal infection ~80%, defects ~85–90% · 11–16 weeks deafness predominates · >20 weeks very rare
Repeat serology 2–3 weeks · rubella IgG protective ~10 IU/mL VERIFY
Medical termination to 63 days (9 weeks); SA termination on request to 22 weeks + 6 days VERIFY
Avoid pregnancy 28 days after MMR · work exclusion until 4 days after rash onset VERIFY

Variants at 5 min: IgG+/IgM− → immune, no further rubella testing, still dating scan; IgM+/IgG− → repeat 2–3 wk before any serious conversation; confirmed seroconversion at 8 wk → pause, tissues, fetal testing or termination, refer with partner, no decision today; confirmed at 24 wk → lead with reassurance, no termination talk, hearing checked after birth

stem: You are a general practitioner in a regional South Australian practice. Your next patient is Jenny Marsden, a 28-year-old woman who is pregnant. She has attended for the results of the antenatal screening blood tests you arranged last week. The results are: syphilis serology — negative; hepatitis B surface antigen — negative; hepatitis C antibody — negative; HIV antibody — POSITIVE; confirmatory testing — POSITIVE. This is confirmed HIV infection.
tasks: Explain the results to the patient
Take a further, focused history
Counsel the patient
time: You have 8 minutes. No physical examination is required.

back.dx: Breaking bad news: newly diagnosed HIV at ~12 weeks in a planned pregnancy. Hidden history: injected drugs and shared needles six years ago; several partners before Ryan, condoms not always; Ryan never tested. Discriminating move: close the empathy phase at ~3 minutes — 'would you prefer we talk about the rest in another consultation?' — then ask permission to continue. Two-thirds of the marks are in the counselling.
plan: Open, rapport, normals — identity; one exchange of rapport; syphilis and hepatitis results named, 'negative is the good result'
Warning shot and set-up — 'I don't have good news'; offer to bring her partner in
The news — 'Both tests positive. You have the HIV infection.' Stop.
Empathy and reframe — name it, tissues, water, silence; manageable (not curable), normal life expectancy; normal pregnancy, healthy baby
★ The transition — offer another consultation; ask permission for questions
Focused history — transfusion, drugs and needle sharing, occupation/needlestick, tattoos/overseas treatment, sexual history and partner testing, previous STI, symptoms
Counselling — three goals; four stages; seven key points
Close — 'normal pregnancy, healthy baby'; support; written information; follow-up with Ryan
ask: Was this a planned pregnancy? Congratulations (one exchange)
Would you like your partner, or anyone else, to be here with you?
'Have I given it to my baby?' → without treatment ~1 in 4; with the full package below 1–2 in 100
Would you prefer that we talk about the rest of it in another consultation? → Is it alright if I ask you a few questions?
Blood transfusion, here or overseas? Any drugs? Ever shared needles? Work — needlestick? Tattoos, piercings, treatment overseas?
Stable relationship? Partner supportive? Other partners, now or past? Condoms? Has your partner ever been tested? Previous STI?
Weight loss, lumps/glands, night sweats, tiredness, rashes, thrush, diarrhoea, cough?
'How did I get it?' → often can't say; it wouldn't change what we do next. Never moralise
pefe: Three goals: her (suppress the virus) · the baby (prevent transmission) · Ryan and previous partners (offer testing)

TODAY: viral load ('the number that guides everything'); confidential notification, anonymous partner notification available; referral to high-risk pregnancy clinic — GP, obstetrician, infectious diseases specialist
DURING: antiretroviral therapy as soon as possible; viral load 2–4 wk after starting, then each trimester and near birth; avoid amniocentesis and CVS; ultrasound safe
BIRTH: mode decided ~36 weeks on viral load — not always a caesarean; low → vaginal; high → caesarean + IV antivirals in labour; no scalp electrodes, no fetal blood sampling, avoid forceps/vacuum

AFTER: infant antivirals within 6 hours (every baby); no breastfeeding — formula, lactation suppression; infant tests over the first year — early antibody tests can look positive from her antibodies, virus test used, certain by ~18 months; early cord clamping, dry and wipe
If time is short protect in order: viral load · specialist referral · ART · delivery depends on viral load · infant treatment 6 h · no breastfeeding · partner testing
fails: No warning shot; ploughing on through the crying; eight minutes of empathy with no plan
Never closing the empathy phase / asking permission to continue
Saying HIV is curable
Moralising about the drug use
Not sending a viral load; saying it is always a caesarean; not saying no to breastfeeding clearly; missing infant treatment within 6 hours; promising absolute confidentiality without qualification
numbers: Transmission 25–30% without intervention; <1–2% with the full package VERIFY
Viral load recheck 2–4 wk after starting/changing, then at least each trimester; delivery decision at 36 wk; elective caesarean if unsuppressed ~>1000 copies/mL VERIFY
Infant ART within 6 h; antibody seroreversion by 18 months
Contact tracing for contrast: chlamydia 6 mo, gonorrhoea 2 mo, primary syphilis 3 mo, HIV none

Variants: 'don't tell Ryan, he'll kill me' → safety first, cannot disclose without permission, notification confidential, anonymous partner notification; known positive undetectable → keep treatment, ID check regimen, plan vaginal birth, infant meds, formula; stopped ART 6 months ago → explore barrier, ID team today; sister breastfed in England → Australian recommendation is formula, raise with ID rather than close down VERIFY; 34 weeks at diagnosis → treat today, may need caesarean, still infant meds and formula

setting: General practice, country practice on the Yorke Peninsula.
stem: You are a general practitioner in a country practice on the Yorke Peninsula. Your next patient is Mary Sullivan, a 24-year-old woman, who has come in for advice. She tells you she has a positive home pregnancy test. She is a known case of irregular periods.
There are no observations provided.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient
Explain to the patient the investigations you would arrange
Provide antenatal counselling
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Early pregnancy advice with undatable pregnancy — irregular cycles (every 2–3 months), cannot remember LMP. Two things the station tests: do you notice you cannot date this pregnancy (dating scan ★), and can you turn a test list into a conversation (STI group consented, not announced ★). Hidden positive finding: 4–5 drinks on Saturdays; hidden worry: heavy drinking two weekends ago before she knew.
plan: Introduction, open question, planned pregnancy?, congratulate
Five Ps then medical, family, lifestyle, mood
The six investigation groups, with consent
Counselling in order: avoid, supplements, vaccines, diet and lifestyle, model of care
Safety-net and close
ask: Was this a planned pregnancy? — check before congratulating (if unplanned: 'are you happy to go ahead with the pregnancy?')
When was your last period? Are your periods regular? How often? Tired? Nausea or vomiting?
In a relationship? Partner supportive? How are things at home? Ever diagnosed with an STI?
Is this your first pregnancy? (never 'do you have any children?') Any medications, OTC, supplements? Last cervical screening? (starts at 25 — not overdue)
Long-term conditions — thyroid, diabetes, heart? High blood pressure? Family medical or genetic conditions?
Alcohol — how much, how often? Smoking? Drugs? Coffee? Exercise? → flag the alcohol: 'I'll come back to that'
Mood, coping with the news; ask about concerns before 7 minutes (the alcohol worry surfaces at ~7:00 otherwise)
pefe: Investigations in six groups with reasons: (1) confirm and date — repeat urine/serum hCG offered; DATING SCAN because dates can't be worked out from irregular periods, everything is timed from it; (2) routine bloods — FBC, blood group and Rh, antibody screen; (3) immunity — rubella, varicella if never had it; (4) STIs WITH CONSENT — syphilis, HIV, hep B, hep C, chlamydia (under 30, urine or self-swab) 'are you happy for me to arrange those today?'; (5) midstream urine — asymptomatic bacteriuria treated even when well, protein; (6) extras — Down syndrome screening OFFERED as a choice, parked for next visit; BP, height, weight today

Counselling: AVOID — alcohol stop completely, no known safe amount, don't worry about drinks before you knew, help offered; no smoking/drugs; tell everyone you're pregnant (doctor, pharmacist, dentist, radiographer) · SUPPLEMENTS — folic acid 0.4 mg first 12 weeks, iodine 150 µg throughout · VACCINES — influenza any stage, whooping cough (partner too), RSV · DIET — avoid raw/undercooked meat, pre-packed salads, soft cheese, raw eggs, high-mercury fish; 1–2 coffees fine; moderate exercise · MODEL OF CARE — shared care / public / private, ~10 visits, 20-week scan, OGTT 24–28 wk, swab 35–37 wk · SAFETY-NET — bleeding, severe pain, severe vomiting, fever
If running out of time, name the remaining headings — a named heading scores
fails: Saying any alcohol is acceptable
Omitting the dating scan
Ordering STI tests without consent
Never checking whether the pregnancy was wanted
Reciting test names without reasons; saying 'we will do' Down syndrome screening instead of offering it
numbers: First antenatal visit before 10 weeks · folic acid 0.4 mg daily first 12 weeks · iodine 150 µg daily throughout
Influenza any gestation · dTpa 20–32 weeks · RSV 28–36 weeks · chlamydia screening if under 30

Down syndrome screening offered from 10 weeks · morphology scan 20 weeks · OGTT 24–28 weeks · GBS swab 35–37 weeks · ~10 visits · caffeine 1–2 cups · cervical screening starts at 25, safe in first trimester

Examiner challenges: why not use her dates? — ovulation unpredictable, LMP estimate could be wrong by weeks, early scan accurate to days before 14 weeks · beta-hCG? — offered, not relied on; a single level doesn't date · gonorrhoea? — not routine, on risk only

Variants: regular cycles/known LMP → no dating scan, say why · unplanned/ambivalent → establish the decision first, no congratulations, no counselling until decided ★ · IUD in situ → exclude ectopic, urgent scan today, station has changed ★ · severe vomiting → assess (pulse, BP, weight, ketones), not diet advice · Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander → Aboriginal Family Birthing Program, Aboriginal health worker, Closing the Gap PBS

stem: You are a general practitioner. Your next patient is Emma Carter, a 27-year-old woman who is 11 weeks pregnant. She attended a few weeks ago and antenatal screening was arranged. She has returned today to discuss non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT).
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Counsel the patient about non-invasive prenatal testing. You have five minutes for tasks 1 and 2. At five minutes you will be given the result of the NIPT
Explain the result to the patient and advise her about further management
time: 8 minutes. The result card arrives at 5:00.

back.dx: NIPT counselling then result interpretation. Card at 5:00 (most recalls): single fetus, sufficient fetal fraction, trisomy 21/18/13 and sex chromosomes all LOW probability, fetal sex female. Discriminating issue: by 4:45 she must already have heard — screening test, reported as low or high probability, low reassuring but not absolute, high is not a diagnosis → CVS or amniocentesis. Hidden: friend said 'it tells you everything'; cousin's boy has Down syndrome.
plan: Introduce, open question, planned pregnancy, congratulate
History — including the two key questions (what do you already know / any concerns; family history of Down syndrome or genetic conditions incl. siblings and their children)
Explain NIPT: what it is, that it is a screening test, how results are reported and what each means, then pros and cons
Card arrives
Read and interpret the result, then further management; ask before revealing sex
Routine antenatal advice and safety-net
ask: Before I explain anything — tell me what you already know about NIPT and Down syndrome, and is there anything you're worried about or want me to cover?
Is there any history of Down syndrome or other genetic conditions in your family — yourself, your siblings, or any of their children?
Correct 'it tells you everything' explicitly — a small number of specific conditions, screening not diagnosis

Brisk: LMP/cycles, nausea/vomiting, relationship/home/STI, first pregnancy (if not: any baby with a genetic condition), cervical screening, medical conditions, medications, folate and iodine, family history, SNAP, coping — stop by ~2:30, skip caffeine and diet
pefe: Counsel: offered to every woman, her choice · Down syndrome = 23 pairs, extra copy of 21st, trisomy · two options: combined test (bloods ~10 wk + NT scan ~12 wk) or NIPT (single maternal blood test) · BOTH SCREENING — neither yes/no, neither 100% · reported low or high probability: low = treated as normal, no further testing, doesn't rule out completely; high ≠ diagnosis → CVS before 14 wk or amniocentesis from 15 wk, both definitive, both small miscarriage risk · pros: T21/18/13 + sex chromosomes, more accurate so fewer invasive tests, fetal sex · cons: $400–500 no Medicare rebate ★, no result in a small number (repeat), harder in twins · still recommend the 12-week scan

Result, in order: one baby, sufficient material → T21 low probability = normal, no further testing → T18, T13, sex chromosomes low → 'low doesn't mean zero, but high confidence' → sex: ask first, offer to write it in a sealed envelope, not 100% accurate
Further management: 12-week scan, morphology 20 wk, OGTT 24–28 wk, swab 35–37 wk, folate and iodine, influenza now, pertussis and RSV later, safety-net (bleeding, severe pain, severe vomiting, fever)
fails: Describing NIPT as diagnostic; saying the baby definitely does or does not have Down syndrome
Reaching the result without ever having said 'screening test'
Not explaining low/high probability reporting before the card arrives
Announcing the sex unasked
Never mentioning cost; leaving the 'tells you everything' misconception uncorrected
numbers: Screening from 10 wk · combined test bloods 10 wk (PAPP-A + free β-hCG), NT scan 11–13+6 · NIPT from 10 wk · CVS 11–14 wk · amniocentesis from 15 wk · quadruple test 14–20 wk (AFP, oestriol, hCG, inhibin A)
NIPT $400–500, no rebate · no result ~1–5% (low fetal fraction — early gestation, higher BMI) · screens T21, T18, T13 + sex chromosomes

Examiner: '99% accurate, why not act?' — accuracy ≠ positive predictive value; at 27 background risk is low so some high results are false positives; always confirm · what is measured? cell-free placental DNA, not fetal red cells (CORRECTION) — confined placental mosaicism causes false positives · does NIPT replace the 12-week scan? no — structure and fetal number

Variants: HIGH probability T21 → normal findings first, warning shot, 'high probability' then immediately 'this is not a diagnosis', silence, CVS/amnio + specialist + genetic counsellor, no decision today, never 'your baby has Down syndrome' ★, termination only if she raises it · no result → not a bad result, repeat (pay again) or combined test · declines → her decision, don't push, 20-wk scan still · twins → harder, discuss with specialists · 18 weeks → NIPT still possible, quadruple test, amniocentesis not CVS

stem: You are a general practitioner in a country practice. Your next patient is Mary Whitfield, a 40-year-old woman, who has come to your general practice with a positive home pregnancy test. This is her first antenatal visit — nothing has been arranged before today.
tasks: Take a history from the patient (3–4 minutes)
At five minutes you will be given the physical examination findings
Counsel the patient in the time remaining
time: 8 minutes. The examination card arrives at 5:00.

back.dx: Advanced maternal age (40) with obesity — card at 5:00: BP 124/78, 1.62 m, 84 kg, BMI 32, dual heart sounds, dipstick negative, urine hCG positive. The second diagnosis is hidden in the BMI line — react to it out loud. Seven key points: early OGTT 14–16 wk · NIPT with emphasis · aspirin for pre-eclampsia · extra growth scans · folic acid 5 mg not 0.4 ★ · weight-gain monitoring · high-risk clinic with more frequent visits, birth 39–40 wk. Hidden agenda at ~3:00: 'Is my baby going to have Down syndrome?'; self-conscious about weight.
plan: Introduce, open question, planned pregnancy, congratulate
Five Ps, then medical — asking specifically about previous or family high blood pressure and high blood sugar — family, lifestyle, mood
Request or receive the examination findings and react to the BMI out loud
Counselling: reassure, then the key points at pace
Routine antenatal investigations named (with consent), safety-net, close
ask: Was this a planned pregnancy? → congratulations. How are you feeling about it? (pick up the fear the moment it appears: 'I'm going to come to exactly that')

LMP, cycles regular, nausea/vomiting, supportive relationship, home, previous STI, first pregnancy? (nulliparity = pre-eclampsia factor — count them: age ≥40, BMI ≥30, nulliparity), cervical screening
Ever been told you had high blood pressure, or a high blood sugar? Thyroid or heart problems?
Medications or supplements — already on folic acid?
Medical or genetic conditions in the family, including any child born with a genetic condition on either side?
Smoke, alcohol, drugs, exercise; coping with the news
pefe: If asked for: BP; height and weight for BMI; cardiovascular — heart sounds, murmurs; urine dipstick esp. protein; repeat urine hCG; no abdominal or pelvic examination at this gestation unless screening due

With the card: 'BP normal at 124/78, heart sounds normal, urine clear — all reassuring. Your BMI today is 32, in the range we call obese; I mention it because it changes a few things I want to arrange' → if she reacts: 'pregnancy is not the time to try to lose weight; we monitor gain and add checks'

Counsel: reassurance sentence first ('many women over 40 have completely normal pregnancies') → three groups we can act on: genetic conditions, diabetes, high blood pressure; age and weight add together → KP1 Down syndrome screening strongly encouraged, still her choice, NIPT preferred (more accurate, other conditions), $400–500 no rebate, screening not diagnosis → KP2 OGTT at 14–16 wk, repeat 24–28 → KP3 aspirin before 16 wk to 34–36 wk, discuss with obstetrician → KP4 extra growth scans → KP5 folic acid 5 mg (BMI >30) first 12 wk + iodine 150 µg → KP6 weight monitoring, not dieting → KP7 high-risk clinic = seen more often; birth planned 39–40 wk
Routine: FBC, group/antibodies, rubella/varicella, syphilis/HIV/hep B/C with consent, MSU; alcohol/smoking/tell everyone/food; influenza, pertussis, RSV; safety-net; review 2 weeks
fails: Giving 0.4 mg folate
Advising weight loss during pregnancy
Delivering the risk list with no reassurance and leaving her frightened
Never addressing her direct question about Down syndrome
Reading the card without commenting on the BMI; 'refer to high-risk clinic' without saying why; opening with 'advanced maternal age and obese pregnancy'
numbers: AMA ≥40 (some references 35) · obesity BMI ≥30 · folic acid 5 mg first 12 wk · iodine 150 µg · early OGTT 14–16 wk, repeat 24–28
Aspirin 100–150 mg nocte, start before 16 wk, stop 34–36 wk; threshold one high-risk or two moderate factors — she has three (VERIFY local 100 vs 150)
Expected gain if BMI ≥30: 5–9 kg · growth scans commonly 28, 32, 36 wk · plan birth 39–40 wk · NIPT higher no-result rate at raised BMI

Examiner: 35 or 40? — no universal cut-off, management driven by risk factors · prescribe aspirin yourself? — discuss with obstetric team, start before 16 wk · why not combined test? — T21 only; NIPT broader, fewer false positives; still 12-wk scan · lose weight? — no, monitor gain · no BMI given? — only 5 mg folate and weight monitoring drop out

Variants: no BMI → 0.4 mg folate, all else same · obese 25-year-old → 5 mg folate, weight monitoring, early OGTT, growth scans, aspirin only with a second factor · asks for amniocentesis → invasive, miscarriage risk, screen first · pre-existing T2DM → 5 mg folate anyway, review medications (stop ACEi/ARB/statin), specialist from start, aspirin (age + nulliparity) · 'am I too old, is this selfish?' → pause, both halves honest, a plan not a guarantee · rural → PATS, Country Health Connect, WCH MFM/SA Clinical Genetics, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
