stem: Your next patient is a 32-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant. She has come for an antenatal check. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m². She has a history of one miscarriage. Her blood pressure is high.
tasks: Take a focused history (four minutes)
At four minutes you will be given the physical examination findings on a card
Counsel the patient
time: Eight minutes. General practice. The examination card arrives at 4:00.

back.dx: Chronic hypertension (4 years) on ramipril 5 mg in the second trimester — the automatic fail lives in never asking the tablet by name, or hearing 'ramipril' and moving on. Card at 4:00: BP 148/94 repeated, pulse 78, 1.64 m/83 kg, BMI 31, heart sounds dual, chest clear, dipstick no protein (excludes pre-eclampsia and renal disease — say so). One miscarriage at 9 weeks, spontaneous. Discriminating issue: announce three components — blood pressure, weight, routine — and get through all three.
plan: Open, confirm identity, 'was this a planned pregnancy and are you happy about it?' before congratulating
Five Ps, one question per turn — inside 2½ minutes
The miscarriage: how many weeks, treatment/procedure, blood group; reassure (1 in 5, no special testing)
Medical conditions/medication → hypertension ladder: how long/before pregnancy, what tablet by name ★, taking regularly, who reviews, any problems → react to ramipril in the room
Complications: chest pain, SOB on exertion, orthopnoea/PND, ankle swelling, blurred vision; family HTN/DM/PET; SNAP; mood
Ask to examine → card. Read it aloud: BP high, heart/chest normal, no protein = not pre-eclampsia, BMI 31 'higher range'

Signpost three components → BP: heart exam, eye check, change ramipril today to labetalol/methyldopa, home BP target <135/85, aspirin → weight: gain 5–9 kg, early OGTT repeat 24–28, growth scans, NIPT encouraged, dietitian → routine: team, bloods/urine, 18–20 wk scan, vaccines, folic acid + iodine, avoid list
Safety-net with specific symptoms; summary; review 2 weeks
back.planNote: only the four-minute history limit is timed in the source
ask: Was this a planned pregnancy, and are you happy about it?
LMP, cycles regular, nausea/vomiting/tiredness, bleeding or pain, relationship/partner/home, STI, first pregnancy?, cervical screening
The miscarriage: how many weeks? any treatment or procedure? blood group?
Any medical conditions or regular medication? → How long? Before this pregnancy? What tablet — do you know the name? Taking it regularly? Who checks it, last reviewed? Ever caused problems?
Chest pain? Shortness of breath on exertion? Lying flat or waking you? Ankle swelling? Blurred vision?
High blood pressure, diabetes or pre-eclampsia in the family? Smoking/alcohol/drugs? Mood and coping? — hidden agenda at ~6:00: 'is the miscarriage going to happen again?'
pefe: Ask to examine: BP, height/weight, heart and chest, urine dipstick → card handed
Say aloud: 148/94 high as expected; heart and chest normal; no protein — kidneys fine, not pre-eclampsia; BMI 31 'higher range' (never 'obese')

Component 1 — BP: chronic hypertension; examine heart, arrange eye check; ramipril not used in pregnancy — change today to labetalol (or methyldopa); home upper-arm monitor, quiet, sitting, 5 min rest, three readings ignore the first; target <135/85; low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia; ramipril question: risk mainly later in pregnancy, stopping now is right, look carefully at 20-week scan
Component 2 — weight: not blame; gain 5–9 kg; early OGTT, repeat 24–28 wk; extra growth scans; NIPT encouraged, her choice; dietitian; pregnancy not the time for weight loss

Component 3 — routine: team (obstetrician, physician, midwife, dietitian); bloods and urine today; 18–20 wk scan; influenza, pertussis, COVID; folic acid + iodine; no alcohol/smoking, listeria and mercury advice in writing
To examiner: baseline hypertensive bloods with protein:creatinine ratio, high-risk clinic referral
fails: Never asking what tablet she takes, or hearing 'ramipril' and moving on ★
Not saying in the room that the drug has to change ★
Not announcing three components / not covering all three ★
Congratulating before checking; saying 'you are obese'; prescribing weight loss
Skipping the clean dipstick and why it matters; no specific safety-net symptoms
numbers: Target <135/85 · severe ≥160/110 · labetalol 100–200 mg 2–3 times daily · aspirin 100–150 mg nightly before 16 wk to 36 wk · folic acid 5 mg (BMI ≥30) to 12 wk · iodine 150 µg · weight gain 5–9 kg · repeat OGTT 24–28 wk · morphology 18–20 wk
One early miscarriage ≈ 1 in 5 pregnancies — no special testing
Safety-net: bad headache, vision changes, pain under ribs, sudden swelling face/hands, reduced movements — same day

Variants: she stopped the tablet herself → 'not no tablet — the right tablet', start labetalol today · card shows 158/102 with 2+ protein at 24 wk → superimposed pre-eclampsia, hospital today for bloods, urine PCR, fetal monitoring — station becomes escalation
Score /10; three starred items

stem: Your next patient is a 30-year-old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant. She has come to see you for her routine pregnancy visit and is complaining of chest discomfort.
tasks: Take a history (six minutes)
Physical examination findings will be given to you on a card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Eight minutes, six of them history. The examination card arrives at 6:00.

back.dx: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in pregnancy — burning retrosternal discomfort worse after eating, acid taste, water brash; no exertional, pleuritic or positional features. Card: BP 118/74, P 84, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 98%, chest clear, MID-SYSTOLIC murmur at left sternal edge (physiological — do not switch diagnosis), fundal height = dates, cephalic, FHR 145, no calf signs, mild symmetrical ankle oedema, dipstick clean. Discriminating issue: run the obstetric and pre-eclampsia block before the reflux questions, and don't show you know the recall. Opens exhausted: 'I just want the pregnancy to end.'
plan: Vitals from examiner before sitting (if abnormal: treatment room)
Respond to her distress before any clinical question — 'you are doing a great job as a mother'

Characterise: site (one finger or area), severity /10, burning/dull/pressing, onset, constant vs intermittent, radiation, modifiers, exertion BEFORE food, leaning forward, eating/breathing → note 'worse after eating', do not follow it
Obstetric history first: how has the pregnancy been, booking bloods, dating scan, Down screening, 18–20 wk scan, sweet drink test, GBS swab, which pregnancy, previous complications
Pre-eclampsia screen: headache, vision/flashes, dizziness, RUQ pain, less urine, new swelling face/hands/legs, baby kicking normally

CVS (SOB exertion — explore once, sweating, palpitations, heart history, orthopnoea) → RS (calf, travel, clots, fever/cough/contacts) → GI seventh (acid taste, water brash, nausea/vomiting, fatty meals, NSAIDs) → MSK (rash, injury, tender to press) → psychogenic (mood, stresses)
Card: read aloud — BP/pulse normal, no fever, oxygen fine, chest clear, no protein, baby well; name the murmur as usually normal in pregnancy and say it doesn't change your thinking
Diagnosis in plain words; differentials by group — pre-eclampsia first ('the one I worried about most'), heart, lungs, stomach, chest wall, stress last; advice; safety-net; summary to examiner
back.planNote: only the six-minute history limit is timed in the source
ask: Could I have her blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?
I understand how stressful and overwhelming this must be — you are doing a great job as a mother

Can you point to it with one finger, or is it an area? /10? Burning, dull ache, or pressing? When did it start, constant or comes and goes? Jaw, shoulder, left arm? Better or worse? Worse on exertion, better with rest? Better leaning forward? Related to eating or breathing?
Before I ask about anything else, tell me how the pregnancy has been going — bloods, dating scan, Down screening, 18–20 wk scan, sweet drink test, GBS swab, which pregnancy, previous complications?
Headaches? Blurring or flashing lights? Dizziness? Pain under the right ribs? Passing less urine? New swelling of face, hands, legs? Is the baby still kicking normally?
Breathless on exertion? (explore once: at rest? wakes you?) Sweating? Racing heart? Heart problems? Pillows? Calf swelling/pain? Travel? Clots in you or family? Fever, chills, cough, contacts?
Bitter or acidic taste? Does your mouth suddenly fill with saliva? Nausea/vomiting? Worse after large fatty meals? Anti-inflammatories? Rash/redness? Injury? Worse pressing or moving? Mood? Stresses?
pefe: Read the card aloud in order: vitals normal, no fever, oxygen fine, chest clear, no protein in urine, baby growing well and heartbeat normal

'I did hear an extra sound when I listened to your heart — that kind of sound is usually completely normal in pregnancy because the heart is pumping much more blood… it doesn't change what I think is going on.' If she is alarmed: nothing about your examination or symptoms points to a heart problem; it goes away after birth
Diagnosis: reflux — the gateway at the bottom of the food pipe loosens with the pregnancy hormone and the baby pushes up on the stomach

Differentials by group: pre-eclampsia (no symptoms, BP normal, urine clear) · heart: arteries, valves, rhythm, heart failure — none of the features · lungs: clot (pregnancy raises risk; no calf signs, oxygen normal), chest infection · stomach: ulcer, gallstones · chest wall: costochondritis, shingles before rash · stress — only after everything else is cleared

Advice: smaller meals more often, don't lie down within 3 hours of eating, raise head of bed, avoid triggers, pregnancy-safe antacids, usually settles after birth · safety-net: bad headache, vision changes, pain under ribs, sudden swelling, breathlessness at rest, reduced movements — same day
fails: Not responding to her distress before clinical questions ★
Asking about food before exertion ★
Reflux questions before the obstetric history ★
Missing the pre-eclampsia screen ★
Changing the diagnosis when the murmur appears ★; chasing 'nine months pregnant' breathlessness into a PE workup; not asking for vitals first
numbers: History six minutes · six groups, obstetric first · FHR 110–160 · systolic murmur usually physiological · diastolic murmur never physiological · D-dimer unhelpful in pregnancy · avoid lying down for 3 hours after eating · ranitidine withdrawn
Variant — 2025 stem with no complaint: she opens 'I just want this pregnancy to end' and withholds the discomfort until validated; done with real warmth she gives it immediately

Variant — card shows a DIASTOLIC murmur: 'comes at a point where we don't expect a normal sound' → echocardiogram, ECG, cardiology referral; reflux may still explain the discomfort but the murmur is a separate unresolved problem (see mitral stenosis station)

Summary to examiner: burning retrosternal discomfort worse after eating with acid taste and water brash; no exertional/pleuritic/positional features; no PET symptoms, normal movements, no clot risk, no infective features; stable, clean dipstick, soft mid-systolic murmur regarded as physiological; GORD in pregnancy; safety-netted for PET, breathlessness at rest, reduced movements
Score /10; five starred items

stem: Your next patient is a 24-year-old woman who has presented for routine antenatal care. She has had a positive home pregnancy test.
tasks: Take a focused history
Physical examination findings will be given to you on a card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Eight minutes. General practice. The examination card is handed over after the history.

back.dx: Rheumatic mitral stenosis, asymptomatic, at 8–10 weeks in a planned first pregnancy. Hidden: childhood murmur after fever and migratory joint pain, monthly injections for years, stopped at ~15, never followed up — she mentions the murmur only when asked about medical conditions. Card: pulse 88 regular, BP 112/70, JVP not raised, tapping undisplaced apex, loud S1, opening snap, low-pitched rumbling MID-DIASTOLIC murmur at the apex, bell, left lateral, held expiration, presystolic accentuation; chest clear, no oedema. Discriminating issue: say out loud that no diastolic murmur is normal in pregnancy, before committing. Hidden fear: being told to end the pregnancy.
plan: Ordinary antenatal history: planned? → congratulate; five Ps one per turn; medical conditions/medication → she says 'murmur' → STOP the five Ps

The murmur ladder: when diagnosed? treatment? (if vague: 'antibiotics for a long time, or injections?') regular follow-up? ever caused problems? → complications hunt: chest pain, SOB exertion, leg swelling, orthopnoea/PND/pillows, palpitations, haemoptysis
Finish the frame: Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander?, family history, diet/exercise/alcohol/smoking, mood; 'I'd particularly like to listen to your heart' → card
Read the card aloud — pulse regular, BP normal, chest clear, no swelling; extra sound at the bottom left of the heart 'at a particular point in the heartbeat'

Diagnosis in plain words (gateway, narrowed, rheumatic fever fits); some murmurs are normal in pregnancy but come at a different point — yours is not one; her questions honestly; differentials in eight groups ending with why the pregnancy murmur doesn't fit; echo first, then ECG, joint clinic; safety-net
ask: Was this a planned pregnancy? → congratulations
LMP, regular, tiredness, nausea/vomiting (how many times), relationship/support/home, STI, first pregnancy, cervical screening

Do you have any medical conditions, or take any medication? → 'murmur' → Do you remember when you were diagnosed? (which joints, did it move?) Any treatment? → Antibiotics for a long time, or injections? When did they stop? Regular follow-up? Ever caused problems?
Chest pain? Shortness of breath on exertion (explore 'not fit' once)? Leg swelling? Breathless at night or lying flat — pillows? Racing or fluttering heart? Ever coughed up blood?

Do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander? Family heart or genetic conditions? Diet, exercise, alcohol, smoking, drugs? Mood and coping? — hidden agenda at ~7:00: 'are you going to tell me I can't have this baby?'
pefe: Card read aloud, then: 'I think you have a condition called mitral stenosis. There is a gateway in your heart called the mitral valve; that gateway has become narrowed… usually long-term damage from a throat infection in childhood — rheumatic fever — which fits the fever, sore joints and the injections'
'Some heart murmurs are normal in pregnancy, but those come at a different point in the heartbeat from yours. Yours is not one of the normal ones.'

Her questions: serious? — important rather than an emergency · the baby? — most women have a healthy pregnancy; the scan tells us how narrow · stop the pregnancy? — nothing found today says that; scan first · why not told? — can stay quiet for years, pregnancy strains the heart · operation? — most don't need one; keyhole option if severe

Differentials in groups (one example each): other valves (aortic) · congenital · cardiomyopathy/heart failure · irregular rhythms (why the ECG) · infection on the valve · anaemia · overactive thyroid · the normal pregnancy murmur — different point in the heartbeat, so doesn't explain yours

Plan: echocardiogram (severity, function) then ECG (AF — the complication that changes management), FBC, TFT; cardiology + obstetrics joint clinic, birth planned at a tertiary centre; safety-net: breathless at rest, lying flat, racing heart, coughing blood — same day
fails: Calling the murmur physiological ★
Not stopping the five Ps when she says 'murmur' ★
Differentials not grouped, or not finishing with why the pregnancy murmur doesn't fit ★
Accepting 'I don't remember' without prompting for antibiotics or injections
Missing palpitations; echo not before ECG; promising or threatening termination
numbers: Mitral area 5th ICS midclavicular line · bell · left lateral · expiration
Mild >1.5 cm² · moderate 1.0–1.5 · severe <1.0 cm² VERIFY
Plasma volume rises 40–50% · beta blocker metoprolol, not atenolol · secondary prophylaxis benzathine penicillin every 21–28 days

Management variant (by severity): echo + ECG → mild: watch, see more often, birth in a big hospital with good analgesia and monitoring · more severe: salt and fluid restriction, no strenuous exercise, rate-slowing tablet, birth where cardiologists are on site · keyhole balloon valvuloplasty in pregnancy if medicines fail · mode of birth decided by specialists — no rule of caesarean; excellent pain relief
AF variant (irregular 120, palpitations, breathless on stairs): less efficient, clot risk → rate control, anticoagulant injection, cardiology today

Summary to examiner: childhood murmur after fever and migratory arthralgia, prolonged prophylaxis stopped in adolescence, asymptomatic; tapping apex, loud S1, opening snap, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation; rheumatic MS; echo, ECG, FBC, TFT, joint clinic, tertiary birth
Score /10; three starred items

setting: Emergency department of a rural South Australian hospital.
stem: Rachel Dunn, 33, is 36 weeks into her second pregnancy. She has presented with abdominal pain.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient — six minutes
Physical examination findings will be given to you on a card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Eight minutes. Two-minute warning. The examination card comes after the six-minute history.

back.dx: Concealed placental abruption (main version E) — four hours of sudden, constant, severe, unrelieved generalised pain, NO bleeding, fetal movements quieter since the pain, smoked ten a day until she found out. Card: distressed, BP 116/72, pulse 108 (early compensation — name it), fundal height 39 cm at 36 wk, uterus tender, no contractions, FHR 148, os closed, no blood or fluid, dipstick negative. The single behaviour that decides all five versions: keep screening after you know the answer — 'that fits, but I still need to rule out a few other things'. The marks are for exclusion, not arrival.
plan: Vitals from the examiner before beginning; name the tachycardia (104)
Acknowledge pain and fear in one sentence; signpost
The pain: where, /10, ache/tightening/tearing, when exactly, constant vs comes and goes → KEY Q1 waves lasting longer and closer together? → KEY Q2 better or worse with anything?
Obstetric block: bleeding? (do not accept 'no bleeding' as reassurance) discharge/fluid? baby moving as usual, last felt? falls, knocks, seatbelt? do you feel safe at home?

Pre-eclampsia set despite an obvious answer; then bowel, liver, urinary groups; antenatal spine; previous pregnancy; BP/kidney history; medications; smoking; travel; 'what were you most worried this might be?'
Examination request — findings not technique, uterine tenderness and contractions by name, speculum with consent; explicitly decline digital VE until praevia excluded → card

Answer the baby question first (heartbeat 148); name abruption plainly, three reasons; the honest 'no bleeding' explanation; smoking answer; differentials in groups; the thirty-second resuscitation; no promises; call Tom in; summary
back.planNote: only the six-minute history and the two-minute warning are timed in the source
ask: Examiner, before I begin, could I have her vital signs?
Where exactly? Out of ten? An ache, a tightening, a tearing? When exactly did it start? Constant, or comes and goes?
Does it come in waves that last longer and arrive closer together?
Does anything make it better or worse — movement, position, eating?
Any bleeding from down below? Any discharge or leaking fluid? Is the baby moving as much as usual — when did you last feel it?
Any falls, knocks to the tummy, seatbelt pulling hard? Do you feel safe at home?
Headaches? Vision — blurring, flashes, spots? Swelling legs/hands/face? Pain under the right ribs? Jaundice? Chest pain/breathlessness? Less urine?
Nausea/vomiting? Bowels, wind, bloating? Fever/chills? Appetite? Groin lump? Dysuria, frequency, haematuria?

Routine bloods, dating scan, 18–20 wk scan, sweet drink test, 36-wk swab? First pregnancy — problems, delivery? BP or kidney problems ever? Medications? Smoking? Recent travel? What were you most worried this might be?
pefe: Findings, not technique: general appearance (distress, pallor, sweating); vitals incl. temperature; abdomen — distension, tenderness over liver and uterus; fundal height, FHR, uterus tender? tense or woody? palpable contractions?; bowel sounds; renal angle tenderness by name; inguinal orifices; speculum with consent and chaperone — os open/closed, blood or fluid; lower limbs; dipstick
'I would not perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded on ultrasound' — say it aloud

Explain: baby's heartbeat first → placental abruption ('the placenta is a bridge between baby and womb wall; part has come away') → three reasons: sudden, constant, severe; 39 cm at 36 wk; tender uterus with no contractions → 'in some abruptions the blood is trapped behind the placenta — the absence of bleeding doesn't reassure me here' → smoking raises risk, she stopped, most have no cause

Differentials in groups: preterm labour (no contractions, os closed), pre-eclampsia (BP and dipstick normal), GI — obstruction, appendicitis; liver/gallbladder; kidney/bladder; uterine rupture kept in mind (no previous caesarean)

Thirty-second management — a resuscitation: call for help, obstetric registrar, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval; two large-bore cannulae; FBC, coags, fibrinogen, UEC, LFT, group and hold with cross-match, Kleihauer; continuous CTG; IV fluids, oxygen if needed; anti-D if rhesus negative; no digital VE; definitive treatment is delivery — obstetric team decides timing
'I can't promise you that, and I won't pretend otherwise' — bring Tom in
fails: 'There's no bleeding, so it's not an abruption' ★
'I'd do a vaginal examination to assess the cervix' ★
Not asking about fetal movements or bleeding
Promising the baby will be fine
'Let's do an ultrasound to confirm the abruption' (insensitive — clinical diagnosis); tocolysis; 'her BP is fine so she's stable'
numbers: 140/90 hypertension · 160/110 severe · target <135/85 · FHR 110–160 · fundal height ≈ weeks, >3 cm discrepancy matters
Abruption risk factors: smoking, hypertension, previous abruption, trauma, multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, cocaine
Corticosteroids if birth anticipated before ~35 wk — betamethasone 11.4 mg IM ×2, 24 h apart VERIFY · anti-D for every rhesus-negative woman with APH · significant bacteriuria 10⁵ CFU/mL
Complications if asked — maternal: haemorrhagic shock, DIC, AKI, Couvelaire uterus, PPH, transfusion/hysterectomy; fetal: hypoxia, growth restriction, preterm birth, stillbirth

THE OTHER FOUR VERSIONS (same stem, changed details): A — 20 wk, GP, fever/dysuria/frequency → pyelonephritis; dipstick blood + protein + nitrites — blood from infection not stone (recheck, image if persists), protein is not pre-eclampsia (BP normal), nitrites tie it to the urinary tract; transfer for admission and IV antibiotics after culture, analgesia, antipyretics, fluids, bloods, CTG — never oral at home, never a stat dose · B — 28 wk, pain while travelling, on iron → constipation: deliver the benign diagnosis with reasons and conviction (hormones + iron, normal card); don't stop iron — change how it's taken, fluid, fibre, safe laxative, review 1 wk · C — 20 wk, travel, no bowel motion for a week → ask 'still passing wind?' and 'vomiting?'; distension out of proportion, weak bowel sounds → bowel obstruction; surgical + obstetric teams today, NBM, IV fluids, CTG · D — 34 wk, ED, bleeding volunteered early → act on it, still work through the rest; waves lengthening; contractions 5-minutely, os 3 cm → preterm labour: in-utero transfer, steroids, antibiotics in labour, continuous monitoring
Three sentences that lose the station: 'no bleeding so not abruption' · 'I'd do a vaginal examination' · 'oral antibiotics and review in two days'

source: Abdominal_Pain_Pregnancy_Recalls_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (main version E; versions A–D on the back)

setting: Rural South Australian general practice. You are the general practitioner.
stem: Jenny Marlowe, 30 years old, is 34 weeks into her first pregnancy. She has presented today with worsening abdominal pain. Antenatal care has been uneventful.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient — six minutes
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like. They will be given to you on a card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Eight minutes. A two-minute warning is given. The card is handed at six minutes.

back.dx: Pre-eclampsia with right upper quadrant pain — two days of heavy constant RUQ ache, three days of headache, floaters and flashes (the discriminating symptom), ankle swelling present on waking, dizzy standing. Vitals at the door: BP 150/90 — say it aloud and declare the branch. Card: alert, no jaundice, RUQ tender no guarding, fundal height 34 cm non-tender no contractions, FHR 142, bowel sounds normal, fundoscopy not performed, brisk reflexes no sustained clonus, pitting oedema to mid-shin, protein 3+. Hidden: sister had pre-eclampsia, delivered at 33 weeks, baby a month in special care.
plan: Introduce, confirm identity; vitals from examiner; 'I note the BP is raised at 150/90, so I'll ask specifically about pre-eclampsia'; open question; one sentence of acknowledgement

The pain — one question per turn: where, /10, ache/burning/cramping in waves, when, constant or comes and goes, worse, moves, better/worse incl. fatty food (if it comes and goes: lasting longer, gaps shorter?); GI run: nausea/vomiting, diarrhoea/constipation, bloating, wind, fever/chills
★ Bleeding? Discharge or fluid? Baby moving — when last felt? (separate questions) Then the pre-eclampsia set incl. swelling present on waking
Antenatal spine, previous pregnancies, medications incl. aspirin/NSAIDs/iron, appetite, groin lump, urinary symptoms, travel, SNAP, safe at home, 'was there something you were worried this might be?'
Examination request in order, findings not technique; because BP is up — fundoscopy, reflexes, ankle clonus; speculum with consent; no digital VE until praevia excluded

Pre-eclampsia in plain words; reasons — two symptoms then two signs; four differential groups with one line each; plan: hospital today, obstetric team, CTG, bloods, PCR, antihypertensives, delivery timing, steroids at 34 wk; six-item safety-net; SA localisation
ask: Examiner, before I begin, could I have her vital signs? → say the BP aloud

Tell me in your own words what's been happening → 'I can hear how worried you are about the baby' (if she asks: 'that's exactly what I'm checking — the heartbeat is one of the first things I'll listen for')
Where exactly? One to ten? Dull ache, burning, or cramping in waves? When did it start? All the time or comes and goes? Getting worse? Move anywhere? Better or worse — fatty food?
Nausea/vomiting? Diarrhoea/constipation? Bloating? Passing wind? Fever/chills?
Any bleeding from down below? Any discharge or fluid leaking? Is the baby moving as much as usual — when did you last feel it move? (don't accept 'I think so')
Headaches? Vision — blurring, flashing lights, floaters? Dizziness? Nausea? Yellowing? Chest pain/SOB? Swelling — is it there when you wake up? Passing less urine? New rashes or bruising?

Booking bloods, dating scan, Down screening, morphology, sweet drink test? Previous pregnancies? Medications incl. aspirin, anti-inflammatories, iron? Appetite? Groin lump? Dysuria/frequency/haematuria? Travel? Smoke/drink/drugs? Safe at home? What were you worried this might be?
pefe: General appearance (conscious state, distress, pallor, jaundice, rash, bruising); repeat BP; abdomen — tenderness, specifically over liver and uterus; uterus — fundal height, FHR, tenderness, palpable contractions; bowel sounds; inguinal orifices, offer PR; because BP raised — fundoscopy, deep tendon reflexes, ankle clonus; lower limbs oedema; dipstick protein/blood/nitrites/leucocytes
'With her consent and a chaperone I'd inspect and pass a speculum — os open? blood or liquor? I would not perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded'
If asked what you're looking for: papilloedema, hyperreflexia and sustained clonus, liver tenderness, protein

Explain: pre-eclampsia only happens in pregnancy, usually second half; several organs at once — BP up, kidneys leak protein, liver swells and sits exactly where the pain is; 'I'm saying that because of' RUQ pain, headaches, flashes/floaters, morning swelling — and BP 150/90, brisk reflexes, 3+ protein

Four groups: pregnancy — early labour, placental separation (no waves, no bleeding) · bowel — appendicitis, blockage, hernia (appetite, bowels, sounds normal) · liver/gallbladder — gallstones, HELLP (needs bloods to exclude; don't call it HELLP without haemolysis, raised enzymes, low platelets) · waterworks — kidney infection or stone (no fever, dysuria, clean nitrites)

Plan: hospital today, ring obstetric team; CTG, FBC/film/LDH/LFT/UEC, urine PCR; safe antihypertensives; delivery is the only cure — team decides timing; steroids at 34 wk; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if she deteriorates; PATS for travel · safety-net: pain worse/constant, bleeding or fluid, baby moves less, headache worse or more flashes, vomiting or fever, 'something is wrong'
fails: Asking for a digital vaginal examination ★
Omitting bleeding or fetal movements — a safety fail even when negative ★
Taking the BP silently and not acting on it
Never asking the concerns question — the sister's story stays unsaid
Saying 'pre-eclampsia' and stopping without reasons; a flat list of twelve diagnoses; calling it HELLP on RUQ pain alone
numbers: 140/90 on two readings · 160/110 severe, treat IV · target <135/85 · 20 weeks — the line above which pre-eclampsia can be diagnosed · FHR 110–160 · fundal height ≈ weeks from ~20 wk, >3 cm discrepancy matters
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM ×2, 24 h apart if birth before 34+6 wk VERIFY · MgSO4 4 g then 1 g/h · 3+ protein → quantify with protein:creatinine ratio

Variants: seizure during the station → eclampsia: call for help, DRSABC, left lateral, oxygen, two large-bore lines, MgSO4 4 g/20 min then 1 g/h, midazolam/diazepam if continuing, IV labetalol/hydralazine, monitor reflexes/RR/urine output, deliver when stable · pain in waves every 5 min, os 3 cm → labour has started, safest place for birth · fundal height 39 cm at 36 wk, tender uterus, no bleeding → concealed abruption, emergency · refuses hospital ('four-year-old at home') → real problem not an excuse, 'how well you feel doesn't tell us how you're doing', bloods and CTG now, back tomorrow, warning signs, PATS and social worker for childcare — her decision, safety-net retained
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

setting: Your general practice, a country town on the Yorke Peninsula.
stem: Ben Halloran, 60, here to discuss the results of a scan.

Background. Ben had an ischaemic stroke some months ago. As part of that work-up he had a CT angiogram of the head and neck. The radiologist has reported an incidental nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid gland. He has no complaint today and no symptoms were recorded.
No observations, no bloods, no examination findings are provided.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Explain to the patient the investigations you would request
time: 8 minutes.

back.dx: Incidental thyroid nodule — clinically euthyroid and asymptomatic, no compressive or red-flag features, but hidden risk factors: radiotherapy to the left neck at 22 after a skin cancer, eleven years as an industrial radiographer, male, 60. Hidden agenda: brother-in-law Trev died of throat cancer, eight months start to finish — he hasn't slept since the letter. Discriminating move: name the kinds of nodule BEFORE listing the tests; TSH always first, then the branch.
plan: Open; heads-up in plain words (a lump in the thyroid, found by chance, most harmless, needs checking); permission to ask questions
Ever told you had a thyroid lump or problem? Scanned or tested?
Local: swelling, pain, skin change
Thyroid function both directions: heat/cold, bowels, palpitations/tremor/sweating/sleep, weight, energy, mood, skin, hair
Cancer questions; the pair: difficulty swallowing? change in voice? plus noisy breathing/lying flat
Risk factors one at a time: radiotherapy to head/neck? occupation now and before, radiation? cancer yourself? thyroid cancer in family? breast cancer? bowel cancer?
The stroke, medications and adherence, reviews, smoking, alcohol, allergies; 'what's been going through your mind since that letter came?' → respond to Trev

STOP the history. Name the kinds of nodule → examination → TSH → branch (uptake scan if fast; ultrasound if normal) → FNA only if suspicious → PATS, safety-net, ring him with the result, check understanding, questions
ask: I do have your results here, and I want to tell you what they show before anything else
Have you ever been told you had a lump or a problem with your thyroid before?
Noticed any swelling in the front of your neck? Pain? Change in the skin?
How do you cope with the weather — heat or cold more than others? Bowels changed? Palpitations, tremor, sweating, trouble sleeping? Weight? Energy, mood, skin, hair?
Lost weight without meaning to? Appetite? Night sweats or fevers? Other lumps, especially above the collarbones?
Two questions I ask everyone with a lump here: any difficulty swallowing? any change in your voice? — ask as a pair; plus noisy breathing or trouble lying flat

Ever had radiotherapy or radiation treatment to your head or neck, at any age? Occupation now and before — worked around radiation? Cancer yourself? Thyroid cancer in the family? Breast cancer? Bowel cancer? — one at a time, never stacked
The stroke: when, what were you left with, medications, taking them every day?, reviews; smoke, alcohol, allergies
What's been going through your mind since that letter came? → 'I'm sorry — that must make this letter very frightening to open'
pefe: Name the kinds first: fluid-filled cyst · overgrown area · inflamed tissue · benign tumour, some of which switch themselves on · a small number are cancers (papillary commonest; follicular, medullary) · very occasionally a cancer from elsewhere
If he asks the odds: 'something like nine in ten are not cancer. I can't promise you which side of that you're on, and I won't pretend I can'

Numbered plan: FIRST examine the neck — size, firmness, tenderness, moves on swallowing, nodes in neck and above the collarbones · SECOND blood test TSH — 'that one test decides what comes next' · THIRD the branch: gland running fast → nuclear (radioiodine uptake) scan, a hot lump is reassuring; TSH normal/low-normal → ultrasound of the neck (what it's made of, how worrying, nearby glands) · FOURTH only if the ultrasound looks suspicious → ultrasound-guided fine-needle sample under local

Wrap: most people are simply watched; bloods here, ultrasound and FNA at a larger centre — PATS; safety-net: grows quickly, voice hoarse, food catching, trouble breathing → sooner or 000; 'I'll ring you myself with the blood result'; check understanding; also address stroke-prevention adherence

Summary to examiner: incidental left nodule on CTA, euthyroid, asymptomatic, no compressive/red-flag features, prior neck irradiation + male + 60; excluding carcinoma; exam → TSH → uptake scan if suppressed or ultrasound with risk stratification → US-guided FNA if indicated; would not repeat CT
fails: No question about swallowing or voice (single-item fail)
Never asking about radiotherapy/radiation — the role-player never volunteers it
Listing tests without saying what you are looking for
Promising it is harmless
Triple-barrelled family cancer question; starting questions cold before the heads-up; ending on the FNA with no safety-net
numbers: Order: examination → TSH → branch → uptake scan (TSH low) or ultrasound (TSH normal/high) → US-guided FNA if indicated
Malignancy ~5–10% of nodules; higher in men, age <20 or >60, after neck irradiation VERIFY · hot = functioning, malignancy uncommon, FNA not routine · cold → ultrasound ± FNA, most still benign

Cytology: Bethesda; FNA cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma → diagnostic hemithyroidectomy · US suspicion: solid hypoechoic, taller-than-wide, irregular margin, microcalcification, extrathyroidal extension, abnormal node
Types: papillary (commonest, best prognosis) · follicular · medullary (MEN 2) · anaplastic · lymphoma · metastasis · syndromes: Cowden (breast), FAP (bowel), MEN 2
Never: CT to characterise · uptake scan with normal TSH · FNA before ultrasound · thyroglobulin as a diagnostic test · blanket reassurance
Clock: heads-up by 0:45 · stop history at 4:40 · last 40 s for understanding, safety-net, follow-up

Variants: TSH suppressed (hot, sweating, 6 kg loss, tremor, loose bowels) → toxic adenoma, nuclear scan not ultrasound, beta-blocker, ECG; recent iodinated contrast — discuss uptake-scan timing with nuclear medicine (Jod–Basedow) · red flags (hoarse 6 wk, food catching, supraclavicular node) → concerned not diagnostic, scan + FNA this week, laryngoscopy, ring him, bring someone · angry patient (letter, 3 weeks, 'cut it out today') → validate, don't defend; surgery risks recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroids, only when tests say so · sibling recall: adrenal incidentaloma — metanephrines, dexamethasone suppression, aldosterone–renin if hypertensive/hypokalaemic; dedicated adrenal CT; never needle before phaeo excluded VERIFY
SA: PATS · Country Health Connect · RAH/FMC/TQEH endocrine surgery · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · TIS 131 450 · healthdirect 1800 022 222

stem: James Doherty, a 66-year-old man, presents complaining of nervousness.
Background. He is a known case of atrial fibrillation. He was taking flecainide; his cardiologist changed him to amiodarone four weeks ago. He has come today for his blood test results.
Results handed to you in the room: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (normal, 0.4–4.0) · Free T4 28 pmol/L (high, 10–20) · Free T3 8.9 pmol/L (high, 3.5–6.5).
tasks: Take a focused history
Interpret the investigation results for the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Roughly 4–4:30 history, 1:30 results, 2:00 diagnosis and differentials.

back.dx: Thyrotoxicosis with INAPPROPRIATE TSH secretion — high T4/T3 with a NORMAL TSH. Two diagnoses, in order: (1) TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma; (2) amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction (honest caveat: amiodarone should suppress TSH, and four weeks is early — but TSH can drift back to normal over months, so it stays on the list). The station is built on one mismatch: in thyrotoxicosis the TSH should be suppressed and his is not. Say it to the examiner, and a lay version to the patient. Hidden agenda: wants the amiodarone stopped today; underneath, frightened his heart is getting worse.
plan: Confirm ID; 'I have your results and we'll go through them — first, what do you mean by nervous: stressed and on edge, shaking hands, or racing heart?'
Timing, pattern, impact (4 weeks, since the switch — note it, don't close on it)
AF anchor: how long, adherence, WHY was flecainide changed, side effects, follow-up; complications — racing, chest pain, SOBOE, oedema, TIA/stroke symptoms, anticoagulant
Track 1 thyroid: heat intolerance, bowels, weight loss, sweating, tremor. Track 2 pituitary: headache, blurred vision, side vision, weakness/numbness
Psychiatry + stimulants: mood, sleep, 'I ask everyone — thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?', home/stress, tea/coffee, alcohol, substances, cold-and-flu tablets

Results in FOUR rungs: gland in the neck makes hormones → yours are high → TSH from the brain controls it → when hormones rise TSH should fall; yours stayed normal — that mismatch is what I must explain. 'Does that make sense so far?'
'Two things on my list' — adenoma (usually not cancer), then amiodarone with the honest caveat. Three ready answers: cancer? stop the tablet? what now? Then the rest of the differentials

Plan: repeat assay on a different platform (ask about biotin), further hormones incl. cortisol, formal visual fields, pituitary MRI, endocrinology; speak to cardiologist yourself; red flags; phone with the repeat result
ask: Can you tell me what you mean by feeling nervous? Stressed and on edge, shaking in your hands, or a racing heart?
How long? Constant or comes and goes? Getting worse? Anything make it better or worse? How is it affecting your day-to-day life?
Why was the flecainide changed? Are you taking the amiodarone regularly, exactly as prescribed?
Still getting racing? Chest pain? Breathless on exertion, ankle swelling? Any weakness/numbness one side, trouble speaking, brief loss of vision? On a blood thinner?
Heat intolerance? Looser/more frequent bowels? Weight loss? Sweating? Shaking hands?
Headaches? Blurred vision, or difficulty seeing to the sides? Weakness or numbness anywhere?
How has your mood been? Your sleep? 'I ask everybody this — any thoughts of harming yourself, or anyone else?'
Who do you live with, any stresses at home or work?
How much tea/coffee? Alcohol? Other substances, cold-and-flu tablets? Any supplements — biotin?
pefe: No examination in this station — results are handed to you

Investigations to name: repeat TFTs on a different assay platform (artefact/biotin), full pituitary hormone profile including MORNING CORTISOL, formal visual field testing, pituitary MRI; endocrinology referral; discuss with cardiologist
To the examiner: 'This is thyrotoxicosis with inappropriate TSH secretion' · 'My first investigation is a repeat assay on a different platform'

Examiner challenge — start carbimazole today? NO: mechanism unknown; if TSH-oma a thionamide lowers T4 and drives TSH higher; if type 2 amiodarone thyroiditis the gland isn't overproducing — thionamide won't help. Repeat assay, involve endocrinology first
fails: Assuming what 'nervous' means and launching a thyroid history without asking
Agreeing 'it's just the tablet' — false reassurance that abandons the normal TSH
Skipping 'why was the flecainide changed?'
Asking mood and sleep but NOT self-harm — marked down hardest
Not asking headache and vision (the pituitary track)
Giving one diagnosis instead of two, in order
Telling him to stop the amiodarone, or not offering to contact the cardiologist
Physiology lecture: drawing the axis, saying 'negative feedback'; jargon without 'in plain English'
numbers: TSH 1.8 normal · fT4 28 · fT3 8.9 both high · 4 weeks on amiodarone — early for drug-induced thyrotoxicosis
Thyrotoxicosis requires a LOW TSH — except in pituitary disease
Amiodarone thyroid phases: hyper → hypo → normal, over months
Five causes of normal TSH + high T4: assay artefact (biotin), sampling/timing, amiodarone late phase, TSH-secreting adenoma, thyroid hormone resistance
Before any thyroid-directed treatment in pituitary disease: check cortisol first
Five history blocks — block 5 is psychiatry

Variant 1 (early recall): TSH 0.02, 8 months on amiodarone = overt amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis; separate type 1 vs 2 with colour-flow Doppler; endocrine + cardiology together before changing the drug
Variant 2: headaches + clipping door frames = bitemporal field defect → urgent fields, MRI, neurosurgery, cortisol first
Variant 3: high-dose biotin, no symptoms = artefact; stop, wait days, repeat on different platform — VERIFY washout interval
'Is it cancer?' — usually benign, treatable, not what I'm worried about today · 'Stop the tablet?' — no, it holds your rhythm; I'll speak to your cardiologist myself
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450

stem: You are a GP. Jenny Alderton, 37, has come in with palpitations and dizziness for three days.
(Version A — shorter stem.)
tasks: Take a focused history (4–5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. 4–5 minutes history, ~30 seconds ECG, remainder diagnosis with a named cause. Ask for vitals before you begin.

back.dx: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response — vitals BP 118/74, P 128 irregular, RR 16, T 36.6, SpO2 98%: stable but tachycardic. Duration THREE DAYS, CONTINUOUS (>48 h — dictates the whole rhythm-control answer). Hidden clue only if asked about associated symptoms: months of exertional chest tightness and breathlessness up the hill, settling on rest → the named cause is probable ischaemic heart disease, with coffee, alcohol and smoking contributing. Father MI in his fifties. Hidden agenda: 'Is this what my dad had?' and can't afford time off work.
plan: 'Before I begin, could I please have the vital signs?' → name 'tachycardic, irregular, haemodynamically stable' out loud
WIPE, open question, empathy line. Choose PALPITATIONS as the structure — dizziness in one clarifying question (spinning vs faint; actually fainted?)
Characterise: tap it out; sudden/gradual; constant or comes and goes (3 days continuous); triggers; associated chest pain, SOB, sweating, presyncope

Cause sweep, fast: heart (exertional pain — how long?, orthopnoea, PND, oedema, murmur/BP), lungs (cough, fever, pleuritic pain, calf, travel, snoring), thyroid (weight, heat, tremor, bowels, neck lump), habits (coffee, alcohol, smoking, drugs), PMH/meds/allergies/FHx

ECG — all seven steps, no pauses: rate (10-second bypass line), rhythm irregularly irregular, no P waves/fibrillatory baseline, PR not measurable, QRS just over 2 small squares, up-sloping ST V2–V3 not pathological, T waves unremarkable → 'AF with rapid ventricular response'

Name it, explain it plainly, then the CAUSE (arteries — chest tightness uphill; caffeine/alcohol/smoking). Differentials delivered as causes: thyroid, hypertension, valve, peri/myocarditis, PE, hormone tumours; also anxiety, hypoglycaemia, anaemia
Safety-net (chest pain, severe SOB, syncope, one-sided weakness/droop → 000), summary, invite questions, answer 'is this what my dad had?'
ask: Can you tap out on the desk what the beat feels like?
Did it come on suddenly or build up? Constant for the three days, or comes and goes? ★
Does anything set it off — coffee, alcohol, exercise, stress?
With the palpitations — chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, feel like you might black out? ★ (this is where the exertional chest tightness comes out)
The dizziness — spinning, or like you're about to faint? Have you actually fainted?
Breathless lying flat, waking at night, ankle swelling? Ever told you have a murmur, high BP, heart problem?
Cough, fever, sharp pain on breathing, calf swelling, long travel? Snore or sleepy in the day?
Weight loss, feeling hot when others don't, tremor, loose bowels, neck lump?
Coffee, alcohol, smoking, other drugs? Other conditions, medications, allergies, heart problems in the family?
pefe: Vitals from the examiner first: BP 118/74, P 128 irregular, RR 16, T 36.6, SpO2 98% RA
ECG seven steps in order: rate → rhythm → P waves → PR → QRS → ST → T; impression AF with RVR

Rate bypass line: 'As the rhythm is irregular, the correct method is to count the QRS complexes across a 10-second strip and multiply by six — may I return to the exact figure?' (ventricular response ~120–140)
If challenged on V2–V3: up-sloping, ramping into the T wave at a fast rate, not horizontal or convex injury; V2–V3 thresholds are higher and vary with age/sex — would not call an infarct
Investigations to name: TSH, echo (pump, valves, clot), FBE, EUC, LFT, fasting glucose and lipids
fails: Taking the dizziness road (vertigo/presyncope/postural drop) and running out of time
Not establishing duration and whether continuous ★
Not eliciting the exertional chest pain ★
Freezing on the rate step — counting boxes, never recovering ★
Over-reading up-sloping ST in V2–V3 as infarct
Giving the label without a named cause ★
Abandoning the systems sweep because you've already guessed AF
numbers: Large square = 0.2 s; 10 seconds = 50 large squares; QRS count × 6
Normal QRS <3 small squares (<120 ms)
ST elevation: ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads; V2–V3 ≥2 mm men ≥40, ≥2.5 mm men <40, ≥1.5 mm women
48 hours = cardioversion safety threshold; unknown duration counts as beyond it
Paroxysmal = self-terminating, usually within 7 days; persistent = beyond 7 days
Her CHA₂DS₂-VA = 0 today (37, no risk factors) — reassess once results back, especially if chest pain is ischaemic

stem: Same practice. A 55-year-old woman presents with palpitations.

The stem is a full page and already contains the history: heavy coffee, alcohol most nights, some chest pain, and hypertension diagnosed years ago and never followed up. (Version B — long stem; summarised here as the PDF summarises it.)
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management plan
time: 8 minutes. Management is the predominant assessment area — roughly five minutes for it. Brevity fails this station.

back.dx: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, driven by untreated hypertension (years of high pressure stretching the heart), with coffee and alcohol adding to it. CHA₂DS₂-VA = 1 (hypertension) → discuss, and recommend starting anticoagulation; +1 more if the stem gives diabetes, vascular disease or heart failure → 2, anticoagulate without debate. Age doesn't score until 65. Duration unknown/long = treat as >48 h.
plan: ECG seven steps, no pauses: 10-second rate line → irregularly irregular → no P waves → PR not measurable → QRS narrow-ish → up-sloping ST V2–V3 not pathological → T unremarkable → 'AF with RVR'

Diagnosis plainly: irregular because the electrical signals are disorganised, top chambers quiver; then the CAUSE — untreated blood pressure, plus coffee and alcohol. Differentials as causes: thyroid, valve, peri/myocarditis, PE, hormone tumours; anxiety, hypoglycaemia, anaemia excluded
Signpost: three parts — find the cause, protect from stroke, treat the beat
Pillar 1: TSH + echo (pump, valves, clot inside); FBE, EUC, LFT, fasting glucose, lipids; treat the BP; cut coffee and alcohol, stop smoking (Quitline), diet, exercise

Pillar 2: clot → stroke; name CHA₂DS₂-VA and the thresholds (0 none · 1 consider · ≥2 give); hers = 1 for hypertension → recommend starting; warfarin (regular tests) vs DOAC e.g. apixaban — echo decides: valve problem → warfarin

Pillar 3: rate control first (beta blocker); rhythm — BOTH duration pathways: <48 h cardiovert now; >48 h or unknown → rate control, anticoagulate, TOE OR 3 weeks anticoagulation, then cardiovert, continue ≥4 weeks after; electrical (sedation, controlled shock) vs pharmacological — echo decides
Safety-net (chest pain, severe SOB, syncope, one-sided weakness/droop → 000); summary; cardiologist; questions
ask: (History is in the stem) Confirm duration if not stated — 'I've no idea' counts as >48 h
'Is it alright if I go through the three parts in turn?'
'What questions do you have for me?'
pefe: ECG interpretation as MED-03
Pillar 1 investigations: TSH, transthoracic echo, FBE, EUC, LFT, fasting glucose, lipids
If pressed on the echo: TTE gives EF, valves, chamber size but cannot reliably exclude LEFT ATRIAL APPENDAGE thrombus — early cardioversion needs a TOE
Warfarin vs DOAC decided by the echo (valvular AF → warfarin)
fails: Finishing management in under two minutes ★
Not naming CHA₂DS₂-VA and the thresholds — you name it for the examiner's score sheet ★
Not naming TSH and echo, or omitting risk-factor modification ★
Not naming rate control, or not explaining the 48-hour rule WITH the reason (pushing a clot out → stroke) ★
Giving only one duration pathway — give both
Label without a cause (untreated hypertension) ★
Saying 'it's about clotting' without the score — the folklore trap
numbers: CHA₂DS₂-VA: 0 none · 1 consider · ≥2 give. Age ≥75 = 2; prior stroke/TIA = 2; age 65–74 = 1; hypertension 1. Australian version drops the female-sex point — say which score you're using
48 h threshold; 3 weeks anticoagulation before cardioversion, ≥4 weeks after
Metoprolol 25–50 mg BD · apixaban 5 mg BD · warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 — VERIFY
Opportunistic AF screening from age 65
Variant 3 'never felt it, you found it on my pulse' — common; assume >48 h; same careful order

Variant 4 refuses the blood thinner (mother bruised on warfarin) — DOACs don't need tests and are more predictable; her decision, but make it with the full picture: the harm prevented is a stroke; go through the numbers together; can change her mind anytime
Quitline 13 7848 · 000

stem: You are the doctor in a general practice. Ray Docherty, 62, has come in with chest pain for the past two to three months. It comes on when he walks up the hill to the shops and settles when he stops.
Vitals: T 36.6 · HR 96 · BP 132/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · BMI 27.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
Outline your investigations and initial management
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · examination 1:00 · diagnosis and differentials 1:30 · investigations and management 1:15 · close 0:15.

back.dx: Stable typical angina BECAUSE OF iron-deficiency anaemia BECAUSE OF a bleeding NSAID ulcer — a three-link chain. Findings: pale, conjunctival pallor · P 96 regular, no postural drop · soft ejection systolic FLOW murmur · chest clear · mild epigastric tenderness · PR: MELAENA · ECG sinus tachycardia, no acute ischaemia · BSL 5.4. Hidden: black tarry offensive stools for a month (only if asked); supermarket ibuprofen most days for 8 months for his knees (only if asked about OTC painkillers after 'nothing really, just a blood pressure tablet'). Agenda: brother's bypass at 64; once melaena surfaces, fear of cancer.
plan: 'May I have his vital signs, including a postural BP?' → open question → acknowledge → signpost: 'questions that might seem unrelated to your chest — they matter'
Characterise: site/radiation, character, provoked/relieved, duration, REST OR NIGHT PAIN, crescendo, associated sweating/nausea/SOB/palpitations → typical and stable
CV risk factors; other chest pain groups in one sweep (fever/viral, leaning forward, travel/calf, haemoptysis, injury/pressing, rash, heartburn)
ANAEMIA BLOCK: tired, more breathless doing usual things, dizzy, palpitations, told you look pale

UPPER GI BLOCK — the pivot: dyspepsia and relation to food; BLACK OR TARRY MOTIONS → characterise (how long, sticky, offensive) and exclude iron/bismuth; haematemesis/coffee grounds; dysphagia; weight/appetite; bowel habit/fresh blood; family GI cancer

Meds asked twice: 'what medications?' then 'anything for pain or joints — including bought at the chemist or supermarket? Ibuprofen, Nurofen, Voltaren, aspirin? How much, how long?' Previous ulcer/H. pylori; allergies; concerns
PEFE box by box incl. PR with consent + chaperone → 'pallor, flow murmur and melaena fit together'
Chain in three linked steps; differentials incl. honest malignancy; Ix and Mx; the aspirin conflict said out loud; safety-net
ask: Where exactly, does it go anywhere, what's it like — heavy, tight, sharp, burning?
What brings it on and what makes it go? How long does it last?
Do you ever get it at rest, or at night, or does it wake you? ★ Is it coming on with less effort than it used to?
Smoking, BP, diabetes, cholesterol; family heart attacks/strokes and at what age; activity; alcohol
More tired than usual? More breathless doing things you used to manage? Dizzy? Palpitations? Anyone said you look pale?
Any indigestion, burning or gnawing upper tummy pain — related to eating?
Have you noticed your bowel motions turning black or tarry? ★ Sticky, offensive? How long? Iron tablets or Pepto-Bismol?
Vomited blood or coffee grounds? Difficulty swallowing? Weight loss/appetite? Bowel habit or fresh blood? Family bowel or stomach cancer?
What medications are you on? … Anything at all for pain or your joints, including bought over the counter? ★ Ever had an ulcer or Helicobacter treatment?
Anything in particular you're worried about?
pefe: General: pale? conjunctival/palmar pallor, glossitis, angular stomatitis, koilonychia
Vitals: pulse rate and rhythm, BP lying and standing
CVS: heart sounds, murmurs (soft ESM = flow murmur in anaemia — say you'd confirm with echo; keep AS open), JVP, oedema, heart failure signs
Respiratory: air entry, added sounds
Abdomen: epigastric tenderness, masses, organomegaly
'With his consent and a chaperone, may I perform a rectal examination — melaena or mass?' ★
Office tests: ECG, BSL, urine dipstick
fails: Closing on coronary disease on 'exertional pain in a 62-year-old' and running on autopilot
Not asking rest/night pain — what grades it stable rather than ACS
Never asking the five anaemia questions; attributing all breathlessness to angina
Hearing 'black stools' and moving on without characterising/excluding iron and bismuth
Accepting 'no medications' — never asking about OTC painkillers ★
Not requesting the rectal examination ★
Calling the murmur aortic stenosis outright
'It's just the anti-inflammatories' — never naming malignancy honestly
Telling him to keep taking the ibuprofen, or never addressing it ★
Starting aspirin, or omitting it silently, instead of naming the conflict
Ordering cardiac stress testing while still anaemic
numbers: Chain: NSAID → ulcer → chronic blood loss → iron-deficiency anaemia → reduced O2 delivery + increased cardiac work → angina
Bloods: FBC (microcytic hypochromic), iron studies (low ferritin), UEC (urea raised in upper GI bleed), LFT, coags, group and hold/cross-match, ECG ± troponin
Scopes: gastroscopy + H. pylori testing; colonoscopy too — iron deficiency in an older adult warrants both tracts

Treatment order: stop NSAID → PPI → iron → transfuse only if symptomatic at rest/compromised (restrictive threshold, slightly higher in cardiac disease — discuss with senior, don't commit to a number) → eradicate H. pylori → GTN spray for episodes → cardiac functional testing AFTER Hb recovers
Knees: paracetamol + topical anti-inflammatory gel + physio
Aspirin: defer; decide jointly with cardiology and gastroenterology with gastroprotection in place
'Is this ACS?' — no: purely exertional, relieved by rest, no rest/night pain, no acute ECG change; low threshold for troponin if anything changes
Safety-net: rest pain that doesn't settle, haematemesis, worsening melaena, faint → ED

stem: Alan Prosser, 58, presents to the Emergency Department with central chest pain worse lying flat and better sitting forward, with a flu-like illness a week ago.
Vitals: T 37.2 · HR 88 · BP 128/76 · RR 18 · SpO2 97%.
ECG handed to you: ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No PR depression, no widespread concave elevation.
tasks: Take a history (4–6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG
Explain the diagnosis and immediate management
time: 8 minutes. The history sounds like pericarditis; the ECG overrides it.

back.dx: Acute INFERIOR STEMI — territorial ST elevation (II, III, aVF) with reciprocal change (I, aVL) = infarct, whatever the story. Pericarditis history + infarct ECG: treat the infarct. Name the mismatch to the examiner: this is exactly why ECG and troponin are part of the pericarditis work-up. Obtain V4R for right ventricular involvement → if RV involved, NO nitrates, give fluid (preload dependent).
plan: Vitals; open question; characterise the pain (positional, pleuritic?, viral prodrome), risk factors, other chest pain groups briefly

ECG aloud: 'Rate 88, sinus, normal axis. ST elevation in II, III, aVF — the inferior leads — with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No widespread elevation, no PR depression. Territorial pattern with reciprocal change = acute inferior STEMI, not pericarditis. I would obtain right-sided leads.'
To the examiner: acknowledge the history suggested pericarditis; the ECG overrides it; treating as infarct
To the patient: tracing shows something more serious — an artery supplying your heart is blocked, a heart attack; the pain didn't feel typical but the tracing is clear; acting now, calling cardiology

Immediate management: resus area, monitoring, O2 only if hypoxic, IV access, aspirin 300 mg chewed, second antiplatelet + anticoagulation per protocol, analgesia; reperfusion — primary PCI if prompt, otherwise thrombolysis + urgent transfer; V4R → avoid nitrates/give fluid if RV; watch for arrhythmia and heart block
Rural SA: thrombolyse here after checking contraindications, simultaneous MedSTAR retrieval to a PCI centre, discuss with receiving cardiologist while treating
ask: Where is the pain, what's it like, does it change with position — worse lying flat, better leaning forward?
Any flu-like illness recently? Fever?
Sweating, nausea, breathlessness? Any pain on exertion before this?
Smoking, BP, diabetes, cholesterol, family history
Any bleeding history, recent surgery, stroke, anticoagulants (thrombolysis contraindications)
pefe: ECG in order: rate → rhythm → axis → ST by territory → reciprocal change → PR segment → impression
Right-sided leads (V4R) for RV involvement
Troponin; continuous monitoring

Variant — the ECG really IS pericarditis: widespread concave ST elevation across territories with PR depression and no reciprocal change → still send troponin and arrange echo (exclude infarction and effusion); treat with NSAID plus colchicine
fails: Calling it pericarditis because the history fits — territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change is an infarct ★
Not obtaining right-sided leads / giving nitrates to an RV infarct
Delaying reperfusion to complete the history
Not naming the history–ECG mismatch to the examiner
Reassuring the patient it's 'just inflammation'
numbers: Inferior leads II, III, aVF; reciprocal I and aVL; V4R for RV involvement
Pericarditis pattern: widespread concave STE + PR depression, no reciprocal change
Aspirin 300 mg chewed; second antiplatelet and anticoagulant per local protocol — VERIFY
Primary PCI if it can be delivered promptly; otherwise thrombolysis and urgent transfer
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — retrieval to a PCI centre (RAH/FMC); country hospital without a cath lab thrombolyses first
RV infarct: preload dependent — fluids, no nitrates

stem: Jenny Hollis, 58, presents to your general practice with palpitations.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 150 · BP 124/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · alert and comfortable.
The ECG you will be handed: rate 150 · regular R-R intervals · no visible P waves · PR not measurable · narrow QRS · ST segments normal.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · ECG 1:00 · diagnosis 0:45 · differentials 1:30 · plan and close 0:45.

back.dx: Supraventricular tachycardia — regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 with no visible P waves (the single deflection between QRSs is the T wave, not a P). Stable. Two planted findings you must earn: EIGHT cups of coffee a day (only the number if asked how much; 'a fair bit' if asked vaguely) and blood pressure once found raised and never followed up (only if asked about BP/PMH). Positional trigger: standing quickly or bending. She refuses to tap the rhythm — ask once, accept, move on. Agenda: neighbour died of a heart attack last year — 'is it a heart attack?' whatever you've said.
plan: Vitals INCLUDING RHYTHM ('you don't know that yet' — accept); state stable; open question; acknowledge
BOX 1: what do you mean — fast, irregular, missing a beat? Tap it out? (refusal → move on)
BOX 2: onset, constant vs episodic, how long and how it stops, first time, worsening
BOX 3: better/worse; standing/bending/lying; exertion vs rest; situation
GROUP 1 full CV block: chest pain/SOB/nausea/sweating; dizzy/syncope; oedema/orthopnoea/pillows; murmur/valve/heart attack; FHx; BP/sugar/lipids (→ untreated BP); smoking/alcohol; fever/viral illness
Groups 2–4: cough/wheeze; calves/travel/clots; heat intolerance/weight loss/diarrhoea/tremor; STIMULANTS QUANTIFIED — cups per day; drugs; puffers; nasal sprays; takeaway/MSG
Groups 5–8: stress/mood/fear of dying; tiredness/exertional SOB; headache/sweats/tremor; missed meals/diabetes drugs; LMP/flushes; allergies; concerns
ECG seven steps → 'regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150, no visible P waves — SVT'
Name it, define it plainly, give the reason (coffee); address the heart-attack fear with reasons; differentials BY SYSTEM; plan incl. BP follow-up and referral; safety-net
ask: May I have her vital signs — BP, pulse rate and the rhythm if available, RR, sats, temperature?
Can you describe what you mean by palpitations — fast, irregular, or missing a beat? Could you tap it out on the desk?
When did it start? All the time or comes and goes? How long, how does it stop? First time? Getting more frequent?
Do you notice it more when you stand up, bend forward or lie down? ★ Worse on exertion — and at rest as well? ★ Any particular place or situation?

Chest pain, SOB, nausea, sweating? Dizzy, ever fainted? Leg swelling, breathless lying flat, how many pillows? Murmur, valve, heart attack? Family heart attacks/strokes? High BP, sugar, fats? ★ Smoke, alcohol? Fever or flu-like illness?
Cough, wheeze? Calf swelling/pain, long travel, previous clots?
Weather preference — hot weather hard to tolerate? Weight loss? Diarrhoea, tremor?
How many cups of coffee, tea or energy drink a day? ★ Recreational drugs? Asthma puffers or nasal decongestant sprays? Salty takeaway before it started?
Stress at home/work? Mood? During an episode, did you ever feel you were going to die?
Unusually tired or breathless on exertion? Headaches, sweating episodes, hand tremor? Missed meals, diabetes treatment? Last period, hot flushes?
Allergies? Other conditions or medications? Anything in particular you're worried about?
pefe: ECG seven steps: rate (two large squares → 150) → regular? (equal R-R) → P waves? (only one deflection between QRSs = T wave; P buried in QRS) → PR not measurable → QRS ~1.5 squares, narrow → ST normal → impression
If your nerve goes: DESCRIBE — 'a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 without visible P waves' earns most of the mark
Bloods: FBC, electrolytes with Mg and Ca, TFTs, glucose ± troponin ± metanephrines
Stable: modified Valsalva → adenosine 6 mg rapid push with flush, then 12 mg, monitored, per protocol with senior — VERIFY; long term: cut stimulants, teach vagal manoeuvres, EP referral for ablation
Unstable (hypotension, ischaemic pain, heart failure, altered conscious state): stop the history — resus, monitoring, O2 if hypoxic, IV, senior help, synchronised DC cardioversion with sedation
fails: Not asking for the rhythm with the vitals
Being derailed by the refusal to tap
Skipping exertion vs rest
Skipping the full CV block / missing the untreated hypertension
Accepting 'a bit' of coffee — not quantifying cups per day ★
Pointing at the T wave, calling it a P, reporting sinus tachycardia ★
Differentials given as a list of other arrhythmias — fail ★ (they are causes of palpitations, by system)
Not addressing 'is it a heart attack?' with reasons
Never returning to the blood pressure in the plan ★
numbers: Three exploring boxes: describe ± tap · onset/episodic/first time/worsening · position/exertion vs rest/situation

Eight groups: CV (ischaemia, HF, valvular, cardiomyopathy, peri/myocarditis, risk factors) · respiratory (PE, COPD) · thyroid · stimulants · psychogenic · anaemia · phaeochromocytoma · hypoglycaemia; plus menopause and fever
Stimulant list: coffee, tea, energy drinks, alcohol, nicotine, illicit stimulants, salbutamol puffers, nasal decongestants, MSG
Phaeo triad: headache, sweating, palpitations
Broad-complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise
'SVT or PSVT?' — paroxysmal describes the episodic pattern; report SVT; AVNRT commonest mechanism
'Do I have to give up coffee completely?' — cut down substantially; 8 cups may be enough on its own
Variant — ECG is AF instead: irregularly irregular, no P, fibrillatory baseline, ~130 → plan changes: rate/rhythm control, echo, TFTs, stroke risk assessment (AF carries stroke risk SVT does not)
Variant — situational only ('when I present at work') → social anxiety, but complete the organic screen and ECG first
Safety-net: chest pain, faint/black out, breathless → back straight away

stem: Jack Ferris, 27, presents to your general practice complaining of awareness of his heartbeat, worried he is having a heart attack.
History yields two to three coffees a day, a pack of cigarettes a day, five glasses of wine most nights. Same SVT on ECG (rate 150, regular, no visible P waves, narrow QRS).
tasks: Take a focused history
Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 10 minutes. Same shape as MED-07. The stated fear is named and answered BEFORE the differentials.

back.dx: Supraventricular tachycardia in a 27-year-old, driven by a stimulant combination — coffee, a pack of cigarettes a day, five glasses of wine most nights. The general rule this version teaches: whenever the stem states a concern about a specific condition (heart attack here; brain tumour in a headache case; cancer in a weight-loss case) you name it and address it with reasons before the patient asks again — never a bare reassurance.
plan: Vitals incl. rhythm; open; acknowledge the fear early
BOX 1 adapted: 'what do you mean by being aware of your heartbeat — do you simply feel it, or is it faster, or irregular?' Then boxes 2–3
Eight groups as MED-07 — stimulants QUANTIFIED: coffees/day, cigarettes/day, standard drinks/night; drugs, puffers, sprays
ECG seven steps → SVT

THE EXTRA STEP before differentials: 'I know you came in worried you were having a heart attack. I don't believe you are: the tracing doesn't show the changes we see with a heart attack, and you don't have the symptoms — no chest pain, sweating, nausea. What you have is a fast heart rhythm — different, and very treatable.'
Differentials by system; the stimulant conversation — each alone can set it off, together much more likely; offer help with smoking and drinking; plan, referral, safety-net
ask: What do you mean by being aware of your heartbeat — do you simply feel it, is it faster, or irregular?
How many coffees a day? How many cigarettes a day? How many glasses of wine, how many nights?
Any recreational drugs, puffers or nasal sprays?
During an episode, did you ever feel you were going to die? Any particular situation?
What are you most worried about?
