Bloods: FBC, electrolytes with Mg/Ca, TFTs, glucose
Vagal manoeuvres taught; adenosine if needed per protocol; EP referral if recurrent
Offer Quitline 13 7848 and alcohol reduction support
fails: Not naming and answering the heart-attack fear with reasons before the differentials ★
Bare reassurance ('you're fine') without the ECG and symptom reasons
Not quantifying all three stimulants
Differentials as a list of arrhythmias
Lecturing about the smoking and alcohol instead of offering to work through reducing all three
numbers: Coffee 2–3/day · cigarettes 20/day · wine 5 glasses most nights — the combination is the cause
Same eight differential groups; same seven ECG steps
Unstable variant (BP 82/50, clammy, chest pain, drowsy, rate 190): stop history, synchronised cardioversion
Quitline 13 7848 · Alcohol and Drug Information Service SA 1300 13 1340 — VERIFY · TIS 131 450

stem: Raymond Doyle, 68, attends your general practice with three days of palpitations and increasing breathlessness on exertion. He describes his heart 'racing steadily, not jumping about'. He has hypertension on perindopril, BMI 33, and drinks around 30 standard drinks a week. An ECG has been performed and is available.
Observations: BP 128/76 · PR 148 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 96% RA · Temp 36.5 °C · no chest pain, alert and well perfused.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Give your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Outline your management
time: 8 minutes, no history. Two-minute plan: stable? → 150 regular = flutter 2:1 → sawtooth leads → 3 days = outside 48 h → rate · rhythm · ANTICOAGULATE · ablate · drivers → drivers in the stem (BP, alcohol, BMI → OSA) plus TFTs.

back.dx: Typical atrial flutter with 2:1 AV block — ventricular rate ~150, metronomically regular, no discrete P waves, continuous sawtooth baseline with no isoelectric segment, negative in II, III, aVF and positive in V1, atrial rate ~300, two flutter waves per QRS, narrow QRS, no acute ischaemia (flutter waves distort ST). Stable. The two things they are testing: do you name the rhythm rather than stopping at 'SVT', and do you anticoagulate. Failing to anticoagulate is a fail regardless of the total.
plan: Say STABLE out loud before interpreting: BP, HR, RR, sats, temp + chest pain, syncope, breathlessness at rest → 'so I can work through this rather than proceed to immediate cardioversion'
ECG read-out: rate, regular, no P, sawtooth, leads, atrial ~300, 2:1, narrow QRS, no ischaemia → 'typical atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction'

'Why not sinus tach?' — sinus is a response and needs a driver (afebrile, comfortable, perfused); sinus varies with respiration, this is metronomic at ~150; if unsure, increase AV block with vagal manoeuvre/adenosine under continuous ECG — diagnostic, not therapeutic

Two SEPARATE lists: differentials of the rhythm (sinus tach, AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia, AF with very rapid response) · causes of the flutter by system (CV: HTN, IHD, HF, valve, recent cardiac surgery; RS: PE, COPD, OSA; endocrine: thyrotoxicosis; drugs/lifestyle: alcohol, caffeine, stimulants, obesity)

To the patient: loop and filter → tired heart (breathless) → clot → stroke → blood thinner. Answer '300? should I be dead?' · 'stroke?' · 'shock it today?' (WHY it must wait) · 'from the drinking?' (honest, with the number: 30 vs limit of 10)

Management five things: rate (beta-blocker; or verapamil/diltiazem; never both; flutter less responsive than AF) · stroke prevention (score + bleeding risk; scores for HTN and age → DOAC; ASPIRIN IS NOT STROKE PREVENTION) · rhythm (outside 48 h → 3 weeks anticoag or TOE, then ≥4 weeks after) · CTI ablation early, curative · drivers (BP, alcohol, weight, OSA screen). Ix: FBC, electrolytes incl. Mg, renal, TFTs, CXR, TTE
ask: (No history task) If examiner allows: chest pain, syncope, breathlessness at rest; alcohol with a number; snoring/witnessed apnoeas
pefe: ECG: rate ~150 regular · no discrete P · sawtooth, no isoelectric segment · negative II, III, aVF, positive V1 · atrial ~300 · 2 waves per QRS · narrow QRS · no acute ischaemic change
Say unprompted: 'Aspirin is not stroke prevention.' 'Adenosine unmasks, it does not terminate.'
Investigations: FBC, electrolytes incl. magnesium, renal function, TFTs, CXR, transthoracic echo

Examiner's five questions, in order: why not sinus tach? · would adenosine treat this? · 3 days — cardiovert today? · is aspirin enough? · how does this differ from AF? (give four divergences — regular vs irregularly irregular, sawtooth vs fibrillatory baseline, atrial ~300 vs 400–600, rate control harder / CTI ablation curative — and state anticoagulation is IDENTICAL)
fails: Not stating haemodynamic stability out loud before interpreting ★
'Sinus tachycardia at 150' or 'SVT' without going further ★ (identify 2:1 block)
Not anticoagulating / not naming a risk score ★ — fail regardless
Not stating aspirin is not stroke prevention ★
Not applying the 48-hour rule (3 weeks or TOE, then 4 weeks) ★
Saying 'not today' without explaining WHY cardioversion must wait
Combining beta-blocker with verapamil/diltiazem
Blurring rhythm differentials with causes
Vague 'do you drink?' — address alcohol with a number
numbers: Atrial rate ~300; 2:1 → 150; 3:1 → 100; variable block gives an irregular response but the sawtooth still distinguishes it from AF
Alcohol 30 standard drinks/week vs recommended limit of 10
Rate control: beta-blocker first line; verapamil/diltiazem if unsuitable; never both
Anticoagulation on the score (HTN + age) → DOAC; bleeding risk assessed; anticoagulation continues after successful ablation if the score says so (AF may follow)
48 h rule: 3 weeks therapeutic anticoag or TOE before cardioversion, ≥4 weeks after
CTI ablation: curative, high success, low complications — raise early, not as last resort

Variant 1 UNSTABLE (BP 78/44, clammy, ischaemic pain): urgent synchronised DC cardioversion with sedation, senior help, anticoagulate around it — 48 h rule does not delay cardioversion in an unstable patient
Variant 2 variable block: rate 110 irregular, sawtooth visible — still flutter
Variant 3 1:1 after flecainide (rate 215, clammy): Class Ic slows the atrial rate so it conducts 1:1 → immediate cardioversion; never flecainide for flutter without an AV nodal blocker
Variant 4 broad complex regular at 150: VT until proven otherwise
Variant 5 day 4 post-CABG: common; correct K/Mg, rate control, exclude sepsis/PE, anticoag decision with the surgical team
Variant 6 refuses anticoagulation (brother bled into brain): respect, correct the misconception (DOACs lower intracranial bleed risk than warfarin), don't push today, review this week

stem: Your next patient is a 35-year-old woman who has presented to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath and chest pain.
Vitals: T 37.4 °C · HR 104 · BP 118/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% on room air · alert.
tasks: Take a relevant history — six minutes
You will be given the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
State your investigations
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · interpret findings 0:45 · diagnosis and reasons 1:00 · differentials 1:30 · investigations 0:30 · close 0:15. Originally an online case — findings arrive on a card, or request them.

back.dx: Pulmonary embolism from a left calf DVT after a two-day car drive Queensland → Melbourne, on a COMBINED pill (Levlen), smoker, mother had a post-op DVT. Findings: anxious, mildly breathless · HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 94%, T 37.4 · loud P2 · left parasternal systolic murmur (TR from RV strain) · dullness and reduced breath sounds left base (infarction + small effusion, NOT pneumonia) · left calf swollen and tender · abdomen soft. Hidden agenda: father died of a heart attack at 52 — 'is this a heart attack?' early and again. Choose CHEST PAIN as the lead complaint out loud; fold breathlessness in with three questions.
plan: Vitals → 'stable but tachycardic, tachypnoeic, mildly hypoxic' → open question → acknowledge → 'I'd like to start with the chest pain, then come back to your breathing'
Full pain analysis incl. BETTER/WORSE — breathing, moving, position, pressing (worse on inspiration and cough)
Breathlessness in three: what do you mean · better/worse · cough, noisy breathing, haemoptysis; dizziness/faint
CVS group: sweating/nausea/racing; smoking/BP/DM/lipids/FHx; fever/viral, leaning forward; orthopnoea/pillows/leg swelling (→ FOLLOW UP the leg: one or both, painful, when); blackouts
RS group — the turn: chest injury; LONG TRAVEL OR LONG PERIODS SITTING STILL (open form, not flights); calf swelling/pain/redness; fevers/chills/phlegm; weight loss/lumps
COST-VMPF immediately: Contraceptive pill BY NAME · Overweight · Surgery/injury/admission · Trauma · Varicose veins · Menstrual/pregnancy · Previous clot · Family history
Finish the sweep: reflux, chest wall, rash, stress; SADMA, PMH, allergies; concerns (the father)

Interpret findings OUT LOUD (P2/murmur = RV strain; basal dullness = infarction/effusion; calf = source; fever from the clot) → diagnosis plain, three reasons, honest answer to the fear → two differentials explained then the rest NAMED → investigations in priority order → stop the combined pill + alternative contraception → safety-net, summary
ask: Where exactly? When and how — sudden or gradual? Sharp, dull, heavy, burning? Travel anywhere? Out of ten?
Anything makes it better or worse — breathing, moving, position, pressing on it? ★
What do you mean by shortness of breath? Better or worse? Cough, noisy breathing, wheeze, coughed up blood? Dizzy or faint?

Sweating, nausea, racing, dizziness with the pain? Smoke? BP, diabetes, cholesterol, family heart disease? Fever or flu-like illness — better leaning forward? Breathless lying flat, pillows, leg swelling? Ever blacked out?
Any injury to your chest? Any long travel or long periods sitting still recently? ★ Any swelling, pain or redness in your legs, especially the calf? ★ Fevers, chills, phlegm? Weight loss, lumps?
Are you on a contraceptive pill — and do you know its name? ★ Overweight? Operations, injuries, admissions? Varicose veins? LMP — any chance you're pregnant? Family clots? Previous clot yourself?
Heartburn/acid, related to eating? Worse on moving or pressing the chest wall? Rash? Stress? Conditions, medications, allergies? Alcohol, drugs?
Is there anything you're worried about?
pefe: If you must request: general appearance and work of breathing; vitals incl. sats and temp; trachea; expansion, percussion, auscultation; heart sounds incl. P2 and any murmur; JVP; BOTH CALVES for swelling, tenderness, asymmetry (the request candidates forget)

Interpret, don't recite: loud P2 + LLSE systolic murmur = raised pulmonary pressure with TR from RV strain; basal dullness = pulmonary infarction with small effusion; swollen tender calf = the source; low-grade fever is caused by the clot

Investigations in priority order: CTPA first → V/Q if contrast allergy, renal impairment or pregnancy → D-dimer rule-out only when suspicion is low (not here) → ECG → bloods: FBC, renal function (guides DOAC choice/dose), LFT (if warfarin considered), coags, troponin → β-hCG → CXR → leg Doppler
Anticoagulate before imaging with high suspicion and no bleeding contraindication
fails: Trying to run both complaint structures — not naming a lead
Skipping better/worse (the highest-yield chest pain question)
Filing 'leg swelling' under heart failure and not following it up
Asking only about flights — immobility is the risk
Accepting 'the pill' without the name (combined must stop; POP need not)
Converting basal dullness + 37.4 into pneumonia
Explaining two differentials beautifully and never naming the rest
Undifferentiated shopping-list investigations (FBC, ESR, CRP, TFTs…) — lead with CTPA
'Probably a muscle strain' or 'just anxiety' — fail
Not stopping the combined pill / leaving her without alternative contraception
numbers: Wells (PE): DVT signs · PE most likely · HR >100 · immobilisation/surgery within 4 weeks · previous VTE · haemoptysis · malignancy; two-level >4 = PE likely → image

PERC (low suspicion only, all 8 negative): age <50 · HR <100 · SpO2 ≥95% · no haemoptysis · no oestrogen · no previous VTE · no unilateral leg swelling · no surgery/trauma needing hospitalisation in 4 weeks
ECG: sinus tachycardia commonest; RV strain, RBBB, T inversion V1–V4; S1Q3T3 uncommon
Treatment: apixaban 10 mg BD 7 days then 5 mg BD; or rivaroxaban 15 mg BD 21 days then 20 mg daily — VERIFY; pregnancy: LMWH (no DOAC, no warfarin)
Duration: at least 3 months if provoked; longer/indefinite if unprovoked or recurrent
Massive PE (SBP <90, syncope, arrest): stop history, resus, high-flow O2, large-bore IV, cautious fluids, senior/ICU, bedside echo for RV strain, thrombolysis; embolectomy if contraindicated/fails
Murmur location: 4th–5th ICS, lower left sternal edge (TR)
Variant 1 recall (raised JVP, soft murmur, swollen ankle): unilateral after immobility = DVT; JVP from RV strain; bilateral oedema + orthopnoea + S3 would point to HF
Variant 2 pregnant: V/Q or perfusion scan to limit breast radiation; LMWH; obstetrics involved
Three reasons to the patient: swollen painful calf · sharp pain worse on breathing in with breathlessness · right-heart strain on examination

stem: You are the doctor in the emergency department. James Okafor, 22, has presented with sudden onset chest pain that started while he was exercising today. He is already on oxygen when you enter the cubicle.
Information available: HR 98 · BP 122/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% · T 36.8 °C · alert and orientated.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Version A: at about five minutes a chest X-ray is provided — explain the X-ray to the patient. Version B: ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you require
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. History stops at 5:00 (the X-ray appears at the prompt whether or not you've finished) · X-ray or PEFE 60–75 s · diagnosis 30–40 s · everything left goes on differentials — the block candidates lose.

back.dx: Primary spontaneous LEFT pneumothorax, no tension — tall slim 22-year-old, daily vaper (since 18, occasional cannabis), rowing machine, no knock. Pain: left, can point to one spot, sudden, sharp stab, 4/10, constant, no radiation, MUCH WORSE ON DEEP BREATH, leaning forward and rest/activity make no difference. PEFE (Version B): trachea midline · reduced expansion L · hyper-resonant L · absent breath sounds L · reduced vocal resonance L · JVP normal, apex undisplaced, no murmur · no calf asymmetry · ECG pending. Hidden agenda: 'Is it my heart? People my age drop dead' — and a Bali trip in three weeks with a learn-to-dive course. The station in one line: say 'pleuritic' out loud, run the whole structure anyway, name the trachea, protect the last two minutes.
plan: Four vitals (BP, pulse, RR, temp) or the online closed statement; WIPE; open question; empathy ONCE, properly
SOCRATES in full — 'is it an area, or can you point to one spot?' — then the THREE named modifiers: deep breath? rest vs activity? leaning forward?
Say the conclusion aloud: 'sharp, well-localised, sudden, worse on breathing in — we call that pleuritic; it points me towards your lungs rather than your heart. I still need to check both.'

CVS block in FULL: SOB/sweating/nausea; BP/DM/lipids/smoking/FHx; cocaine/amphetamines; fever/flu, leaning forward; orthopnoea/PND/oedema/congenital; ever fainted, esp. on exercise; FAMILY HISTORY OF SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH (ask here, not at the end)

Respiratory: calves, travel, immobility, family clots, haemoptysis; WHAT EXERCISE and any knock/tackle; previous pneumothorax self/family; smoke/vape/cannabis; fever/cough/phlegm; 'unlikely at your age but I ask everyone' weight loss/lumps/night sweats
GI (heartburn, waterbrash, food), MSK (rash, pressing, twisting), psych (stress, mood); SADMA, PMH, allergies, concerns

BELL — X-ray script, six steps, 60–75 s, trachea named even though normal; answer 'am I going to be alright?' with two reasons (trachea central, BP normal) then finish. Version B: PEFE by named items, interpret the card aloud

Diagnosis 30–40 s plain → three reasons (sharp, pleuritic, X-ray/PEFE) → HCM, PE, infection each with a reason → the rest as a rapid list → drain, admit, repeat X-ray, stop vaping, no flying until healed, no diving ever without surgery, safety-net
ask: Where exactly — an area, or can you point to one spot? When, what were you doing, sudden or gradual? Sharp/dull/heavy/tight/burning? Go anywhere? Out of ten? Constant or waves, worse?
Anything better or worse? Specifically — does a deep breath make it worse? Change with rest or activity? Does leaning forward help? ★

SOB, sweating, nausea? BP/diabetes/cholesterol? Smoke? Family heart disease? Cocaine or amphetamines? Fever/chills/flu-like illness? Breathless walking/lying flat, wake at night, ankle swelling, born with a heart condition? Ever fainted, especially during exercise?
Any family history of sudden cardiac death — anyone who died suddenly and young, during sport or in their sleep? ★
Calf swelling/pain? Long flights/car trips, surgery, immobility? Clotting problems in the family? Coughed up blood?
What exercise were you actually doing — and did you take any knock or tackle to the chest? ★
Ever had a collapsed lung, or anyone in the family? Smoke, vape, cannabis? Fever, cough, coloured phlegm? Weight loss, lumps, night sweats?
Tummy pain, vomiting, heartburn, sour fluid? Related to food? Rash on the chest, worse on pressing or twisting? Stress at home or uni, mood? Medications, allergies, past history, operations?
What are you worried it might be?
pefe: X-ray six lines: (1) 'This is the X-ray of your chest' (2) three shades — white bone, grey soft tissue, black air (3) landmarks — heart, spine, WINDPIPE and whether it's central (4) normal side — markings to the edge, sharp angle at the base (5) abnormal side — lung edge visible, no markings beyond it, air in the space (6) 'that's a pneumothorax'. The finding is ABSENT MARKINGS beyond a visible pleural edge, not blackness — trace apex to costophrenic angle for the subtle apical one

Poor paper film: 'The print quality makes fine detail difficult — clinically your symptoms and examination point to a left pneumothorax, and that's what I can see at the edge; I'd review the digital image'

Version B PEFE by name: general appearance/distress/cyanosis/drowsy; vitals on air and on O2; expansion symmetrical? TRACHEA midline or deviated? bruising/focal tenderness? percussion resonant/hyper-resonant/dull? breath sounds present and equal, added sounds, rub? vocal resonance? JVP, apex, S1/S2, murmurs; abdomen; oedema and calf asymmetry; ECG?

Interpret aloud: reduced expansion + hyper-resonance + absent breath sounds + reduced vocal resonance on the left, trachea midline, BP normal = left pneumothorax without tension; hyper-resonance = air (dull would be fluid/consolidation/haemothorax)
fails: Shortcutting to lung questions once 'pleuritic' is reached — the structure is the mark
Never acknowledging the fear, or sympathising after every answer and reaching 5:00 with half a history
Asking only the open 'better or worse?' and accepting 'nothing really'
Leaving sudden cardiac death to the end and running out of time
Not asking what exercise / any knock (separates spontaneous from traumatic)
Skipping malignancy or psychogenic questions because he's 22
Not commenting on the trachea (Version B: not asking 'midline or deviated?' — the pass-or-fail question) ★
Radiology language to a frightened 22-year-old
Accepting 'air entry reduced on the left' as the whole examination — expansion, trachea, percussion, vocal resonance are four separate marks
The beautiful 40-second physiology explanation that eats the differential time; never finishing the list ★
Tension variant: 'I'd get an urgent chest X-ray to confirm' — the sentence that fails the station ★
numbers: Signs: reduced expansion · hyper-resonant · absent breath sounds · reduced vocal resonance · trachea midline. Dull instead → effusion, consolidation, haemothorax

Tension = hypotension + trachea deviated AWAY + distended neck veins → clinical diagnosis, no imaging: needle decompression 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line (2nd ICS MCL traditional alternative), then intercostal catheter — decompression is temporising
Drain: safe triangle, 5th ICS anterior to mid-axillary line, small-bore 8–14 Fr; symptomatic or unstable → intervene; otherwise conservative/ambulatory with review
Recurrence ~30%, mostly within 1–2 years; vaping/smoking cessation is the single best prevention
Flying: not until resolved, typically a week beyond; diving: never without definitive surgery

Variant 2 HCM: central tightness on running, eased on stopping, near-syncope, uncle died in sleep at 38, NOT pleuritic → ECG + echo; autosomal dominant, commonest cause of SCD in young athletes; ESM louder on standing/Valsalva, softer on squatting (opposite of AS); ECG LVH, deep narrow Q, TWI; cardiology, no competitive sport, avoid dehydration/nitrates/diuretics, screen first-degree relatives

Variant 3 traumatic haemopneumothorax: tackle, bruising, focal rib tenderness, DULL base → large-bore IV, G&H/cross-match, FBE, coags, erect CXR ± CT, large-bore tube, surgeons early (ongoing drain loss = theatre), check flail segment and sub-diaphragmatic injury

Variant 4 pericarditis: two days, central, better leaning forward, worse flat, post-viral, febrile, rub with resonant chest → ECG (saddle STE, PR depression), troponin, inflammatory markers, echo for effusion; NSAID + colchicine, exercise restriction
Safety-net: more breathless, worse pain, faint, racing heart, blue lips/fingers → 000

stem: Your next patient is a 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset chest tightness and shortness of breath that began while watching a movie at home. He has had similar episodes before and was told nothing was wrong. His parents are separated, he lives alone, works as an accountant, and has been under stress.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 96 · BP 126/78 · RR 18 · SpO2 99% RA · alert, anxious.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the pathophysiology of the condition
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · diagnosis 1:00 · differentials 1:15 · pathophysiology 1:15 · management and close 0:30.

back.dx: Panic attack → PANIC DISORDER with agoraphobic avoidance (Daniel Pike, 25). Peak within 5–10 minutes, settled over half an hour; pounding heart, sweating, dizziness, trembling, PERIORAL AND FINGER TINGLING (hyperventilation fingerprint), derealisation. Five or six attacks over three months, mostly out of the blue (desk, train, supermarket queue); two prior ED visits with normal tests. Three key questions make the diagnosis: fear of dying? worried about another? changed behaviour? (stopped cinema, drives instead of train). Also: 5–6 coffees + energy drinks; 'I'm generally an anxious person' (bait for GAD — screen by criteria, don't relabel). The trap: the psychosocial stem is bait — run a CHEST PAIN history and reach the psychogenic bucket LAST. Hidden agenda: convinced doctors keep missing a heart problem; privately frightened he's going mad.
plan: Vitals → open question → acknowledge the 'nothing wrong' frustration explicitly → signpost: tightness, then breathing, then rule out important causes
Full pain analysis INCLUDING 'how long did it take to reach its worst?' and how it settled
Breathlessness in three questions
CVS + RS sweep (note the tingling — use it later); GI, MSK/rash; caffeine/energy drinks QUANTIFIED, drugs, alcohol, recently stopped anything; thyroid symptoms
ANNOUNCE the negative organic screen out loud, then ask permission to move to the episodes
Characterise: how many, over what period, out of the blue or triggered, what was happening in the film, trembling/choking/unreal
THE THREE KEY QUESTIONS verbatim → agoraphobia screen → GAD by criteria → stressors → mood → self-harm

Diagnosis: attack, then disorder; 'your symptoms are real'; 'not in your head — in your body' → differentials of CHEST PAIN with why each is less likely (still do ECG, TFTs) → pathophysiology (alarm system, adrenaline, over-breathing/CO2, vicious cycle; peaks ~10 min, not dangerous) → CBT, MHTP, SSRI low and slow if needed, no benzos, cut caffeine, limit tests, safety-net
ask: Where exactly? When and how quickly? How long did it take to reach its worst? ★ Tight/sharp/heavy/burning? Travel? Out of ten? Better or worse — breathing, moving, position, pressing? How long, how did it settle?
What do you mean by shortness of breath? Better/worse? Cough, noisy breathing, wheeze?

Sweating, nausea, racing, dizziness with it? Smoke, BP, DM, lipids, family heart disease? Fever/flu, better leaning forward? Flat/pillows/leg swelling, ever fainted esp. exercise? Long travel/sitting still, calf swelling/pain, haemoptysis? Chest injury? Fevers, chills, phlegm, weight loss, lumps?
Abdominal pain, vomiting, acid/heartburn, related to eating? Worse on moving or pressing? Rash?
How much coffee or energy drink a day? ★ Recreational drugs, alcohol? Recently stopped anything? Weight loss, feeling hot, tremor, loose bowels?
'I've asked about your heart, lungs, stomach and chest wall and haven't found anything pointing that way — now I'd like to ask about the episodes themselves. Is that all right?' ★
How many, over what period? Out of the blue or a trigger? What was happening in the film? Trembling, choking, things not quite real?
During the attack, did you feel you were going to die — were you afraid of dying? ★
Since then, have you been worried about having another attack? ★
Have you changed any routines or behaviour because of that worry? ★

Places you avoid — public transport, crowds, queues, shopping centres, far from home alone? Apart from the attacks, excessive hard-to-control worry about everyday things — how long? Restless, tired, irritable, tense, poor sleep? What's been happening at home and work? Mood? Thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn't worth living?
pefe: No examination task. Investigations: ECG · FBC, electrolytes/renal, TFTs, glucose · drug screen if indicated — then STOP; 'I don't want to keep repeating tests, because that feeds the worry'

Differentials of the COMPLAINT, each with why it's less likely: ACS/angina (25, no risk factors, non-exertional, no radiation — still ECG) · PE (no travel, no calf, no haemoptysis, sats normal) · pneumothorax (no injury, normal exam/sats) · pericarditis (no viral illness, no positional change) · arrhythmia (possible — ECG) · reflux/ulcer (no heartburn, no meal relation) · chest wall (pressing doesn't reproduce) · thyrotoxicosis and caffeine (bloods) · GAD possible alongside — the attacks define it

Technical pathophysiology if asked: amygdala/sympathetic activation → catecholamine surge (tachycardia, ↑CO, sweating, tremor); hyperventilation → hypocapnia, respiratory alkalosis → cerebral vasoconstriction (light-headedness, derealisation), ↓ionised Ca (perioral/peripheral paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm); catastrophic misinterpretation → positive feedback; conditioned anticipatory anxiety and avoidance → panic disorder → agoraphobia
fails: Taking a psychiatric history instead of a chest pain history because you recognised the recall ★
Not acknowledging the 'nothing wrong' frustration
Skipping time-to-peak
Hearing the tingling and moving on
Omitting caffeine/stimulants and thyroid rows
Not announcing the negative organic screen before switching
Saying 'probably anxiety' without the three key questions ★
Relabelling as GAD on 'I'm an anxious person'
'It's just anxiety' / 'there's nothing wrong' / 'try to relax' — marked communication failures ★
Differentials given as a list of anxiety disorders
Prescribing benzodiazepines; repeating investigations
numbers: Panic attack: abrupt surge peaking within minutes (typically <10), ≥4 of 13 symptoms, characteristically fear of dying/losing control
Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks + ≥1 month of worry about further attacks OR maladaptive behaviour change
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 of public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, queues/crowds, outside home alone; typically 6 months
GAD: excessive hard-to-control worry about multiple matters ≥6 months with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, tension, sleep disturbance — discrete attacks not a core feature
Organic mimics: arrhythmia · thyrotoxicosis · hypoglycaemia · asthma · stimulant use or withdrawal

Management: validate → CBT first line → Mental Health Treatment Plan → SSRI if needed, start low go slow, warn of early worsening → avoid benzodiazepines (dependence, safety behaviour reinforcing avoidance) → cut caffeine/alcohol/stimulants → follow-up
'Will I have to take tablets forever?' — CBT is first line; medication only if needed and reviewed
Variant 1 lifelong worrier: panic disorder primary, possible comorbid GAD — name and treat the attacks first, same approach helps both
Variant 2 snake scene, lifelong fear: specific phobia — triggered attack, similar therapy
Variant 3 organic swap: pleuritic pain, 16-hour drive, right calf ache, SpO2 93% → Wells, CTPA, treat as PE until proven otherwise

setting: You are the doctor working in the Emergency Department.
stem: Jack Mitchell, 40 years old, has presented complaining of chest pain for the last two days. He is a known case of schizophrenia.
Vital signs available from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient
Explain your initial management to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Roughly six minutes of history; diagnosis and management share the last two minutes.

back.dx: Stable angina (ischaemic heart disease) in a man whose cardiometabolic risk is driven by risperidone — central heaviness to the neck, 6/10, brought on by walking and stairs, settles in a few minutes with rest, NEVER at rest, longest episode five minutes. Vitals normal (BP 138/86, PR 82, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 98%). Risk load: father MI at 50, pack a day since 20, 6–8 beers most nights, takeaway diet, no exercise, 20 kg gain on risperidone, nobody has checked lipids or sugar in years. Discriminating question: 'do you ever get this pain when you are resting?' — that answer is the diagnosis. Version B: a voice at night and 'people are giving me this pain' — validate, gently decline the belief, carry on. Hidden agenda: frightened of dying like his father; frightened of being dismissed as 'in my head again'.
plan: Vitals from the examiner BEFORE greeting; intro, name, confidentiality statement (unless risk of harm to you or someone else)
'Tell me more about this pain' — silence; empathy line
SOCRATES as one fluent run; then the discriminator out loud: pain at rest? longest episode?
Signpost, then four schizophrenia questions: when diagnosed, treatment, taking it regularly, side effects (weight, postural dizziness, tremor, dry mouth), GP/psychiatrist follow-up
Three-question screen in order: harm to self or others → hear/see/feel things others don't → anyone trying to harm or control you. Version B: one sentence of validation, note it, move on
CVS risk factors as one continuous run: family MI/stroke, BP/cholesterol/diabetes, smoking, alcohol, drugs, diet, exercise
System sweep in one breath: ACS features, pericarditis, heart failure, PE, chest injury/cough, weight loss/lumps, GORD, MSK/rash; other conditions, meds, allergies
Diagnosis: name it, plain-words mechanism, THREE reasons (pain character, risk factors, the antipsychotic); five-second differential insurance line

Management in three headings: find it (ECG + troponin now, stress test ± echo) · protect the heart (aspirin, statin, GTN, Quitline, alcohol, diet, walking) · fix the cause (do NOT stop risperidone; speak to psychiatrist re switch e.g. aripiprazole, mental health review) · 000 safety-net · summary, questions
ask: Before I begin, could I have Jack's vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?
Everything we talk about stays between you and me — unless there's a risk of harm to you or to someone else. Is that alright?
Jack, tell me more about this pain. → 'I'm sorry to hear that, and I completely understand your concern. I'll do my best to find the cause today.'
Point to exactly where? Sharp, burning, or a heaviness? Out of ten? Travel anywhere? Comes and goes or constant? Brings it on? Makes it better?
★ This next question is important: do you ever get this pain when you are resting — sitting still, or lying in bed at night? And what's the longest one has lasted?

I saw you have schizophrenia — can I ask a few quick questions? It may actually be relevant to your chest pain. When were you diagnosed? What treatment? Able to take it regularly? Side effects — weight gain, dizzy on standing, shaky hands, dry mouth? See your GP and psychiatrist regularly?

★ I ask everyone this: any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else? Do you ever hear, see or feel things other people don't? Do you ever feel anyone is trying to harm you, or controlling you?
Version B reply: 'That sounds frightening, and I can hear how distressing it is. I don't see it the same way you do — but I have no doubt the pain is real, and I'm taking it seriously.'

Anyone in the family had a heart attack or stroke? Ever told high BP, cholesterol or diabetes? Smoke — how much, how long? Alcohol — how much a week? Recreational drugs? What do you usually eat in a day? Any regular exercise?

With the pain: sweating, SOB, nausea, racing heart? Fever or recent flu-like illness, worse lying flat / better sitting forward? Breathless lying down at night, leg swelling? Long travel, calf pain or swelling? Chest injury, cough, phlegm? Weight loss, appetite, lumps? Tummy pain, vomiting, acid taste, related to eating? Rash, worse on pressing or moving? Other conditions, medications, allergies?
pefe: No examination task. Ask for vitals only — treat 'just a history station' as the trap; he could be infarcting

Diagnosis to patient: 'ischaemic heart disease — stable angina. One of the blood tubes supplying your heart has narrowed, not blocked. When you walk the heart needs more oxygen than the narrowed tube can deliver — that shortage is the heaviness. When you rest it settles.' No atherosclerosis / ischaemia / stenosis

Three reasons: character of the pain (central, heavy, to the neck, exertional, relieved by rest) · risk factors (father at 50, smoking, weight, diet) · the medication he takes for schizophrenia raises heart risk
Differential insurance line (5 s): 'no sign you're having a heart attack, though we'll check; I also thought about inflammation around the heart, a clot on the lung and reflux — they don't fit'

Management: FIND — ECG now, troponin (pain new within 48 h), exercise stress ECG (treadmill, faster and steeper every 3 min) often with echo; CT coronary angiography increasingly first-line locally · PROTECT — aspirin, statin, GTN spray for pain, stop smoking (Quitline 13 7848), cut alcohol, diet, build to 30 min walking most days · FIX THE CAUSE — risperidone raises weight, cholesterol, sugar and heart risk; 'I won't change it and you mustn't stop it — stopping suddenly can make you unwell'; speak with psychiatrist about switching (e.g. aripiprazole) + mental health review
Safety-net: pain at rest, >10 min, or with sweating/vomiting/breathlessness → 000, don't drive. Summary + invite questions
If the examiner challenges investigations: ECG + serial hs-troponin to exclude ACS because symptoms are new; functional testing (stress ECG/echo) establishes stable angina; CTCA per local pathway
fails: Never asking about pain at rest and episode duration ★
Omitting the harm-to-self / harm-to-others question ★
Saying the pain is stress, anxiety or part of his illness ('it's in my head again')
Stopping or promising to stop the risperidone; changing it yourself rather than via the psychiatrist
Chasing a full MSE after the delusion and abandoning the chest pain; colluding with or arguing against the belief
Skipping vitals; skipping diet and exercise; giving the diagnosis with no reasons; MONA / aspirin-plus-troponin as the whole plan; no stress test named
numbers: 6 min history · ~1 min diagnosis · ~1 min management · 4 questions per known condition · 3 psych screen questions · 3 reasons · 3–4 differentials in 5 s
Stress ECG positive: ST depression ≥1 mm horizontal or downsloping; Bruce protocol increments every 3 min VERIFY

Aspirin 100 mg daily (300 mg stat if ACS) · atorvastatin 40–80 mg nocte · metoprolol 25–50 mg BD · GTN 400 microg SL q5 min up to 3, 000 if pain persists 10 min after first dose · 150 min moderate activity/week VERIFY

Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring: baseline, 3 months, then at least annually · premature FHx: first-degree male <55, female <65 (father 50) · life-expectancy gap in severe mental illness 15–20 years, mostly cardiovascular

Variant 1 pain at rest, woke him at 3 am, 30 min → no longer stable angina: ECG within 10 min, IV access, serial hs-troponin, aspirin 300 mg chewed, GTN, analgesia, monitor, urgent cardiology — manage as ACS, keep him in

Variant 2 'everyone would be better off without me' → stop, explore ideation, plan, intent, means, previous attempts, protective factors; same-day mental health assessment; still finish the chest-pain thread

Variant 3 'take me off the tablets' / refuses treadmill → don't stop; speak to psychiatrist; respect refusal, explore the worry, still start heart protection · Variant 4 clozapine + fever → clozapine myocarditis (first 2 months): troponin, CRP, ECG, echo, psychiatry + cardiology before any further dose

setting: You are the doctor on duty at a rural hospital.
stem: Bernard Hollis, 68, has attended with two days of lethargy and generalised muscle weakness following an episode of gastroenteritis last week. He has chronic kidney disease stage 4 and takes ramipril, spironolactone, metformin and atorvastatin. His blood results have just returned and are on the desk.
K⁺ 7.2 · Na⁺ 134 · urea 24.1 · creatinine 312 · eGFR 16 · HCO₃ 16 · corrected Ca 2.18. BP 104/62 · PR 52.
tasks: Interpret the results and any further investigation to the examiner
State the likely causes
Outline your immediate management
Explain the situation to the patient
time: 8 minutes. The ECG is only handed over if you ask for it.

back.dx: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes — AKI on CKD 4 (prerenal from gastroenteritis), ACE inhibitor + spironolactone, metabolic acidosis; hidden ibuprofen for his knee (only if you ask about NSAIDs). ECG (must be requested): rate 52, P waves flattened/low amplitude, PR prolonged, QRS broad ~130 ms without bundle-branch morphology, tall narrow-based symmetrical peaked T waves in mid-precordial leads. The station is decided by your FIRST sentence: monitor + 12-lead ECG immediately, and 'was the sample haemolysed?' — before you finish reading the panel.
plan: Reading time
Write five things: ECG + monitor now, ask haemolysis · PROTECT · SHIFT · REMOVE · doses · stop ramipril/spironolactone/NSAIDs/trimethoprim · four causes
First sentence
'The potassium is 7.2 — severe. I'd attach cardiac monitoring and get a 12-lead ECG immediately, and check whether the sample was haemolysed'
ECG

Rate · P · PR · QRS · T, in that order → 'changes of severe hyperkalaemia, needs treatment now'. If asked 'ischaemic T waves?' — hyperacute T waves are broad-based and asymmetrical; the flat P, long PR and wide QRS make hyperkalaemia the explanation
Biochemistry
Creatinine 312 / eGFR 16 = advanced renal impairment; urea 24 with prerenal pattern = AKI on CKD; HCO₃ 16 = metabolic acidosis shifting K⁺ out of cells; mild hyponatraemia fits volume depletion
Causes
Four at once: CKD 4 baseline · AKI on top (gastro, poor intake) · ramipril + spironolactone additive · acidosis. Then ask: OTC NSAIDs, recent trimethoprim, potassium salt substitutes
Management

Three jobs: PROTECT calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–3 min on the monitor, repeat at 5 min if ECG unchanged, lasts 30–60 min, does NOT lower K⁺ · SHIFT 10 units short-acting insulin in 50 mL 50% glucose IV over 15–30 min, hourly BGL for ≥6 h unprompted, plus salbutamol 10–20 mg neb; consider bicarbonate given HCO₃ 16 (weak evidence) · REMOVE oliguric, eGFR 16 → haemodialysis is definitive, renal team + retrieval now. Withhold ramipril and spironolactone, cautious volume, recheck K⁺ at 1–2 h
Patient

Explain the effect, never the number: 'a salt called potassium is much higher than it should be … upsets the electrical rhythm of your heart … calcium protects the heart while the rest works … two of your tablets hold potassium in — stopping both today, don't restart until reviewed'. Answer heart attack / my fault / Adelaide honestly; offer to call someone
ask: ★ Examiner, before I go through these in full — the potassium is 7.2, which is in the severe range. I would attach cardiac monitoring and obtain a 12-lead ECG immediately, and I would check whether the sample was reported as haemolysed.

Examiner's three questions after management, in order: 'Does the calcium lower his potassium?' → No — stabilises the myocardium, serum level unchanged, must always be given alongside something that shifts or removes K⁺, never instead. 'Commonest complication of your treatment?' → hypoglycaemia from insulin, often delayed, hence hourly BGL for 6 h. 'ECG had been normal — would you still treat?' → yes, K⁺ 7.2 is treated on the level; a normal ECG is not permission to wait

To the patient: 'Am I going to have a heart attack?' → 'Not a heart attack in the usual sense — this affects the rhythm rather than blocking an artery. I don't want to understate it — at this level the rhythm can become dangerous, which is why you're on a monitor and I'm treating you now. It is very treatable.'

'Is it something I did? I couldn't keep anything down.' → 'You have not done anything wrong. Being unwell and dehydrated strained kidneys that were already struggling, and two of your tablets hold potassium in — that combination caused this.'

'Do I have to go to Adelaide?' → 'Possibly. If the potassium doesn't come down with treatment, dialysis is the most effective way to remove it and that means transferring you. I'm arranging that conversation now so we aren't delayed. Is there someone you'd like me to call?'
If he looks blank at '7.2 — is that bad?' you have quoted the number instead of the effect — restart in lay terms
pefe: No history or examination task — results, causes, management, explanation
Investigations to name: 12-lead ECG + continuous monitoring first; haemolysis check; repeat K⁺ at 1–2 h; VBG/ABG; urine output; BGL hourly ×6 h; consider digoxin level if relevant
Drugs to stop: ramipril, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim; hold metformin with eGFR 16 and acute illness VERIFY

Version B run (K⁺ 6.1, well 44-year-old woman, pre-procedure bloods): order of operations — ECG and observations FIRST, ask about haemolysis/delayed processing/platelet and white cell counts, THEN repeat with wide-bore needle, no prolonged tourniquet or fist clenching, prompt transport — THEN conclude pseudohyperkalaemia; do not treat and do not cancel the procedure until a clean result; if repeat high, it's real → renal function, medications, adrenal causes
SA: renal team and MedSTAR retrieval early rather than after failed medical therapy; PATS for the transfer; family call
fails: Not asking for an ECG and monitoring in the first response — a fail regardless of the total ★
Calcium gluconate without dose and route; or not stating that calcium does NOT lower potassium ★
No hourly glucose monitoring, unprompted ★
Not withholding ramipril and spironolactone ★
Naming one cause and stopping; reading the whole panel before asking for the ECG; quoting '7.2' at the patient; false reassurance on the heart-attack question
Not naming dialysis as definitive here; not involving renal / retrieval early
numbers: Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–3 min, repeat at 5 min, protects 30–60 min · insulin 10 u short-acting + 50 mL 50% glucose over 15–30 min, hourly BGL ≥6 h · salbutamol 10–20 mg neb (additive) · sodium bicarbonate considered when acidotic, weak evidence · dialysis definitive VERIFY
Severe ≥6.5 or any ECG change; moderate 6.0–6.4 (Version B 6.1) VERIFY · recheck K⁺ 1–2 h
ECG sequence: peaked T → flat P → long PR → wide QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole
Four causes here: CKD 4 · AKI on CKD (urea 24, creatinine 312, eGFR 16, prerenal) · ACEi + spironolactone · acidosis HCO₃ 16 · plus hidden ibuprofen

Variant 1 sine wave K⁺ 8.4, drowsy, hypotensive = peri-arrest: calcium immediately and repeated, insulin–dextrose and salbutamol simultaneously, call for help + arrest trolley, emergency dialysis · Variant 2 digoxin toxicity K⁺ 6.4, nausea, yellow-green vision: hyperkalaemia marks severity → digoxin-specific antibody fragments definitive; avoid reflex calcium, discuss with toxicology · Variant 3 DKA K⁺ 5.9, glucose 28, pH 7.12: total body K⁺ depleted, follow DKA protocol, replace K⁺ once <5.5 and passing urine · Variant 4 well dialysis patient K⁺ 6.9, normal ECG, dialysis tomorrow: chronic tolerance, not permission to wait — monitor, treat medically, bring dialysis forward · Variant 5 angry patient ('your tablets nearly killed me'): validate, both tablets prescribed for good reasons, kidneys took a hit, they need reviewing when things change
Pass guide: 17/22 items and all five starred · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Poisons Information 13 11 26 · TIS National 131 450

setting: You are an HMO in a metropolitan emergency department.
stem: A 52-year-old man has presented complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath that started one hour ago. The pain began while he was chopping wood.
Vital signs: BP 135/85 · pulse 78 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 97% on room air · T 36.8°C. He has no history of bleeding disorders.
The ECG is handed to you with the stem.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes. About one minute on the ECG, then the management. No history taking, no physical examination.

back.dx: Acute anterolateral STEMI — ST elevation in I, aVL and V2–V6 with reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF; most likely proximal LAD; sinus rhythm ~65–70, normal axis, normal PR, narrow QRS, no established Q waves. Treat as time-critical: primary PCI within 90 min (metro). James Whitfield, self-employed builder, smoker 15/day, untreated BP, father died of MI at 58, no bleeding problems, no sildenafil. Hidden agenda: terrified of dying like his father; money — two jobs booked, no income if he stops. Discriminating behaviour: 'six things, one at a time' — every drug with dose and route, the sildenafil question attached to the nitrate, oxygen refused with the 92% threshold, PCI translated.
plan: Park the patient in one sentence: 'I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly — I've been asked to look at your heart tracing with my examiner first, give me one minute.' If 'am I having a heart attack?' → 'that's exactly what I'm checking and I'll tell you straight away'

ECG in fixed order: details/date/calibration → rate → rhythm → axis → PR → QRS → ST segments (elevation V2–V6, I, aVL; reciprocal III, aVF) → no Q waves → impression anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD, time-critical

Say 'heart attack' plainly with plain-words mechanism; 'I've already let the cardiac team know'; acknowledge the father. Then: (1) aspirin 300 mg chewed + clopidogrel 600 mg (2) GTN 400 microg SL q5 min ×3 — ask Viagra/Cialis in last 24 h FIRST, say the other contraindications (3) IV access (4) troponin + FBC/UEC/lipids/coags — 'we are not waiting for it'; morphine 2.5–5 mg IV, ondansetron 4–8 mg IV

(5) oxygen only if SpO2 <92%, repeat ECG 1–2 hourly (6) PCI within 90 min: fine tube from wrist/groin, dye, balloon or stent — translate every word; cardiology consent. 'Are you cutting my chest open?' → no, a needle puncture at the wrist

'Am I going to die?' — no false promise: serious, caught early, treatment works well, I'm staying with you. Offer to call Karen. Ask for concerns (money → social work). One-line summary. If time remains: DAPT 12 months then aspirin, statin, ACEi, beta-blocker, cardiac rehab, smoking, driving — never drift into history taking
ask: Hello James — I'm one of the doctors looking after you. I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly. Give me one minute with my examiner and I'll come straight back with the plan.

Examiner, this is a 12-lead ECG; I'd confirm patient details, date and calibration. Rate ~65–70 (R–R about 4½ large squares). Regular, P before every QRS — sinus. Axis normal. PR normal and constant, QRS narrow. ST elevation V2–V6 and I, aVL — ≥1 mm limb, ≥2 mm V2–V3; reciprocal ST depression III and aVF. No established Q waves. Impression: acute anterolateral STEMI, likely proximal LAD, time-critical.

The tracing shows that you are having a heart attack. One of the blood tubes supplying your heart muscle has become blocked by a clot, so part of that muscle isn't getting blood and oxygen — that's the pain. It is serious. It is also very treatable and we're starting right now. I've already let the cardiac team know.
There are six things I'm going to do in the next few minutes. Let me take them one at a time.

★ Before I give you the spray — one question I have to ask everybody: have you taken Viagra, Cialis or anything similar in the last 24 hours? ('why?' → together they can drop your blood pressure dangerously low)
How long for the blood test? → 'It doesn't change what we do today — we're not waiting for it. The tracing is enough to act on; waiting would cost you heart muscle.'
Shouldn't I be on oxygen? → 'It's 97% which is good; extra oxygen doesn't help and can narrow the heart arteries — if it falls below 92% I'll start it.'

Am I going to die? → 'I'm not going to pretend this isn't serious — it is. But you got here fast, we've caught it early, and the treatment works well. I'm going to stay with you.' Is there anyone you'd like me to call? Any questions or concerns?
pefe: No history, no examination — the vitals are in the stem
ECG: ST elevation I, aVL, V2–V6; reciprocal depression III, aVF; sinus ~65–70; normal axis; narrow QRS; no Q waves → anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD
Investigations: ECG within 10 min of arrival, repeat 1–2 hourly; troponin (named, then discounted as a reason to wait), FBC, UEC, lipids, coags; continuous monitoring

Reperfusion Version A: primary PCI — target 90 min, acceptable if reachable within 120 min of first medical contact; translate 'percutaneous coronary intervention' → fine tube from the wrist, dye, ballooning, stent = tiny metal scaffold; awake but comfortable; cardiology consents

Long-term if time allows: aspirin + clopidogrel 12 months then aspirin 100 mg lifelong, atorvastatin 40–80 mg / rosuvastatin 20–40 mg, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker once stable, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking (Quitline 13 7848), diet, activity, driving restrictions VERIFY

Summary: 'your tracing shows a heart attack; aspirin and clopidogrel to stop the clot growing, a spray and morphine for the pain, and the cardiac team is preparing to reopen the artery within the hour. I'll be right here.'
fails: Giving the nitrate without asking about sildenafil in the last 24 hours ★
'I'll give you a blood thinner' — any drug without dose and route scores nothing ★
Never saying the words 'heart attack'; launching into aspirin before the diagnosis
Implying you will wait for the troponin; putting a normoxic patient on oxygen; three minutes on the ECG
Saying 'percutaneous coronary intervention' and stopping there; answering 'am I going to die' with 'no'
Turning to the examiner without parking the patient; drifting into history taking; finishing early
numbers: Aspirin 300 mg chewed · clopidogrel 600 mg before PCI (300 mg with lysis; 75 mg no load if >75) · GTN 400 microg SL q5 min ×3, tablet 300–600 microg · morphine 2.5–5 mg IV · ondansetron 4–8 mg IV · oxygen only if SpO2 <92% VERIFY
ECG within 10 min · PCI if reachable within 120 min of first medical contact, target 90 min · fibrinolysis within 30 min if not, angiography at 3–24 h VERIFY
STEMI criteria: ST elevation ≥1 mm in two contiguous limb leads, ≥2 mm in V2–V3 (men ≥40) VERIFY · anterolateral = I, aVL, V2–V6; reciprocal III, aVF
GTN contraindications to say aloud: PDE-5 inhibitor within 24 h (48 h tadalafil VERIFY), RV infarction, hypotension, bradycardia or extreme tachycardia
Variant — he says YES to sildenafil this morning: withhold the spray, say why, morphine for pain, everything else unchanged, state it in the cardiology handover
DAPT 12 months then aspirin 100 mg lifelong · atorvastatin 40–80 mg · ACEi · beta-blocker · cardiac rehab VERIFY
Pass guide: 18+ of 23 checklist items with every bold item; <5 bold items = fail · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848 · TIS National 131 450

setting: You are an HMO in a rural hospital. Your closest tertiary centre is 400 km away.
stem: A 55-year-old man has been brought in by ambulance complaining of chest pain that started suddenly one hour ago while he was working. He is a known hypertensive.
Vital signs: BP 160/95 · pulse 88 · RR 20 · SpO2 93% on oxygen · T 36.9°C.
The ECG is handed to you with the stem.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner or the medical student
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management
time: 8 minutes. About one minute on the ECG; the diagnosis is a separately marked task here. No history taking, no physical examination.

back.dx: Acute anterolateral STEMI (ST elevation I, aVL, V2–V6; reciprocal depression III, aVF; sinus, narrow QRS, no Q waves) — 400 km from PCI, so fibrinolysis is the reperfusion strategy: alteplase or tenecteplase with enoxaparin, after the FOUR bleeding questions, then transfer for angiography at 3–24 h. Same six steps as the metro version; task 2f is replaced entirely. Hidden agenda as before: father died of MI at 58; self-employed, money. Harder run: bleeding ulcer admission last week → do NOT lyse unilaterally; escalate to cardiology + retrieval and keep treating everything else.
plan: Park the patient in one sentence; 'give me one minute with my examiner'
ECG in fixed order → acute anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD, time-critical

Diagnosis task (separately marked): 'the tracing shows you are having a heart attack' + blood tube blocked by a clot + serious but very treatable + 'I've already let the cardiac team and retrieval know'; acknowledge the father

Six things, one at a time: aspirin 300 mg chewed + clopidogrel 300 mg with lysis; GTN 400 microg SL q5 min ×3 after the sildenafil question; IV access; troponin (not waiting) + bloods; morphine 2.5–5 mg IV + ondansetron 4–8 mg IV; oxygen — SpO2 93% on oxygen: continue, wean to keep ≥92% VERIFY; repeat ECG

Reperfusion: 'nearest hospital that can physically reopen it is 400 km — four hours. If we can't get you there within two hours, waiting does more harm than travelling does good. So we treat you here with a clot-dissolving medicine through the drip.' Four bleeding questions in ten seconds → alteplase bolus then infusion over 60–90 min (or tenecteplase single bolus) + enoxaparin; monitor for reperfusion arrhythmias; repeat ECG and troponin; cardiology re transfer for angiogram in the next day or so

'Four hours? Can't you fly me?' → retrieval is being arranged, but the medicine can be given now and now is what matters. 'What if it doesn't work?' → straight to transfer for the procedure; I'll know within ~90 min. Am I going to die / call Karen / concerns / summary
ask: Hello — I'm one of the doctors looking after you. I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly. Give me one minute with my examiner and I'll come straight back with the plan.

ECG to the examiner/medical student: details, date, calibration → rate → rhythm sinus → axis → PR → QRS narrow → ST elevation I, aVL, V2–V6 with reciprocal depression III, aVF → no Q waves → acute anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD, time-critical

The tracing shows that you are having a heart attack. One of the blood tubes supplying your heart muscle has been blocked by a clot. It is serious. It is also very treatable and we are starting right now.
Six things, one at a time — drug, dose, route every time
★ Before the spray: have you taken Viagra, Cialis or anything similar in the last 24 hours?

★ Four bleeding questions, ten seconds: 'Any bleeding in the brain, stroke or brain tumour? Any bleeding disorder, or bleeding anywhere now? Any stomach ulcer or bleeding from the bowel? Any major surgery or serious head injury in the last three months?'

'Good — nothing there that stops us. So: alteplase, a starting dose into the vein followed by a drip over the next hour to hour and a half, and a second blood thinner called enoxaparin alongside it. You'll stay on the monitor because the rhythm can misbehave as the artery opens; we'll repeat the tracing and blood test, and I'll be speaking with the cardiac team about transferring you for an angiogram in the next day or so.'
Is there anyone you'd like me to call? Any questions or concerns? → summary
pefe: No history or examination beyond the stem vitals and the four bleeding questions

Reperfusion decision stated aloud: PCI not reachable within 120 min of first medical contact (400 km, ~4 h) → fibrinolysis within 30 min of arrival, then angiography at 3–24 h; retrieval arranged in parallel

Absolute contraindications to say: prior intracranial haemorrhage, known structural cerebral vascular lesion or malignancy, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, active bleeding or bleeding diathesis, significant closed head/facial trauma within 3 months, suspected aortic dissection VERIFY

Harder rural run — bleeding ulcer last week: 'the clot-dissolving medicine carries a real risk of restarting that bleeding, so this is not a decision I make on my own. I'm calling the cardiac team and our retrieval service now so we can weigh the two risks together and get you moved as fast as possible. Everything else — aspirin, pain relief, monitoring — carries on.' Examiner watches for: recognise the conflict, refuse to lyse unilaterally, escalate, keep treating
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval and cardiology advice; RFDS; RAH/FMC cath lab; PATS for the family; social work for the self-employed income worry; TIS National 131 450
fails: Offering PCI when the stem has told you there is none within reach ★
Thrombolysing without asking the four bleeding questions; or lysing unilaterally in the bleeding-ulcer variant ★
GTN without the sildenafil question; any drug without dose and route ★
Never saying 'heart attack' — a separately marked task in this version
Waiting for the troponin; saying 'percutaneous coronary intervention' or 'thrombolysis' without translating; answering 'am I going to die' with 'no'
Finishing early; drifting into history
numbers: Alteplase: 15 mg IV bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 min, then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 min (max 100 mg) · tenecteplase single weight-based IV bolus · always with enoxaparin VERIFY
Aspirin 300 mg chewed · clopidogrel 300 mg with lysis (600 mg before PCI; 75 mg no load if >75) · GTN 400 microg SL q5 min ×3 · morphine 2.5–5 mg IV · ondansetron 4–8 mg IV VERIFY
Fibrinolysis within 30 min of arrival when PCI cannot be delivered within 120 min · angiography at 3–24 h after lysis · rescue PCI if <50% ST resolution at 60–90 min VERIFY
Oxygen: target SpO2 ≥92%; he is 93% on oxygen — continue and titrate, don't remove it reflexively VERIFY
Four bleeding questions: brain bleed/stroke/tumour · bleeding disorder or bleeding now · stomach ulcer/bowel bleeding · major surgery or head injury within 3 months
Variant — yes to sildenafil: withhold GTN, morphine instead, everything else unchanged, say it in the handover

setting: You are the Hospital Medical Officer in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan Australian hospital.
stem: James Whitfield, a 55-year-old man, has presented with the sudden onset of central chest pain that began approximately 20 minutes ago. He is anxious and says his father died of a heart attack.
BP 124/78 · pulse 98 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 98% room air · temp 37.8 °C · BGL 5.6 (exact vitals vary between recalls — the pattern is stable with a low-grade fever).
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
You will be shown an ECG — give the examiner your overall impression and the key features that support it
Explain your likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Version A — the ECG is handed over after the history (mini-bell / prompt at about 4 minutes in the face-to-face format). Stop the history when the bell goes.

back.dx: Acute pericarditis, most likely viral — the case that looks exactly like an MI until the last SOCRATES question. Central, crushing, sudden, 20 min, constant, 7/10, to left arm and jaw … then BETTER LEANING FORWARD, worse lying flat, sharper on deep breath, flu ten days ago, feverish and tired, no CV risk factors (never smoked, clear check-up). The role-player sits leaning forward clutching his chest — look at him. ECG: rate ~100, sinus, normal PR/QRS, concave ST elevation I, II, V2–V6 (crosses territories), no reciprocal depression except aVR, PR depression. Discriminating behaviour: finish SOCRATES before opening the differential; never say 'definitely not a heart attack' before the troponin.
plan: Vitals from examiner → 'haemodynamically stable'; wash; intro, confirm name; open question; acknowledge the father's death — 'I'll come back to that'; signpost + consent
SOCRATES to the end — the box is sealed until E: 'anything make it worse? better? — I notice you're sitting forward holding your chest, is it easier like that? and lying flat? deep breath or cough?'
Associated + prodrome: cold/flu in last 1–2 weeks, feverish, tired

Kill list in one block: MUST ASK CVS (exertional pain before today, sweating/nausea/doom, tearing to back, arms different, palpitations, blackouts, oedema, orthopnoea/PND) · MUST ASK resp (sudden SOB, haemoptysis, calf pain/swelling, travel/surgery/immobility, fever/cough/sweats/weight loss) · GI (burning, meals, acid, forceful vomiting before pain, black stools) · MSK/skin (injury, lifting, tender on pressing, rash/burning skin) · psych (stress, panic, tingling)
SADMA (cocaine/amphetamines; anticoagulants), PMHx (DM/HTN/lipids, previous MI, cardiac surgery, autoimmune, cancer, TB, HIV, renal), FHx with age, ICE 'what are you most worried this might be?'
Bell → excuse yourself → ECG in seven steps → impression in four words: widespread · doesn't match a territory · no reciprocal · concave (+ PR depression)

Diagnosis in plain words + THREE reasons (leans forward, recent flu — most are viral, the tracing) · honest troponin line · long DDx one clause each, killers first · plan: troponin, CXR, echo, FBE/ESR/CRP, admit, colchicine + NSAID, no strenuous exercise · safety-net · summary · questions
ask: Examiner, before I begin — may I have the vital signs: BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?
That sounds very frightening and I can see you're uncomfortable. I'm going to take a history and then examine you so I can come to a diagnosis and make a plan — is that okay?
Where exactly? When — sudden or gradual? Sharp, dull, crushing, tight? Move anywhere? Constant or comes and goes? Out of ten?

★ Anything make it worse? Anything make it better? — 'I notice you're sitting forward and holding your chest — is the pain easier when you lean forward like that? And what happens if you lie flat?' Does it change with a deep breath or cough?
★ Any cold or flu-like symptoms in the last week or two? Felt feverish or unusually tired?

Exertional chest pain before today? Sweating, nausea, a feeling of doom? Tearing pain through to the back? Pain different in each arm? Palpitations? Blackouts? Leg swelling? Breathless lying flat or waking at night?
Sudden breathlessness? Coughing up blood? Calf pain or swelling? Long flights, car trips, surgery, time in bed? Fever, productive cough, night sweats, weight loss?

Burning pain, worse lying down or after meals? Acid coming up? Forceful vomiting before the pain? Black stools? Injury, heavy lifting? Tender when pressed? Rash or blistering? Stress, panic, tingling?

Smoke? Alcohol? Cocaine or amphetamines? Regular medicines — any blood thinners? Allergies? Diabetes, BP, cholesterol, previous heart problems or surgery, autoimmune disease, cancer, TB, HIV, kidney problems? Family — heart attack or sudden death, and at what age? What are you most worried this might be?

'So it's definitely not a heart attack?' → 'It looks much more like pericarditis — but the two can look very similar and I won't tell you a heart attack is excluded until the troponin blood test is back. That test is the main reason I'd like to keep you in hospital.'
pefe: ECG read-out, fixed order: rate ~100 → regular → P before every QRS → PR normal → QRS normal → ST: 'more than 1 mm limb, more than 2 mm chest — elevation in I, II, V2–V6; concave; no reciprocal depression apart from aVR which I disregard; PR segment depression' → 'overall impression acute pericarditis: widespread, doesn't match a single coronary territory, concave, no reciprocal changes'
aVR pearl: it looks from the opposite direction, so ST depression and PR elevation in aVR are expected, not the reciprocal change of infarction

Explain: 'the heart sits inside a thin covering, a bit like a sac; in pericarditis that covering becomes inflamed and that is the pain'. Three reasons: better leaning forward/worse flat · flu ten days ago and most cases are viral · the tracing shows the changes of this condition, not a heart attack

DDx to patient, one clause each: heart attack (tracing pattern; confirm with troponin) · clot on the lung (no leg swelling, travel, surgery; sats normal) · tear in the main blood vessel (not tearing, not to the back) · collapsed lung (no injury, equal breath sounds) · then in one sweep: tear in the food pipe, heart failure, tight valve, chest infection, growth in the lung, reflux, ulcer, shingles, chest-wall cartilage, stress

Investigations: ECG · troponin (essential — raised = myopericarditis) · echo (effusion, tamponade) · CXR · FBE, ESR, CRP · UEC/LFT/BGL baseline before colchicine/NSAID · cultures if febrile and unwell. Managed in hospital because you need the troponin now

Treatment: colchicine + NSAID — ibuprofen 400–600 mg TDS with food until symptoms settle and CRP normalises then taper (aspirin 600–900 mg TDS if post-MI), plus gastric protection; colchicine 0.5 mg BD (0.5 mg daily if <70 kg or poorly tolerated) for 3 months VERIFY; no steroids first-line (recurrence); restrict strenuous exercise; admit, serial troponin, cardiology; GP in a week, repeat CRP; complete the colchicine course

Safety-net: pain much worse or different, increasing SOB, faint/dizzy/blackout, palpitations, high fever, leg or abdominal swelling → back immediately. Tamponade in the station: 'stop, call for help, MET call, IV fluids, urgent bedside echo, cardiology for pericardiocentesis'
fails: Diagnosing MI at 'radiates to the left arm' — never asking relieving factors ★
Omitting the troponin; saying 'it's definitely not a heart attack' ★
Not looking at the patient leaning forward; being put off by the pleuritic quality; being talked out of it by risk factors
A one-word ECG answer; not saying the four words (widespread, no territory, no reciprocal, concave)
Two differentials only, or over-explaining each; talking over the mini-bell; skipping vitals
No safety-net, no summary, jargon
numbers: ST elevation significant: >1 mm limb leads, >2 mm chest leads · pericarditis ECG: widespread concave elevation + PR depression, aVR reversed, no reciprocal · MI: territorial, convex, reciprocal depression

Pericarditis vs MI: posture (better forward / none) · pleuritic (often / no) · prodrome (viral, fever / exertional, diaphoresis) · rub (yes / S4, failure) · troponin (normal unless myopericarditis / rise and fall)
Causes: viral commonest · autoimmune (SLE, RA) · bacterial/TB · post-MI (early or Dressler) · uraemia · malignancy · radiotherapy · post-cardiac surgery · trauma · drugs
Colchicine 0.5 mg BD × 3 months (0.5 mg daily if <70 kg) · ibuprofen 400–600 mg TDS with PPI · aspirin 600–900 mg TDS if post-MI · no steroids first-line VERIFY

Tamponade = Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds) + pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg fall on inspiration → MET call, fluids, echo, pericardiocentesis · myopericarditis = raised troponin, arrhythmia, poor LV → admit, cardiology, no exercise · purulent = high fever, rigors → cultures, IV antibiotics, drainage
Version B of this station (4-min history + ask examiner + explain) is MED-18 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

setting: You are the Hospital Medical Officer in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan Australian hospital.
stem: James Whitfield, a 55-year-old man, has presented with the sudden onset of central chest pain that began approximately 20 minutes ago. He is anxious and says his father died of a heart attack.
BP 124/78 · pulse 98 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 98% room air · temp 37.8 °C · BGL 5.6.
tasks: Take a focused history — 4 minutes only. A mini-bell will sound at 4 minutes
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings (you will be given findings only if you ask for them specifically)
Explain your likely diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Mini-bell at 4:00 — stop the history immediately. Obtaining the ECG is not your task in this version.

back.dx: Same case as MED-17 — acute viral pericarditis presenting as an MI mimic. Four-minute history means prioritise: intro/consent → complete SOCRATES (relieving factors are the diagnosis) → life-threatening CVS and respiratory screen → GI/MSK only if time. Then PEFE by name: the pericardial friction rub is the mark — 'any added sounds?' may get you 'no'. Findings: no distress, no cyanosis, alert; vitals unchanged; JVP not raised; apex not displaced, no heave; S1 S2 normal, no murmur, PERICARDIAL FRICTION RUB PRESENT; equal air entry; abdomen normal; no oedema; no pulsus paradoxus; ECG pending.
plan: Vitals → wash → intro → open question → acknowledge the father → signpost + consent (30 s)
SOCRATES to the end, including the acted clue (leaning forward) and deep breath/cough; recent flu, fever, fatigue
Killers: exertional pain before today, sweating/nausea, tearing to back, palpitations/blackouts, oedema/orthopnoea; sudden SOB, haemoptysis, calf, travel/surgery/immobility, cough/fever
SADMA (drugs, anticoagulants), PMHx, FHx age; GI/MSK if any time; ICE
Bell — 'Thank you James, my apologies, I'll just speak with my examiner' → ten-step PEFE, findings not technique, rub by name, pulsus paradoxus as bonus
Diagnosis + three reasons (posture, viral prodrome, rub — ECG pending) · honest troponin line · DDx list killers first · plan + safety-net · summary
ask: Examiner, may I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, saturations, temperature?
★ Anything make it better? I notice you're sitting forward holding your chest — is it easier like that? What about lying flat? Deep breath or cough?
★ Any cold or flu-like illness in the last couple of weeks? Feverish, tired?

One-breath PEFE if short of time: 'Examiner — general appearance and vitals; cardiovascular inspection, palpation and auscultation, and specifically is there a pericardial friction rub; respiratory air entry and added sounds; lower limbs for oedema.' The rub must survive the compression

Full PEFE order: 1 general — distress, cyanosis, pallor, alert? 2 vitals 3 CVS inspection — JVP raised? apex visible? 4 palpation — apex displaced? parasternal heave? 5 auscultation — S1 S2, murmurs, added sounds, specifically a pericardial friction rub? 6 resp — equal air entry, added sounds? 7 abdomen 8 lower limbs — oedema, calf tenderness? 9 bedside — ECG available? 10 bonus — pulsus paradoxus?
If asked what a rub is: superficial scratching/creaking, left sternal edge, sitting forward in end-expiration, evanescent — highly specific
pefe: Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled sounds here = tamponade → stop, MET call, fluids, urgent echo, cardiology for pericardiocentesis
Diagnosis to patient as MED-17; third reason becomes 'when I listened to your heart I could hear the rubbing sound of the inflamed lining' while the tracing and blood test are pending
Plan: ECG, troponin, echo, CXR, FBE/ESR/CRP; admit for serial troponin; colchicine + NSAID; restrict exercise; safety-net (pain worse/different, SOB, faint, palpitations, fever, swelling)
fails: Talking over the 4-minute bell and never reaching the explanation ★
Not asking for the friction rub by name ★
Never asking relieving factors; saying 'definitely not a heart attack'; no troponin in the plan
Chit-chat with the examiner; asking technique instead of findings; not excusing yourself to the patient first
Short differential list; no safety-net or summary
numbers: 4-minute priority order: 1 intro + consent · 2 complete SOCRATES · 3 CVS + respiratory killers · 4 GI/MSK — sacrifice these if the bell beats you
Two signs that matter: pericardial friction rub (ask by name) · pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg (effusion/tamponade)
Colchicine 0.5 mg BD × 3 months · NSAID + PPI · no steroids first-line VERIFY · see MED-17 for the full ECG read-out, DDx table and doses
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450
