stem: Lily, a 50-year-old woman, presents with on-and-off chest pain. Her father had a heart attack recently. She is worried she is having a heart attack too.
An ECG has already been done — it will be handed to you approximately 4–5 minutes into the station. Vital signs are provided on request.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Interpret the ECG to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses, including an explicit response to her concern about a heart attack
time: 8 minutes. 0:00–1:00 stability, WIPE, acknowledge the fear · 1:00–5:00 history · 5:00–6:00 ECG read and explained to her · 6:00–7:15 diagnosis, reasons, her concern, management · 7:15–8:00 rapid differential list, summary.

back.dx: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — months of on/off burning retrosternal + epigastric pain, 4–5/10, not progressive, doesn't wake her, no radiation, worse lying down, better leaning forward (the planted pericarditis red herring), 'not sure' about food (deliberately vague — keep asking), acid brash YES, water brash YES, regurgitation sometimes; 3–4 coffees a day, a drink most nights, regular ibuprofen for her knee (the modifiable cause); no CV risk factors; father's MI at 78 (ask the age); no alarm features. ECG completely normal (BP 128/78, PR 76, RR 16, SpO2 99%, T 36.7). Discriminating behaviours: ask acid brash and water brash by name; call the ECG normal with confidence; de-escalate her fear with TWO named reasons, never the ECG alone.
plan: Vitals → wash → intro, confirm name/DOB → purpose + consent → comfort → open question → she volunteers the fear → structured reassuring statement (names the emotion, names the dad, gives a plan, promises to return, asks permission)
SOCRATES incl. the night-waking red flag (chronic pain) — probe all three axes: activity/rest, position, food; don't accept 'not sure'
Cardiac symptom screen (all negative) → every risk factor: HTN, DM, lipids, smoking, alcohol, weight, activity, FHx + 'how old was your father?'
Other CVS (pericarditis — fever/viral/pleuritic; AS; HF; dissection; arrhythmia) → respiratory (pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, cancer screen doubles as GI alarm screen)

GI block — where it's decided: abdominal pain/N&V → ★ acid or bitter taste? ★ mouth filling with saliva? regurgitation on bending? cough/hoarse/wheeze → alarm features: food sticking, painful swallowing, weight loss, black tarry sticky stools, vomiting blood → PUD discriminators (to the back, dull ache, night pain) → biliary → GORD risks: coffee, spicy/fatty/late meals → ★ medications incl. OTC → rash, worse on pressing/moving, mood/stress; SADMA, PMHx, allergies
ECG: read systematically, then to Lily in plain words with the honest limit ('one normal tracing doesn't rule out heart disease forever — it's one piece')

Four moves: name it → explain the valve → reasons (burning, posture, acid/water brash, coffee/alcohol/ibuprofen) → her concern: two reasons + offer CV risk check → management → safety-net → rapid DDx list → summary
ask: Lily, I completely understand how frightening chest pain can be, especially after what happened to your dad. Let me ask a few questions, then I'll look at your heart tracing. We'll work out the cause together, and I promise I'll come back to your concern. Is that alright?

Where exactly — point with one finger? Sudden or gradual, when? Burning, crushing, tight, sharp, tearing? Travel anywhere — arm, jaw, neck, back? Constant or on and off, getting worse? Does it ever wake you from sleep? Worse? Better — antacids, peppermint? Out of ten?
Walking uphill or stairs — and settles with rest? Lying flat, bending, leaning forward? After meals, before, large or late meals? (all three axes, every time)
SOB, nausea/vomiting, sweating, palpitations, dizziness, blackouts, ankle swelling, orthopnoea, PND, exercise tolerance?

High blood pressure? Blood sugar? Cholesterol? Smoke, ever? Alcohol per week? Weight? How active? Heart disease in the family — ★ how old was your father when it happened? ('it matters most under 55')

Fever or viral illness, sharp pain worse on deep breath? Chest pain, breathlessness or blackouts on exertion? Pillows, PND, ankle swelling? Sudden tearing pain to the back? Racing or skipping? Cough, sputum, fever? Sudden SOB, haemoptysis, calf pain, travel, surgery, pill/HRT, previous clot, cancer? Weight loss, appetite, night sweats, hoarse voice, neck lumps?

★ Do you get an acidic or bitter taste at the back of your mouth? ★ Have you noticed your mouth suddenly filling with saliva? Does food or fluid come back up when you bend or lie down? Chronic dry cough, hoarse in the morning, wheeze at night?
★ Does food ever stick? Hurt to swallow? Weight loss without trying? Bowel motions black, tarry and sticky like tar? Vomited blood? Persistent vomiting? Family history of stomach or food-pipe cancer?

Pain through to the back, or a deep dull ache rather than burning? Right upper tummy pain after fatty meals, yellow eyes, pale stools? Tea/coffee — how much? Spicy, fatty, fried, chocolate, late meals? ★ Any medications at all, including over the counter or from the pharmacy? Rash or blistering? Worse when you move, twist or press? Mood, stress at home or work?
pefe: ECG to the examiner/yourself: details, calibration → rate ~75 → regular → P before every QRS, sinus → PR normal → QRS normal, no Q waves → no ST elevation or depression in any territory → T waves normal → QTc normal → 'a completely normal ECG'. Don't over-read mild concave ST elevation in V5–V6 (benign early repolarisation) as pericarditis

ECG to Lily: 'this is a tracing of your heart's electrical activity. The good news is it's completely normal — rate about 75, rhythm regular and coming from the right place, and importantly none of the changes we'd expect if the heart muscle wasn't getting enough blood or you were having a heart attack. One honest thing: a normal tracing today doesn't rule out heart disease forever — it's one piece of the picture'

Diagnosis: 'reflux — a valve between food pipe and stomach that keeps acid where it belongs; when it doesn't close properly acid comes back up and the food pipe, which isn't built for acid, gets irritated — that's the burning'. Reasons: burning quality · posture (acid moves up when gravity isn't helping) · acid taste + mouth filling with saliva are quite specific · coffee, alcohol, ibuprofen

Her concern — two reasons: (1) tracing normal (2) more important — character doesn't fit heart pain (heavy/crushing, on exertion, eases with rest, to arm/jaw) vs hers (burning, months, not activity-related, changes with position). 'That said, because of your dad I'd like to check your overall heart risk properly — bloods and BP' = partnership

Management: STOP the ibuprofen (paracetamol; look at the knee) · lifestyle: cut coffee, reduce alcohol, avoid provoking foods/chocolate/peppermint/fizzy drinks, smaller meals, nothing within 3 h of lying down, head of bed up 15–20 cm on blocks, weight, loose clothing · antacid/alginate PRN · PPI once daily 30–60 min before breakfast for 4–8 weeks then step down (esomeprazole 20 mg / pantoprazole 20–40 mg / omeprazole 20 mg) VERIFY · FBC, H. pylori (UBT or stool antigen — withhold PPI 2 weeks) VERIFY, lipids, HbA1c, UEC for absolute CV risk · review 4–6 weeks; no response or alarm features → endoscopy
Examination to state: CVS, resp, abdomen incl. epigastric tenderness, chest-wall palpation, skin for zoster, BMI, BP

DDx list to Lily briskly: heart (tracing normal, pain doesn't fit) · sac around the heart (no fever/viral) · stomach ulcer (possible with ibuprofen — usually to the back, dull ache) · clot on lung, collapsed lung, chest infection (no sudden SOB, cough, fever) · gallbladder · chest-wall muscle/joint · shingles (no rash) · stress/anxiety. 'Reflux fits best'
fails: Never asking the reflux questions — acid brash and water brash ★
Reassuring on the ECG alone; 'there's nothing wrong with your heart' / 'it's just reflux' ★
Abandoning the structure — jumping to GI on 'burning', or locking onto pericarditis on 'better leaning forward'
Not asking the father's age; skipping alarm features in a 50-year-old; missing the OTC ibuprofen
Over-reading a normal ECG as pericarditis; not addressing her stated concern explicitly
Jargon (GORD, retrosternal, melaena); no ambulance threshold; running out of time before the differentials
numbers: Premature CVD: first-degree male <55, female <65 · father 78 = not premature · 'melaena' → 'black, tarry, sticky, like tar'
Two-axis rule: tracks with meals and posture → oesophagus; tracks with exertion and rest → heart. Radiation: arm → cardiac; jaw shared; epigastrium → oesophageal
PPI trial 4–8 weeks then step down · H. pylori test off PPI 2 weeks · review 4–6 weeks · endoscopy if alarm features, new onset >50 with persistent symptoms, or failed PPI VERIFY
Drugs that worsen reflux: NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, anticholinergics, doxycycline, potassium supplements
Safety-net: exertional pain, to arm/jaw, sweating, SOB, faint → 000, don't drive · food sticking, vomiting blood, black tarry stools → urgent review · not better in 4–6 weeks → come back
Version B (28-year-old man, 6-min history, squeezing pain to the jaw, relieved by peppermint tea) is MED-20 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with chest pain for 30 minutes — better now.
Vital signs are stable (stated in the stem). An ECG is provided — normal.
tasks: Take a history for 6 minutes
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Six-minute history, then diagnosis and differentials.

back.dx: GORD in a young man whose pain SOUNDS cardiac — squeezing, radiates to the jaw — but with no sweating, no nausea/vomiting, no other MI features, and positive acid/bitter taste, water brash, relief with peppermint tea. Normal ECG. The recall that caused panic: candidates who never ran the GI block were left with 'an MI with no MI symptoms' and froze. Oesophageal pain can reach the jaw — it's the ARM that discriminates towards cardiac. Same structure as MED-19: run cardiac → respiratory → GI every time, and still ask every risk factor.
plan: Confirm stability quickly (don't dwell) → WIPE → open question → acknowledgement line
SOCRATES; all three axes — exertion/rest, position, food
Cardiac symptoms (sweating, nausea, SOB, palpitations, syncope) → ALL risk factors incl. FHx with age → ★ recreational drugs (cocaine, amphetamines) asked non-judgementally
Respiratory differentials (PE, pneumothorax — tall/thin/smoker, pneumonia, cancer screen)
GI: acid/bitter taste, water brash, regurgitation, relation to meals, ★ what relieved it (peppermint), alarm features, PUD, biliary; GORD risk factors; medications incl. OTC
MSK/rash, mood/stress, SADMA, PMHx, ICE → 6:00 diagnosis + reasons → DDx briskly, killers first → plan (lifestyle, PPI trial, review) → safety-net → summary
ask: Tell me more about the pain. Where — point or area? Squeezing, burning, sharp, tearing? Travel anywhere — arm, jaw, back? How long, constant? What were you doing? What made it better — anything you took or drank?
Any sweating, nausea or vomiting, breathlessness, racing heart, dizziness or blackouts with it?
High BP, diabetes, cholesterol ever? Smoke? Alcohol? Weight? Heart attacks or strokes in the family — at what age? I ask everyone: any recreational drugs — cocaine, speed, ice?
Sudden breathlessness, coughing blood, calf pain, travel, previous clots? Fever, cough? Tall and thin, previous collapsed lung?

★ Acidic or bitter taste at the back of your mouth? ★ Mouth suddenly filling with saliva? Food coming back up? Relation to meals? Food sticking, weight loss, black tarry stools, vomiting blood? Coffee, alcohol, spicy/late meals? Any medications, including over the counter?
Rash? Worse pressing or twisting? Stress at home or work, mood?
pefe: No examination task — vitals stated stable, ECG provided normal; state that a normal ECG does not exclude ischaemia and that the history is what settles it
Diagnosis + reasons: acid taste, water brash, relief with peppermint (relaxes the oesophagus), no sweating/nausea/SOB, no risk factors, normal ECG; 'oesophageal pain can go to the jaw'

Young-but-not-low-risk list to keep in mind and screen: cocaine/amphetamine coronary spasm, familial hypercholesterolaemia, myocarditis/pericarditis, spontaneous pneumothorax, PE, connective tissue disorder with dissection
Management as MED-19: lifestyle, antacid PRN, PPI 4–8 weeks, review 4–6 weeks; safety-net with 000 threshold and GI alarm features
fails: Never asking the GI questions and freezing on 'an MI with no MI symptoms' ★
Skipping cardiovascular risk factors or the recreational drug question because 'he's 28'
Reassuring on the ECG alone; 'there's nothing wrong with your heart'
Committing to GORD before the cardiac and respiratory screens; jargon; no safety-net
numbers: Jaw radiation is shared by cardiac and oesophageal pain; arm radiation discriminates towards cardiac
Peppermint and GTN both relax oesophageal smooth muscle — relief by either never proves the pain is not cardiac
PPI trial 4–8 weeks · review 4–6 weeks · endoscopy if alarm features or failed trial VERIFY
See MED-19 for the full GORD back · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

setting: Emergency department, Australian metropolitan hospital. You are the ED junior doctor.
stem: James, a 49-year-old man, has brought himself to ED with severe central chest pain that started 30 minutes ago.
Vital signs are available from the examiner on request. An ECG will be provided after the history.
tasks: Take a focused history — 5 minutes. A warning bell sounds at 5 minutes
Interpret the ECG to the examiner — step by step, out loud, in a fixed order
Explain your likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient in plain language
time: 8 minutes. History 5:00 (bell) · ECG ~1:00 · explanation ~2:00.

back.dx: Acute inferior STEMI — super-typical pain: central area not a point, 7–8/10, tightening/crushing, 30 min constant, to jaw and left shoulder, worse walking better resting AND at rest now; SOB, sweating, nausea; four discriminators all negative (breathing, position, eating, movement). KEY POINT of every chest-pain station: the five risk factors — dad and uncle MI, hypertension + cholesterol on tablets, 15/day for 25 years, beers at weekends, overweight. Vitals: BP 128/76, pulse 52 (bradycardia is a clue — RCA supplies SA/AV nodes), RR 18, T 36.8, SpO2 97%. ECG: rate ~50, regular sinus, PR normal, QRS wide (esp. chest leads — bundle branch, describe and move on), ST elevation II, III, aVF (III and aVF marked), reciprocal depression I and aVL, plus depression V2–V4 (possible posterior extension), no ST elevation in V1 (no RV clue).
plan: Vitals from examiner ('stable though bradycardic') → wash → intro, name/DOB → consent → open question → acknowledgement line

SICORA: site (point or area?) → intensity → character (crushing or sharp?) → onset/course → radiation → aggravating/relieving; if 'haven't noticed' → 'does activity make it worse and rest better?' → 'pain at rest right now?'
Four discriminators every time: deep breath? leaning forward? eating? movement/pressing?

Systems screen 1–2 questions each in fixed order: CVS (SOB/sweat/nausea/palpitations; fever/flu/leaning forward; orthopnoea/pillows/oedema; syncope on exertion) → resp (calf, travel, clots; trauma; fever/cough/noisy breathing; weight/appetite/lumps/haemoptysis) → GI (abdo pain/vomiting; acid taste/saliva; meals) → MSK/skin (movement/pressing; rash) → psych (stress, mood)
★ KEY POINT — five risk factors: FHx heart attack/stroke · sugar/BP/fats · smoking amount and years · alcohol · overweight
Recreational drugs (cocaine/amphetamines) · medications incl. sildenafil · allergies · 'anything else you'd like to tell me?'

Bell → ECG seven steps → impression → to patient: name it, one sentence, three reasons (typical pain, risk factors, ECG) → reason 1–2 DDx then rapid list, life-threatening first → what happens now, safety-net, summary
ask: Examiner, before I begin I'd like the patient's vital signs please: BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation.
I understand how concerning chest pain can be, James. Let me ask you a few questions, I'll try to find the cause and make the best plan for you, and I'll address your concerns as quickly as I can.

Where is the pain — a point you can put a finger on, or an area? One to ten? Crushing, or sharp? When exactly did it start — constant or on and off since, getting worse? Does it travel anywhere? Anything make it better or worse? → ★ Does activity make it worse and rest make it better? ★ Do you have pain at rest right now?
Is it related to breathing — deep breath worse? To position — leaning forward better? To eating? Worse on movement or pressing on the chest?
Any SOB? Sweating? Nausea? Racing heart? Fever, chills, flu-like symptoms? Breathless lying flat, how many pillows, leg swelling? Ever fainted, especially with exercise?

Calf swelling or pain? Long travel, family history of clots? Chest injury? Fever, cough, noisy breathing? Weight loss, appetite, lumps, coughed up blood? Tummy pain, vomiting? Acidic or bitter taste, sudden saliva? Related to eating? Rash? Stress at home or work, mood?
★ Family history of heart attacks or strokes? Past history of high sugar, high blood pressure or high fats in the blood? Smoke — how much, how long? Alcohol — how much? Are you currently overweight?
Recreational drugs? Any medications — including anything like Viagra? Allergies? Anything else you'd like to tell me today?
'Am I going to be alright?' → 'I understand this is frightening. You came in early and we have a well-established treatment pathway that we're starting right now' — then the three reasons
pefe: Seven-step ECG, never the impression first: 1 rate (300 ÷ large squares → ~50) 2 rhythm regular 3 P waves → sinus 4 PR < 1 large square 5 QRS — 'wide, particularly in the praecordial leads' 6 ST elevation — name every lead and the territory: II, III, aVF = inferior 7 look deliberately at the opposite territory: reciprocal depression I and aVL; also V2–V4 · extra step for inferior MI: 'is there ST elevation in V1?' — QR pattern but no elevation → no RV clue · THEN 'acute inferior STEMI'
Don't open with 'I'd check the name and date' — if at all, say it last

Diagnosis script: 'most likely a myocardial infarction — the same as a heart attack. One of the blood tubes of your heart has become blocked so the muscle isn't getting enough oxygen, and that's the pain.' Three reasons: typical pain (central, to jaw and shoulder, worse with activity) · risk factors (family, BP, cholesterol, smoking) · the ECG shows the changes

DDx: reason the first one or two (pericarditis — no fever/flu; PE — no travel; pneumothorax — no injury) then list: aortic dissection, oesophageal rupture; heart failure, narrowed valve; chest infection, growth in the lung; reflux, stomach ulcer; rib-joint inflammation, shingles; panic attack. Life-threatening first. When the bell goes mid-sentence: finish the phrase, 'that's my list of differentials', stop

Management if extended: resus bay, monitor, defib to bedside, IV ×2, ECG within 10 min (repeat; V4R for inferior), aspirin 300 mg chewed, titrated IV opioid + antiemetic, nitrate only if BP adequate and no RV infarct/PDE-5 inhibitor, oxygen only if hypoxic, activate STEMI pathway + cardiology NOW — troponin never delays reperfusion; PCI within targets else fibrinolysis; CCU, not for discharge; DAPT, statin, beta-blocker, ACEi; cardiac rehab; screen family

One-line lay DDx: pericarditis 'inflammation of the covering of your heart' · pneumothorax 'a collection of air in the chest' · PE 'a clot in your lungs' · dissection 'a tear in the main blood tube of your body' · rupture 'a tear in your food pipe' · HF 'your heart isn't pumping normally' · GORD 'stomach acid irritating your food pipe' · shingles 'reactivation of the chickenpox virus' · costochondritis 'inflammation of the rib joints' · AS 'a narrowed heart valve'
fails: Skipping cardiovascular risk factors — the single commonest reason candidates fail the MI case ★
Not checking haemodynamic stability before the first question ★
Jumping to the ECG impression; not naming reciprocal changes
Narrow cardiac-only differential; over-explaining two differentials and no list when the bell rings
'Don't worry, I'm sure it's nothing'; talking over the bell; no plan or safety-net sentence
numbers: Rate = 300 ÷ large squares · PR normal < 1 large square (200 ms) · QRS narrow < 3 small squares (120 ms) · significant ST elevation >1 mm limb, >2 mm chest VERIFY
Territories: inferior II, III, aVF ↔ reciprocal I, aVL, check V1/V4R for RV · anterolateral I, aVL, V1–V6 ↔ reciprocal III, aVF ± II · pericarditis widespread concave, NO reciprocal, aVR depressed
Inferior MI: RCA → SA/AV node → bradycardia/heart block · RV infarct = preload dependent → no nitrates, give fluids · ST depression V1–V4 may be posterior extension → V7–V9
Aspirin 300 mg chewed · ECG within 10 min · no routine oxygen if normoxic · nitrate contraindications: hypotension, RV infarct, PDE-5 inhibitor within 24–48 h VERIFY
DDx order: MI · pericarditis · PE · pneumothorax · dissection · oesophageal rupture → HF, AS → pneumonia, lung cancer → GORD, PUD → costochondritis, shingles → panic
Case B (unclear ECG, anterolateral STEMI, HTN/DM/lipids) is MED-22 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

back.dx: Acute anterolateral STEMI hiding behind a poor tracing — the station built to catch 'pericarditis!'. History: centre and left chest, an area, 8/10, squeezing, 30 min constant, to the left arm, worse moving better resting, pain at rest now, a bit SOB and sweaty; discriminators negative; risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia (on tablets), pack a day for 20 years, overweight, dad MI at 60. Vitals BP 142/88, PR 92, RR 20, T 36.6, SpO2 96%. ECG: steps 1–5 normal; ST elevation ~1 small square in I and aVL, and V2–V6 — widespread → 'pericarditis or anterolateral infarct — let me look at the inferior leads' → II acceptable, ~1 mm depression in III and aVF → reciprocal change present → NOT pericarditis. The discriminator in one sentence: widespread elevation WITH reciprocal depression = infarct; WITHOUT = pericarditis.
