SICORA + 'activity worse, rest better?' + 'pain at rest now?' + four discriminators
Associated symptoms → systems screen in one rapid run (CVS → resp → GI → MSK → psych)
★ Risk factor block: FHx with age, sugar/BP/fats, smoking, alcohol, weight → drugs, meds incl. Viagra, allergies, anything else

Bell → 'I'll zoom in and go through this systematically' → steps 1–5 → elevation lead by lead vs the isoelectric line → 'widespread, so pericarditis vs anterolateral infarct — inferior leads' → III and aVF depressed → anterolateral STEMI

'You're having a heart attack' + three reasons (squeezing to the arm and worse with activity; BP, diabetes, cholesterol, smoking; the ECG) → reason 2–3 DDx then the list → aspirin, analgesia, monitor, cardiology called, cath lab, CCU → safety-net → questions
ask: Examiner, may I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?
I understand how concerning chest pain can be. Let me ask a few questions so I can find the cause and make the best plan for you.

Where — a point or an area? One to ten? Crushing or sharp? Travel anywhere? Constant since it started? ★ Activity worse, rest better? ★ Pain at rest right now? Related to breathing, leaning forward, eating, pressing?

SOB, sweating, nausea, racing heart? Fever/chills/flu? Breathless flat, leg swelling? Fainted with exercise? Calf pain, travel, clots? Injury? Cough, blood? Weight loss? Tummy pain, vomiting, acid taste? Pressing/rash? Stress, mood?

★ Family history of heart attacks or strokes? High sugar, high BP, high fats? Smoke — how much, how long? Alcohol? Overweight? Medications — including anything like Viagra? Recreational drugs? Allergies? Anything else?
'Are you sure?' → 'I understand this is a shock. I'm confident for three reasons…'
pefe: Poor-image technique: say you're zooming in; compare each ST segment to the isoelectric (TP) line, not to expectation; one small square named in a lead is a real finding; anchor on what you can genuinely see and build to neighbouring and opposite leads; never invent a finding

Model paragraph: 'technically difficult, but rate, rhythm, P waves, PR and QRS are normal. ST elevation of about one small square in I and aVL, and across V2–V6. Because the elevation is widespread I specifically examined the inferior leads for reciprocal change — about 1 mm of ST depression in III and aVF. Reciprocal change argues against pericarditis. Diagnosis: acute anterolateral STEMI'

Case B full explanation under 60 s: heart attack — blood tube blocked → three reasons → dissection (not likely), PE (no travel), pneumothorax (no injury) reasoned → then food-pipe tear, covering of the heart, narrowed valve, heart failure, pneumonia, lung cancer, rib joints, shingles, reflux, ulcer

Anterolateral vs pericarditis vs inferior: elevation I, aVL, V1–V6 convex/straight with reciprocal III, aVF ± II · widespread concave, no reciprocal, aVR depressed · II, III, aVF with reciprocal I, aVL, check V1
Plan: aspirin, pain relief, monitor, cardiology called, cath lab, CCU, tell us if pain worsens or faint; management detail as MED-21
fails: Calling widespread elevation pericarditis without checking the opposite leads ★
Skipping the risk factor block ★
Leading with the impression; freezing on a poor-quality tracing; dismissing one small square because it isn't dramatic
Cardiac-only screen; no list when the bell rings; talking over the bell; no plan or safety-net
numbers: The one question this station tests: 'have I looked at the opposite leads?' — reciprocal present = infarct; absent + concave + aVR depression = pericarditis
Compare to the isoelectric TP segment · 1 small square = 1 mm = a real finding when named in a lead
Three modifiable risk factors here (HTN, DM, lipids) + smoking + weight + FHx at 60 · dad at 60 is not premature (<55) but still counts as family history
Aspirin 300 mg chewed · ECG within 10 min · activate STEMI pathway before troponin · see MED-21 for the full drill and management
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

source: STEMI.pdf (Case B — unclear ECG, anterolateral STEMI)

setting: You are a GP at a suburban general practice in Australia.
stem: Mr Daniel Reid, a 40-year-old man, has presented today complaining of chest pain.
Vital signs recorded by the practice nurse: temp 37.8 °C · HR 88 · BP 128/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% RA · BGL not done. Haemodynamically stable — you may proceed with a focused consultation.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (~4 min)
Review the physical examination findings provided on the screen (Version B face-to-face: ask the examiner for the findings)
Explain your provisional diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
Outline your investigations and initial management, including safety-netting
time: 8 minutes. About 4 minutes of history, then findings, explanation, plan and safety-net.

back.dx: Herpes zoster of the right T4 dermatome — sharp stabbing pain from the right nipple round to the back, same side, never crossing the midline, started last night, 8–9/10, constant, worse overnight, ALLODYNIA (the bedsheet brushing the skin), burning/itching for a day or two before, flu last week, feverish and tired. Co-diagnosis the station is built around: why is a 40-year-old reactivating varicella? — 5 kg weight loss, night sweats, exhaustion, a lump under the right arm (firm 2 cm axillary node on exam) → lymphoma/leukaemia screen. Childcare worker; pregnant sister staying at home. Version B trap (2019): examiner says 'no rash' — the pain precedes the rash by 2–3 days; the diagnosis stands. Findings on screen: low-grade fever; vesicular rash on one side of the chest not crossing the midline (= dermatomal — decode it); CVS and resp normal; ECG normal.
plan: Vitals acknowledged → wash → intro, name/DOB → open question → empathy → consent; chest exposure with privacy and chaperone offer
SOCRATES: point to it → 'does it ever cross to the other side?' → sharp/stabbing → allodynia → 'tingling, burning or numb?' → severity, sleep

Exclude the killers even though you 'know': exertional? to jaw/arm, sweating, nausea? SOB, haemoptysis? calf, travel, surgery? ★ 'you had the flu — worse lying flat, better sitting forward?' (pericarditis) · heartburn, meals, swallowing · injury, lifting, coughing

Shingles layer: rash or blisters seen? ★ occupation ★ contacts (pregnant, newborns, young children, immunosuppressed) → ★ malignancy red flags: weight loss, drenching sweats, lumps in neck/armpit/groin, bruising/bleeding, fevers, tiredness → diabetes symptoms → steroids/immunosuppressants → HIV/BBV risk with a preface → chickenpox as a child, previous shingles, vaccine → eye/ear symptoms
SADMA, PMHx (DM, cancer, HIV, autoimmune, transplant, renal), FHx, who's at home, 'what were you most worried this might be?' (heart attack — address it first later)

Findings: decode 'vesicles one side, not crossing midline' = dermatomal, right T4; note the axillary node. Version B: ask by name (general/cachexia, vitals + BGL, lymph nodes + hepatosplenomegaly, CVS incl. rub, resp, chest wall — rash? crosses midline? tenderness incl. light touch, neuro with dermatomal sensory testing, abdomen, ECG, urinalysis)

Heart worry first (exam + ECG normal, pattern doesn't fit) → shingles in plain words → DDx → the second conversation: why now, honest 'is it cancer?' → investigations → four-part management → contacts, work, notification → safety-net incl. PHN → summary, written info, review 2–3 days
ask: Show me exactly where. Does it ever cross over to the other side of your chest? Tight or heavy, or sharp? ★ 'Even the bedsheet hurts' → is the skin also tingling, burning or numb? Out of ten, and has it stopped you doing anything?

Does it come on when you exert yourself? Spread to jaw, neck, left arm? Sweating, nausea, faint? Shortness of breath, coughing blood? Calf swelling or pain, long flights, surgery, time in bed? ★ You had the flu — is it worse lying flat and better sitting forward? Heartburn, related to eating, difficulty swallowing? Injury, heavy lifting, hard coughing?
Noticed any rash or blisters on that area? ★ What do you do for work — children or healthcare? ★ Contact with anyone pregnant, any newborns or young children, anyone with a weak immune system?

★ 'Some questions may seem unrelated' — lost weight without trying? Drenching night sweats? Lumps in neck, armpits or groin? Unusual bruising or bleeding? Persistent fevers? More tired than usual? Drinking or passing urine more? Known diabetes? Steroids, chemotherapy, arthritis or bowel-disease drugs, injections affecting the immune system? 'I ask everyone — anything in your background that might affect your immune system, such as blood-borne virus risk?' Chickenpox as a child? Shingles before? Vaccinated? Rash near the eye, forehead, tip of nose, eye pain, vision change? Ear pain, hearing, dizziness, facial weakness?
Smoke, alcohol, drugs, medications, allergies? Past conditions? Family — heart disease, clots, cancer? Who's at home? What were you most worried this might be?

'Is it cancer?' → 'I can't tell you today and I don't want to alarm you. These symptoms need proper investigation rather than ignoring. Some causes are straightforward — diabetes, a recent infection. Others involve the blood or lymph glands, and those are the ones I want to find or rule out, because finding them early matters.'
pefe: Version B ordered request: 1 general — distress, cyanosis, pallor, drowsy, cachexia 2 full vitals incl. BGL 3 lymph nodes cervical/supraclavicular/axillary/inguinal + hepatosplenomegaly 4 full CVS incl. JVP and pericardial rub, calves 5 resp 6 chest wall — 'is there any rash? does it cross the midline? tenderness on palpation and to light touch?' 7 neuro upper/lower limbs + dermatomal sensory testing over the band 8 abdomen 9 ECG, BGL, urinalysis

'No rash' answer: 'The absence of a rash does not exclude shingles — the pain typically precedes the rash by a few days. My provisional diagnosis remains herpes zoster, and I would warn him a rash is likely over the next 2–3 days and review within 48–72 h so antivirals start inside the window'

Explain: heart worry first → 'shingles — when you had chickenpox the virus went to sleep in the nerve roots near your spine; years later it can wake up and travel along one nerve — that's why the pain is a band on one side that stops dead in the middle, and why the skin is so sensitive. The pain usually comes first and the rash a few days later.' DDx: heart, clot on the lung, sac around the heart, lung infection, reflux, chest-wall cartilage — unlikely on history, exam and ECG

Investigations — two jobs, say both: (1) confirm/exclude mimics: ECG (mandatory), swab from a de-roofed vesicle for VZV PCR (don't wait for it — clinical diagnosis), troponin only if ischaemic suspicion (2) why now: FBE + film, BGL/HbA1c, HIV serology with consent, ESR/CRP, LDH, UEC (antiviral dosing), LFT, CXR (mediastinal nodes) → urgent haematology if abnormal

Management: 1 antiviral — famciclovir 500 mg TDS × 7 days (or valaciclovir 1 g TDS × 7, or aciclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7); within 72 h of rash if immunocompetent, any duration if immunocompromised; renal dose adjustment VERIFY 2 analgesia — not paracetamol alone: regular paracetamol + NSAID, paracetamol/codeine for breakthrough with constipation advice, early amitriptyline/gabapentin/pregabalin if severe 3 skin — cool compresses, calamine, clean/dry, loose clothing, non-adherent dressing, don't scratch 4 contacts — until every blister has crusted avoid pregnant women who haven't had chickenpox, newborns, unvaccinated young children, immunosuppressed; cover, hand-wash, no shared towels; 'the fluid gives chickenpox, not shingles' · off work while lesions can't be covered, medical certificate, check childcare requirements · notifiable in SA (say you'll comply) VERIFY · review 2–3 days · Shingrix once recovered if eligible (NIP ≥65, ATSI ≥50, immunocompromised ≥18) VERIFY

Safety-net: rash near eye/forehead/nose tip (Hutchinson's) or eye pain/vision → same-day ophthalmology · rash spreads, crosses midline, >20 lesions → disseminated, admit IV aciclovir · facial weakness, hearing, vertigo → Ramsay Hunt, ENT · hot red spreading skin/pus · high fever, confusion, new SOB, worsening chest pain. PHN warning: 'the rash settles but the nerve pain can outlast it — come back, there are specific medicines'
fails: Not exploring an underlying cause for zoster at 40 — no concern over weight loss and tiredness, no malignancy/immunosuppression screen — documented CRITICAL ERROR ★
Ruling out shingles because the examiner says 'no rash' ★
No ECG in a chest pain station; committing to shingles before excluding ACS, PE, pericarditis
Paracetamol alone for severe neuropathic pain; delaying antivirals for the PCR
No contact advice, no occupation question, no notification; exposing the chest without consent/chaperone offer
'It's only a rash'; jargon (herpes zoster, dermatomal, dorsal root ganglion) untranslated; no PHN warning, no review date
numbers: 72 hours — antiviral window from rash onset (immunocompetent); any duration if immunocompromised (diabetes, steroids, malignancy, HIV count)
Famciclovir 500 mg 8-hourly × 7 · valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly × 7 · aciclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7 · reduce in renal impairment · IV aciclovir if disseminated/immunocompromised VERIFY
Dermatomes: T4 nipple · T6 xiphisternum · T10 umbilicus · C6 thumb · L4 medial malleolus — name 'right T4' to the examiner
Rash: grouped vesicles on an erythematous base → pustules → crusts over 7–10 days; pain precedes rash by 2–3 days (up to a week); infectious until crusted
Red-flag distributions: ophthalmic (Hutchinson's sign, nose tip) · Ramsay Hunt (ear vesicles + facial palsy) · disseminated (>20 lesions outside the dermatome / crossing midline)
Shingrix NIP: ≥65, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ≥50, immunocompromised ≥18 VERIFY · SA Health notification · PATS/Country Health Connect · ACCHS · TIS National 131 450

source: Herpes Zoster.pdf (Version A on-screen findings; Version B 'no rash' on the back)

stem: Your next patient is Margaret Doyle, 65, who was admitted two weeks ago with pneumonia, treated with antibiotics, discharged, and is now well. She has a permanent pacemaker for a bradyarrhythmia and uses CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea. She plans to travel interstate in two weeks. Two chest X-rays are available: the admission film and a repeat film taken this week.
Observations: T 36.6 °C · P 72 regular · BP 128/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% room air.
tasks: Explain the two chest X-rays to the patient
Take a relevant focused history
Counsel her about the risks of travelling and advise her accordingly
time: 8 minutes. 0:30 films · 1:30 pneumonia box · 2:30 pacemaker/CPAP · 3:45 risk factors/SADMA · 4:30 the trip · 5:15 verdict and counselling · 7:30 summary and safety-net.

back.dx: Fit to travel — resolved right middle lobe pneumonia (admission film: dense white patch right mid-zone, pacemaker box with two leads; this week's film: cleared, sharp heart border), symptoms settled, SpO2 97%. Two things she will NOT volunteer: CPAP only two nights a week (mask digs into her nose) and ten cigarettes a day for forty years. 'Somac' = pantoprazole — say it. Cairns, ten days, three-hour flight, staying with sister Anne — and a beginner scuba dive is booked (surfaces only if you ask what she'll do). Discriminating behaviours: hold the verdict until the history is done; ask 'how many nights a week' not 'do you use it'; ask what she plans to do; letter + written red flags because she'll be 2,500 km away.
plan: WIPE, confirm name; open question; agenda: films → recovery, heart and sleep apnoea, the trip → clear answer + something in writing

Films: three colours → heart, spine, windpipe → normal left lung first → right mid-zone white patch → NAME the pacemaker → second film: black again, sharp heart border → 'cleared completely' → 'I think the answer will be yes — let me check a few things first'
Box 1 pneumonia: admitted/discharged, days of antibiotics and finished?, cough, sputum, BLOOD, SOB walking/lying flat, fever/chills/sweats, chest pain, appetite and WEIGHT
Box 2: pacemaker — when, last check, tablets, racing/fluttering, dizzy spells/blackouts; CPAP — 'how many nights a week do you actually use it?' → two → acknowledge, flag you'll come back
Box 3: asthma/emphysema, diabetes, kidney/liver, cancer, steroids, stroke/memory/choking; medications (Somac = pantoprazole); flu and pneumonia vaccines; smoke — how much; alcohol; occupation
Box 4: where, when, how long; flying or driving; who with, staying with whom; WHAT will you do; insurance, enough medication

Verdict: yes — 'no rule that you must wait a set time after a pneumonia'. Letter (admission, antibiotics, pacemaker, CPAP settings). Red flags + 000 + tell your sister. No scuba (snorkelling fine; formal dive medical if she insists, later). CPAP: consequences, mask refit/nasal pillows/humidifier, sleep service referral, take it on the plane. Smoking: ask-advise-assess-assist-arrange in 90 s, Quitline 13 7848, NRT. Flu vaccine today, check pneumococcal and COVID. Tropical advice, flight advice
Summary in one breath; 'have I missed anything you were worried about?'
ask: 'On an X-ray there are really only three colours: white is bone, grey is soft tissue like heart and muscle, black is air. Here is your heart, your spine, your windpipe down the middle. Your left lung is completely black — normal. Compare the right: a dense white patch here in the middle — that's where the infection was. And this box with two wires into your heart is your pacemaker, correctly placed, wires intact.'

'Second film — same colours, same landmarks, same pacemaker — but the area that was white is black again, and the heart edge is sharp. Your pneumonia has cleared completely. I think the answer will be yes; before I commit, let me ask about your recovery, your heart and sleep apnoea, and the trip.'

When admitted, when home? Days of antibiotics — finished? Still coughing, bringing anything up? ★ Any blood in it? Breathless walking or lying flat? Fever, chills, night sweats since? Chest pain? Appetite and weight?

Pacemaker — when put in, last checked? Any heart tablets, taken daily? Racing, fluttering, funny beating? Dizzy spells or blackouts? ★ 'And the sleep apnoea — how many nights a week do you actually use the CPAP?' → 'Thank you for being honest — I want to come back to that, there are things we can do about the mask'

Asthma or emphysema? Diabetes, kidney, liver, cancer? Steroid tablets? Stroke, memory trouble, choking on food or drink? What medications? ('Somac is pantoprazole — that settles acid') Flu and pneumonia vaccinations up to date? ★ Do you smoke, how much? Alcohol? What did you do for work?
★ Where are you going, when, how long? Flying or driving? Who with, staying with whom? What are you planning to do while you're there? Travel insurance, enough of your medications?
'Yes, you can make this trip. Symptoms settled, oxygen normal, repeat film clear — there is no rule you must wait a set time after a pneumonia; what matters is that you've recovered, and you have.'

'One thing I'd steer you away from: the scuba dive. Diving puts the lungs under pressure and so soon after a pneumonia there's a real risk of lung injury. Snorkelling on the surface is fine. If you genuinely want to dive you need a formal dive medical first — and I'd rather that waited.'
pefe: No examination task. If the examiner asks for a doctor-level read: erect PA films; admission — right middle lobe consolidation with loss of the right heart border, dual-chamber pacemaker in situ with leads in the right atrium and right ventricle, no effusion; repeat — resolution of consolidation, right heart border restored
The letter: admission dates, antibiotic given, pacemaker (model/date), CPAP settings, medications, allergies, GP contact; hand over to any doctor in Cairns

Red flags, written: cough returning or worsening · more breathless · fever or chills · chest pain · coughing up blood · feeling faint → see a doctor; severe → 000; tell Anne so she can act if you can't

CPAP counselling: two nights a week = the discomfort without the benefit; untreated OSA → repeated overnight desaturation, higher BP, strain on a heart that already needs a pacemaker, more chest infections; fixes — different mask size, nasal pillows, humidifier; refer back to the sleep service for a refit; take the machine on the plane (airlines carry it as medical equipment — noted in the letter)

Smoking, 90 seconds: 'I won't lecture you, but at ten a day smoking is the biggest single thing making another pneumonia likely — and the one thing we can change. Have you thought about stopping?' → Quitline 13 7848 (they ring you back), nicotine patch + lozenge/gum, review a fortnight after she's home. Never moralise; if she says 'after the trip', accept it as a start

Vaccines and travel: influenza today (adjuvanted from 65), check pneumococcal (funded at 70; from 50 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander; earlier with risk conditions) and COVID booster; up there — avoid coughs and crowded indoor places while the lungs finish healing, repellent, don't drink from creeks, wet season keep cuts covered and out of mud; on the flight drink water and walk about
SA: Country Health Connect for the sleep-service referral pathway if rural; healthdirect 1800 022 222; TIS 131 450
fails: Answering 'yes, off you go' after the films and losing the history — or never giving a clear verdict at all ★
Accepting 'yes I've got the machine' — never asking how many nights ★
Never asking about smoking, or not quantifying it
Not asking what she'll do on the trip — the dive advice is the only patient-specific advice in the station
Safety-net with nothing written; no letter; no red flags; no 000

Starting the film with the abnormality; not naming the pacemaker; not comparing the two films; turning smoking into a full cessation consult; lecturing (she becomes defensive: 'I've heard all this before')
numbers: Quitline 13 7848 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450 · 000

Radiographic clearance normally 4–6 weeks · repeat film at 6 weeks in smokers over 50 · CURB-65 and SMART-COP ≥3 are severity tools at presentation, NOT travel tools · cabin altitude equivalent 1,500–2,500 m VERIFY
Influenza annually, adjuvanted from 65 · pneumococcal funded at 70 (50 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults; earlier with risk conditions) VERIFY current NIP
Long-term PPI is a modest pneumonia risk factor · OSA untreated → hypertension, arrhythmia, higher infection risk · CPAP adherence target ≥4 h/night on ≥70% of nights VERIFY

Variant 1 examiner: 'what is her risk score?' → 'there is no validated risk score for travel after pneumonia; I assessed her under four headings — complete resolution, comorbidity control, ongoing risk factors, demands of the trip — and she is fit, with two modifiable risks addressed'

Variant 2 still symptomatic, shadow not cleared: 'my advice is different from what you hoped' — persistent cough and incomplete clearance at 65 with a smoking history → bloods and CT chest before travel to be certain nothing sits behind the infection; postpone a few weeks; book the scan this week
Variant 3 overseas: destination vaccines, food/water, mosquitoes, insurance with declared pre-existing conditions, medications in hand luggage with a letter, nearest reliable facility

stem: Jenny Alcott, 60, has been brought to your practice. She has been breathless for two months and has been coughing up red / pink sputum.
Observations on request: BP 124/76 · pulse 96 regular · RR 22 · SpO2 91% on room air, 95% on 2 L via nasal prongs · T 36.9 °C. Face-to-face she is on an oxygen mask.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 5 minutes)
A chest X-ray is provided at 5 minutes — explain it to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. History 5 min · film ≤1 min · diagnosis, reasoning and differentials 2 min.

back.dx: Small right pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer — two months of progressive exertional breathlessness ('can't get enough air'), now some breathlessness at rest, pink/streaky red sputum five or six times in a fortnight (a few drops, no clots), dry cough, 5 kg weight loss since Easter, poor appetite, very tired; retired aged-care nurse; smoked ten years in her twenties; no asbestos, no fevers/sweats/travel, one pillow, no oedema. Film: blunted right costophrenic angle, sharp left angle, trachea central. DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: 'pleural effusion' is a sign, not a diagnosis — name the finding, then name the cause as 'a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung', justified from her own findings.
plan: Vitals — REACT to SpO2 91%: 'her saturations are low, so I'd keep her oxygen on while we talk'. WIPE, open question, acknowledge the fear, promise a process

Beat one (90 s): describe the breathlessness (air in / tightness / not enough air), duration, constant, worse?, modifiers → 'does rest help — are you ever breathless at rest?' → sputum: how many times, pink or red, streaks/clots, how much → cough, wheeze
Beat two (70 s): CANCER BLOCK FIRST — weight loss quantified, appetite, lumps, previous cancer, occupation now AND before, asbestos, arm numbness/eyelid/face (Pancoast)

Beat three: chest pain/palpitations/dizziness; family atopy; smoke now OR EVER; childhood chest infections; fever, sore throat, night sweats, travel, TB contact; pillows, leg swelling; rash, joints; tiredness; SADMA only if spare
Film in ≤1 min: three colours → heart, spine, airway central → normal LEFT side first, sharp angle → right angle missing, filled in → 'fluid around the lung — a pleural effusion'

'Breathlessness can have a number of causes — but in your case I have a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung' → three reasons (weight loss, blood in sputum, fluid on the film) → pause, acknowledge, support person → differential list → plan (bloods, CT, US-guided pleural tap, urgent respiratory referral) → safety-net → teach-back
ask: Examiner, before I begin, may I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature? → acknowledge the low saturation
'I'm so sorry to hear that, and I understand how worrying it must be. Let me ask a few questions, then I'll go through your chest X-ray with you, find the cause and make the best plan.'

Is it difficulty getting the breath in, tightness, or not enough air? How long? Constant or on and off? Worse? Better or worse with anything? ★ 'You've said it's worse walking — does rest make it better? Are you ever breathless at rest, sitting still?'
The pink phlegm — how many times? Pink or frankly red? Streaks or clots? A few drops, a teaspoon, or more? Cough with it? Noisy breathing or wheeze?

★ Cancer block: lost weight without trying — how much, over what period? Appetite? Lumps or bumps? Ever had cancer before? Occupation now — and before that? Asbestos? Numbness or weakness in the arm, anyone comment on your eyelid or face?
Chest pain, racing heart, dizziness? Family asthma, eczema, hay fever? ★ 'Do you smoke now, or have you ever smoked?' Recurrent chest infections as a child?
Fevers, chills, sore throat, runny nose? Night sweats, overseas travel, TB contact? Breathless lying flat — how many pillows? Leg swelling? Rashes, joint pains? Unusually tired?

Film: 'This is an X-ray of your chest. Three colours — white is bone, grey soft tissue, black is air. This big shadow is your heart, down the centre your spine, this line your main airway, sitting nicely central. Start with the normal side: on your left the lung is dark and there's a sharp angle at the bottom where lung meets chest wall. On your right that sharp angle is missing — filled in. That happens when fluid collects around the lung — we call it a pleural effusion.'
pefe: No examination task. If examiner wants a doctor-level read: erect PA, adequate inspiration and penetration, no rotation; blunting of the right costophrenic angle with a meniscus; trachea and mediastinum central; no pneumothorax; no focal bony lesion — small right pleural effusion. Never say this to the patient
Speak in HER sides — the patient's right is on the image left; the marker R sits over her right

Diagnosis: 'I do have a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung. I want to explain why, because it isn't a guess: you've been losing weight without trying, you've been coughing up what I believe is blood, and your X-ray shows fluid around the lung. I can't tell you today that that's what it is — but I'm not going to wait either.' → 'I can see that's a shock, I'm sorry to be telling you this today. Take a moment. Is there someone you'd like with you? I'll write everything down.'

Differentials, spoken: infection in the chest including TB (no fevers, sweats, travel) · heart not pumping well (one pillow, no ankle swelling) · liver or kidney problems, underactive thyroid · asthma · smoking damage · scarring from dusts at work · repeated chest infections · low in blood

Plan: FBE, UEC, LFT, TFT; CT chest; ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration by a specialist (protein, LDH, cytology ×3, MC&S, pH) — 'tells us what the fluid is and often what's causing it; draining some will help your breathing'; urgent respiratory referral; review in a few days regardless; safety-net — much more breathless, more blood, chest pain, fever → straight to hospital

Version B (James Whitlock, 70): massive LEFT effusion with mediastinal shift to the right — 'a large white shadow covering most of the lung, pressing it upward, and your heart has been pushed across'; answer = primary lung cancer OR metastatic prostate cancer (name both, say you can't separate them from the film), third differential occupational lung disease incl. mesothelioma (boilermaker, asbestos) → see MED-26
SA: urgent respiratory referral RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; Aboriginal Liaison Officer if relevant; TIS 131 450
fails: Never saying 'pleural effusion' on the film; or stopping at 'fluid in your lung' without naming the CAUSE ★
Cancer block left to the end 'if there's time'; weight loss not quantified; haemoptysis not characterised; 'do you smoke?' without 'ever' ★
'You have lung cancer' as a verdict — or 'probably nothing serious' as false reassurance; ploughing from the word cancer straight into the list without a pause
Omitting the rest-breathlessness question; forgetting pillows (HF) or travel (TB)
Jargon on the film (costophrenic, opacification); reversing her sides; film over a minute; not reacting to SpO2 91%
Skipping the differential list after naming cancer; no plan, no safety-net
numbers: Film script ≤1 min: three colours → three landmarks → normal side → abnormal side → NAME IT · white = bone, grey = soft tissue, black = air · heart, spine, trachea
Fluid visible ~200 mL on PA, ~50 mL lateral · white-out: shift AWAY = effusion, TOWARDS = collapse, none = consolidation VERIFY

Exudate: cancer, infection/empyema, TB, infarct, connective tissue · transudate: heart failure, liver failure, nephrotic, hypothyroidism · Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, fluid LDH >⅔ ULN VERIFY
Signs: reduced expansion, stony dull, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance · drain ≤1–1.5 L per sitting · cytology ×3 VERIFY

Four beats: complaint 90 s · cancer block 70 s · sweep 2 min · film + diagnosis + list + plan 3 min · self-check when the film appears: weight quantified, haemoptysis, previous cancer, occupation before, smoking ever

Variant B 'just tell me straight — is it cancer?' → 'I don't know yet — I need the scan and a sample of the fluid. But I won't pretend: cancer is the thing I'm most concerned about, which is why I'm arranging things urgently. You'll hear it from me as soon as I know' · Variant C 78 F, four pillows, oedema, bilateral small effusions, big heart → heart failure, not the cancer recall
Four questions for any named past condition: when · treatment · follow-up · complications

source: Chest_Xray_Pleural_Effusion_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Version A — Jenny Alcott, small right effusion)

stem: James Whitlock, 70, presents to your clinic. He has been breathless since last week. A colleague has already arranged a chest X-ray, which will be given to you at five minutes.
Observations on request: BP 138/82 · pulse 92 regular · RR 20 · SpO2 93% on room air · T 36.7 °C.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 5 minutes)
Explain the chest X-ray to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. History 5 min · film ≤1 min · diagnosis and differentials 2 min. The stem's 'last week' is a trap — the true timeline is three months.

back.dx: Massive left pleural effusion (near-total opacification, lung compressed, heart and mediastinum pushed to the right) — three months of worsening air hunger, much worse this past week, golf course down to the driveway, sometimes breathless at rest, dry cough; 'a bit' of weight loss = 3–4 kg over 2–3 months, appetite down; PROSTATE CANCER six years ago (surgery + radiotherapy, annual urology, PSA stable, no known spread, no bone pain); 'I don't smoke' = pack a day for 30 years, stopped 5 years ago; 'retired' = boilermaker, dust, fumes, probably asbestos; no haemoptysis, no fevers/sweats/travel, one pillow, no oedema. Answer: primary lung cancer OR metastatic prostate cancer — name BOTH and say you can't separate them from the film; third differential occupational lung disease (mesothelioma, asbestosis, plaques). He understates everything — make him quantify.
plan: Vitals (react to 93%); WIPE; open question; acknowledge; signpost the film
Clarify the TRUE duration; describe, constant, progression, modifiers; rest question + breathless at rest; cough, wheeze

Cancer block: weight — 'a bit' → how much, over what period; appetite; lumps; haemoptysis (ask it even though it's not in the stem); previous cancer → prostate → FOUR questions (when, treatment, follow-up, complications/spread) + bone pain; occupation now → 'and before you retired?' → boilermaker → asbestos, dust, fumes
Sweep: chest pain/palpitations/dizziness; family atopy; smoke now — 'have you ever?' → 30 pack-years; childhood infections; fever/sweats/travel/TB; pillows, oedema; rash/joints; tiredness

Film: three colours, three landmarks, normal RIGHT side first, then 'a large white shadow covering most of your left lung, pressing it upward, and your heart pushed across away from that side — fluid around the lung, a pleural effusion'; 'is that why I can't breathe?' → yes, draining will help

'My main concern is the possibility of a cancer in the lung — or a spread of your prostate cancer to the lung' → reasons (4 kg, previous cancer, 30 years smoking, large fluid collection) → honest that you can't tell which → beat of silence, 'I'm sorry to be telling you this' → occupational lung disease third (boilermaker: dust/asbestos scarring or a cancer of the lining of the lung) → rest of the list → plan → safety-net → support person, write it down
ask: Examiner, may I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, saturation, temperature? → 93% acknowledged

Describe the breathlessness — air in, tightness, or not enough air? ★ 'And how long, exactly?' (stem says last week; answer is three months) Constant or on and off? Worse? Better or worse with anything? Does rest help — ever breathless at rest? Cough? Wheeze?

★ Lost weight without trying? → 'a bit' → 'How much, and over what period?' Appetite? Lumps? ★ Ever coughed up blood? ★ Ever had cancer anywhere in the past? → 'When were you diagnosed? What treatment? Regular follow-up with GP and specialist? Any complications or sign of spread?' → 'Any bone pain — back, hips, ribs?'
★ Occupation now? → 'retired' → 'And what did you do before you retired?' → boilermaker → 'Were you ever exposed to asbestos, or to fumes and dusts?'

Chest pain, racing heart, dizziness? Family asthma, eczema, hay fever? ★ 'Do you smoke now, or have you ever smoked?' → pack a day 30 years, stopped 5 years ago. Childhood chest infections? Fevers, chills, sore throat, runny nose? Night sweats, travel, TB contact? Lying flat — pillows? Leg swelling? Rashes, joints? Tired?

Film: 'Three colours — white bone, grey soft tissue, black air. Heart, spine, main airway. On your right the lung is dark and healthy with a sharp angle at the bottom — normal. On your left there's a large white shadow covering most of the lung, pressing it upward, and your heart has been pushed across a little away from that side. That white area is fluid collecting around the lung — a pleural effusion.'

'James, breathlessness can have a number of causes. But in your case my main concern is the possibility of a cancer in the lung — or a spread of your prostate cancer to the lung. It isn't a guess: you've lost around four kilos without trying, you have a previous cancer, you smoked heavily for thirty years, and your X-ray shows a large collection of fluid. From the X-ray alone I can't tell which of those two it is — both are genuinely possible. That's what the next tests are for.'

'The other thing high on my list, because you were a boilermaker, is a lung condition caused by dust and asbestos — scarring, or a specific cancer of the lining of the lung. Beyond that: infection including TB; the heart not pumping well; smoking damage; asthma; repeated chest infections; being low in blood.'
pefe: No examination task. Doctor-level read if asked: near-complete opacification of the left hemithorax with a meniscus superiorly, mediastinal shift to the right, right lung clear, no visible rib lesion — massive left pleural effusion

If challenged on the boilermaker: 'boilermaking was a high asbestos-exposure trade in Australia, so alongside dust-related interstitial disease I'd specifically consider mesothelioma, asbestosis and benign pleural plaques — a unilateral effusion in that occupational context raises mesothelioma until excluded; it also has occupational compensation implications (ReturnToWorkSA / asbestos-related disease claims)'

Plan: bloods incl. FBE, UEC, LFT, PSA; CT chest ± abdomen/pelvis; ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration (protein, LDH, cytology ×3, MC&S) and therapeutic drainage ≤1–1.5 L per sitting; urgent respiratory referral; multidisciplinary lung cancer / urology input; safety-net — much more breathless, haemoptysis, chest pain, fever → hospital; support person (his wife); written summary

Role-player behaviour: understates; if you rush past the cancer word without acknowledgement he looks away and gives short answers; if you use jargon he asks 'sorry, what does that mean?'; near the end asks 'what else could it be?' / 'is it the cancer come back?'
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if he deteriorates in a regional setting; PATS for tertiary appointments; RFDS; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; TIS 131 450
fails: Naming only one cancer — not saying both primary lung and metastatic prostate, or not saying you can't separate them ★
Taking 'I don't smoke', 'I'm retired', 'a bit' at face value — missing 30 pack-years, the boilermaker, the 4 kg ★
Prostate cancer dropped and not followed by the four questions and bone pain
Accepting 'last week' from the stem; omitting the rest question; omitting haemoptysis because it wasn't in the stem
Not saying 'pleural effusion'; jargon; reversing sides; film over a minute; not describing the mediastinal shift
No occupational lung disease in the differential; no pause after bad news; no plan or safety-net
numbers: Version B: 70 M · 3 months · 3–4 kg loss · prostate cancer 6 years · 30 pack-years · boilermaker · massive left effusion with shift · answer = both cancers + occupational third
White-out with shift AWAY = effusion; TOWARDS = collapse; no shift = consolidation · massive effusion = >⅔ hemithorax VERIFY
Mesothelioma latency 20–40 years after asbestos · boilermaking, shipbuilding, lagging, Wittenoom = high-exposure history VERIFY
Four questions for a named past cancer: when · treatment · follow-up · complications/spread — then bone pain for prostate
Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5 · LDH ratio >0.6 · fluid LDH >⅔ ULN · cytology ×3 · drain ≤1–1.5 L per sitting VERIFY
Calibrated phrase: 'a concern about the possibility of' — never 'you have cancer', never 'probably nothing'
Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450

source: Chest_Xray_Pleural_Effusion_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Version B — James Whitlock, massive left effusion, dual diagnosis)

stem: Gerald Munro, 60, presents with shortness of breath for three months. The previous doctor has already requested a full blood count, thyroid, liver and renal function — all normal. Spirometry has also been requested and will be given to you.
Spirometry: FEV1 predicted 2.60 L, pre-bronchodilator 1.35 (52%), post 1.37 (53%) · FVC predicted 3.35, pre 2.50, post 2.54 · FEV1/FVC predicted 0.83, measured 0.54.
tasks: Take a history and rule out your differentials
Interpret the spirometry — to the examiner face-to-face, to the patient online
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes. History 5 · chart 1.5 · explanation 1.5.

back.dx: Moderate COPD — 40 pack-years ('gave it up two years back' — you must ask 'did you ever?'), three months of progressive exertional air hunger (stops at the top of the drive), not at rest, morning cough with clear phlegm; fitter at the works forty years with asbestos in the old sheds (ask occupation); no red flags, one pillow, no oedema, one BP tablet; father had emphysema. Chart: ratio 0.54 vs predicted 0.83 → obstructive; FEV1 1.35 → 1.37 = 20 mL, 1.5% → not reversible (<200 mL and <12%) → COPD not asthma; post-BD ratio <0.70 confirms; post-BD FEV1 53% = moderate. The examiner marks the WORKINGS: 'step one, the ratio measured against predicted…'. Hidden agenda: he blames himself and is frightened of ending up like his father.
plan: Vitals even though it's 'three months'; intro; 'how can I help?'; acknowledge the frustration of a pile of normal bloods and no answer; agenda
Heart or lung: tightness vs difficulty getting air in; duration; constant; worse?; better/worse; at rest?; cough, wheeze, phlegm
Cancer and occupation: weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, haemoptysis, previous cancer; occupation now and before; dust, fumes, stone, asbestos, mask

'Do you smoke, or did you?' → 'did you ever? how much, how long?' → say '40 pack-years' aloud; chest pain, palpitations, dizziness; pillows, ankle swelling; childhood infections; atopy/family asthma; fevers, sweats, travel, TB; joints, rashes; tiredness, bleeding; medications, allergies, FHx (father — emphysema)

Chart: FIVE SECONDS OF SILENCE → name the columns → step 1 ratio vs predicted → obstructive → step 2 FEV1 pre vs post (never the ratio again) → 0.02 L = 20 mL, 1.5% → below both thresholds → COPD → post-BD ratio <0.70 confirms → 53% = moderate

Diagnosis with TWO reasons (40 pack-years; airway narrowing that barely moved with Ventolin) → 'is it going to get worse?' honest: doesn't reverse, slope is in our hands, stopped smoking already, inhalers, pulmonary rehab, vaccines → differentials with one reason each (~8) → plan and summary to examiner
ask: Before I start, could I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?

Tell me about the breathlessness — is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in? How long, constant or comes and goes, getting worse? What makes it better or worse — and are you short of breath at rest as well? Cough, wheeze, noisy breathing, phlegm?
★ Lost weight without trying? Appetite? Lumps or bumps, night sweats? Have you coughed up any blood? Any previous cancer?
★ What is your occupation, and what did you do before that? Worked with dust, fumes or stone? Asbestos? Mask or respirator?
★ Do you smoke, or did you? → 'gave it up' → 'And before that — how much, and for how long?' → 'That's forty pack-years, which is important and I'll come back to it'

Chest pain on exertion, palpitations, dizziness? Worse lying flat — how many pillows? Ankle swelling? Childhood chest infections or repeated pneumonias? Hay fever, eczema, asthma in the family? Fevers, sweats, travel, TB contact? Joint pains, rashes? Tiredness, bleeding? Medications incl. anything long-term? Allergies? Family history?

Chart to the examiner: 'Before I interpret this, let me orientate myself to what I've been given: pre- and post-bronchodilator columns, predicted values, percentage predicted in brackets, and all three values I need — FEV1, FVC and the ratio. Step one, the ratio measured against predicted: 0.54 against 0.83 — decreased, so an obstructive pattern; obstruction is now certain. Step two, because the ratio is decreased, I compare FEV1 before and after the bronchodilator — the predicted values and the ratio are no longer relevant. 1.35 to 1.37 litres: 0.02 litres, that is 20 millilitres, about 1.5 per cent. Under 200 mL and under 12 per cent — no significant reversibility, so COPD rather than asthma. Post-bronchodilator ratio remains below 0.70, which confirms COPD; post-bronchodilator FEV1 53 per cent predicted = moderate airflow limitation.'

To the patient (online): 'Three numbers — total air you can blow out, air in the first second, and the ratio. Your ratio is lower than expected for your age and height — narrowing in your airways. We gave you a puff of Ventolin and repeated it; your numbers barely moved, about 20 millilitres. Asthma usually improves a lot with that puffer, this hasn't. So the pattern fits COPD.'
pefe: No examination task

Diagnosis: 'most likely COPD — chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. In plain terms your lungs have been damaged by many years of smoking. Two reasons: a pack a day for forty years, the single biggest cause; and your breathing test shows narrowing that barely improved with the puffer — that pattern points to COPD rather than asthma'

'Is it going to get worse?' → 'I'll be honest: COPD doesn't reverse. But how fast it progresses is very much in our hands — the biggest thing is you've already stopped smoking, which changes the slope more than any tablet. Inhalers make day-to-day breathing easier, pulmonary rehabilitation genuinely improves what people can do, vaccinations keep you out of hospital'

Differentials, one reason each: lung cancer (no weight loss, no haemoptysis — still CXR) · IHD and heart failure (no chest pain, no oedema, sleeps flat) · asthma (puffer test) · interstitial lung disease from asbestos (HRCT, keep an eye) · bronchiectasis · infections incl. TB · sarcoidosis · anaemia (FBC normal)

Summary to examiner: CXR; consider HRCT for the asbestos history; reinforce abstinence; inhaled bronchodilator (LAMA first-line; LAMA/LABA if still symptomatic); pulmonary rehabilitation; influenza, pneumococcal, COVID vaccination; written COPD action plan; review; Lung Foundation resources VERIFY
SA: pulmonary rehab via Country Health Connect / local hospital; Quitline 13 7848 (already quit — relapse prevention); PATS for respiratory review; TIS 131 450
fails: Reading numbers out and appending a guess — 'ratio 0.54, FEV1 1.35, I think COPD' ★
Comparing the ratio pre and post bronchodilator instead of FEV1 ★
Quoting one threshold, or getting the units wrong (0.02 L is 20 mL, not 0.02 mL) ★
Not asking 'did you ever smoke?' — missing 40 pack-years ★
Dropping the cancer questions / haemoptysis because the bloods were normal ★
Not pausing to read the chart layout; naming the pattern not the disease; fewer than six differentials; breezy 'nothing to worry about' ('my father died of this'); jargon ('you've lost me, doc')
numbers: Three values only: FEV1 · FVC · FEV1/FVC · % predicted = measured ÷ predicted × 100 · reversibility = (post − pre) ÷ pre × 100 · significant = ≥200 mL AND ≥12% · bronchodilator repeated after 10–15 min VERIFY

This chart: ratio 0.54 vs 0.83 · FEV1 1.35 → 1.37 L = 20 mL, 1.5% · post-BD ratio <0.70 = COPD · severity on post-BD FEV1 %: ≥80 mild · 50–79 moderate · 30–49 severe · <30 very severe → 53% moderate VERIFY (GOLD)
Pack-years = packs/day × years: 1 × 40 = 40 · FeNO ≥40 ppb supports asthma · mesothelioma latency 20–40 years VERIFY

Variant 1 restrictive (45-yo stonemason, engineered benchtops): ratio 0.90 vs 0.79 = increased → not obstructive; FEV1 and FVC both ~half predicted → restrictive; confirm with lung volumes and gas transfer, HRCT; ILD/silicosis; notify SafeWork SA, ReturnToWorkSA claim, screen co-workers; engineered stone prohibited nationally VERIFY
Variant 2 reversible: FEV1 3.00 → 3.70 = 700 mL, 23% → exceeds both thresholds → asthma

Variant 3 spirometry pending, CXR handed over: flattened hemidiaphragms, hyperlucent fields, long narrow tubular heart, >6 anterior ribs above the diaphragm → hyperinflation, emphysema/COPD — describe first, don't just say 'COPD'
Variant 4 normal chart: doesn't exclude asthma (normal between episodes) → FeNO or bronchial challenge; revisit cardiac and non-respiratory causes

stem: Mrs Margaret Ellis, 72, presents with shortness of breath and cough.
A chest X-ray will be provided. Observations available from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a history (5 minutes)
Interpret and explain the chest X-ray to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes. Reading 2 min · history 5 · CXR 1 · diagnosis and differentials 1–2.

back.dx: Lung cancer — six months of gradually worsening exertional breathlessness (walks the dog, now stops twice), cough with 'yellowish' phlegm that is BLOOD-STREAKED for the last fortnight (disclosed only if you ask a second, specific question about blood), 7–8 kg unintentional weight loss over four months, 30 pack-years (quit five years ago), builder with old asbestos exposure; one pillow, no oedema, no fevers, no chest pain. Film: a MASS in the lung field, no effusion — a mass is grey on grey, scan both fields deliberately, especially behind the heart, apices and hila. Hidden agenda: a brother had lung cancer. Discriminating behaviour: warning shot → the word cancer → apology → SILENCE → check in.
plan: Observations from the examiner; WIPE; 'are you short of breath sitting here now?'; open question; acknowledge; agenda

Breathlessness in three boxes: describe (what it feels like, constant, what can't you do now, walking distance, lie flat, wake at night) · time (sudden/gradual, worse) · what changes it (exertion, lying, dust, work; better; puffers)
★ The sputum: 'what colour exactly?' → 'and have you ever seen any blood in it — even streaks or specks, even once?'

Systems: infection (fever, chills, soaking sweats, TB contact, travel) · heart (chest pain, ankle swelling, pillows, palpitations) · clot (calf, surgery, immobility, flights) · reflux/airway (heartburn, post-nasal drip, voice) · blood count (tired, dizzy, black/bloody stools)

★ Red-flag block: weight — how much, how long; night sweats; hoarseness; dysphagia; bone/shoulder/arm pain; headaches, morning vomiting, weakness; face/arm swelling, chest veins; smoke or ever — pack-years said aloud; work over your life — asbestos, dust, fumes
Close: conditions, medications incl. puffers/OTC, allergies, family lung problems/cancer, who's at home, 'anything you were particularly worried this might be?' → brother
Film to the patient: three colours → normal side, sharp angle → 'on this side something that shouldn't be there — an abnormal mass, a growth, in the lung. That raises the possibility of a cancer'

'Is there anyone you'd like with you?' → 'I'm afraid what I've found is more serious than a simple chest infection' [pause] → the word → 'I'm sorry to have to say that' [pause — don't fill it] → 'what's going through your mind?' → not a diagnosis yet → differentials briskly → urgent CT + respiratory referral + MDT → 'I'll ring you personally' → safety-net → longer appointment, support person → questions
ask: Before I start, may I have her observations — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?

What does the breathlessness feel like, when did you first notice it? All the time or comes and goes? What can't you do now that you could six months ago? How far on the flat before you stop? Can you lie flat — wake at night short of breath? Sudden or gradual, getting worse? What makes it worse — exertion, lying down, dust, work? Better? Tried any puffers?
★ Tell me about the cough. Bringing anything up? What colour exactly? — And have you ever seen any blood in it, even streaks or specks, even once?

Fevers, chills, night sweats that soak the sheets? TB contact, travel? Chest pain or tightness, ankle swelling, how many pillows? Palpitations? Calf pain or swelling, recent surgery, immobility, long flights? Heartburn, post-nasal drip, change in your voice? Tiredness, dizziness, black or bloody stools?

★ Lost any weight without trying — how much, and over how long? Night sweats? Voice hoarse? Trouble swallowing? New bone pain, or shoulder/arm pain? Headaches, morning vomiting, weakness anywhere? Swelling of face or arms, veins standing out on the chest? Do you smoke, or have you ever — how many a day, how many years? → 'so around thirty pack-years'. What work over your life — asbestos, dust, fumes?
Other conditions? Medications incl. puffers and anything you buy? Allergies? Family lung problems or cancer? Who's at home, how are you managing? Anything you were particularly worried this might be?

Film: 'Margaret, this is an X-ray of your chest. Three colours: white bone, grey soft tissue, black air. On this side — the normal side — the normal dark shadow of your lung and a nice sharp angle at the bottom. But on this side I can see something that shouldn't be there: an abnormal mass, a growth, in the lung. And that raises the possibility of a cancer.'

'Before I go on — is there anyone you'd like with you for this, or would you rather I go ahead? … I'm afraid what I've found is more serious than a simple chest infection. [pause] Together with the weight loss, the blood in your phlegm and your smoking history, my main concern is that this could be a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that.' [pause] → 'That's a lot to take in. What's going through your mind?'
pefe: No PEFE task in Version A — the film replaces it. If the examiner asks for a doctor-level description: erect PA, a rounded/spiculated opacity in the [zone], no effusion, trachea central, look for hilar enlargement, rib lesions, contralateral nodules

'How long have I got?' → 'I understand why you're asking, and I'm not going to give you a number I can't stand behind. We don't yet know what this is, and if it is a cancer, what matters is the type and whether it has spread — that's exactly what the scan and the sample will tell us. What I can promise is that I won't keep anything from you'

Differentials to the patient: a heart problem (no chest pain, normal heart exam) · COPD from smoking · asthma (no wheeze) · infection incl. TB · abscess · scarring of the lungs · mesothelioma, linked to asbestos · heart failure · low blood count — 'today's finding is the one I want to act on straight away'

Plan: urgent CT chest with contrast (± upper abdomen), urgent respiratory referral, tissue via bronchoscopy/CT-guided biopsy, lung cancer MDT; FBE, UEC, LFT, Ca; 'I'll ring you personally with the scan result'; safety-net — more than a small amount of blood, worse breathing, chest pain, face/arm swelling → straight back/ED; longer appointment this week, bring her daughter; written information; Cancer Council 13 11 20

Variant 1 — she asks at 3 min 'just tell me straight, is it cancer?': 'I can hear that's what's frightening you and I won't dodge it. It's one of the things I need to rule out — that's exactly why I'm asking about the weight and the phlegm. I can't answer properly before I've looked at your X-ray, and I don't want to guess. Give me a few more minutes and I'll tell you honestly where I stand'

Variant 2 — CXR reported normal: 'No, it doesn't change my management. A plain film misses a significant proportion of lung cancers — small, central, apical, behind the heart or diaphragm. In a smoker with unintentional weight loss and haemoptysis a normal film is not reassuring; urgent CT with contrast and respiratory referral, and I'd tell her that so she doesn't leave falsely reassured'

Variant 4 — she declines: 'That's your decision and I'll respect it — I want to make sure it's informed. What's behind it? … A diagnosis doesn't mean treatment you don't want; knowing also lets us control symptoms far better. Is there anything you'd want to arrange if time were shorter? Nothing has to be decided today — come back this week with your daughter; my door stays open'. SA: PATS, RFDS if regional; Aboriginal Liaison Officer; TIS 131 450
fails: Never asking specifically about blood in the sputum — stopping at 'yellowish' ★
Never asking about weight loss, or not quantifying it ★
Never saying the word cancer (evasion), or saying it with no warning shot and no pause (bluntness) ★
Giving a prognosis or a number; false reassurance; filling the silence
'I used to smoke' not converted to pack-years; no occupational/asbestos history; brother never elicited
Finishing without urgent CT and urgent specialist referral; no safety-net; leaving the mass undescribed on the film
numbers: Pack-years = packs/day × years · this case ~30 · Quitline 13 7848 · Cancer Council 13 11 20 · TIS 131 450

National Lung Cancer Screening Program (from 1 July 2025): 50–70, ≥30 pack-years, current or quit within 10 years, ASYMPTOMATIC only, low-dose CT every 2 years — a symptomatic patient needs a diagnostic CT, not screening VERIFY

Non-small cell ≈85% of lung cancers · red flags: haemoptysis, weight loss, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal), dysphagia, bone pain, Pancoast (shoulder/arm, Horner's), SVC obstruction, cerebral metastases (headache, morning vomiting, weakness)
A mass on CXR: grey against grey — scan behind the heart, apices, hila; a normal film does not change the diagnosis with weight loss + haemoptysis

Variant 3 SVC obstruction ('face puffy in the mornings, collar tight'): facial/upper limb oedema, non-pulsatile distended neck veins, chest wall collaterals, conjunctival oedema, Pemberton's sign → oncological emergency: sit upright, oxygen if hypoxic, urgent CT with contrast today, respiratory + oncology now (steroids, stenting, radiotherapy), hospital not outpatient VERIFY

Breaking bad news sequence: permission/support person → warning shot → the word → apology → silence → 'what's going through your mind?' → not yet a diagnosis → plan with timeframe → safety-net → longer appointment

stem: Mr James Doherty, 50, presents with breathing difficulty.
Observations available from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes online / 4 minutes face-to-face)
Request the physical examination findings from your examiner (online: they appear on screen)
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes. History 6 (online) or 4 (face-to-face) · PEFE hand-over 1 · diagnosis and differentials 1–2.

back.dx: Malignant left pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer — same history as MED-28: six months of worsening exertional breathlessness, cough with yellowish then blood-streaked phlegm (ask about blood specifically), 7–8 kg over four months, 30 pack-years quit five years ago, builder with asbestos, one pillow, no oedema; brother died of lung cancer (hidden). PEFE: no distress, no clubbing, BP 110/70, P 84, RR 12, T 36.9, SpO2 98%; LEFT base — decreased expansion, dull, ABSENT breath sounds, DECREASED vocal resonance, trachea midline; CVS normal; no oedema. Interpret aloud before you turn back: 'the four signs of a pleural effusion — and why is the fluid there?'
plan: Observations; WIPE; 'short of breath sitting here?'; open question; acknowledge ('my wife made me come' → 'I'm glad she did')

Three boxes on the breathlessness; ★ sputum colour then blood; systems screen; ★ red-flag block with weight quantified, pack-years aloud, occupation/asbestos; close with concerns → brother. Face-to-face 4-min: intro → breathlessness → sputum/blood → weight/smoking/asbestos → concerns; sacrifice the tail
'James, just give me one moment — I'll speak with my examiner and be right back. Apologies.' → turn → one fluent request block → findings → INTERPRET ALOUD → turn back: 'thank you for waiting'

Support person → warning shot → 'fluid around the bottom of your left lung — that's why you're breathless. What concerns me is why … my main concern is that this could be a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that' → silence → 'what's going through your mind?' → not yet a diagnosis

'How long have I got?' → no number, honesty promised → differentials briskly → urgent CT + urgent respiratory referral + pleural aspiration (diagnostic and therapeutic) + MDT → 'I'll ring you with the result' → safety-net → longer appointment, bring your wife → summary → questions
ask: Before I start, may I have his observations — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, saturation and temperature?
★ Are you bringing anything up? What colour exactly? — And have you ever seen any blood in it, even streaks, even once?
★ Lost weight without trying — how much, over how long? Smoke, or ever — how many a day, how many years? → pack-years aloud. What work have you done — any asbestos, dust or fumes?
Was there anything you were particularly worried this might be? → 'my brother had lung cancer' → 'thank you for telling me — I'll come back to that directly'

★ To the examiner, one breath: 'General appearance — respiratory distress, cyanosis, cachexia, finger clubbing, palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy? Vitals — BP, pulse rate and rhythm, respiratory rate, temperature, saturation on room air. Respiratory — chest movements symmetrical? trachea midline? percussion note? breath sounds and added sounds? vocal resonance? Cardiovascular — JVP raised, apex displaced, heart sounds, murmurs or gallop? Peripheries — leg swelling, calf tenderness? Office tests — ECG, spirometry or peak flow, urine dipstick?'

★ 'Thank you. Reduced expansion, dullness, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance at the left base are the signs of a pleural effusion. Given the weight loss, the haemoptysis and the smoking history, my principal concern is a malignant effusion secondary to lung cancer.' → turn back

'Before I go on — is there anyone you'd like with you for this, or would you rather I go ahead? … I'm afraid what I've found is more serious than a simple chest infection. [pause] The examination shows fluid collected around the bottom of your left lung, and that's why you're breathless. What concerns me is why that fluid is there. Together with the weight loss, the blood in your phlegm and your smoking history, my main concern is that this could be a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that.' [pause]

'That's a lot to take in. What's going through your mind?' → 'This isn't a diagnosis yet — we need a scan and a sample of that fluid to know for certain. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I didn't tell you honestly what I'm thinking.'
pefe: Effusion signs: reduced expansion · stony dullness · absent breath sounds · reduced vocal resonance · trachea pushed away if large. Consolidation: dull · bronchial breathing · crackles · INCREASED vocal resonance. Collapse: trachea pulled towards
Three hand-over traps: turning away without excusing yourself · a long conversation with your back to the patient · forgetting to turn back and re-engage before you explain

Differentials: heart problem (no chest pain, normal CVS exam) · COPD · asthma (no wheeze, no history) · infection incl. TB · abscess · lung scarring · mesothelioma (asbestos, builder) · heart failure · low blood count

Plan: urgent CT chest with contrast; urgent respiratory referral; ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration — protein, LDH, cytology ×3, MC&S (Light's criteria; exudate expected) — diagnostic and eases breathing, ≤1–1.5 L per sitting; bloods; MDT; 'I'll ring you personally'; safety-net — more than a small amount of blood, breathing worsens, chest pain, face/arm swelling; longer appointment this week; bring his wife; Cancer Council 13 11 20

Role-player: withholds blood unless asked specifically; 'a bit' of weight; five-second silence after cancer — if you fill it he goes flat and monosyllabic; asks 'how long have I got?' and marks down any number; ends with 'am I going to be alright?'
SA: urgent respiratory/pleural clinic RAH, FMC, Lyell McEwin; PATS and RFDS if regional; TIS 131 450
fails: Never asking specifically about blood in the sputum; never asking/quantifying weight loss ★
Hearing 'absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance' and saying 'thank you' — not interpreting aloud as effusion and asking why ★
Never saying cancer; or no warning shot and no pause; giving a number for prognosis ★
Turning to the examiner without excusing yourself; not turning back; omitting vocal resonance and lymph nodes from the request
No pack-years; no occupation/asbestos; concerns never elicited
No urgent CT and urgent referral; no safety-net; no support person/longer appointment
numbers: Light's criteria (exudate if any one): pleural/serum protein >0.5 · pleural/serum LDH >0.6 · pleural LDH >⅔ ULN serum LDH · drain ≤1–1.5 L at one aspiration VERIFY
30 pack-years · 7–8 kg / 4 months · SpO2 98% (a normal saturation does not exclude a malignant effusion)
National Lung Cancer Screening Program: 50–70, ≥30 pack-years, current or quit ≤10 y, asymptomatic, LDCT 2-yearly — he is symptomatic → diagnostic CT VERIFY
Trachea: pulled towards collapse; pushed away by large effusion or tension pneumothorax
Variant 3 SVC obstruction — puffy face, tight collar → emergency: upright, oxygen, CT today, respiratory + oncology now

stem: Your next patient is Ron Petrie, a 66-year-old man, who has presented to you complaining of shortness of breath.
Spirometry report provided: FEV1/FVC ratio reduced · post-bronchodilator FEV1 improvement of 3% and 120 mL from baseline · pattern obstructive, without significant reversibility.
tasks: Explain the spirometry to the patient
Take a relevant history (five minutes for tasks 1 and 2 together)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings (or read them from the screen)
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes (2 min reading). Spirometry ≤90 s · history to 5:00 · PEFE ~1 min · explanation ~2 min.

back.dx: Lung cancer on a background of COPD — 'AND ALSO', not 'it's COPD'. Spirometry is genuinely COPD (obstructive, +3%/+120 mL fails both thresholds). History: 3 years of slowly worsening exertional breathlessness, dry cough, courier driver (before that roadworks, before that a workshop with old lagging), 10/day since age 20, NO haemoptysis, one pillow, no oedema, no fever — and 6–7 kg unintentional weight loss over a few months, trousers loose, appetite down (NOT volunteered). PEFE: CLUBBING, reduced expansion, trachea midline, percussion normal, vocal resonance normal, crackles mid-zone LOCALISED (only if you ask localised vs generalised), SpO2 95%, CVS normal. Three findings COPD cannot explain: weight loss, clubbing, localised crackles. Belief: 'it's the smoking catching up with me'. Hidden agenda: losing his licence = losing the job, three years off the pension.
plan: Spirometry in 90 s: two things measured; proportion out in the first second reduced = resistance = obstructive; reliever repeated — improved only 3%/120 mL, we need ≥12% AND ≥200 mL; didn't reverse → in a smoker = COPD; if it had reversed → asthma

'Even though that test points to COPD, I don't want to assume it explains everything' → breathlessness: how long, constant, worse, walking distance then vs now, lie flat/pillows, waking, ankle swelling, cough dry/productive, blood, wheeze

★ Cancer block: weight without trying → how much, over how long → appetite; lumps neck/collarbones; sweats/fevers; bone pain; voice; job now — and before that — and before that; asbestos by name (construction, mining, welding, shipping, lagging, brake linings); previous cancer

Briskly: chest pain/palpitations/dizziness; asthma/hay fever; recurrent infections/daily phlegm; joints/rash/dry eyes; fever/travel/TB; calf/flights/surgery; tired/pale/bleeding; cigarettes and years, tried to stop; medicines; past; family; home and work; 'what do you think is going on, what worries you most?'

'Give me one moment — I'll ask my examiner and come straight back' → ordered request incl. clubbing, nodes, 'are the added sounds localised or generalised?', vocal resonance → INTERPRET BEFORE TURNING BACK: clubbing is not a feature of COPD → lung cancer top of the list; localised crackles → localised lesion; with weight loss → leading diagnosis lung cancer on a background of COPD

Support person? → 'Your test does show COPD, and you were right about the smoking — we'll treat that' [pause] → 'But COPD doesn't explain everything: 6–7 kg, the fingertip changes, crackles in one area' [pause] → 'what I'm most concerned about is a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that. We don't know it yet' → silence → other differentials: bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, TB — all can club

Plan: CXR + bloods today; CT chest/upper abdomen this week; bronchoscopy/biopsy if positive; specialist team. COPD: Quitline 13 7848, NRT/varenicline, vaccines, pulmonary rehab. 'Should I tell Denise?' → his call, welcome her at the scan visit; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20. Safety-net: blood, sudden worsening, chest pain, fever → ED. Summary: two diagnoses
ask: 'This test measures how much air you can blow out in total, and how much of it you can get out in the very first second. In your case the proportion coming out in the first second is reduced — the air is meeting resistance on the way out; the airways are narrowed. We call that an obstructive pattern. Then we gave you a reliever puffer and repeated it. It improved by only about three per cent, a hundred and twenty millilitres — we look for at least twelve per cent and two hundred millilitres before we call that a real response. Narrowing that does not reverse, in someone who has smoked, is COPD.'
★ 'Now, even though that test points to COPD, I don't want to assume it explains everything.'
★ 'There are some questions I ask everybody with these symptoms. Have you lost any weight without trying to? … How much, over how long? … How is your appetite?'

Lumps in the neck or above the collarbones? Night sweats, fevers? Bone pain? Voice changed? What's your job now — and what did you do before that? Ever worked around asbestos — lagging, old brake linings, construction, welding? Ever had a cancer? Has there ever been any blood in the phlegm?
How many cigarettes, for how many years? Tried to stop? And finally — what do you think might be going on, and what are you most worried about?

★ To the examiner: 'General appearance — respiratory distress, cyanosis, cachexia, clubbing, palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy? Vitals incl. saturation on room air. Respiratory — chest movements symmetrical, trachea midline, percussion note, breath sounds, added sounds — and are they localised or generalised? — vocal resonance. Cardiovascular — JVP, apex, heart sounds, murmur or gallop. Lower limbs — oedema, calf tenderness.'

★ 'Thank you. Two of those findings are significant. Clubbing is not a feature of COPD — in a patient with obstructive lung disease it obliges me to look for another cause, and top of that list is lung cancer. And the added sounds are localised; in COPD I would expect them generalised, so localised crackles point to a localised lesion. Taken with the weight loss, my leading diagnosis is now a lung cancer on a background of COPD.'

'You do have COPD, and we will treat it — and there are things here that COPD does not explain, so I am also concerned about a cancer.' → 'From my fingers?' → 'It sounds strange, I know. But clubbing is a signal the body gives, and it's one we take seriously. What's going through your mind?'
pefe: Findings given only when asked and only what you ask for: clubbing present; no cyanosis, distress, cachexia or lymphadenopathy; BP 132/78, P 82, RR 18, T 36.7, SpO2 95% RA; reduced expansion, trachea midline, percussion normal, breath sounds present with crackles in the mid zone — localised; vocal resonance normal; JVP not raised, apex undisplaced, dual heart sounds; no oedema; ECG sinus
'How long have I got?' → no number; type and spread decide; the scan will tell us; 'I won't keep anything from you'

Plan with timeframes: CXR and bloods today · CT chest and upper abdomen this week · sample through a camera into the airways if positive · specialist MDT · COPD: stopping smoking is the single thing that changes its course — Quitline 13 7848, patches, tablets · influenza/pneumococcal/COVID · pulmonary rehab · review as soon as the scan is back, wife welcome

Driving: the licence worry — don't pre-empt; if he raises it, acknowledge honestly that fitness to drive depends on what is found and how he is, and that you'll help him through Austroads/ReturnToWork if needed VERIFY
SA: Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 (anonymous); Yorke Peninsula → PATS for CT/respiratory in Adelaide; Country Health Connect; TIS 131 450
fails: 'It's COPD' — diagnosing COPD and stopping ★
Never asking about weight loss (it is not volunteered) ★
Hearing 'clubbing' and saying 'thank you' — not interpreting it ★
Never asking whether the crackles are localised or generalised ★
Four minutes on the spirometry; wrong reversibility threshold; skipping the differential blocks because 'we already know'
Cancer buried ('a few possibilities, we'll run tests') or announced with no warning shot; filling the silence; inventing a prognosis; no safety-net; no plan timeframe
numbers: Reversibility ≥12% AND ≥200 mL from measured baseline — this case +3%/+120 mL fails both · COPD = post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.7 · chronic cough >8 weeks

Clubbing: Lovibond angle >180°, Schamroth's window obliterated · causes to name: lung cancer, bronchiectasis, ILD/fibrosis, TB/empyema/abscess (NOT COPD) · localised crackles = localised lesion; COPD crackles generalised
Effusion: reduced expansion, stony dull, absent BS, reduced VR · consolidation: dull, bronchial breathing, increased VR · Light's: protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, LDH >⅔ ULN VERIFY

Effusion variant Version 1 (no weight loss, orthopnoea, more pillows): heart failure with transudative effusion first, COPD second — still sample the fluid · Version 2 (weight loss added): malignant effusion first, HF second, COPD third — weight loss is incompatible with the fluid retention of decompensated HF (cardiac cachexia is late) → see MED-31
Pass guide: 20+ of 28 with every bold item; missing the weight-loss question or hearing clubbing without interpreting it fails on its own
Quitline 13 7848 · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · My Aged Care 1800 200 422 · TIS 131 450
