setting: General practice. (Stem reconstructed from the variant section — the notes give findings and history, not a verbatim door stem.)
stem: A 50-year-old man who smokes presents with shortness of breath, worse lying flat, and a productive cough. He has been using more pillows.
Version 1: no weight loss. Version 2: significant unintentional weight loss added — one line in the history changes the whole ranking.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Same spine as MED-30; the examination findings are identical in both versions — the history decides the answer.

back.dx: Findings in both versions: reduced chest expansion at the LEFT base, dull to percussion, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance, trachea central = left pleural effusion. VERSION 1 (orthopnoea, increasing pillows, NO weight loss): heart failure with a secondary transudative effusion first, COPD second (smoking, productive cough) — still sample the fluid because malignancy stays on the list. VERSION 2 (weight loss added): malignant pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer first, heart failure second, COPD third — weight loss is not compatible with the fluid retention of decompensated heart failure (cardiac cachexia is late and in established disease). Same four signs, different ranking; the marks are in saying why, out loud, to the examiner.
plan: Vitals; WIPE; open question; acknowledge
Breathlessness: duration, course, exertion, ★ orthopnoea and pillow count, PND, ankle swelling; cough — colour, blood; wheeze

★ Cancer block: weight loss — ask it, quantify it; appetite; lumps; sweats; haemoptysis; occupation/asbestos; smoking pack-years; cardiac — chest pain, palpitations, previous MI/hypertension; infection; VTE; concerns

Excuse yourself → examiner block (appearance, clubbing, nodes, vitals, expansion, trachea, percussion, breath sounds, added sounds localised/generalised, vocal resonance, JVP, apex, heart sounds, oedema) → interpret: 'the four signs of a pleural effusion at the left base' → RANK with reasons before turning back

Version 1 to the patient: fluid around the left lung → with breathless lying flat and extra pillows, most likely the heart isn't pumping as strongly, fluid backs up — heart failure, treatable; also COPD; 'whenever there's fluid like this in someone who's smoked I have to rule out a cancer — sample and scan'. Version 2: support person → warning shot → fluid → 'because you've also lost weight without trying, and your smoking history, the possibility I'm most concerned about is a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry. We don't know it yet' → HF and COPD also → sample + CT this week

Plan: pleural aspiration (protein, LDH, cytology), CXR, CT chest, echo + BNP, ECG, FBE/UEC/LFT/TFT; diuretic and cardiology if HF; urgent respiratory referral if Version 2; smoking cessation; safety-net; summary
ask: Is the breathlessness worse lying flat? How many pillows — has that number gone up? Do you wake at night gasping? Ankle swelling? Any chest pain, palpitations, previous heart problems or high blood pressure?
★ Have you lost any weight without trying? How much, over how long? Appetite? (Version 1: no. Version 2: yes — significant)
Cough — what colour, any blood ever? Do you smoke — how many, how long? What work — asbestos, dust, fumes?
★ Examiner: '…percussion note, breath sounds, added sounds — localised or generalised — and the vocal resonance? Is the trachea central?'

★ Version 1 interpretation: 'Reduced expansion, dullness, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance at the left base are the four signs of a pleural effusion. With orthopnoea and increasing pillow use, and no weight loss, my leading diagnosis is heart failure with a secondary transudative effusion. COPD is second given the smoking and productive cough. I would still sample the fluid, because malignancy remains on my list.'

★ Version 2 interpretation: 'The same four signs give a left pleural effusion. However, in a 50-year-old smoker with significant unintentional weight loss, my leading diagnosis is now a malignant pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer. Heart failure is second and COPD third. Weight loss is not compatible with the fluid retention of decompensated heart failure — cardiac cachexia occurs, but late and in established disease.'

Version 1 to the patient: 'What I found is fluid collected around the bottom of your left lung, and that's what's making you breathless. Together with being breathless lying flat and needing extra pillows, I think the most likely cause is that your heart isn't pumping as strongly as it should, which lets fluid back up — we call that heart failure, and it's treatable. I'm also considering damage from smoking, COPD. And I have to be straight with you: whenever there's fluid like this in someone who's smoked, I have to rule out a cancer, so I'm going to take a sample of the fluid and arrange a scan.'

Version 2 to the patient: 'Before I go on — is there anyone you'd like with you? … What I found is fluid around your left lung. [pause] Because you've also lost weight without trying, and because of your smoking history, the possibility I am most concerned about is a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that, and we don't know it yet. I'm also thinking about a heart problem, and about COPD. The tests are designed to tell them apart — a sample of the fluid, and a CT scan, both this week.'
pefe: Findings (both versions): reduced expansion left base · dull · absent breath sounds · reduced vocal resonance · trachea central. Also ask JVP, apex, gallop, oedema — raised JVP/S3/oedema push toward HF; clubbing/nodes/cachexia push toward cancer
Transudate causes: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic, hypothyroidism · exudate: malignancy, infection/empyema, TB, PE, connective tissue · Light's criteria decide

Version 1 plan: CXR, ECG, echo, BNP, UEC/FBE/TFT/LFT, pleural aspiration (still), loop diuretic, daily weights, fluid/salt advice, cardiology, smoking cessation, spirometry for COPD; safety-net — worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis

Version 2 plan: urgent CT chest with contrast, urgent respiratory referral, pleural aspiration for cytology ×3, MDT; echo/BNP still to exclude HF as contributor; warning shot, pause, no prognosis; support person; Cancer Council 13 11 20
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if hypoxic/unstable in a rural site; PATS; TIS 131 450
fails: Reaching the wrong ranking without stating the reasoning — you can be wrong and pass, you cannot pass without visible reasoning ★
Version 1: not still sampling the fluid / not saying cancer is still on the list in a smoker ★
Version 2: not asking about weight loss, or hearing it and leaving heart failure on top ★
Not asking pillows/orthopnoea; not requesting vocal resonance; not interpreting the four signs aloud
Version 2 cancer named without warning shot or buried; prognosis invented
Running the two versions back to back with a partner — use separate days (from the notes)
numbers: Four effusion signs: reduced expansion · stony dull · absent breath sounds · reduced vocal resonance · trachea central (small) or pushed away (large)
Heart failure = fluid-retaining state → weight GAIN (hence diuretics and daily weights); unintentional weight LOSS argues against decompensated HF; cardiac cachexia is late

Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5 · LDH ratio >0.6 · pleural LDH >⅔ ULN → exudate if any one VERIFY · HF effusions usually bilateral, right > left; a unilateral left effusion is less typical for HF — another reason to sample VERIFY
BNP/NT-proBNP and echo for HF; CXR — cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B, bilateral effusions
Ranking Version 1: HF → COPD → (malignancy still on list) · Version 2: lung cancer → HF → COPD

stem: Robert Hale, 60, a farmer in rural Queensland, presents with shortness of breath. He had a myocardial infarction one year ago treated with thrombolysis, and has had no GP follow-up since.
Vitals: BP 140/90 · PR 96 · RR 14 · T 36.5 °C · SpO2 99% room air.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. History 6 min online / 4 min face-to-face · leave 2 minutes for task 3.

back.dx: Congestive heart failure from ischaemic cardiomyopathy — six months of progressive exertional air hunger ('can't get enough air in', NOT tight like the heart attack), stops halfway up the paddock, not at rest unless overdone; orthopnoea on THREE pillows, PND, both ankles swell by evening; no chest pain/palpitations/dizziness; no cough/wheeze/haemoptysis/weight loss. The clue in the stem: thrombolysed MI a year ago at the base hospital — RAN OUT of tablets three or four months in, no script since, no GP (three-hour round trip). Wheat farm + a few hundred cattle, asbestos in the old sheds, never had the Q fever vaccine; 30 pack-years, quit after the MI; father MI at 62. PEFE: JVP >3 cm, displaced apex, parasternal heave, S3 gallop, bibasal creps, hepatomegaly + positive hepatojugular reflux, bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin. The station turns on 'I was also thinking about…' said once per differential, after you already know it's heart failure. Hidden agenda: can he keep working the farm; guilt about the tablets.
plan: Vitals from the examiner; sit; 'how can I help?'; the fixed acknowledgement line

★ 'Is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in?' → then how long, constant, worse, better/worse, walk distance then vs now → ★ 'breathless at rest as well?' → cough, wheeze, phlegm

★ The MI: when, treatment then, medications NOW, taking them every day, GP check-ups → thank him, normalise. Then IHD questions (chest pain on exertion, racing, dizzy, blackouts) AND heart failure questions (lying flat, pillows, wake gasping, ankle swelling)

Cancer block anyway: weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, haemoptysis, previous cancer. Occupation: hay/grain/birds, asbestos, cattle/sheep/goats + Q fever vaccine; childhood infections; fever/travel/TB; smoke or did; joints/rash; tired/bleeding; PMHx, allergies, FHx

'Given the history I'd like to start with the cardiovascular examination' → appearance → JVP → apex, heave → heart sounds, murmurs, gallop/S3 → respiratory (movement, percussion, breath sounds, added, VR) → abdomen (hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux) → legs — 'is the oedema pitting?' → ECG + spirometry

Diagnosis in plain words + THREE reasons → 'sounds like the heart's about to stop' → reframe → 'should I have come sooner?' → no blame, fix the follow-up → 'I was also thinking about…' × 8+ → summary to examiner
ask: Before I begin, could I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation? → 'Thank you for coming in to get this assessed today, Robert. I understand this is worrying for you. Let me ask you some questions and examine you, and we'll find the cause together — is that alright?'
★ Tell me about the breathlessness. First of all — is it more a tightness in your chest, or is it difficulty getting the air in?

How long have you had it? All the time or comes and goes? Getting worse? What makes it worse and better? How far could you walk six months ago, and how far now? ★ And are you short of breath when you're resting as well? Any cough, wheeze or noisy breathing, any phlegm — what colour?

★ Can I ask about your heart attack? When did you have it? What treatment did you have at the time? What medications are you on for it now? Are you managing to take them every day? Have you been having regular check-ups with a GP? → 'Thank you for being straight with me — that's more common than you'd think'

Since the heart attack — chest pain with the breathlessness, especially on exertion? Racing of the heart? Dizziness or blackouts? Is the breathlessness worse when you lie down — how many pillows? Wake in the night gasping? Swelling in your legs or ankles?
★ Lost weight without trying? Appetite? Lumps or bumps? Night sweats? Have you coughed up any blood? Ever had cancer of any kind?

What's your occupation? Work with hay, grain or birds? Ever exposed to asbestos? Contact with cattle, sheep or goats — and have you had the Q fever vaccination? Chest infections as a child? Fevers or chills? Travel or TB contact? Smoke, or did you? Joint pains or rashes? Tiredness, bleeding? Other conditions — BP, diabetes, kidneys? Allergies? Family?

'Given the history, I'd like to start with the cardiovascular examination. General appearance — respiratory distress, cyanosed, drowsy? Inspection — is the JVP raised? Palpation — apex beat displaced? Parasternal heave? Auscultation — first and second heart sounds normal, any murmurs, gallop rhythm or third heart sound? Respiratory — symmetrical movements, percussion, breath sounds and added sounds, vocal resonance? Abdomen — tenderness, hepatomegaly, positive hepatojugular reflux? Lower limbs — oedema, and is it pitting? And two office tests: ECG and spirometry.'
pefe: Findings: no distress, not cyanosed, alert · JVP raised >3 cm · apex displaced · parasternal heave · HS normal, no murmurs, gallop with S3 · movements symmetrical, percussion normal, bibasal crepitations, VR normal · hepatomegaly, positive hepatojugular reflux · bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin · ECG and spirometry requested

Traps: examining the lungs in detail and the heart briefly · asking leg-size difference (a DVT question — here it's pitting and bilateral) · findings on a printed card → read silently, 'thank you, I've noted the findings', don't narrate

Diagnosis: 'most likely you have a condition called heart failure. After a heart attack the muscle of the heart is damaged, and the heart doesn't pump blood around the body properly. The reasons: your breathlessness has a very particular pattern — worse lying flat, three pillows; swelling in both legs; and on examination raised pressure in the vein in your neck, an extra heart sound, crackles at the bases of your lungs, an enlarged liver and fluid in your legs'

'Sounds like the heart's about to stop' → 'I'm glad you said that, because it's a bad name for it. It doesn't mean your heart is about to stop — it isn't pumping as strongly as it should, and there are very good treatments that make people feel better and live longer. Part of why this has happened is you've been without your heart tablets for most of the year, and that's something we can put right' · 'Should I have come sooner?' → 'You've come in now, and that's what matters. I'm not here to give you a hard time about the distance'

'I was also thinking about…' ischaemic heart disease again (no chest pain/racing — still checking) · rhythm problem · valve problem · lung cancer (smoked; no weight loss/haemoptysis) · COPD and asthma (no wheeze) · hypersensitivity pneumonitis from grain and hay dust · lung scarring · bronchiectasis · infections — pneumonia, Q fever from the cattle, TB · anaemia. Forgot to ask about something (sarcoidosis)? Name it anyway — don't re-take the history

Summary to examiner: 60-year-old farmer, six months progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea on three pillows, PND, bilateral ankle oedema, one year post thrombolysed MI with no secondary prevention or follow-up; signs of biventricular failure; CHF from ischaemic cardiomyopathy, recurrent IHD second; ECG, echo, CXR, spirometry, FBE/UEC/glucose/lipids/TFT; restart secondary prevention + guideline HF therapy; cardiac rehab, HF service, telehealth cardiology; Q fever vaccination discussion · SA equivalents: Country Health Connect, PATS, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
fails: Not asking tightness vs difficulty getting air in ★
Not exploring the MI — when, treatment then, treatment now, compliance, follow-up ★
Not asking about haemoptysis ★
Fewer than six further differentials — stopping after 'heart failure' ★
Hearing 'better with rest' and not asking about breathlessness at rest; skipping the cancer block because the picture is complete
Examining lungs in detail and heart briefly; not asking pitting; judgemental about the tablets or the distance ('it's not as simple as that from where I live'); untranslated jargon; no ECG
numbers: Vitals BP 140/90 · PR 96 · RR 14 · T 36.5 · SpO2 99% — a normal saturation does not exclude heart failure · JVP abnormal >3 cm above the sternal angle · three pillows · six months progressive · 30 pack-years

Definitive test: echocardiogram · four pillars of HFrEF: ACE inhibitor or ARNI · beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol CR, nebivolol) · MRA · SGLT2 inhibitor · frusemide relieves congestion but does not change prognosis VERIFY
Action plan: >2 kg gain in 2 days → call · fluid restriction ~1.5 L/day if congested · daily weights
Rural exposures to name: hypersensitivity pneumonitis (grain, hay, birds) · Q fever (cattle, sheep, goats; vaccine Q-VAX) · asbestos in old sheds · history and differentials are separately scored

Variant 2 — he admits stopping the tablets: 'that's far more common than people admit, and it isn't a telling-off. What got in the way — cost, the trip, side effects, or just life? … longer script, a pharmacy that can post them, telehealth review so you're not driving three hours for five minutes'

Variant 3 — 'Am I going to be able to keep working the place?' → can't promise today; most people with treated heart failure keep doing a great deal — treatment usually improves what you can do; tests and medication first, then work out the farm together; 'what do you drive, and how far?' (fitness to drive VERIFY)
Variant 4 — printed card: read silently, 'thank you, I've noted the findings', straight to diagnosis · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450

setting: General practice (online format). Stem reconstructed from the variant section — the notes give the findings and the shape of the case, not a verbatim door stem.
stem: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents with shortness of breath, some chest heaviness, and ankle swelling.
Examination findings (given when requested): bilateral ankle oedema, tachycardia, a murmur. Nothing else.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient, and your investigations to the examiner
time: 8 minutes. Same spine as MED-32; the difference is that the findings do NOT settle the diagnosis, so the explanation must stay honestly broad.

back.dx: The vague version — cardiovascular disease, cause not yet determinable: chest heaviness in a 70-year-old hypertensive with bilateral oedema, tachycardia and a murmur could be ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, a cardiomyopathy, a valve lesion, or an arrhythmia ('your heart is running fast today'). The mark is for saying 'I don't have enough yet to tell you which, and I'd rather test than guess' — then the lung list with lung cancer at the top, then a targeted investigation set to the examiner. Same history structure as MED-32: tightness vs air hunger, rest breathlessness, IHD and HF questions, cancer block, exposures, smoking.

'The most likely cause of your breathlessness is a problem with your heart — cardiovascular disease. Within that it could be narrowing of the heart's arteries, it could be heart failure, it could be a problem with the heart muscle, or a rhythm disturbance — your heart is running fast today. I don't have enough yet to tell you which, and I'd rather test than guess. I was also thinking about the lungs: lung cancer at the top of that list, then COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis and scarring of the lungs.'

To the examiner: 'An ECG, because this could still be ischaemic heart disease; an echocardiogram to assess for heart failure and the murmur; 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring given his long-standing hypertension; a chest X-ray, which may show cardiomegaly or an effusion as well as screening the lungs; spirometry; and a full blood examination for anaemia.'

stem: Lily, 28, presents with shortness of breath since last night, which began while she was sitting on the couch and has not settled.
Observations on request: BP 118/74 · pulse 104 · RR 22 · SpO2 95% room air · T 37.1 °C.
tasks: Take a complete history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis and differentials

back.dx: Pulmonary embolism from a right calf DVT — constant, worsening breathlessness since last night, started at rest on the couch, worse moving but present sitting still, slight dry cough, slight pleuritic ache; FOUR withheld findings, each needing its own specific question: right calf swollen and achy for two days ('thought I'd pulled something') · flew back from the States three days ago AND took a sleeping tablet and slept the whole way (only if you ask what she did on the flight) · on Levlen, a COMBINED pill (only if you ask which) · mum had a DVT after an operation (only if you ask family clots). Not pregnant (LMP two weeks). Hidden agenda: 'do you think it's just a panic attack? work's been stressful' at ~5 min. Described as the highest-failure case in the breathlessness cluster; if you could say one thing to pass: DVT signs and symptoms. Disposition = ambulance to ED today, not an outpatient scan.
plan: Observations → 'mildly tachycardic and tachypnoeic, not shocked'; WIPE; 'short of breath sitting here?'; open question; acknowledge. Don't deliberate acute vs chronic — run the structure

Breathlessness: describe; constant/comes and goes; worse; first time; better/worse — exertion AND at rest; lying flat; ★ 'what were you doing exactly before it started?'; cough, sputum, BLOOD, wheeze, chest pain worse on breathing in
★ 'Any swelling or pain in your calves or legs?' → which leg, when, painful/red/warm, sore to squeeze or walk

★ COST VMPF in under 60 s: Contraception — which one? · Overweight — 'would you say you're currently overweight?' · Surgery/hospital last 1–2 months · Travel — 'and what did you do during the trip?', immobility/illness/cast · Varicose veins · Malignancy/weight loss · Pregnancy — LMP, any chance · Family or personal clots

Rule out the rest: chest injury, smoking; wheeze/night cough/atopy/asthma FHx; fever/chills/sweats; tightness, palpitations, ankle swelling, fainting, sudden deaths <40; rash/itch/lip swelling/new food or drug; tiredness, dizziness, heavy periods, black stools; weight loss/sweats; stress, panic; conditions, meds, allergies, home; 'anything you were worried this might be?'

ask: Before I begin, may I have her observations — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, saturation and temperature? → 'I understand how stressful that must be. Let me ask you some questions and we'll work out the cause together and make a plan.'

Is it tightness in the chest, difficulty getting the breath in, or not getting enough air? All the time or comes and goes? Getting worse? First time? Worse when you walk — and is it there at rest? Worse lying flat? ★ What were you doing exactly before it started?
Any cough? Bringing anything up — ★ have you seen any blood in it? Noisy or wheezy breathing? Chest pain — worse when you breathe in deeply?
★ Have you had any swelling or pain in your calves or legs? — Which leg? When did you first notice it? Painful, red or warm? Sore when you squeeze the calf, or when you walk?

★ Are you taking any contraceptive pill — do you know which one, or its name? Would you say you're currently overweight? Any surgery or hospital stay in the last month or two? Any long travel recently — and what did you do during the trip? Any days off your feet — illness, a cast, bed rest? Prominent or dilated veins in your legs? Previous cancer, or weight loss you didn't intend? When was your last period — any chance you could be pregnant? Have you, or anyone in your family, ever had a clot in the leg or lung?

Injury to the chest? Smoke? Wheeze, night cough, hay fever, eczema, asthma in the family? Fever, chills, sweats? Chest tightness, palpitations, ankle swelling, fainting? Sudden deaths in the family under 40? Rash, itching, swelling of lips or tongue — new food or medication? Tiredness, dizziness, heavy periods, black stools? Weight loss, night sweats? Unusual stress, episodes of panic with a racing heart? Other conditions, medications, allergies? Who's at home? Anything you were particularly worried this might be?

'Lily, most likely you have a condition called a pulmonary embolism — in plain terms, a clot in one of the blood vessels of your lung. The clot almost certainly formed in your leg and then travelled up — which fits with the swelling and ache in your right calf. It formed because you were sitting still for a very long time on that flight, especially having slept through it. Being on a combined contraceptive pill adds to that risk, and so does your mum's history of clots. None of this is something you did wrong — it's a set of things stacking up.'

★ 'This is serious and it's very treatable, but it has to be dealt with today — not next week. I'm calling an ambulance and sending you to the emergency department now; I don't want you driving. They'll do a CT scan of the blood vessels in your lungs, and if it confirms the clot they'll start a blood-thinning medication, usually a tablet, for at least three months. We'll need to stop your combined pill — stop it now, condoms until we sort a replacement — and I'll make sure you have an alternative arranged.'

Variant 1 — she offers the panic attack: 'Panic attacks absolutely can cause exactly this, and I'm keeping it on my list. But I want to be honest about why I'm not settling on it today: a swollen painful calf, a very long flight asleep and immobile, and a combined pill. That combination makes a clot in the lung a real possibility. We rule that out first; if it's clear, then we talk properly about the anxiety — which matters too'

Variant 3 — wants to go home: 'I understand, and I'm sorry — but no. A clot in the lung can be stable one hour and dangerous the next; the risk isn't how you feel in this chair, it's the next few hours. The scan is only at the hospital and the treatment shouldn't wait. I'd rather you didn't drive in case you become more breathless or faint — that's why I'm calling an ambulance. Work will keep. Can I ring your partner to meet you there?'
Contraception replacement: progestogen-only pill, implant, hormonal IUD all safe; combined pill, patch and ring are the oestrogen risk

Agreeing she can go home, hesitating, or arranging an outpatient scan; letting her drive ★
Never mentioning stopping the combined pill and replacing it ★
Taking the panic-attack offer; dismissing a young woman's symptoms — or the opposite, never keeping panic on the list
Not asking pregnancy/LMP; asking her BMI; wasting time deciding acute vs chronic; no safety-net or summary

setting: You are the GP. Same practice as MED-34.
stem: Lily, 28, presents with sudden-onset shortness of breath for two hours.
Examination findings will appear on screen at 6 minutes. Observations on request.

Interpret the examination findings that appear on screen at 6 minutes
Explain your diagnosis and differentials

back.dx: Pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction — same withheld history as MED-34 (right calf, flight asleep, Levlen combined, mum's DVT) but here she HAS coughed up blood ('red, mixed in with the phlegm'). Findings on screen: dullness left lower lobe · loud P2 · left parasternal systolic murmur. The trap: dullness at a base reads as pneumonia, and the case is built to see whether one sign overturns a history pointing elsewhere. Say aloud: loud P2 = acute pulmonary hypertension; parasternal systolic murmur = tricuspid regurgitation from RV strain; basal dullness = pulmonary infarction ± small effusion rather than consolidation (no bronchial breathing, no increased vocal resonance offered). Hold the diagnosis. Ambulance to ED.

Describe/timing/exertion/rest/lying flat/what were you doing; cough → sputum → ★ blood → YES, red mixed with phlegm → how much, how many times; wheeze; pleuritic pain
★ Legs; ★ COST VMPF under 60 s incl. which pill, what she did on the flight, family clots, LMP/pregnancy

★ Any cough? Bringing anything up — have you seen any blood in it? → 'How much — streaks, a teaspoon, more? How many times? Is it fresh red or dark?'

★ Interpretation aloud: 'A loud P2 reflects acute pulmonary hypertension, and a left parasternal systolic murmur fits tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular strain — both are recognised in pulmonary embolism. The dullness at the left base is most consistent with pulmonary infarction, possibly with a small associated effusion, rather than consolidation — if it were consolidation I would expect bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance, and neither is present. Taken with the history, these findings support rather than contradict a pulmonary embolism.'

'Most likely you have a pulmonary embolism — a clot in one of the blood vessels of your lung. It almost certainly formed in your leg and travelled up, which fits the swelling in your right calf. The blood you coughed up is from a small area of lung the clot has damaged. It formed because you were still for a very long time on that flight, especially asleep; the combined pill and your mum's history add to that. None of this is something you did wrong.'

'I did consider a chest infection — the examination found some dullness at the bottom of your left lung, which can happen with pneumonia, but you have no fever and the other findings point to the clot. Also a collapsed lung, asthma, a heart problem, a severe allergy, a low blood count, a panic attack which I'd only settle on once the clot is excluded, and at the far end a cancer.'

They'll scan the blood vessels in your lungs and start a blood thinner for at least three months. Stop the combined pill now; condoms until we arrange an alternative. Tell the staff straight away if the breathing worsens, you get chest pain, feel faint, or cough up more blood. Who can I call to meet you there?'

setting: Emergency department. The role-player is a final-year medical student (Alex), not a patient.
stem: A 68-year-old man with tachypnoea. History of hypercholesterolaemia, hypertension and previous myocardial infarction.

SpO2 89% RA · BP 132/84 · HR 112 · RR 28 · T 36.8 °C. Distended neck veins; apex not displaced; systolic murmur at the apex; S1 and S2 muffled with an S3 gallop; bibasal dullness and crepitations; pitting oedema to the knees.
tasks: Explain your diagnosis to the medical student
Explain your immediate management plan
time: 8 minutes. 0:20 name it in full · 0:40 the chain · 2:00 map the signs · 3:30 murmur and muffled sounds · 4:30 investigations · 5:00 numbered management · 7:00 long-term · 7:30 check understanding.

back.dx: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema secondary to decompensated heart failure — say BOTH halves. The student opens with 'isn't this pneumonia?' and is briefed to ask 'but why does that happen?' whenever you list a sign without joining it. Six-link chain: substrate (HT, cholesterol, old MI) → LV can't eject → pressure backs into LA → pulmonary veins → capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds oncotic pressure → fluid into interstitium then alveoli → gas exchange fails (RR 28, SpO2 89%). Murmur = functional mitral regurgitation from a dilated annulus. Muffled sounds → test Beck's triad aloud (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds): two of three but BP 132/84 → not tamponade; still ask the echo for pericardial fluid. Management as a NUMBERED sequence with sitting upright first.
plan: 'What did you make of him?' → pneumonia → 'reasonable, keep it live — but I think this is acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema secondary to decompensated heart failure. Here is the chain'
The six links; then 'how do you tell it from consolidation?' → fine, bibasal, symmetrical crackles WITH raised JVP, S3, oedema; consolidation is focal, bronchial breathing, fever

Hang every sign on the chain: JVP + oedema = systemic venous side of the same pressure · S3 = rapid filling into a stiff dilated ventricle · creps = alveoli opening against fluid · basal dullness = transudative effusion

Murmur: systolic, apex (5th ICS MCL), radiates to axilla → functional MR. 'Prolapse?' → click + late systolic murmur, younger patient, not expected. Muffled sounds → Beck's triad → normotensive → not tamponade → echo anyway
Management numbered 1–7; 'why nitrate before frusemide?' → redistribution vs volume, nitrate acts in minutes; 'morphine?' → no longer routine; what I'm NOT doing

Investigations with reasons: ECG + serial troponin (ACS commonest precipitant), FBE/UEC before diuresing, LFT/TFT, gas + lactate, CXR (alveolar oedema, Kerley B, cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, effusions), ECHO — EF, wall motion, MR severity, pericardial fluid

Long-term once euvolaemic: four pillars, beta-blocker NOT today; loop diuretic for congestion only; rehab, daily weights 2 kg/2 days, vaccines, device assessment later → summary → 'does that hang together?'
ask: 'Hi Alex. Before we go back in, let's take two minutes on this gentleman — what I think is going on and why, then what I want done in the next ten minutes. Stop me whenever. What did you make of him?'
★ 'My diagnosis is acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, secondary to decompensated heart failure. Let me show you how the stem gets us there.'

★ 'Once pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds the oncotic pressure holding fluid in the vessel, fluid crosses into the interstitium and then into the alveoli. That is the pulmonary oedema, and it is why gas exchange fails — hence the tachypnoea, the tachycardia and the saturation of 89%.'
'Each sign is a link in the chain, not a separate finding. The third heart sound is rapid filling into a stiff, dilated ventricle.'

★ 'Beck's triad is hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds. He has two of three, but he is normotensive, so this is not tamponade. I will still ask the echocardiogram to look for pericardial fluid.'

★ 'One, sit him upright with his legs dependent — free, immediate, reduces preload. Two, oxygen titrated to 92–96%. Three, IV access, cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG. Four, glyceryl trinitrate 300–600 micrograms sublingually or a 400 microgram spray, repeated, provided his systolic stays above 100. Five, IV frusemide 40 mg, or a dose matching his usual daily oral dose, with a catheter to chart urine output. Six, stop any intravenous fluids. Seven, if still hypoxic or working hard, CPAP at 5–10 cm of water — and call cardiology.'

'Things I am not doing: no IV fluids, no NSAIDs, and I am not starting a beta-blocker today — those go in once he is euvolaemic. Morphine is no longer routine; observational data associate it with worse outcomes, more ventilation and longer stays. I'd reserve it for severe distress or ischaemic pain, at a low dose.'
'Does that hang together? Anything you want me to go back over?'

Long-term: HFrEF four pillars — ACE inhibitor or sacubitril–valsartan where indicated · beta-blocker with HF evidence (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol CR, nebivolol) low and slow once euvolaemic · MRA · SGLT2 inhibitor · loop diuretic for congestion = symptom control not disease modification · cardiac rehab · daily weights (2 kg in 2 days trigger) · vaccination · device assessment later VERIFY

Variant 3 — explain it to the patient instead: switch register completely — 'your heart isn't pumping as strongly as it should, so fluid is backing up into your lungs and that's why you feel breathless. We're going to sit you up, give you oxygen, and give you a water tablet through the drip to shift that fluid. You'll pass a lot of urine and should start to breathe more easily quite quickly' — no hydrostatic pressure, no ejection fraction

Variant 2 — cardiogenic shock (BP 78/50, cool, lactate 4.2, oliguric): say the words 'cardiogenic shock' aloud — NO nitrate; oxygen and NIV as tolerated; cautious or withheld diuretic until perfusion improves; inotrope/vasopressor; urgent bedside echo; cardiology and ICU immediately; in SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to a cath lab

Misquoting Beck's triad (it is HYPOtension); calling it tamponade in a normotensive man — or dismissing the muffled sounds without ordering the echo

setting: Inpatient ward. The role-player is a final-year medical student.
stem: A 54-year-old man admitted with fever, cough and dizziness; CXR confirms lower lobe pneumonia. MI five years ago, on enoxaparin, has received 3 litres of normal saline. No chest pain but cannot lie flat.
Observation chart: RR 12→25 · HR 102→124 · systolic 120→104 · SpO2 97–99% on room air · temperature settling.
tasks: Interpret the observation chart
Perform the relevant examination
Explain your differential diagnoses to the medical student
time: 8 minutes. Chart in trends with one synthesis sentence · examination (cardiorespiratory + fluid status) · bucketed differentials · first action is to stop the fluids.

back.dx: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from IATROGENIC fluid overload (3 L saline in a man with a previous MI) — leading diagnosis; ACS and arrhythmia next on the cardiac side; respiratory causes stay live (progressive pneumonia, parapneumonic effusion/empyema, PE — prophylactic enoxaparin does not exclude it); others: sepsis with septic cardiomyopathy, ARDS, anaemia. The chart: two rising parameters (RR, HR) and one falling (systolic) = deteriorating, meets escalation criteria; preserved SpO2 97–99% does NOT reassure — early pulmonary oedema is a tachypnoea problem before it is a saturation problem. Orthopnoea is the history clue. The student is briefed to argue for more fluid ('he's septic and his pressure is falling') — that is the trap.
plan: Chart in trends, not numbers: RR 12–15 → 21–25; HR 102 → 124; systolic 120 → 104; SpO2 preserved — 'and I would specifically say that does not reassure me'; temperature settling → 'this patient is deteriorating and meets our criteria for escalation' → call for senior help / MET per local criteria

Examination, stated then performed: general appearance and work of breathing; fluid status — JVP, hepatojugular reflux, peripheral oedema, mucosa; CVS — apex, heave, S3, murmur; respiratory — expansion, percussion (basal dullness, effusion side), breath sounds, crepitations (bibasal vs focal), bronchial breathing, VR; calves; catheter/urine output; bedside echo if available; ECG
Differentials bucketed to the student: respiratory (kept live) → cardiovascular (leading: fluid overload APO; then ACS, arrhythmia) → other (sepsis/septic cardiomyopathy, ARDS, anaemia)
'Shouldn't we give more fluid?' → the trap answered; first action: STOP the saline, sit up, assess filling; small aliquots with reassessment only if genuinely hypovolaemic

Then the APO sequence: sit up, O2 to target, monitor, ECG, GTN if systolic >100 (here 104 — cautious), IV frusemide, catheter, CPAP if needed; investigations — ECG, troponin, FBE/UEC, gas + lactate, CXR, cultures, echo; escalate to registrar/ICU; summary
ask: ★ 'This is the adult observation and response chart. Working down: respiratory rate has climbed from 12–15 on day one to 21–25 today. Heart rate 102 to 124. Systolic has drifted from 120 to 104. Saturation is preserved at 97–99% on room air — and I would specifically say that does not reassure me, because early pulmonary oedema is a tachypnoea problem before it is a saturation problem. Temperature is settling. Two rising parameters and one falling: this patient is deteriorating and meets our criteria for escalation.'

'I'll examine him now — general appearance and work of breathing; fluid status: JVP, hepatojugular reflux, oedema; heart: apex, heave, third heart sound, murmur; chest: expansion, percussion, breath sounds, crackles and whether they're bibasal or focal, bronchial breathing, vocal resonance; calves; urine output.'

★ 'He was admitted with a pneumonia, so I keep respiratory causes live: progressive pneumonia, a parapneumonic effusion or empyema, and pulmonary embolism — prophylactic enoxaparin does not exclude that. But the story has changed: he cannot lie flat, he has had a myocardial infarction, and he has received three litres of saline. So on the cardiovascular side: acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from iatrogenic fluid overload — my leading diagnosis — then acute coronary syndrome and arrhythmia. Under other: sepsis with septic cardiomyopathy, ARDS, and anaemia. My first action is to stop the intravenous fluids.'

★ Student: 'He's septic and his blood pressure is falling — shouldn't we give more fluid?' → 'That is exactly the trap. He has already had three litres, he cannot lie flat, and his respiratory rate is climbing faster than his pressure is falling. In a man with a previous infarct, that combination is fluid overload, not hypovolaemia. I want the saline stopped, him sat up, and an assessment of his filling — JVP, hepatojugular reflux, oedema, and a bedside echo if we have one. If he really were hypovolaemic I would give small aliquots with reassessment after each, never a continued infusion.'
'Does that hang together? Anything you want me to go back over?'
pefe: Perform, don't just request: expected findings in this version are not scripted — describe what you look for and interpret whatever is given: raised JVP + bibasal creps + S3 → overload; focal bronchial breathing + fever → pneumonia progression; stony dull base → effusion (parapneumonic vs transudate → tap); unilateral calf swelling → PE

Investigations: ECG (ischaemia, AF), troponin, FBE, UEC (before diuresis), CRP, blood cultures, VBG/ABG with lactate, CXR now vs admission (new bilateral interstitial/alveolar shadowing, effusions, cardiomegaly), BNP, echo (EF, wall motion, pericardial fluid); consider CTPA if PE remains plausible after the above

Management once overload confirmed: stop fluids · sit upright · O2 92–96% · monitor · GTN only if systolic >100 (104 — cautious, reassess) · IV frusemide 40 mg with catheter · CPAP if working hard · continue antibiotics for the pneumonia · escalate — registrar, MET/ICU, cardiology; hold further enoxaparin decisions with the team if effusion needs tapping
Version C (numbers card): fluid balance +5 L over 48 h — same logic, bigger load
SA: MET criteria per hospital; rural — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 early for a deteriorating post-MI patient
fails: Reading every number aloud instead of trends + one synthesis sentence; not calling it deterioration/escalation ★
Being reassured by SpO2 97–99% ★
Agreeing to more fluid; not stopping the saline as the first action ★
Dropping the respiratory bucket because 'it's the heart' — or dropping PE because he's on enoxaparin
Not asking/eliciting orthopnoea as the pivot; examining chest only, no fluid status
Continuous fluid infusion for hypotension in an overloaded post-MI patient
numbers: Chart: RR 12→25 · HR 102→124 · SBP 120→104 · SpO2 97–99% RA · temp settling · fluid load 3 L (Version C +5 L/48 h)
Early APO = tachypnoea before desaturation · orthopnoea = the history flag · two rising + one falling = escalate

Buckets: respiratory (progressive pneumonia · parapneumonic effusion/empyema · PE) · cardiovascular (iatrogenic overload APO · ACS · arrhythmia) · other (sepsis/septic cardiomyopathy · ARDS · anaemia)
Hypovolaemia vs overload: JVP, hepatojugular reflux, oedema, orthopnoea, bedside echo (IVC, LV) · fluid challenge = 250 mL aliquot with reassessment, never an infusion VERIFY
APO sequence: sit up → O2 92–96% → monitor/ECG → GTN if SBP >100 → IV frusemide 40 mg + catheter → stop fluids → CPAP 5–10 cmH2O → cardiology VERIFY

source: Acute_Pulmonary_Oedema_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Version B — inpatient ward, iatrogenic fluid overload, observation chart)

stem: Jack Reid, an 18-year-old man, presents with sudden breathlessness while exercising. SpO2 93% — he is already on oxygen.
Other observations from the examiner on request. A chest X-ray will be shown.
tasks: Take a history (5 minutes)
Explain the chest X-ray to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes. Four beats: stability + opening 35 s · complaint 55 s · acute three then full sweep 3.5 min · film, diagnosis, list, plan 3 min.

back.dx: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax, trachea central — right side. Positives only: sudden, mid-game an hour ago, constant, not improving, worse moving, breathless AT REST (symptomatic → drives the management branch), slight dry cough, sharp right-sided pleuritic pain. Everything else is NO — no tackle, no calf/travel/family clots, no allergies/rash, no fever/coryza, no palpitations/dizziness/syncope, no family sudden death, no atopy, not tired, doesn't smoke or vape, HEADSS fine. Vitals: BP 118/72, P 104, RR 24, T 36.6, SpO2 93% on 6 L Hudson — react aloud. The discriminating issue is the TRACHEA: on the film, name it in the midline before you describe the black shadow. 'Sudden' in the stem = ask the ACUTE THREE first (pneumothorax, PE, anaphylaxis).
plan: 'Examiner, may I have BP, pulse, RR and temperature — I have the saturation in the stem' → 'tachypnoeic and hypoxic, I'd keep the oxygen running'; WIPE; 'I can see you're on oxygen — we'll keep that going'; open question; acknowledge; signpost the pace
Describe (tightness / air in / not enough air); EXACTLY when; constant; worse; better/worse → ★ rest question + breathless at rest → cough, noisy breathing/wheeze
★ ACUTE THREE: knock or tackle to the chest? · calves, long trips/flights, family clots (+ pill and pregnancy in a woman) · known allergies, rash, itch

Infection (fever/chills, sore throat/runny nose, overseas travel — not night sweats in a one-hour history); cardiac — chest pain, racing, dizziness, blackout, ★ 'has anyone in your family died suddenly, particularly young?'; family atopy; tiredness; ★ smoke or vape; weight/appetite; mini-HEADSS LAST and brief (home, school/bullying, mood)

Film ≤1 min: three colours → heart, spine, ★ TRACHEA in the midline 'which matters for how urgently we treat this' → left lung out to the chest wall → right: black shadow between lung and chest wall → 'a pneumothorax'. 'How did air get in?' → two sentences, stop

Diagnosis + two reasons + 'airway central, not under pressure' → differentials each with a reason against from his own answers → plan: O2, analgesia, reassess; needle/tube if still symptomatic, else observe ~4 h then home with repeat film + appointment → red flags → no flying until cleared, never scuba → 'does that make sense?'
ask: Examiner, before I begin, may I have the blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature? I have the oxygen saturation in the stem. → 'He's tachypnoeic and hypoxic, so I'd keep the oxygen running throughout.'

'Good morning, I'm Dr —. Am I speaking with Jack? I can see you're on oxygen — we'll keep that going. Tell me more about your breathing.' → 'I understand how concerning this must be. Let me ask some questions, we'll work out what's happening and make the best plan together. Some will sound unrelated — with breathlessness this sudden there are a few serious things I need to rule out quickly.'

Can you describe it — tightness, difficulty getting the breath in, or not getting enough air? ★ Exactly when did it start? Constant or on and off since? Getting worse? Anything make it better or worse? ★ Does rest make it better — and are you breathless at rest, sitting here now? Cough? Noisy breathing or wheeze?

★ Did you take any knock or injury to the chest — were you tackled or did you land badly? Any pain or swelling in your calves? Long trips or flights? Anyone in the family with blood clots? Any known allergies? Rash or itching anywhere?

Fevers or chills? Sore throat, runny nose? Travel overseas? Chest pain with this? Racing or pounding heart? Dizziness? Did you black out when it started? ★ And — this one's important — has anyone in your family died suddenly, particularly young?

Family asthma, eczema, hay fever? Unusually tired lately? ★ Do you smoke — or vape? Lost weight or appetite? How are things at home? Stress at school, anyone giving you a hard time — any bullying? How's your mood been generally?

★ Film: 'Jack, this is an X-ray of your chest. Three colours — white bone, grey soft tissue, black air. This shadow in the middle is your heart, this is your spine, and this line running down the centre is your main airway. I'm checking that it's sitting in the midline — and it is — because that makes a real difference to how urgently we need to treat this. On your left the lung goes right out to the chest wall, sitting against the inside of the ribs the way it should. But on your right there's a black shadow between the lung and the chest wall — the lung isn't sitting against the ribs any more. That black area is air that's escaped and collected around the lung, and the name we give that is a pneumothorax.'

'Most often it happens on its own, without any injury. There are tiny bubbles on the surface of the lung that can burst, and air leaks out into the space around it. It's more common in young, tall, slim people, and often during exercise.' — two sentences, stop
pefe: No PEFE task in Version A — the film replaces it. Doctor-level read if asked: right pneumothorax with a visible visceral pleural line and absent peripheral lung markings, trachea and mediastinum central, no effusion, no rib fracture

Diagnosis: 'most likely a pneumothorax — air trapped between your lung and your chest wall. Two reasons: it came on very suddenly during exercise, and — the main one — I can see the air collection on your X-ray. Your main airway is central, so it isn't building up under pressure'

Differentials each with a reason AGAINST: clot on the lung — no travel, no leg swelling, no family clots · severe allergic reaction — no allergies, rash, itch · chest infection — no fever, no cold symptoms · asthma attack — no wheeze, no family asthma · heart — rhythm, or a thickened heart muscle that runs in families — no palpitations, dizziness, blackout, family sudden death · low in blood — not tired

Plan: keep oxygen, analgesia, reassess; still symptomatic → aspiration/needle or small-bore intercostal catheter (treat by symptoms and stability, NOT size); settles and stable → observe ~4 h → home with repeat film, follow-up appointment, written red flags; safety-net: suddenly worse, bad chest pain, faint → tell someone now; no flying until cleared; never scuba dive; smoking cessation cuts recurrence; 'can I play footy?' → after review and repeat film; 'will it happen again?' → it can, hence follow-up
If the bell is close: 'pneumothorax' → one reason → 'I considered a clot, allergic reaction, infection, asthma and heart causes — none fit' → oxygen, analgesia, possible drainage, follow-up
SA regional: discuss with the receiving hospital; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if intervention needed and not available locally; TIS 131 450
fails: Never mentioning the trachea on the film ★
Never saying the word 'pneumothorax' ★
Not asking the acute three first — reaching chest injury/calves/allergies at four minutes ★
Omitting family history of sudden cardiac death; omitting smoking because he's 18 ★
Not reacting to SpO2 93% / not asking the other vitals; 'you've overdone it'; reassuring before knowing anything
Differentials without reasons against; jargon (hyperlucency, pleural line); film over a minute; leading with HEADSS; no plan/safety-net/flying-diving advice
numbers: Acute three: pneumothorax · PE · anaphylaxis · signs: reduced expansion, hyper-resonant, absent breath sounds, reduced VR · trachea pushed AWAY + hypotension + distress = tension → needle first, film later

Treat by symptoms and stability, not size · stable + asymptomatic → observe 4 h → discharge + repeat film + appointment + red flags · symptomatic after analgesia or unstable → pleural intervention VERIFY (BTS/local pathway)

Needle decompression: 2nd ICS mid-clavicular, just above the 3rd rib — or 5th ICS anterior axillary in adults (chest wall thickness) · intercostal catheter: safe triangle — pec major, lat dorsi, 5th ICS · underwater seal
Advice: no flying until cleared · never scuba dive again · stop smoking/vaping · ECG yes, spirometry NO in the acute patient

Variant B tension (24 M after a tackle, BP 82/50, P 132, RR 34, neck veins, trachea to the right, absent BS left): 'that changes everything — treating as tension, no X-ray, call for help, high-flow O2, immediate needle decompression left, cannula left in, then intercostal catheter in the safe triangle, reassess'

Variant C PE (26 F, pleuritic, 3 days post-flight, combined pill, swollen calf): Wells → straight to CTPA, treat while waiting if no contraindication · Variant D HOCM (19 M, collapse at training, uncle died at 32, exertional tightness): ECG today, echo, urgent cardiology, no competitive exercise until assessed, family screening
Vitals here: BP 118/72 · P 104 · RR 24 · T 36.6 · SpO2 93% on 6 L · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

stem: Chloe Barrett, 27, presents with sudden onset breathlessness.
There is no X-ray. Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes. History 4 min — acute three front-loaded, pill and pregnancy added · PEFE request in a fixed order with the trachea named · diagnosis, differentials with reasons against, plan.

back.dx: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax, LEFT, trachea central — same near-all-negative history as Jack (sudden, constant, at rest, dry cough, pleuritic pain; no injury/clots/allergy/fever/cardiac/atopy/smoking), but in a woman the PE block must include the contraceptive pill and pregnancy. Findings (only what you ask for): reduced expansion left, trachea CENTRAL, hyper-resonant left, absent breath sounds left, reduced vocal resonance left; CVS normal; abdomen normal; calves equal. Without asking the tracheal position you cannot exclude tension — that is the discriminating item. Don't skip abdomen and lower limbs 'because they aren't respiratory'; don't request spirometry in an acute patient.
plan: Vitals → react; WIPE; open; acknowledge; signpost. 4-minute history: describe, exactly when, constant, worse, modifiers, rest + at rest, cough, wheeze
★ Acute three + the female additions: chest injury · calves, travel, family clots, ★ contraceptive pill (which one), ★ LMP / could you be pregnant · allergies, rash, itch
Fever/coryza/travel; chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, syncope, ★ family sudden death; atopy; tired; ★ smoke/vape; weight; brief HEADSS if time
'Apologies Chloe, I'll just speak with my examiner for a moment' → ordered request incl. ★ tracheal position → interpret aloud → turn back

Diagnosis with reasons (sudden on exertion; reduced expansion, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds on the left; trachea central so not under pressure) → differentials with reasons against → plan: ED/hospital for CXR, oxygen, analgesia, observe vs intervene; no flying/scuba; safety-net
ask: Examiner, before I begin, may I have the blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and saturation?

★ Exactly when did it start? Does rest make it better — and are you breathless at rest now? Did you take any knock or injury to the chest? Any pain or swelling in your calves, long trips or flights, family blood clots? ★ Are you on the contraceptive pill — which one? When was your last period, any chance you could be pregnant? Any known allergies, rash or itching?

Fevers, chills, sore throat, runny nose, travel? Chest pain, racing heart, dizziness, blackout? ★ Has anyone in your family died suddenly, particularly young? Family asthma/eczema/hay fever? Unusually tired? ★ Do you smoke or vape?

★ 'Examiner: general appearance — respiratory distress, cyanosis, drowsy? Vital signs. Respiratory — on inspection and palpation, are chest movements symmetrical? What is the tracheal position? Percussion note? Breath sounds and added sounds? Vocal resonance? Cardiovascular — raised JVP, displaced apex, normal first and second heart sounds, any murmur or gallop? Abdomen — swelling, redness, tenderness, masses, palpable liver edge? Lower limbs — any size difference between the calves, or oedema? Office tests — may I have an ECG?'

★ Interpretation: 'Reduced expansion, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance on the left, with a central trachea and normal haemodynamics — that is a left pneumothorax without tension.'

'Chloe, most likely you have a pneumothorax — air trapped between your lung and your chest wall. It came on very suddenly, and on examination the left side of your chest is moving less, sounds hollow, and I can't hear breath sounds there. Your windpipe is central, which tells me it isn't building up under pressure.'

'I considered a clot on the lung — no travel, no leg swelling, and your calves are equal; a severe allergic reaction — no allergies or rash; a chest infection — no fever; asthma — no wheeze; heart causes including a thickened heart muscle that runs in families — no palpitations, blackouts or family sudden death; and being low in blood — you're not tired.'

'You need a chest X-ray today to confirm it and measure it, so I'm sending you to the emergency department now with oxygen and pain relief — I'll ring ahead. If you're still short of breath there they'll let the air out with a small tube or needle; if you settle they'll watch you a few hours and see you back with a repeat film. If your breathing suddenly gets worse, you get severe chest pain or feel faint, tell someone immediately. Don't fly until you've been cleared, and you shouldn't scuba dive after this.'
pefe: Expected findings: reduced expansion left · trachea central · hyper-resonant left · absent breath sounds left · reduced vocal resonance left · CVS normal · abdomen normal · calves equal · ECG available

If the examiner gives 'trachea deviated to the right, BP 82/50, distended neck veins' → tension: no X-ray, call for help, high-flow O2, immediate needle decompression left (2nd ICS MCL or 5th ICS anterior axillary), cannula left in, then intercostal catheter in the safe triangle with underwater seal, reassess; GP setting → 000 and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 while decompressing
Disposition from GP: transfer to ED for CXR (erect PA ± expiratory), not observation in the practice; ambulance if hypoxic/symptomatic; ring ahead
Traps: not asking the tracheal position · skipping abdomen and lower limbs · requesting spirometry · forgetting the pill and pregnancy in the PE block
SA regional: nearest ED with chest drain capability; MedSTAR for retrieval if intervention not available locally; TIS 131 450
fails: Not asking the tracheal position — cannot exclude tension ★
Not asking the acute three in the first minute; not asking the pill and pregnancy ★
Omitting family sudden cardiac death; omitting smoking ★
Requesting spirometry in an acutely breathless patient; skipping abdomen and legs
Turning to the examiner without excusing yourself; not interpreting the findings aloud; not turning back
Differentials without reasons against; no transfer plan; no red flags; no flying/diving advice
numbers: Pneumothorax signs: reduced expansion · hyper-resonant · absent breath sounds · reduced VR · trachea central (simple) vs pushed away (tension)
Tension = clinical diagnosis: distress, hypotension, tachycardia, distended neck veins, deviated trachea → needle first, film later
Needle: 2nd ICS MCL just above the 3rd rib, or 5th ICS anterior axillary line · ICC: safe triangle (pec major, lat dorsi, 5th ICS)
Female PE block: combined pill/patch/ring (oestrogen), pregnancy/postpartum, plus calves, travel, surgery, family clots
Advice: no flying until cleared · never scuba dive · stop smoking/vaping · recurrence ~30% after a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax VERIFY
Variants C (PE) and D (HOCM) as on MED-38 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · 000

source: Acute_SOB_Pneumothorax_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Version B — Chloe Barrett 27, examination from the examiner, no X-ray)

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. You are the GP.
stem: Jane Marsh, a 47-year-old woman, presents with cough.
Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Three beats: the four boxes 75 s · the differential sweep, red flags first, 3.5 min · the others 75 s · then deliver. Examination and management have never been asked.

back.dx: ACE-inhibitor cough (lisinopril, one year) as the most likely — PLUS post-nasal drip ('stuff running down the back of my throat, especially mornings') PLUS a post-viral cough (bad cold two weeks ago — only disclosed if you ask 'now, or recently?'). Three months, every day, dry, occasional teaspoon of clear phlegm, never blood, no unusual sound, not nocturnal-waking, slightly worse mornings; no red flags, never smoked, office manager (retail before), no asbestos. Vitals normal. The discriminating issue: AMC plants SEVERAL findings — the station scores how many differentials you excluded, not which diagnosis you landed on. Hearing 'lisinopril' and winding down the history is the fail the station was redesigned to catch. Deliver: one most likely + contributors + the exclusion list with reassuring negatives. Do NOT tell her to just stop the tablet — substitute it.
plan: Vitals; WIPE; 'tell me more about your cough' → 'worried there's something wrong with my lungs' → acknowledge, promise to work it out, signpost the breadth; no reassurance before a single question

Box 1 timing: how long, constant or on and off, worse, ★ at night / wakes you. Box 2 triggers: open, then specific — work, outdoors, seasons, exercise, lying down. Box 3 character: dry or chesty → C·C·C·V·O (colour, consistency, ★ content/blood, volume — teaspoon vs eggcup, odour). Box 4 sound: honking, whooping, barking. The brothers: SOB, noisy breathing
★ Lung cancer block: weight, appetite, lumps, tired, haemoptysis, previous cancer, occupation now AND before, asbestos. Heart failure: chest pain, exertional SOB, pillows, ankle swelling

Infections: fever/chills/sweats, ★ sore throat or runny nose — now, or recently?, body aches, post-tussive vomiting, travel, TB/sick contacts. Airways: nocturnal/exertional, family atopy, smoke now or ever + passive/occupational, childhood infections

★ THE OTHERS — protect this block: medications → lisinopril → note flatly, KEEP GOING; heartburn, acid taste, water brash; ★ secretions down the back of the throat, facial pain, blocked nose; rashes/joints; birds, hay, grain, mouldy dust; stress, mood, impact
SADMA only if time — note social wine and move on. Deliver: most likely + reason → contributors → exclusion list → CXR + spirometry → switch the tablet → teach-back
ask: Examiner, before I begin, may I have the vital signs? → 'I'm sorry to hear that, Jane, and I'm glad you've come in to have it looked at. I'll ask quite a few questions and we'll work out the cause together. Some will seem unrelated to a cough — there are a lot of possible causes and I'd like to go through them properly. Is that alright?'

How long? On and off, or there constantly — weeks when you're fine? Getting worse? ★ Do you cough at night, or does it wake you from sleep? Anything make it better or worse? Is there a particular place or situation that sets it off — at work, outdoors, certain seasons, exercise, lying down?

Is the cough dry, or chesty — do you bring anything up? What colour — clear or yellow-green? Thin and watery or thick and sticky? ★ Have you ever noticed any blood in it? A teaspoonful, or more like an eggcupful? Bad smell? A slightly unusual question — what does the cough sound like: a loud honking cough, one explosive bark? A whooping sound at the end? Harsh and barking? Any shortness of breath or noisy breathing?

★ Now some questions I ask everyone with a persistent cough: lost any weight or appetite? Lumps or bumps? Unusually tired? Ever coughed up blood? Ever had cancer in the past? What's your occupation now — and what did you do before that? Ever exposed to asbestos? Chest pain? Breathless on exertion? Breathless lying flat — how many pillows? Swelling in your legs?

Fevers, chills, night sweats? ★ Sore throat or runny nose — now, or recently? Body aches, joint pains? Do you ever vomit after a coughing bout? Travel overseas, contact with anyone unwell or with TB? Worse at night or on exercise? Family asthma, eczema, hay fever? ★ Do you smoke now, or have you ever — does anyone smoke at home or at work? Recurrent chest infections as a child?

★ Are you on any medications at all? → lisinopril → (note flatly, continue) Heartburn? Acid or bitter taste? Sudden rush of saliva? ★ Do you feel secretions dripping down the back of your throat? Facial pain or blocked nose? Rashes or joint pains? Birds at home, or hay, grain, mouldy dust at work? How is this affecting your life — stress at home or work, how's your mood?

'The most likely cause of your cough is the blood pressure tablet you take. Lisinopril belongs to a family of medicines with a well-recognised side effect of a persistent dry cough — roughly one in ten people. Yours fits: months long, every day, dry. It can start at any point — days, or many months later. But I don't think it's only that. The secretions running down the back of your throat — post-nasal drip — irritate the throat and cause a cough in their own right. And the viral illness two weeks ago can leave a cough behind for several weeks. So there are probably three things contributing, which is quite common.'

★ 'I also want you to know what I was looking for and what I don't think this is. I was particularly concerned to rule out lung cancer, because a cough that won't settle always deserves that — you haven't coughed up blood, lost weight or appetite, you've never smoked and had no asbestos exposure, which is all reassuring. I considered heart failure — no chest pain, no breathlessness lying flat, no ankle swelling. Infections — pneumonia, whooping cough, TB — no fevers, night sweats, vomiting after coughing, travel or sick contacts. Asthma, smoking-related lung disease and bronchiectasis — nothing supports those. And reflux, an allergic reaction in the lungs from dust or birds, and sarcoidosis. I'd like a chest X-ray and breathing tests to be certain, and to change that tablet to one that doesn't cause cough — it usually settles within a month of switching. Does that make sense?'
pefe: No examination task. If asked: ENT (nasal mucosa, post-nasal drip, pharynx), chest, cardiac, peak flow/spirometry

Management if asked: switch lisinopril → ARB (e.g. candesartan/irbesartan), don't simply cease; intranasal corticosteroid ± saline for post-nasal drip/rhinitis; post-viral cough — time, review; CXR (any cough >3 weeks), spirometry; review 4–6 weeks; red flags → return VERIFY

Findings-dial versions (same stem, same questions): Setting 1 lisinopril only · Setting 2 lisinopril + reflux triad (heartburn, bitter taste, water brash) → 'both are contributing and we'd treat both' · Setting 3 (scripted) lisinopril + PND + post-viral · Setting 4 lisinopril + wheat farm + father and brother MIs in their fifties → name hypersensitivity pneumonitis as a real possibility; heart failure considered and unlikely (no chest pain, orthopnoea, oedema)
If she pushes for one answer: the medication is the main one because of the duration and daily pattern; the others add to it
SA: CXR via local radiology; Country Health Connect; TIS 131 450; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 only in the red-flag version
fails: Winding the history down after 'lisinopril' ★
Omitting the cancer block — automatic fail; not asking haemoptysis ★
Telling her to simply stop the tablet ★
Reassuring before asking anything ('I'm sure it's nothing'); ignoring the lung worry
Asking 'runny nose?' only in the present tense — missing the post-viral finding; 'do you smoke?' without ever/passive; occupation now only
Omitting the sound box; jargon (productive, wet, haemoptysis, post-nasal drip); alcohol counselling detour; a single diagnosis with no exclusion list
numbers: Chronic cough >8 weeks · subacute 3–8 · acute <3 · CXR for any cough >3 weeks · ACE-inhibitor cough ~1 in 10 (5–20% across sources), onset days to months, settles 1–4 weeks after switching to an ARB, occasionally up to 3 months VERIFY
The '-prils': perindopril · ramipril · lisinopril · enalapril · captopril · big three with a normal CXR: post-nasal drip · asthma · reflux

Phlegm C·C·C·V·O: colour · consistency · content · volume (teaspoon vs eggcup) · odour · cough sounds: honking = psychogenic · whoop = pertussis · barking = croup/laryngeal · bovine = recurrent laryngeal nerve
Pertussis: the 100-day cough — paroxysms, whoop, post-tussive vomiting, PCR, notifiable · reflux triad: heartburn · acid taste · water brash · COPD: post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.7
Target: ≥5 differentials from ≥4 groups · self-check at 4 min: haemoptysis, weight loss, occupation before, medications, heartburn, secretions behind the throat
Red-flag version → MED-41 · habitual cough version → MED-42

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Stem reconstructed from the red-flag variant (Setting 5 / Variant D) — the notes give the findings, not a verbatim door stem.
stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a cough of ten weeks. She has smoked for 25 years. She has coughed up blood twice, has lost 6 kg without trying, and her voice has become hoarse.
Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Identical structure to MED-40 — but the delivery abandons reassurance and moves to urgent imaging.

back.dx: Lung cancer until proven otherwise — haemoptysis ×2, 6 kg unintentional weight loss, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), 25 pack-years, 10-week cough. Run the identical four-box → red-flag → infection → airways → others structure; the answers decide the delivery. The failure this variant tests: delivering the reassurance script from the standard version. Warning shot, the word cancer, pause, no prognosis, CXR today + urgent CT + specialist review, support person.
plan: Vitals; WIPE; open question; acknowledge the fear; signpost
Four boxes: timing (10 weeks, nocturnal), triggers, character with C·C·C·V·O — ★ blood: how many times, how much, fresh or dark, clots — sound (hoarse/bovine?), SOB/noisy breathing/stridor

★ Cancer block in full: weight quantified, appetite, lumps (neck/supraclavicular), tired, previous cancer, occupation now and before, asbestos; hoarseness duration, dysphagia, bone pain, shoulder/arm pain, headache/morning vomiting, face/arm swelling; ★ smoking now or ever, how many, how long → pack-years aloud; heart failure questions

Infections (fever, sweats, TB contact, travel — TB is a real differential with haemoptysis and weight loss); airways; the others (medications — ACEi still asked; reflux; PND; birds/dusts; mood/impact); FHx; concerns

Support person → warning shot → 'the combination of coughing up blood, losing weight without trying, the change in your voice and your smoking history means I'm concerned about a serious cause in the lung, including the possibility of a cancer' → pause → not able to tell today, not waiting → differentials → CXR today, urgent CT, specialist review → safety-net → summary
ask: Before I begin, may I have the vital signs? → 'I'm glad you've come in — let me ask quite a few questions so we can work out what's going on together'
★ Tell me about the blood — how many times, how much (streaks, a teaspoon, more), fresh red or dark, any clots? When was the last time?

★ How much weight, over how long? Appetite? Lumps in the neck or above the collarbones? Ever had cancer? Occupation now — and before? Asbestos? How long has your voice been hoarse — constant? Any trouble swallowing? Bone pain, shoulder or arm pain? Headaches, morning vomiting, weakness? Swelling of the face or arms?
★ Do you smoke now, or have you ever — how many a day, for how many years? → 'that's about 25 pack-years'

Fevers, night sweats? TB contact, travel? Chest pain, breathless on exertion, pillows, ankle swelling? Medications? Heartburn, acid taste, saliva? Secretions down the throat? Birds, dusts? How are you coping, mood? Anyone in the family with lung disease or cancer? What are you most worried this might be?

★ 'Before I go on — is there anyone you'd like to have with you? … I want to be honest with you. The combination of coughing up blood, losing weight without trying, the change in your voice and your smoking history means I'm concerned about a serious cause in the lung, including the possibility of a cancer. I'm not able to tell you that today — but I'm not going to wait either.' [pause]

'That's a lot to take in. What's going through your mind?' → 'How long have I got?' → 'I'm not going to give you a number I can't stand behind. What matters is what this is and whether it has spread — the scan will tell us. I won't keep anything from you.'

'I'd like a chest X-ray today, and I'll arrange an urgent CT scan of your chest and a specialist review. The other things I've considered are TB and other infections, which can also cause blood and weight loss; smoking-related lung damage; a growth on the voice box itself; and a clot — the tests will tell those apart. If you cough up more than a small amount of blood, become more breathless, or get chest pain or fever, go straight to the emergency department. Is there someone who can come with you?'
pefe: No examination task; if asked — cachexia, clubbing, cervical/supraclavicular nodes, hoarse voice, stridor, chest signs (effusion, collapse, monophonic wheeze), Horner's, SVC signs, hepatomegaly

Investigations: CXR today; urgent CT chest + upper abdomen with contrast; FBE, UEC, LFT, Ca, coags; sputum cytology and AFB ×3 (TB); urgent respiratory referral (bronchoscopy/biopsy) and ENT for the hoarse voice (laryngoscopy); lung cancer MDT
Differentials to name: lung cancer · laryngeal cancer · TB · bronchiectasis/chronic bronchitis with infection · PE with infarction · lung abscess · COPD · (ACEi if on one — still not the answer here)
Hoarseness >3 weeks in a smoker = laryngoscopy regardless VERIFY · smoking cessation offered at every visit — Quitline 13 7848, NRT, varenicline — without lecturing
SA: urgent respiratory at RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin, PATS, Cancer Council SA 13 11 20, TIS 131 450
fails: Delivering the reassurance script — 'probably your tablet / a virus' — to a smoker with haemoptysis, weight loss and hoarseness ★
No warning shot / never saying cancer / inventing a prognosis ★
Not quantifying the haemoptysis and weight loss; not converting smoking to pack-years
Omitting TB from the differential; omitting the laryngeal cause of the hoarse voice
Outpatient routine CXR only — no urgent CT, no specialist referral, no timeframe
No safety-net; no support person; no summary
numbers: Red flags: haemoptysis · unintentional weight loss · hoarseness · dysphagia · cough >3 weeks in a smoker · night sweats · lymphadenopathy
25 pack-years · 6 kg · 10 weeks · haemoptysis ×2 — any haemoptysis in a smoker >40 → CXR then CT regardless of film VERIFY
National Lung Cancer Screening Program (LDCT 2-yearly, 50–70, ≥30 pack-years, asymptomatic) — NOT for her; she needs diagnostic CT VERIFY
Hoarseness: recurrent laryngeal nerve (left, aortic arch) from mediastinal tumour/nodes; or primary laryngeal cancer — laryngoscopy
TB: haemoptysis, weight loss, sweats, contacts — sputum AFB ×3, notify · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · Quitline 13 7848
Breaking bad news: permission → warning shot → the word → apology → silence → check in → plan with timeframe → safety-net

setting: General practice. Stem reconstructed from Variant C (the 2019 one-off) — findings given, not a verbatim door stem.
stem: A 25-year-old man, an accountant, presents with a cough that has been present for five years. He denies any stress.
Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Identical structure; the entire history is normal, and the diagnosis is one of exclusion.

back.dx: Habitual (habit) cough — a diagnosis of exclusion after a completely normal five-year history: no red flags, no infection, no airway disease, no medications, no reflux, no post-nasal drip, no exposures, and he explicitly denies stress. Deliver it as a habit, not a psychiatric problem, and do NOT attribute it to stress when he has denied it. Still arrange a CXR and spirometry because this is a diagnosis you only make once everything else is excluded. Ask the sound box — a loud honking, barking cough that disappears in sleep supports it.
plan: Vitals; WIPE; open; acknowledge (five years is exhausting and embarrassing); signpost

Four boxes — timing (five years, constant, ★ does it happen during sleep?), triggers (situations, attention, meetings), character (dry, C·C·C·V·O incl. blood), ★ sound (honking, explosive single bark, whoop, barking), SOB/wheeze
Red flags anyway: weight, appetite, lumps, haemoptysis, previous cancer, occupation now and before, asbestos; heart questions

Infections; airways (nocturnal/exertional, atopy, smoking/vaping/passive, childhood infections, pertussis vaccination); the others — medications, reflux triad, PND, rashes/joints, birds/dusts; impact, mood, stress (accept his denial), sleep

Deliver: 'having gone through everything, I can't find any features pointing to a problem in your lungs, your heart, an infection, reflux or a medication. When a cough goes on this long with nothing else to find, one recognised explanation is a habitual cough…' → CXR + spirometry to be certain → exclusion list → plan (behavioural approaches, review) → teach-back
ask: Before I begin, may I have the vital signs? → 'Five years is a long time to put up with this — let's go through it properly'

★ Does the cough happen while you're asleep — has anyone ever heard you cough in your sleep? Does it disappear when you're absorbed in something? Worse when you're aware of it, in meetings, on the phone?

★ What does the cough sound like — a loud, honking cough, one single explosive bark? A whoop at the end? Harsh and barking? Dry or chesty — colour, thickness, any blood, how much, smell? Short of breath, noisy breathing?
Weight or appetite loss? Lumps? Tired? Ever coughed up blood? Previous cancer? Occupation — and before? Asbestos? Chest pain, exertional breathlessness, pillows, ankle swelling?

Fevers, sweats, sore throat now or recently, vomiting after coughing, travel, TB contact? Worse at night or on exercise? Family asthma/eczema/hay fever? Smoke or vape now or ever, anyone at home? Childhood chest infections, whooping cough, vaccinations?

Any medications at all? Heartburn, acid taste, sudden saliva? Secretions down the back of the throat, blocked nose, facial pain? Rashes, joints? Birds, hay, grain, mould? How is it affecting work and life? How's your mood — and any stress? (he denies — accept it) How do you sleep?

★ 'Having gone through everything, I can't find any features pointing to a problem in your lungs, your heart, an infection, reflux or a medication. When a cough goes on this long with nothing else to find, one recognised explanation is a habitual cough. That means there is no physical problem in your lungs — after a chest infection people sometimes get into the habit of clearing their throat, and the cough simply stays. I'd still like a chest X-ray and breathing tests to be certain, because this is a diagnosis we only make once everything else is excluded.'
