'What I was looking for and don't think this is: lung cancer — no blood, no weight loss, never smoked; heart failure; infections including whooping cough and TB; asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis; reflux, post-nasal drip, a medication cough, allergic reactions to dusts or birds, sarcoidosis. Does that make sense?'
pefe: No examination task; if asked — ENT, chest, cardiac normal; observe the cough (loud, honking, absent when distracted)
Investigations to close the loop: CXR, spirometry ± bronchodilator; consider FeNO; ENT review if any laryngeal symptoms; no need for CT with a normal film and no red flags VERIFY

Management: explain the mechanism without blame; behavioural — suppression techniques, sipping water, substitute swallow, awareness training; speech pathology referral (behavioural cough suppression therapy); avoid unnecessary medication; review 4–6 weeks; reconsider if any new feature VERIFY
Frame: habit, not psychiatric; he denied stress — don't insist on it; offer that if stress ever becomes relevant, it's worth raising
SA: speech pathology via Country Health Connect; TIS 131 450
fails: Attributing it to stress after he has explicitly denied stress ★
Naming habitual cough without first running and excluding the full structure ★
Skipping the cancer block because he's 25 and never smoked; omitting haemoptysis
Omitting the sound box and the sleep question — the two discriminators for this diagnosis
Framing it as 'psychological' / 'in your head'; not arranging CXR and spirometry
No exclusion list; no plan; no review
numbers: Habitual/psychogenic cough: loud honking or barking, absent during sleep, disappears with distraction, normal investigations, often post-infective onset — a diagnosis of exclusion VERIFY
Chronic cough >8 weeks · CXR for any cough >3 weeks · big three with a normal CXR: post-nasal drip · asthma (cough-variant) · reflux — exclude each by history and spirometry/FeNO/trial
Cough sounds: honking = psychogenic/habit · whoop = pertussis · barking = croup/laryngeal · bovine = recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
Pertussis vaccination: dTpa booster; the '100-day cough' is a differential in adults VERIFY
Behavioural cough suppression therapy (speech pathology) has evidence for refractory chronic cough VERIFY

stem: Peter Callaghan, a 62-year-old man, has had three months of increasing breathlessness and a cough. He has lost about 6 kg without trying. He has smoked around 20 cigarettes a day for forty years and worked as a boilermaker in his twenties. You have already taken a history and examined him. His chest X-ray is on the screen in front of you.

Examination: no distress at rest, no cyanosis; reduced chest expansion at the left base; trachea central; dullness to percussion at the left base; absent breath sounds there; reduced vocal resonance. Cardiovascular examination normal, no leg oedema.
tasks: Interpret the chest X-ray
Explain the chest X-ray to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
Outline your management plan
time: 8 minutes (2 min reading). The film is task 2 of four — keep it to 60–90 seconds. Seven moves: permission → three colours → airway midline → normal side → abnormal side → name it → next step.

back.dx: Left pleural effusion — homogeneous opacification of the left lower zone, blunted costophrenic angle, rising lateral meniscus, no air bronchogram, trachea central, right lung clear, left heart border obscured — AND the concern about why it is there: lung cancer most likely (6 kg, 40 pack-years), then heart failure, infection incl. TB, mesothelioma (boilermaker — asbestos lagging), liver/kidney causes. Peter is flat and guarded, arms folded, has looked it up and is convinced it's cancer, hasn't told Denise; hidden agenda: will he see his first grandchild, due in April. 'Airway midline' is the sentence nobody says. Naming the effusion and stopping answers half the question.
plan: To the examiner if asked: PA erect, name/date/old films, RIPE quality (not rotated, six anterior ribs, adequate exposure), trachea central, bones/soft tissues, the left lower zone finding with meniscus and no air bronchogram, right clear, left heart border obscured → left pleural effusion

Permission: 'I'd like to show it to you, because it's easier to understand when you can see it' → three colours → ★ 'this dark line down the centre is your main airway — sitting straight down the middle, which is what we want' → normal RIGHT side first, sharp angle → left: angle filled in, white curving up → 'fluid around the outside of the lung, pressing on it — why you've been so breathless — a pleural effusion' → tie it to the examination (dull, no breath sounds)

'So you drain it and I'm fixed?' → 'we will take fluid off and that will help — but I have to be honest with you about something first' → support person? → ★ 'the fluid isn't the whole problem — the question is why it's there' → pause → cancer named, apology, 'we don't know it yet' → silence → 'what's going through your mind?'
'How long have I got?' → no number → differentials to the patient: heart backing fluid up · infection incl. TB · mesothelioma — asbestos as a boilermaker · liver/kidney fluid retention

Plan: ultrasound-guided fluid sample (inflammatory vs pressure fluid; cancer cells; infection) → CT chest + upper abdomen → bloods → respiratory referral, MDT — all this week → safety-net → 'should I tell Denise?' → his decision, welcome her at results, Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 → concerns (grandchild) → smoking help → summary
ask: 'Thanks for waiting, Peter. Your X-ray is back and I've had a good look at it. I'd like to show it to you, because it's easier to follow when you can see it. Is that all right?'

'This is a picture of your chest. There are really only three colours. White is bone — ribs, collarbone, spine. Grey is soft tissue, like your heart here in the middle. And black is air, which is what healthy lung looks like.'

★ 'This dark line running down the centre is your main airway — your windpipe. It's sitting straight down the middle, and that is exactly what we want. Now this side first — your right. The lung is dark all the way down, and this sharp little angle at the bottom, where the lung meets the chest wall, is nice and pointed. That side looks normal to me.'

★ 'But on this side — your left — that same angle isn't sharp any more. It's filled in and it's white, and the white goes up in a curve like this. That white is fluid, sitting around the outside of the lung and pressing on it — and that's why you've been getting so short of breath. The medical name is a pleural effusion, which just means fluid around the lung. It matches what I found when I examined you — that side was dull when I tapped it and I couldn't hear the breath sounds.'

★ 'Before I go on — is there anyone you'd like to have with you, or would you rather I keep going? … The fluid isn't the whole problem. The question is why it's there, and that's what decides what happens next. [pause] Putting together the fluid, the six kilos you've lost and forty years of smoking, the possibility I'm most concerned about is a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that to you. We don't know it yet — but I'm not going to pretend it isn't what I'm thinking.' [pause — don't fill it]

'That's a lot to take in. What's going through your mind?' → 'How long have I got?' → 'I'm not going to give you a number I can't stand behind. What matters is what type this is and whether it has spread — and that's exactly what the scan and the sample will tell us. What I can promise is that I won't keep anything from you.'

'The other explanations I'm thinking about: a heart problem, where fluid backs up into the lungs; an infection, including tuberculosis; a condition of the lining of the lung called mesothelioma, which is linked to the asbestos you may have met as a boilermaker; and problems of the liver or kidneys that make the body hold fluid. The tests are designed to tell those apart.'

'Here's what I'm going to do. First, a small sample of the fluid with a fine needle, guided by ultrasound so it's safe — it tells us whether it's inflammatory fluid or fluid from pressure, and we look for cancer cells and infection. Second, a CT scan of your chest and upper abdomen. Third, blood tests. Fourth, a referral to the respiratory team — and if this is what I'm worried about, a specialist team who manage exactly this. All this week; this is not something we wait on. If your breathing gets worse, you cough up blood, or get chest pain or fever — straight to the emergency department. And I'd like to see you again when the results are back so we go through them together.'
pefe: Examination is given in the stem: reduced expansion, dull, absent breath sounds, reduced VR at the left base, trachea central = effusion; CVS normal, no oedema → against heart failure

Examiner-register film read: 'PA erect adult film; confirm name and date, compare old films; adequate — not rotated, six anterior ribs, adequately exposed; trachea central; bones and soft tissues unremarkable; homogeneous opacification of the left lower zone with a blunted costophrenic angle and a rising lateral meniscus, no air bronchogram; right lung clear; left heart border obscured so cardiac size unreliable; conclusion — left pleural effusion'. Consolidation would show an air bronchogram and no meniscus — say both

Effusion work-up: ultrasound-guided tap → protein, LDH, cytology ×3, Gram stain/culture, pH; Light's criteria; CT chest + upper abdomen; FBE, UEC, LFT, albumin, Ca; drain ≤1–1.5 L per sitting; respiratory referral; lung cancer MDT; PATS for travel from Yorke Peninsula

Disclosure: 'Denise doesn't know I'm here — should I tell her?' → his decision, no right answer today, most find it harder alone, welcome her at results; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 (anonymous). 'Will you tell me straight?' → yes. Grandchild in April → acknowledge what he actually wants to know without promising
Smoking: 'should I stop?' → yes, and concrete help — Quitline 13 7848, NRT, varenicline — no lecture. Don't go back and take more history

Variants: (1) mass instead of effusion — 'a round white shadow in the upper part of the lung, about golf-ball size … I'm afraid that shouldn't be there … concerned this could be a cancer' · (2) pneumothorax — 'a fine line is the edge of your lung; everything outside it is black with none of the normal markings — air has leaked out, the lung has partly collapsed; very treatable'; hypotensive + deviated trachea → don't describe the film: 'tension pneumothorax, clinical diagnosis, decompress before imaging' · (3) cardiomegaly to a student — erect PA first, CTR >0.5; in a 5-year-old two weeks after a sore throat → acute rheumatic fever with carditis; look for venous diversion, Kerley B, effusions; pericardial effusion mimics — echo · (4) normal film, patient not — 'normal and reassuring, but a chest X-ray can miss small cancers, early scarring and clots; given the weight loss and cough I still want a CT'
fails: Missing the warning shot, or never saying the word cancer ★
Naming the effusion and stopping — not saying 'and I'm concerned about why it's there' ★
Starting the film with the abnormality; omitting 'airway midline'; abnormal side before normal ★
Calling it consolidation (no meniscus/air-bronchogram reasoning); jargon (opacity, effusion, costophrenic — 'you've lost me')
Filling the silence; inventing a prognosis; false reassurance in variant 4 ('your X-ray is clear so there's nothing to worry about')
Fewer than three other causes; no asbestos/mesothelioma; no fluid sample and CT; no timeframe; no safety-net; film over 90 seconds
numbers: Three densities: white bone · grey soft tissue · black air · RIPE: Rotation (clavicles equidistant from spinous process), Inspiration (5–6 anterior / 8–10 posterior ribs), Picture (PA erect), Exposure (hemidiaphragm just visible through the heart)

CTR >0.5 = cardiomegaly, erect PA only · right hemidiaphragm higher (liver) · meniscus + no air bronchogram = effusion · air bronchogram = consolidation · trachea pushed away: tension pneumothorax, massive effusion · pulled towards: collapse, fibrosis, pneumonectomy
Silhouette sign: right heart border = right middle lobe · left heart border = lingula · hemidiaphragm = lower lobe
Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5 · LDH ratio >0.6 · pleural LDH >⅔ ULN → exudate · drain ≤1–1.5 L per sitting VERIFY · mesothelioma latency 20–40 years

Lay-sentence bank: consolidation 'cloudy white area is infection filling the tiny air sacs' · pneumothorax 'fine line is the edge of your lung, air has leaked out' · cardiomegaly 'heart shadow takes more than half the width' · hyperinflation 'lungs over-blown, diaphragm pushed flat' · mass 'round white shadow that shouldn't be there' · hilar nodes 'swollen glands at the centre of both lungs' · oedema 'fluid backed up because the heart isn't pumping it forward' · free gas 'air where there shouldn't be — something has perforated' · normal 'reassuring but doesn't rule everything out, I still want a scan'
Pass guide: 17+ of 23 with every bold item; missing the warning shot or the word cancer fails on its own · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · Quitline 13 7848 · TIS 131 450 · PATS

source: Chest_Xray_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Peter Callaghan — left pleural effusion; four variant films on the back)

stem: Mr James Halloran, 62, retired shearing contractor from Kadina. BMI 32. Ex-smoker, 40 pack-years, stopped two years ago. Admitted three weeks ago with shortness of breath, worse on stairs and exertion. Cardiology has cleared him. Family history of heart and lung disease. Using Ventolin with minimal effect. Here for his results.
Spirometry: FEV1 1.52 → 1.64 L (predicted 2.60); FVC 2.27 → 2.42 L (3.40); ratio 67 → 68 (predicted 76); change +120 mL, +3%. ABG on room air: pH 7.33 · PaCO2 58 · PaO2 62 · HCO3⁻ 30 · BE +4.
tasks: Explain the investigations to the patient
Explain your management plan in detail
time: 8 minutes. 0:00 open · 0:45 spirometry · 1:50 gas · 2:40 name COPD and check · 3:25 PIVOT to management whether or not you've finished · 6:50 action plan and safety net · 7:45 summarise.

back.dx: COPD — fixed airflow obstruction (post-BD ratio 68 vs 76, reversibility 120 mL / 3% fails both thresholds) with a partially compensated chronic respiratory acidosis / type 2 respiratory failure (pH 7.33, PaCO2 58, HCO3 30 = kidneys compensating = long-standing, not new). PaO2 62 does NOT meet the home-oxygen threshold — say so confidently. The trap: Task 1 is 90 seconds that feels like the whole station; Task 2 is five minutes most candidates give ninety seconds. Hidden agenda: his brother ended up on home oxygen and died at 71 — 'am I going to end up dragging a bottle round?' (asked at ~6 min if you never ask what worries him). Never used a spacer, never been watched using the puffer. Snores; mood a bit flat; shearing-shed dust; father MI at 66.
plan: WIPE, identity, consent; 'two parts — tests, then the plan, and most of our time on the plan'; 'what have you been told, and what were you hoping to get out of today?' → ask what worries him most

Spirometry: total air out ÷ first-second air = ratio 67 vs ~76 → reduced → obstructive → 'airways narrowed'; after the puffer +120 mL/3% vs ≥200 mL and 12% → not significant → COPD not asthma; say 'post-bronchodilator'

Gas: oxygen + carbon dioxide (waste gas); CO2 staying in → mild acid → pH 7.33 vs 7.35–7.45 → respiratory acidosis → IMMEDIATELY the bicarbonate 30 = kidneys compensating slowly = long-standing and settled; PaO2 62 — no oxygen needed

Name it: 'COPD — long-term narrowing from years of smoking, far enough along that CO2 is building a little. What does that word mean to you?' → cancer? → not on these tests, same smoking history raises the risk, that's why we keep reviewing → oxygen fear → addressed kindly

Five headings signposted: (1) puffers — Ventolin reliever via SPACER; add salmeterol BD every day; tiotropium if not enough; NO inhaled steroid (say why if asked); 'show me how you use it' (2) fitter and lighter — pulmonary rehab 8 weeks, 2–3/week, content; exercise physiologist; dietitian (BMI 32); rural access: Country Health Connect, telehealth, PATS (3) prevent — stay stopped (Quitline 13 7848 if slips); three vaccines named with intervals: influenza yearly (free), pneumococcal now + a few months + ≥5 years, COVID booster (4) support — Lung Foundation Australia + fact sheets (5) action plan

Written action plan: worse breathing/cough/phlegm than usual = flare-up → reliever 4–8 puffs q3–4 h → prednisolone 50 mg daily × 5 → amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 5 ONLY if phlegm increased AND changed colour; both boxes today; 000 for sudden severe breathlessness, chest pain, confusion/drowsiness, reliever not lasting 3 h; GP Management Plan; review 4–6 weeks; ★ teach-back
ask: 'I'll do this in two parts — the tests, then the plan, and most of our time goes on the plan. Before I start — what have you already been told, and what were you hoping to get out of today?' → 'And what worries you most?'

★ 'Your ratio is 67, and we'd expect around 76 — so it is reduced. A reduced ratio means an obstructive pattern; in plain terms your airways are narrowed. After the puffer we look for at least 200 millilitres and 12 per cent; yours is 120 and 3 per cent, so it is not significantly reversible. Narrowing that does not open up with a puffer is what we call COPD. I used the post-bronchodilator ratio, because that is the diagnostic criterion.'

★ 'Carbon dioxide is the waste gas your lungs are meant to breathe out. Because your airways are narrowed, some is staying in. It dissolves to make an acid, so your blood is slightly acidic — pH 7.33 where we'd want 7.35 to 7.45; we call that respiratory acidosis. Now the useful part: your bicarbonate is up at 30. That is your kidneys compensating, and it only happens slowly — so this is long-standing, not something new and dangerous.'

'Am I going to end up on oxygen like my brother?' → ★ 'Home oxygen is only for people whose oxygen level is genuinely low, and it's assessed formally by a specialist team. Yours is not at that level. Most of what happens from here depends on the plan we make today.'
'Is it cancer?' → 'Not on these tests. The same smoking history does raise that risk, which is exactly why I'll keep reviewing you.'

★ 'Keep the blue Ventolin for symptoms — through a spacer, far more gets into your lungs. I'm adding a long-acting puffer, salmeterol, morning and night every day whether or not you feel breathless — that's the one that changes how far you can walk. Before you go, show me how you use it.' 'Are these steroids?' → 'No — and I'm deliberately not starting an inhaled steroid; that's reserved for people with repeated flare-ups or a particular blood cell raised.'

★ 'Flu vaccine every year, free for you. Pneumococcal — one now, another in a few months, a third at least five years later. And your COVID booster.' 'Pulmonary rehabilitation has better evidence for your breathlessness than any third puffer.' 'Do I have to go to Adelaide?' → 'Not necessarily — regional and telehealth-supported programmes through Country Health Connect; PATS for travel and accommodation if you do.'

★ 'Both things have to happen: more phlegm and a colour change. Antibiotics taken when you don't need them stop working when you do. Can you tell me back what you'd do if your phlegm turned green tomorrow?'
pefe: No examination task — results interpretation and counselling. Inhaler technique check counts as the examination: shake, slow deep breath, hold ~10 s, spacer

Summary to the examiner: '62-year-old ex-smoker, 40 pack-years, exertional breathlessness, cardiac disease excluded. Post-bronchodilator spirometry: ratio 68 against a lower limit of 76 with only 120 mL and 3% reversibility — fixed airflow obstruction. Gas: partially compensated chronic respiratory acidosis with type 2 respiratory failure. Diagnosis COPD. Started a long-acting bronchodilator with spacer-delivered reliever; referred pulmonary rehabilitation, exercise physiology, dietetics; influenza, pneumococcal and COVID vaccination; written action plan with prednisolone and amoxicillin rescue pack; GP Management Plan, review 4–6 weeks; lung cancer kept under review'

Variant A — raised TLC, low DLCO: 'those two lines tell me which type of COPD — air trapping and damaged air sacs = emphysema; the other type is chronic bronchitis where phlegm is the main problem; both sit under COPD and we treat them the same way'

Variant B — still smoking: 'everything else helps; only one thing changes how fast the damage continues, and that's stopping. How do you feel about it? … combination NRT or a tablet plus Quitline 13 7848 roughly trebles the chance; and while you're smoking home oxygen isn't safe or available'

Variant C — two admissions last year, eosinophils 0.4: the one situation where adding an inhaled steroid is worth it → combination inhaler; trade-off slightly higher pneumonia and thrush risk — rinse after each dose

Variant D — 'how long have I got?': no number; what changes it — stopped smoking (done), rehab, vaccination; plenty live many years well managed; 'is there something specific behind the question?' · SA: Country Health Connect, PATS, Lung Foundation 1800 654 301, Quitline 13 7848
fails: Spending the station on Task 1 — no pivot at 3:25; management given ninety seconds ★
Offering home oxygen (PaO2 62 doesn't meet the threshold) ★
Saying 'acidosis' without the compensation point; 'obstructive' without a plain-English tail ★
Rescue pack without doses, without the two-limb antibiotic trigger, or without teach-back ★
Letting him think the new inhaler replaces Ventolin; no spacer; no technique check; starting an inhaled corticosteroid
'Vaccinations' as one word; Lung Foundation not named; never asking what worries him — the oxygen fear lands at 7:30; ignoring rural access
numbers: COPD: post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.70 · reversibility ≥200 mL AND ≥12% · this chart: 68 vs 76, +120 mL / +3% · pH 7.35–7.45 · PaCO2 35–45 · HCO3 22–26 · home O2 threshold PaO2 ≤55 mmHg (or ≤59 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia) · target SpO2 88–92% VERIFY
Salmeterol 50 microg BD · tiotropium 18 microg daily · ICS only if ≥2 exacerbations or eosinophils ≥0.3 · rehab 8 weeks, 2–3 sessions/week VERIFY

Action plan: salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer q3–4 h · prednisolone 30–50 mg mane × 5 days, no taper · amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 5 days (or doxycycline) ONLY with increased volume AND colour change · 000 triggers: severe breathlessness, chest pain, confusion/drowsiness, reliever <3 h VERIFY
Vaccines: influenza yearly (NIP-funded with COPD) · pneumococcal — 13vPCV then 23vPPV at 2–12 months, second 23vPPV ≥5 years (check current schedule) · COVID booster per age/eligibility VERIFY
Emphysema (↑TLC, ↓DLCO) vs chronic bronchitis — same treatment · GP Management Plan/Team Care Arrangement funds allied health
Quitline 13 7848 · Lung Foundation Australia 1800 654 301 · Country Health Connect · PATS · TIS 131 450

stem: You are a general practitioner. Your next patient is Ken Ballard, a 60-year-old man, with fever, cough and shortness of breath for three days, coughing up yellow phlegm, more than usual. He has known COPD and uses puffers. Investigations are available.
T 37.8 °C · SpO2 93% RA · RR 22 · HR 92 · BP 130/80 · WCC 14.5 · CRP raised · COVID-19 PCR negative · CXR: hyperinflated, no consolidation.
tasks: Interpret the investigations to the patient
Explain the reasons for his condition
Explain your further management
time: 8 minutes. 0:30 agenda + his concern · 2:30 results ending on 'no consolidation' · 4:00 flare-up and trigger · 6:30 three medicines, inhaler check, written plan · 7:15 red flags and follow-up · 8:00 smoking, vaccines, rehab, summary.

back.dx: Infective exacerbation of COPD without consolidation — all three Anthonisen cardinal symptoms (more breathless, more phlegm, purulent) → antibiotic + prednisolone + reliever; meets no admission criteria → home with a written three-zone action plan. Hidden: he thinks it's pneumonia (father died of it); the brown preventer is taken 'most mornings' = half the time, never used a spacer; still smokes 15/day for 40 years (three quit attempts, longest six weeks). Baseline SpO2 93–94% — ask it. Three things that must physically happen: say 'no consolidation — this is not a pneumonia'; watch him use his inhaler and correct it; write and hand over a three-zone plan with doses and a 000 trigger.
plan: Intro, identity, consent; agenda covering all three tasks + 'something written to take home'; ★ 'what were you most worried it might be?' → pneumonia → 'I'll answer that directly'

Results in lay terms: T 37.8 fits infection · SpO2 93% — 'for your lungs a reasonable number — what does it usually sit at?' → same as baseline, no oxygen today · WCC 14.5 = infection-fighting cells responding, not a danger measure · CRP raised · COVID negative · CXR: hyperinflation = chronic, not new; ★ 'no white patch anywhere — you do not have pneumonia'

Flare-up explained: airways permanently narrowed and inflamed (smoking) → infection → swell, more phlegm, narrower → temporarily much worse than normal; trigger named: three changes together = infective flare-up = why antibiotic. 'Why do I keep getting these?' → smoking, adherence/technique, vaccination, rehab — sort at review
'Do I need hospital?' → admission criteria listed (breathless at rest, confusion/drowsiness, cyanosis, new leg swelling, not responding, nobody at home) → meets none → home, wife present

Three medicines with numbers: salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer q3–4 h then PRN · prednisolone 50 mg mane × 5 days, no wean, side effects named (sleep, appetite, mood, sugar) · amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 5 days because colour changed. 'Do I have to take steroids?' → short course, benefit, side effects short-lived, his call

★ 'Show me how you take your puffer — I ask everyone' → correct: shake, slow deep breath, hold 10 s, spacer given. ★ Write green/amber/red with doses; red = breathless at rest/talking, reliever not helping or <3-hourly, chest pain, drowsy/confused/blue lips → 000. Review 48–72 h booked; healthdirect 1800 022 222 after hours. Later: Quitline 13 7848 + PBS pharmacotherapy (no lecture), flu/pneumococcal vaccines, pulmonary rehab. Summary + 'what have I not covered?'
ask: 'Ken, I've got all your results. I'd like to go through them, explain what I think has caused this, then agree a plan — including something written for you to take home. Before I start, what were you most worried it might be?'

'Your oxygen level is 93 per cent — for someone with your lungs that's a reasonable number. Can I ask what it usually sits at when you're well?' 'Is that low? Do I need oxygen?' → 'It's the same as your usual, which is reassuring — and no, not today. In COPD we're happy with a number in that range.' 'Fourteen — dangerous?' → 'Higher than normal, but a sign your immune system is working, not a measure of danger on its own.'

★ 'Two things on the X-ray. First, your lungs look bigger and blacker than usual with flattened diaphragms — they're holding on to air they can't push out. That's your COPD; it's been there a long time, it isn't new today. Second — and this is what I was looking hardest for — there is no white patch anywhere on this film. That's what we'd see with pneumonia. You do not have pneumonia.'

'This is a flare-up of your COPD, set off by an infection in the airways. Three things have changed together: more short of breath, more phlegm, and the phlegm has turned yellow. Those three together are what tell me it's an infective flare-up — and they're the reason you're getting an antibiotic as well as everything else.'

★ 'The things that would make me admit someone are being breathless at rest, confusion or drowsiness, blue lips, new swelling in the legs, not responding to treatment, or having nobody at home. You don't meet any of those, so I'm happy to treat you at home — provided you take the plan with you and someone is around tonight.'

★ 'Three things, starting today. One, your reliever — 4 to 8 puffs through a spacer, every 3 to 4 hours while you're like this, then back to as needed. Two, prednisolone, 50 milligrams each morning for 5 days — settles the swelling; five days then stop, no weaning; it can affect sleep, appetite and mood and push your sugar up for a few days. Three, amoxicillin, 500 milligrams three times a day for 5 days, because that phlegm has changed colour.'

★ 'Before you go, can you show me how you take your puffer? I ask everyone — it's the commonest reason treatment doesn't work.' → 'That's close. Two changes: shake it first, and breathe in slowly and deeply rather than fast, then hold for about ten seconds. And always through the spacer — I'll give you one today.'

★ 'I'm writing this down for you, because at two in the morning nobody remembers what the doctor said. Green — well: usual breathlessness and phlegm, daily preventer, reliever as needed, off cigarettes. Amber — flare-up starting: more breathless, more phlegm, or colour change → reliever 4–8 puffs every 3–4 hours, prednisolone 50 mg each morning for 5 days, start the amoxicillin, ring us. Red — breathless at rest or talking, reliever not helping or needed sooner than three hours, chest pain, drowsy, confused or blue lips — that's 000. I'll see you in 48 to 72 hours either way; after hours healthdirect 1800 022 222.'
pefe: No examination task beyond the inhaler technique check; findings are the investigations in the stem
Why not admit: no rest dyspnoea, no confusion, no cyanosis, no oedema, SpO2 at baseline, supportive wife at home; reassess at 48–72 h

Variant 1 — 'why can't I just have the antibiotic?': 'You are getting one because the phlegm has changed colour. But the antibiotic only deals with one part — the swelling in the airways is what's making you breathless, and that's what the steroid and reliever treat. Antibiotic alone and you stay breathless longer.' If only ONE cardinal symptom and no purulence → no antibiotic; bronchodilator + prednisolone, explain, safety-net

Variant 2 — deteriorating (drowsy, confused since lunch, SpO2 88%): possible type 2 respiratory failure → controlled oxygen 88–92%, ABG, ADMIT; nebulised bronchodilators, IV/oral steroid, antibiotics, NIV if pH <7.35 with PaCO2 >45; country site → ring receiving physician early, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

Variant 3 — present to the examiner instead: 'infective exacerbation of COPD without radiographic consolidation, all three Anthonisen cardinal symptoms present, meeting no admission criteria' → three drugs with doses, inhaler check, written action plan, 48–72 h review
Smoking: 'most people who succeed have several goes first — that isn't failure, it's the normal pattern' → proper appointment, medication support, Quitline 13 7848; if lectured he shuts down
fails: Never saying 'no consolidation — this is not pneumonia' — describing hyperinflation and stopping ★
Not watching and correcting inhaler technique; no spacer ★
No written three-zone plan, or a plan without doses or a 000 trigger ★
'Steroids and antibiotics' without doses/durations; not saying no taper; side effects unnamed
Panicking at 93% or promising oxygen; not asking baseline saturation
Not asking his concern; admission criteria not given; no 48–72 h review; lecturing about smoking
numbers: Salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer q3–4 h · prednisolone 30–50 mg mane × 5 days, no taper · amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 5 days, or doxycycline 200 mg day 1 then 100 mg BD × 5 days · oxygen target 88–92% · ABG if SpO2 <92% or drowsy · NIV if pH <7.35 with PaCO2 >45 VERIFY
Anthonisen cardinal symptoms: ↑ dyspnoea · ↑ sputum volume · ↑ purulence → antibiotic if 2 of 3 including purulence (here all 3)
Admission criteria: dyspnoea at rest · confusion/drowsiness · cyanosis · new peripheral oedema · failure to respond · inadequate home support · significant comorbidity · SpO2 well below baseline
Review 48–72 h · rehab and maintenance review 4–6 weeks · brown preventer taken half the time — adherence and technique addressed at review
Prednisolone side effects at 5 days: insomnia, appetite, mood, hyperglycaemia — short-lived; no adrenal suppression concern at this duration VERIFY
Quitline 13 7848 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450

stem: You are a general practitioner. Your next patient is Jenny, a 57-year-old woman, who has booked an urgent consultation after she coughed up blood. It happened while she was eating dinner.
Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. 45 s opening · ten history boxes · examination with ENT added · diagnosis with four reasons, then differentials.

back.dx: Pulmonary tuberculosis — two teaspoons (~10 mL) of bright red blood with a little phlegm, coughed not vomited, streaks once or twice before; 5 kg over one to two months, appetite down, tired, drenching night sweats, slight cough; missionary work in Cambodia 'to help sick people' (she will never say TB — ask what the work involved); never smoked, no asbestos, one pillow, no clots/thinners/rashes. Examination completely normal (vitals normal, no clubbing/nodes, ENT clear, chest clear) — 'a normal examination doesn't reassure me: early TB and a central lung cancer both examine normally'. Lung cancer must be named aloud (weight loss). Hidden agenda: her late husband died of lung cancer. Three lines that must be said: 'did you cough it up, or vomit it?' · 'any recent travel, contact with people who've been unwell — what did that work involve?' · 'I'm also concerned about the possibility of lung cancer'.
plan: Vitals — RR and SpO2 first, then BP, pulse, temp; open question; the concern statement (safe hands, NOT 'I'm sure it's nothing'); 'please tell me it's not something awful' → 'I can't answer that yet, but I promise I'll tell you exactly what I think before you leave'
The bleed: when, first time, colour, ★ volume with anchors (a few drops or a large amount?), mixed with phlegm; the event: doing what, ★ choking, nosebleed, ★ coughed or vomited

Cancer block: weight → ★ over what period; appetite, lumps, tired, occupation now AND before, asbestos, cough/SOB/noisy breathing, previous cancer, Pancoast pair (hand numbness/weakness, drooping eyelid/pupil)

Infection block: fever/chills, ★ night sweats, sore throat/runny nose/facial pain/PND, ★ travel, sick contacts, animals → ★ 'what did that work involved?' → join it up aloud: sick people in a TB-endemic country + 5 kg + sweats + haemoptysis

Rapid pairs: smoking now/ever; childhood infections/daily phlegm (bronchiectasis); clot (legs, travel, FHx); heart failure (chest pain, exertion, pillows, ankles); blood thinners, bleeding tendency; rashes/joints/haematuria (vasculitis); chest injury; PMHx/meds/allergies/FHx

Examination request incl. ★ ENT (nasal speculum, throat, posterior bleed, sinus tenderness), clubbing, cachexia, cervical/supraclavicular nodes, respiratory with VR, CVS, hepatomegaly, calves, ECG/spirometry → 'a normal examination doesn't reassure me'

Diagnosis: TB with four reasons → ★ lung cancer named → differentials one line each with the reason against → answers (curable; airborne — mask today, public health contact tracing; cancer will be checked) → CXR, bloods, sputum ×3, CT → safety-net → 'any worries or questions?' → husband → summary
ask: 'Before I start, could I have her vital signs — respiratory rate and oxygen saturation first, and also blood pressure, pulse and temperature, since she is bleeding and infection is on my list.' → 'I can see how stressful and scary this must be. I'm going to ask you a few questions and examine you, and I'd like to reassure you that you are in safe hands — we'll work out what's causing this together.'

When exactly? First time? Bright red or darker? ★ How much — a small amount like a few drops, or a large amount? Mixed with phlegm? What were you doing exactly? ★ Any choking beforehand? Any bleeding from your nose? ★ Did you vomit any blood, or was it definitely coughed up?

★ Have you lost any weight lately? → 'How much, and over what period of time?' Appetite? Lumps or bumps? Unusually tired? What's your occupation now — and what did you do before that? Asbestos? Cough, breathlessness, noisy breathing? Ever had cancer? And two unusual ones — numbness or weakness in your hands, and a drooping eyelid or a difference in your pupils?

Fever or chills? ★ Night sweats — waking up drenched? Sore throat, runny nose, facial pain, secretions down the back of the throat? ★ Have you travelled anywhere recently? Contact with people who've been unwell, or with animals? → ★ 'Can I ask what that work involved?' → 'So you've been directly caring for unwell people in a country where tuberculosis is common, you've lost five kilos, you're getting night sweats, and now you've coughed up blood. Those four things together are important, and I'll come back to them.'

A few quick ones: ever smoked, now or in the past? Repeated chest infections as a child, phlegm most days? Leg swelling or pain, recent long travel, family clots? Chest pain, breathless on exertion or lying flat — how many pillows? Ankle swelling? Blood thinners? Bleeding disorders, bruising, nosebleeds? Rashes or joint pains? Blood in your urine? Chest injury? Other conditions, medicines, allergies, family?

★ Examiner: 'General appearance — distress, cyanosis, drowsiness, pallor; clubbing, cachexia, cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Because bleeding from the nose or throat is on my list I'd like to add an ENT examination: on speculum examination of the nose, any source of bleeding; on examining the throat, any source of bleeding or visible posterior bleed; any sinus tenderness. Respiratory — symmetrical movements, tracheal position, percussion, breath sounds, added sounds, vocal resonance. Cardiovascular — JVP, apex, S1 S2, murmurs, gallop. Abdomen — swelling, tenderness, hepatomegaly. Lower limbs — calf size difference. ECG, and spirometry if available.' → ★ 'A completely normal examination doesn't reassure me here — early tuberculosis and a central lung cancer can both examine normally, so my diagnosis rests on the history and on imaging.'

★ 'Jenny, the most likely diagnosis is tuberculosis — a type of lung infection. Four reasons: contact with sick people in a country where TB is common; five kilos lost; night sweats; and coughing up blood. I also want to be honest that I'm concerned about the possibility of lung cancer, mainly because of the weight loss, so I'll check for that too — less likely than the infection, but I won't leave it unchecked.'

'Isn't TB a Victorian disease?' → still common in many parts of the world, we see it here, and it is curable. 'Will I give it to my grandchildren?' → spreads through the air — mask here today; if confirmed, the public health team will offer testing to people close to you; routine, to protect them. 'Is it cancer?' → 'one of the things I have to rule out, and I will — I'm not going to pretend it isn't on my list. But the picture fits an infection best.'
pefe: Findings: comfortable, not pale, no clubbing, no nodes · ENT no source of bleeding, no sinus tenderness · chest symmetrical, trachea central, resonant, normal breath sounds, no added sounds, VR normal · JVP not raised, apex undisplaced, dual heart sounds · abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly · calves equal · ECG sinus · spirometry unavailable · vitals RR 16, SpO2 97%, BP 128/78, P 84, T 37.1

Differentials to the patient with the reason against: bronchiectasis (no childhood infections) · COPD (never smoked) · heart failure (one pillow, no ankle swelling) · PE (no leg swelling, no recent travel) · nose/throat bleed (nothing found) · vasculitis/lupus (no rashes, joints, haematuria) · lung cancer stays ON the list

Plan today: CXR, FBE/UEC/LFT/CRP/coags, sputum ×3 for AFB smear, culture and NAAT, HIV test with consent, CT chest; mask/airborne precautions today; notifiable if confirmed — SA Health TB Services do contact tracing; safety-net — large volume or breathless → back immediately / 000; review as soon as results are back; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 if the cancer path opens

Variant 1 — cancer switch (20/day since 17, hoarse six weeks, never left the country, clubbing + hard fixed left supraclavicular node): warning shot → 'the combination … makes me worried about a growth in the lung — a lung cancer. I don't know that yet' → CXR today, urgent CT, specialist referral, bring someone → questions; Cancer Council SA + lung cancer nurse consultant

Variant 2 — it was haematemesis (vomited, coffee-grounds with food, epigastric burning, daily ibuprofen, black stools): 'that changes the whole picture — bleeding in the stomach or upper bowel, most likely a peptic ulcer' → observations for shock, FBE/UEC/LFT/coags/group & hold, stop ibuprofen, PPI, urgent gastroscopy VERIFY

Variant 3 — massive haemoptysis (large volume into a bowl, RR 32, SpO2 88%, BP 92/58, P 124): STOP the history — call for help + ambulance, protect the airway, high-flow O2, two large-bore cannulae, bloods + cross-match, fluid/blood, bleeding side DOWN, reverse anticoagulation, urgent transfer for bronchoscopy or bronchial artery embolisation; rural → MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 immediately VERIFY · Variant 4 — Pancoast (ulnar-side numbness and hand weakness, ptosis, months of shoulder ache): apex tumour invading lower brachial plexus (C8/T1) and sympathetic chain → Horner's (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis — NOT 'facial asymmetry'); add Horner's check and C8/T1 upper-limb neuro; urgent CT and referral
fails: 'I'm sure it's nothing serious' — false reassurance in a 57-year-old with haemoptysis ★
Never asking coughed vs vomited, or never asking what the Cambodia work involved ★
Never naming lung cancer aloud ★
Weight loss not given a time period; volume without the drops-or-large anchor; choking and nosebleed omitted
No ENT examination request; dropping cancer/clot/heart questions once TB is suspected
Naming TB and stopping — no reasons, no differentials with reasons against; no sputum ×3, mask, safety-net; never asking her worries (husband)
numbers: 2 teaspoons ≈ 10 mL · 5 kg over 1–2 months · weight-loss red flag >5% body weight in 6–12 months · massive haemoptysis >100 mL/h or 200–600 mL/24 h, or any volume with compromise → bleeding side DOWN VERIFY
TB work-up: sputum ×3 AFB smear, culture, NAAT · CXR ± CT · HIV · N95/airborne isolation · notifiable · treatment 6 months: 2 months RHZE then 4 months RH + pyridoxine VERIFY

Haemoptysis differentials: TB · lung cancer · bronchiectasis · COPD/bronchitis · pneumonia/abscess · PE · heart failure/mitral stenosis · anticoagulation/bleeding disorder · vasculitis (GPA, Goodpasture) · ENT source · trauma
Pancoast: C8/T1 (ulnar hand) + Horner's = ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis · hoarseness = recurrent laryngeal nerve
NLCSP: 50–70, ≥30 pack-years, current or quit within 10 years, asymptomatic only — not for a symptomatic patient VERIFY
Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · SA Health TB Services · TIS 131 450

source: Haemoptysis_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Jenny Marsden — TB after missionary work; four variants on the back)

setting: Emergency Department. You are the HMO.
stem: Your next patient is a 20-year-old woman with cough and shortness of breath. She developed flu-like symptoms three days ago and is now short of breath and feels feverish.
Her oxygen saturation is 92% on room air.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Request the investigations you would order
You are handed a chest X-ray — explain it to the patient
Explain the diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Opening + stability 0:50 · complaints to 2:20 · four boxes to 3:50 · examination + investigations to 6:20 · film (≤45 s), diagnosis, differentials, close.

back.dx: Community-acquired pneumonia, multilobar (right mid zone + smaller left basal patch), severity to be scored — Emily Novak, 20: cold Thursday, cough Saturday, breathless since yesterday, febrile 38.9, RR 26, HR 112, BP 112/68, SpO2 92%; green thick sputum 'a couple of tablespoons at a time', no blood, can lie flat, Panadol helped briefly. Three things NOT volunteered: right-sided pleuritic pain (only if asked) · vapes daily ('I don't smoke' first) · finals in two weeks (only if you ask her concerns). On the combined pill → complete the PE screen, then say aloud why PE is less likely once there is focal consolidation. Housemate had bad flu. PEFE: reduced expansion, dull, bronchial breathing + coarse crackles, INCREASED vocal resonance right mid zone, trachea midline. The task that fails people is investigations: nine relevant items in four headings with reasons (urea = CURB-65, albumin = SMART-COP) — not 'chest X-ray' and stop, and not twenty tests.
plan: Intro; ★ stability statement — 'your oxygen is a little low: resus cubicle, oxygen, full observations'; vitals from the examiner → 'febrile, tachycardic, raised RR, BP maintained'; open question; empathy; 'is it serious?' → 'exactly what I'm going to find out — I'll tell you straight'
Four complaints: cough and SOB — onset, constant, worse; air in vs tightness; rest vs exertion; lie flat; sputum C·C·C·V·O; fever measured, paracetamol response

Box 1 upper airway: sore throat, blocked nose, facial pressure, ear pain/discharge, neck lumps. Box 2 lower: wheeze, haemoptysis, ★ sharp pain on breathing in, ★ calves, asthma ever. Box 3 atypical: diarrhoea/vomiting, headache/confusion, aches, travel/hotels/spas, sick contacts, birds/farm animals/potting mix. Box 4 risk: ★ smoke — or VAPE; alcohol; long-term conditions (asthma, diabetes, heart, kidney, liver); medications incl. steroids/immunosuppressants; ★ the pill; flu and COVID vaccines
Closed examination questions in order (see PEFE) → 'dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance over one zone is consolidation'

★ Investigations — four headings, nine items, one breath (bedside · imaging · microbiology · bloods with the urea and albumin reasons); film handed mid-list → 'thank you — before I read this, may I finish my investigations?'

Film in plain English ≤45 s (three colours, heart/spine/airway, normal left, grey shadow right = infection, smaller patch left base = pneumonia). 'Only old people?' → no; admission → won't guess, score severity first. Diagnosis: CAP with the bug groups; differentials in named groups incl. PE and why less likely, sepsis; plan (oxygen, tests, antibiotics after cultures, severity score); safety-net; ★ 'anything else worrying you?' → exams
ask: ★ 'Good morning, I'm Dr —, one of the doctors in the Emergency Department. You're Emily, and you're 20? Before anything else I want to make sure you're safe. I'd like to move you into the resuscitation cubicle, put some oxygen on, and get a full set of observations. Then I'll ask some questions, look at your tests, and tell you what I think. Is that all right?' → 'Examiner — could I have the temperature, respiratory rate, pulse and blood pressure?'

Is it difficulty getting air in, or more a tightness? At rest, or only on moving? Can you lie flat? Dry, or bringing something up — colour, thickness, amount, any blood, any smell? Have you measured your temperature? Taken anything — did it bring it down?

Sore throat? Runny or blocked nose? Facial pressure? Ear pain or discharge? Lumps in your neck? Any noisy or wheezy breathing? Coughed up any blood? ★ Any sharp pain when you breathe in? ★ Any pain, swelling or tenderness in your calves? Ever had asthma or wheezed before?

Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting? Bad headache, felt confused? Aching all over? Recent travel, hotels or spas? Anyone around you unwell? Contact with birds, farm animals, potting mix or compost? ★ Do you smoke — or vape? Alcohol? Long-term conditions — asthma, diabetes, heart, kidney, liver? Medications, including steroids or anything for your immune system? ★ Are you on the pill? Flu and COVID vaccinations up to date?

★ 'I asked about the pill and your calves because a clot on the lung can look like this.' (after the examination: 'the fever, the green phlegm and a clear patch of infection on the film fit pneumonia much better — I'll keep the clot in mind')

★ Examiner, closed questions: 'General appearance — respiratory distress? cyanosis? drowsy? dehydrated? ENT — throat redness, swelling, exudate? nasal discharge? ears — discharge, red or bulging drum? Chest — is expansion symmetrical? where is the trachea? is there dullness, and in which zone? are breath sounds vesicular or bronchial, any added sounds? is vocal resonance increased, normal or decreased? Cardiovascular — S1, S2, murmur? Abdomen — distension, tenderness, masses?'

★ 'At the bedside — full observations including respiratory rate, continuous pulse oximetry, bedside glucose, an ECG, and an arterial blood gas. Imaging — chest X-ray, PA and lateral. Microbiology — sputum Gram stain, culture and sensitivities; two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics; nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and COVID-19; urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella. Bloods — full blood examination; urea, electrolytes and creatinine — the urea specifically because it is a CURB-65 item; liver function tests including albumin, a SMART-COP item; CRP as a baseline; and a lactate if I'm concerned about sepsis.'

'Let me show you. Bone is white, soft tissue grey, and air is black. This is your heart, this line your spine, this your main airway. On the left, the normal black lung and a sharp angle at the bottom. On the right, instead of black there's a grey shadow — where the air has been pushed out and replaced by infection. There's a smaller patch at the bottom of the left side too. That is pneumonia — an infection in the lung tissue itself.' → 'Isn't pneumonia only for old people?' → 'Commoner in older people, but healthy young adults get it — which is exactly why we treat it properly.' → 'Am I going to have to stay in? I've got finals' → 'Thank you for telling me — I'll factor it in. I won't guess: your oxygen is low and more than one part of the lung is involved, so once the gas and bloods are back I'll score the severity and give you a straight answer.'
pefe: Findings: mild respiratory distress, no cyanosis, alert, hydrated · T 38.9, RR 26, P 112, BP 112/68, SpO2 92% · ENT normal · reduced expansion right mid zone, trachea midline, dull right mid zone, bronchial breathing with coarse crackles right mid zone, increased vocal resonance right mid zone · heart sounds normal, abdomen soft

Diagnosis to the patient: 'a community-acquired pneumonia — an infection of the lung tissue picked up out in the community rather than in hospital; I can't yet tell you which bug: typical bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus), atypical (Legionella, Mycoplasma), or a virus such as influenza or COVID-19' — attach a severity: to be scored (CURB-65/SMART-COP) before disposition

Differentials to the patient in groups: above the voice box — throat, tonsils, sinuses (had those first, don't explain low oxygen or the shadow) · in the lungs — asthma, collapsed lung, inhaled object, whooping cough, TB, abscess · circulation — clot on the lung (asked pill, calves, travel; fever + green phlegm + focal patch fit pneumonia better) · overall — sepsis (cultures and lactate). To the examiner, technical order: PE · sepsis · typical CAP · atypical (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Q fever, psittacosis) · viral LRTI · upper airway infection by site · asthma · pneumothorax · abscess/empyema · TB · pertussis · pulmonary oedema · malignancy with post-obstructive pneumonia in an older smoker

Plan: oxygen 92–96%, tests, empirical antibiotics after cultures (amoxicillin 1 g 8-hourly ± doxycycline for low severity; benzylpenicillin IV + doxycycline for moderate; ceftriaxone + azithromycin for high), severity score → home vs ward; review 48 h; repeat film 6 weeks; vaping — irritates the airway, revisit; safety-net — breathing worse, confused/drowsy, can't keep fluids down, fever won't settle → straight back VERIFY

Traps: promising she'll be fine; abandoning pneumonia for PE (or ignoring the pleuritic pain + pill); asking which came first (spend it on orthopnoea/exercise tolerance); radiology jargon at the patient; three minutes on the film
fails: 'Chest X-ray' and stop — or treating the film's arrival as the end of the investigations task ★
Reciting every test you can name (thyroid, amylase, coags, 'septic screen just in case') ★
Open 'I'd examine the respiratory system' — no closed questions; omitting vocal resonance ★
No stability statement despite SpO2 92%; promising she'll be fine
Accepting 'I don't smoke' without the vaping question; not asking the pill/calves/pleuritic pain — or dropping pneumonia for PE
Ending on 'you have pneumonia' with no severity, disposition, safety-net; never asking her concern (exams)
numbers: CURB-65: confusion · urea >7 · RR ≥30 · BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic · age ≥65 · SMART-COP: SBP <90 (2), multilobar (1), albumin <35 (1), RR ≥25/30 by age (1), tachycardia ≥125 (1), confusion (1), O2 low (2), pH <7.35 (2) → ≥3 = risk of needing intensive respiratory/vasopressor support VERIFY

Antibiotics (Australian): low severity amoxicillin 1 g PO 8-hourly × 5 days ± doxycycline 100 mg BD; moderate benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly + doxycycline; high ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily × 7 days; severe penicillin allergy moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily · antibiotics within 1 h in septic shock · O2 92–96% · review 48 h · repeat CXR 6 weeks VERIFY
Consolidation signs: dull · bronchial breathing · coarse crackles · INCREASED vocal resonance (effusion: decreased) · trachea midline

Nine investigations, four headings: bedside (obs, oximetry, BGL, ECG, ABG) · imaging (CXR PA + lateral) · microbiology (sputum MC&S, blood cultures ×2 pre-antibiotic, respiratory viral PCR incl. influenza/COVID, urinary antigens pneumococcus + Legionella) · bloods (FBE, UEC — urea, LFT — albumin, CRP, lactate)

Atypical clues: diarrhoea/headache/confusion (Legionella), hotels/spas (Legionella), birds (psittacosis), farm animals (Q fever), potting mix (Legionella longbeachae), young adult dry cough (Mycoplasma)
Version B → MED-48 · Version C → MED-49 · TIS 131 450

source: Pneumonia_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Version A — Emily Novak, ED HMO, five tasks)

setting: Hospital ward. The patient's daughter is at the bedside; an antibiotic table is on the screen.
stem: A 70-year-old man has been diagnosed with a high-severity community-acquired pneumonia. He is confused and disoriented. eGFR 50. Documented allergy to amoxicillin and penicillin.
His daughter is with him. An antibiotic table is displayed on the screen.
tasks: Take a three-minute history (from the daughter)
Explain the condition and why it is high severity to the daughter
Explain your antibiotic choice
time: 8 minutes. Consent and role check first · 3-minute collateral history · severity explained with the criteria he meets · the two allergy questions, then the antibiotic with dose, route and duration.

back.dx: High-severity CAP in a confused 70-year-old with renal impairment and a labelled penicillin allergy — the station is the ALLERGY HISTORY: 'what actually happened, and how soon after the dose?' A rash three days later = non-severe delayed reaction → ceftriaxone is safe (no shared side chain with amoxicillin): ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily × 7 days, step down to oral when stable. Lip/tongue swelling within twenty minutes and an ambulance = anaphylaxis → avoid all beta-lactams → moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. Before anything: check she is his substitute decision-maker and has his consent to discuss. Severity: confusion, age ≥65, ± RR/BP/urea/O2/multilobar — name the criteria he meets.
plan: Intro; ★ 'before we talk about your father — can I check you're his substitute decision-maker, and that you have his consent for me to discuss his condition with you?'; acknowledge her worry

Collateral history (3 min): onset and course, cough/sputum/fever/breathlessness, when the confusion started and his baseline cognition, oral intake/urine output, comorbidities (heart, lung, kidney — eGFR 50, diabetes, immunosuppression), medications, smoking/alcohol, vaccinations, recent hospital/antibiotics, travel/animals/potting mix; ★ the allergy: what happened, how soon, how treated, any antibiotics since; advance care wishes

Explain: pneumonia = infection in the lung tissue; 'high severity' = the scoring criteria he meets — confusion, age, breathing rate/oxygen/blood pressure/kidney function as applicable → why that matters: higher risk, needs IV antibiotics, monitoring, possible ICU; honest about the confusion being part of the illness

Antibiotic choice reasoned aloud from the allergy history and the table: ceftriaxone + azithromycin (non-severe delayed rash) OR moxifloxacin (anaphylaxis); dose, route, duration; renal note (eGFR 50 — no ceftriaxone adjustment; check others); cultures before antibiotics; oral switch when stable
Supportive care (oxygen, fluids, monitoring, ICU threshold), what to expect, updates, questions, summary
ask: ★ 'Before we talk about your father — can I check you're his substitute decision-maker, and that you have his consent for me to discuss his condition with you?'

'When did he first become unwell? What has the cough been like — is he bringing anything up, what colour? Fevers, shivers? How is his breathing compared to normal? When did you first notice him confused — and what is he normally like: does he manage at home, remember things, recognise people?'

'Is he eating and drinking? Passing urine as usual? Any other conditions — heart, lungs, kidneys, diabetes? What medications does he take? Does he smoke or drink? Has he had his flu and pneumonia vaccines? Any recent hospital stays or antibiotics? Any travel, birds, animals, gardening with potting mix?'

★ 'His notes say he's allergic to penicillin. What actually happened when he took it — a rash, an upset tummy, or swelling of the lips or face, wheezing, collapse? And how soon after the dose — within an hour or two, or days later?'

'Your father has a pneumonia — an infection in the lung tissue itself. We call it high severity because of the things we score: he's confused, he's over 65, and his breathing/oxygen/blood pressure/kidney results add to that. High severity means a higher risk of the infection spreading to the blood, and that he needs antibiotics through a drip, close monitoring, and possibly the intensive care team if he worsens. The confusion is part of the illness and usually settles as the infection is treated.'

★ 'That was a rash, three days later — a non-severe delayed reaction. That means I can safely use ceftriaxone: it shares no side chain with amoxicillin. I'd give ceftriaxone 1 gram intravenously daily plus azithromycin 500 milligrams intravenously daily, for seven days, switching to tablets once he's stable.'
★ 'If instead he'd had swelling and collapse — anaphylaxis — I would avoid all penicillin-type drugs and use moxifloxacin 400 milligrams intravenously daily.'

'Alongside that: oxygen, fluids through the drip, blood cultures before the first dose, a chest X-ray and bloods, regular observations, and a low threshold to involve intensive care. I'll keep you updated. What questions do you have?'
pefe: No examination task; the stem gives the severity label — your job is to justify it with named criteria (CURB-65 ≥3 / SMART-COP ≥3) from the information available and ask for anything missing (RR, BP, SpO2, urea, CXR extent)

Antibiotic table logic: high-severity CAP = ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (or benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly if no allergy) + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily; non-severe delayed penicillin reaction → cephalosporin acceptable; immediate/severe (anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN, DRESS) → no beta-lactams → moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily; tropical/immunocompromised → add cover per guidelines VERIFY
eGFR 50: ceftriaxone no adjustment; azithromycin no adjustment; moxifloxacin no adjustment; avoid nephrotoxins, monitor fluids and renal function; dose-adjust if gentamicin ever considered VERIFY

Supportive: O2 92–96%, IV fluids for hypotension/poor intake, VTE prophylaxis, delirium care (orientation, family presence, avoid sedatives), ICU criteria (SMART-COP ≥5, septic shock, respiratory failure) VERIFY
SA: ID/respiratory consult; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if in a country hospital and ICU-level care may be needed; TIS 131 450
fails: Prescribing before asking what actually happened with the penicillin and when ★
Discussing him with the daughter without checking her role and his consent ★
Choosing a beta-lactam after an anaphylaxis history — or refusing ceftriaxone after a mild delayed rash ★
Antibiotic without dose, route, duration; no cultures before antibiotics; no oral switch plan
'High severity' without naming the criteria he meets; not explaining the confusion
History overrunning three minutes; no supportive care; no ICU threshold; no update plan
numbers: CURB-65: Confusion · Urea >7 · RR ≥30 · BP <90/≤60 · age ≥65 → ≥3 high severity · SMART-COP ≥3 VERIFY
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily × 7 days · moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily (severe allergy) · benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly + doxycycline if no allergy (moderate) VERIFY

Allergy history: reaction type (rash / GI / angioedema / wheeze / collapse / SJS) · timing (immediate <1–2 h vs delayed days) · treatment needed · tolerated any beta-lactam since · cross-reactivity amoxicillin–cephalosporin driven by side chains; ceftriaxone shares none with amoxicillin VERIFY
eGFR 50 = CKD 3a — no adjustment for ceftriaxone/azithromycin/moxifloxacin; caution with NSAIDs, gentamicin
Substitute decision-maker in SA: Advance Care Directive appointee, guardian, or 'person responsible' hierarchy under the Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 VERIFY
Antibiotics within 1 h in septic shock · review 48 h · CXR repeat 6 weeks · TIS 131 450

source: Pneumonia_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Version B — high-severity CAP, penicillin allergy, antibiotic table, daughter)

setting: Hospital ward. The patient's son is present.
stem: A 70-year-old man has been admitted with a cough productive of green sputum. His advance care directive requests all treatment, irrespective of outcome. Low blood pressure, low saturation, high temperature, raised respiratory rate.
Examination: left lower zone dullness, crepitations, reduced expansion. His son is present.
tasks: Explain the diagnosis, with reasons, to the son
Advise the immediate and short-term management
time: 8 minutes. Consent and role check · read the directive aloud · diagnosis with reasons (symptoms + observations + signs) · immediate resuscitation-level management · short-term antibiotics and escalation plan. Do NOT offer palliative care — the near-identical recall with a not-for-resuscitation directive is a different station.

back.dx: Severe community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis (hypotension, hypoxia, fever, tachypnoea; left lower lobe consolidation) in a 70-year-old whose advance care directive requests ALL treatment. The marked behaviour: read the directive aloud and say you will follow it; then immediate management at resuscitation level — resus area, monitoring, IV fluids for the low BP, high-flow oxygen, blood cultures then empirical IV antibiotics without waiting, CXR, ABG, UEC, CRP, lactate; short-term — ceftriaxone + azithromycin IV 7 days with oral switch, ICU if deteriorates, intubation and ventilation within what he has asked for; regular updates to the son. The failure this version tests: offering palliative care.
plan: Intro; ★ check the son's role/consent; acknowledge; ★ 'I have read your father's advance care directive, and I can see he has asked for all treatment that may help him. We will be following that.'

Diagnosis with reasons: green phlegm + fever + fast breathing (the story) · low BP, low oxygen, high temp, raised RR (the observations = severe, infection affecting the whole body — sepsis) · dull, crackles, reduced movement at the left lower lung (the examination = infection in that part of the lung) → 'a severe pneumonia of the left lower lung, with the infection affecting his circulation'

Immediate (say it as happening now): resuscitation area, continuous monitoring; IV access ×2; IV fluids for the low pressure (bolus, reassess); high-flow oxygen for the low saturation; blood cultures ×2 then IV antibiotics straight away — empirical; CXR, ABG, FBE, UEC, LFT, CRP, lactate, glucose, sputum, viral PCR, urinary antigens; catheter/urine output; senior + ICU notified

Short-term: ceftriaxone + azithromycin IV 7 days → oral when stable; reassess response at 48 h; ICU if deteriorates — non-invasive or invasive ventilation, vasopressors — 'within what he has asked for'; VTE prophylaxis, delirium care, nutrition, physio; repeat CXR 6 weeks
Communication: regular updates, involve him in decisions, name the ward/team contact; 'is there anything else I can do to support you?'; summary
ask: 'Before we talk about your father, can I check that you're the person he'd want me to speak with, and that you're comfortable for me to discuss his condition with you?'
★ 'I have read your father's advance care directive, and I can see he has asked for all treatment that may help him. We will be following that.'

'Your father has a pneumonia — an infection in the lung tissue. Three reasons: the story — green phlegm, fever and fast breathing; the examination — the lower part of his left lung is dull to tap, crackly to listen to and moving less, which is where the infection sits; and his observations — his blood pressure and oxygen are low and his temperature and breathing rate are high, which tells me the infection is affecting his whole body. That combination makes it a severe pneumonia.'

★ 'Right now: he goes to the resuscitation area with continuous monitoring. His blood pressure is low, so intravenous fluids. His oxygen is low, so high-flow oxygen. We take blood cultures and then start strong antibiotics into the vein without waiting for results — that's called empirical treatment. And we take a chest X-ray, a blood gas, kidney tests, inflammatory markers and a lactate.'

★ 'Ceftriaxone and azithromycin into the vein for seven days, switching to tablets once he's stable. If he deteriorates we would move him to intensive care; if his breathing becomes too laboured to sustain we may place a tube in his airway and support his breathing with a machine — and that is within what he has asked for.'
'I'll keep you in the loop with regular updates and involve you in decisions. Is there anything else I can do to support you?'

'Is he going to be alright?' → 'He is seriously unwell, and I won't pretend otherwise. Severe pneumonia at his age carries real risk. But we're treating it fully and quickly, exactly as he asked, and many people in his position do recover. I'll tell you straight as things change.'

Summary: severe left lower lobe pneumonia with sepsis; fluids, oxygen, cultures then IV antibiotics now; ceftriaxone + azithromycin for a week; intensive care and breathing support if needed, in line with his directive; regular updates
pefe: Findings are in the stem: hypotension, hypoxia, fever, tachypnoea; left lower zone dullness, crepitations, reduced expansion. Ask for the numbers if not given (BP, SpO2, RR, T, HR, confusion, urine output) to justify severity

Sepsis bundle: cultures before antibiotics; antibiotics within 1 h; 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension/lactate ≥4 with reassessment; lactate; oxygen; urine output; vasopressors for MAP <65 after fluids (ICU) VERIFY

Antibiotics: high-severity CAP — ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (or benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly + azithromycin) × 7 days; tropical/aspiration/immunocompromised modifications per guidelines VERIFY

Escalation consistent with the directive: NIV/HFNC, intubation and ventilation, vasopressors, renal support if needed; ICU consult early; document the directive; goals of care reviewed with the treating team AND family but treatment not withheld

SA: Advance Care Directives Act 2013 — a binding directive requesting treatment guides but does not compel futile treatment; treating team decides clinically appropriate care in line with wishes VERIFY; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for ICU retrieval from a country site; TIS 131 450
fails: Offering palliative care / comfort measures in a man whose directive requests all treatment ★
Not reading or acknowledging the directive aloud ★
Delaying antibiotics for results; antibiotics before cultures; no IV fluids for hypotension; no oxygen for hypoxia ★
Diagnosis without the three reasons (story, examination, observations); not naming sepsis/severity
No ICU/escalation plan; no mention that ventilation is within his wishes
Not checking the son's role/consent; jargon (empirical, consolidation) untranslated; no update plan
numbers: Sepsis: SBP <90 / MAP <65 · lactate ≥2 (≥4 severe) · RR ≥22 · altered mentation (qSOFA) · fluids 30 mL/kg crystalloid then reassess · antibiotics within 1 h VERIFY
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily × 7 days → oral (amoxicillin/doxycycline) when stable · moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily if severe beta-lactam allergy VERIFY
CURB-65 here: RR ≥30?, BP <90/≤60 ✓, age ≥65 ✓, ± confusion, ± urea · SMART-COP: SBP <90 (2), O2 low (2), RR (1), multilobar? → ≥5 = ICU consideration VERIFY

Immediate list: resus area · monitoring · 2× IV · fluids · high-flow O2 (target 92–96%) · cultures ×2 · empirical IV antibiotics · CXR · ABG · FBE/UEC/LFT/CRP/lactate/glucose · sputum · viral PCR · urinary antigens · catheter
Advance care directive requesting all treatment → follow it; do NOT offer palliation (that is the NFR variant) · O2 92–96% · review 48 h · CXR 6 weeks

source: Pneumonia_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Version C — severe CAP with sepsis, advance care directive requesting all treatment, son)

setting: Surgical ward. You are the medical officer; the nurse has asked you to review. The observation chart is available.
stem: James Whitmore, 45, was admitted after a cholecystectomy performed yesterday. The nurse has recorded a high temperature and has asked you to review him.
Observation chart: temperature 39.5°C on return to the ward, now 40.0°C · respiratory rate 15–20 initially, now 20–25 · SpO2 95% throughout, now drifting below 95% on room air.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
Outline your management plan
time: 8 minutes. Stability line 0:00 · fever block · post-op review block (pain and analgesia is the diagnosis being handed to you) · chest → heart → urine → wound → legs → cannula → drug/transfusion reaction · examination in fixed order with vocal resonance and the four abdominal asks · diagnosis + differentials grouped by time since surgery · management with analgesia FIRST.

back.dx: Post-operative day 1 fever with rising RR and falling SpO2, pain limiting deep breathing, decreased air entry and crepitations left mid-zone with vocal resonance NOT increased → atelectasis (the 'wind' of the timeline). Differentials grouped by time since surgery — immediate/first hours: drug or transfusion reaction, malignant hyperthermia, pre-existing infection; early to day 3: atelectasis, pneumonia, cannula thrombophlebitis, necrotising SSI (within 48 h), cardiac event (Version B); late after day 3: UTI (catheter), wound infection, VTE, intra-abdominal collection / bile leak, C. difficile. Antibiotics are withheld and the reason is said aloud. Discriminating behaviour: asking the cardiac questions in a station that 'looks respiratory', and putting analgesia first in the plan.
plan: Gel; ★ stability statement to the examiner ('continuous observations, monitored bed if he deteriorates — I have the chart, I'll proceed'); intro; open question; concern statement
Fever block: feels feverish? rigors/shaking chills? onset? ★ fever before the operation? getting worse?

Post-op review block: nausea/vomiting · bowels/wind · abdominal pain beyond the wound · dizziness · eating and drinking · out of bed · ★ 'are you in pain now — are the painkillers helping?' → react aloud: 'that's really important — I think the pain is part of the cause'
Chest: cough (dry/productive, colour), SOB, noisy breathing, lung disease, smoking. ★ Heart: chest pain or tightness even briefly, palpitations, previous cardiac disease

Urine (dysuria, frequency, offensive, loin pain, ★ catheter), wound (discharge, redness, swelling), legs (calf pain/swelling, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis), travel ('an infection picked up before surgery can present like this'), ★ cannula and WHEN it went in, ★ prior fever after surgery / transfusion / new medicine; PMH, meds, allergies

Examination in order: general (distress, cyanosis, pain) → vitals → respiratory in full incl. ★ vocal resonance → CVS → abdomen with the four asks (★ wound, suprapubic, renal angle, masses) + drain → cannula site → calves → urine dipstick

Diagnosis in plain English: 'because of the pain you haven't breathed deeply and a small part of the lung has collapsed down — common, treatable'. ★ Differentials named to the patient: chest infection (CXR), urine/wound infection, drip site, clot in leg/lung, drug reaction, strain on the heart

Management: ★ analgesia first, paracetamol for fever, CXR + bloods + urine MCS, monitoring with O2 if needed, physio for deep breathing and supported coughing (describe the technique, then the device), sit up and mobilise, no smoking (patches/Quitline), review this afternoon, safety net verbatim, 'any questions or concerns?' (hidden agenda: has something gone wrong, time off work), summary
ask: ★ 'Before I begin I'd like this patient on continuous observations, and I'd move him to a monitored bed if he deteriorates. I have the chart, so I'll proceed.'
'Do you feel feverish yourself? Any shivering or shaking chills? When did you first notice it? Did you have any fever before the operation? Is it getting worse?'
★ 'Are you in pain right now — are the painkillers helping?' → 'That's really important — I think the pain is part of what's causing this, and we'll fix it.'
★ 'Any chest pain or tightness, even briefly? Have you noticed your heart racing? Any previous heart trouble?'
'Any redness or pain at the drip site — and do you know when it was put in?' / 'Have you ever had a fever after an operation, a blood transfusion, or starting a new medicine?'
★ 'Can I have the vocal resonance, please?' / 'Is there suprapubic tenderness, and is there renal angle tenderness?'
'I've grouped my differentials by how long it is since the operation.'

'Collapsed sounds frightening, but it means a small area has gone airless — it re-inflates once you can breathe deeply again.' / 'Do I need antibiotics?' → ★ 'Not for this — antibiotics don't treat a collapsed lung. If the X-ray shows an infection, that changes.'

Safety net: 'Tell the nurses immediately if your breathing gets worse, you get chest pain, your heart races, the wound leaks or gets much more painful, or you feel faint. I'll be back to review you.' Do not promise a discharge date.
Summary: day 1 post-cholecystectomy fever, most likely atelectasis from pain-limited breathing; CXR and bloods, better analgesia, physio and mobilising, review this afternoon
pefe: Given: uncomfortable not distressed, no cyanosis. Chest movements symmetrical, trachea central; decreased air entry left mid-zone with crepitations; vocal resonance NOT increased. Heart sounds dual, no murmur. Abdomen soft, wound clean and dry, no suprapubic/renal angle tenderness, no masses, drain minimal serous. Cannula site clean. Calves soft and equal. Dipstick negative.

Variant — the vocal resonance switch (day 3): decreased air entry left base, coarse creps, vocal resonance INCREASED, bronchial breathing, green sputum → consolidation = hospital-acquired pneumonia: sputum + blood cultures, CXR, antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines HAP with local resistance in mind VERIFY

Variant — day 4 bile leak: generalised abdominal tenderness, ileus, bile-stained (green) drain → blood cultures, lactate, FBE/CRP/UEC/LFT/lipase, CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast, fasted + IV fluids, surgical registrar NOW — not physio and reassurance

Variant — septic turn mid-station (BP 85/50, HR 132): ★ stop the history, name the change, name the pathway, name who you call — high-flow O2, 2× large-bore IV, cultures, lactate, fluid bolus, empirical IV antibiotics within the hour, IDC, surgical reg + ICU, rural: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 early
Investigations: CXR, FBE, CRP, UEC, LFT, blood cultures if rigors/T ≥38.5, urine MCS, sputum if productive; ECG/troponin only if cardiac features (Version B)
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848 · TIS 131 450
fails: Omitting the cardiac questions because the chart 'looks respiratory' ★
Not asking 'are you in pain / are the painkillers helping', or hearing 'it hurts to breathe in' and not reacting ★
Naming atelectasis and stopping — no differentials given to the patient ★
Starting antibiotics for atelectasis, or leading the plan with physiotherapy rather than analgesia ★
Skipping the stability statement; or spending two minutes on DRS ABC in a history station
Not asking for vocal resonance, the four abdominal asks, cannula site + date, calves; 'full abdominal examination' and stopping
Continuing the history through a deteriorating patient (septic variant)
numbers: Stem obs: T 39.5 → 40.0°C · RR 15–20 → 20–25 · SpO2 95% → falling
Timeline: immediate (first hours) · early (to day 3) · late (after day 3) — 'wind, water, wound, walking, wonder drugs' mapped onto it
Paracetamol 1 g q6h, max 4 g/24 h · SpO2 target 92–96% · cannula resite by 72 h (local policy 72–96 h)

Escalation: SBP <90 · HR >130 · RR >25 · lactate ≥2 · new confusion · necrotising SSI within 48 h · febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction rise ≤1°C · malignant hyperthermia dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV · C. difficile oral vancomycin 125 mg QID × 10 days
'Fever does not exclude a pulmonary embolism.'
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848 · TIS 131 450

setting: Surgical ward, day 2–3 after cholecystectomy. You are the medical officer. Stem reconstructed from Version B in the variant section — the notes give the changed answers and findings, not a verbatim door stem.
stem: James Whitmore, 45, is two to three days post-cholecystectomy and has developed a fever. The nurse asks you to review him.
Observations: temperature 38.4°C · pulse 112 · BP 168/96 · respiratory rate 16 · SpO2 97% on room air.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
Outline your management plan
time: 8 minutes. Same nine-box spine as MED-50. The station is won or lost at the cardiac block: he only reveals the chest tightness if you ask. Normal RR, normal saturations and a normal chest mean you cannot call this atelectasis.

back.dx: Post-operative fever day 2–3 with tachycardia, hypertension, a normal chest, and — only on direct questioning — twenty minutes of chest tightness overnight with palpitations, a father with MI at 50, and antihypertensives withheld peri-operatively. Working diagnosis: peri-operative myocardial infarction / acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise (post-op MI is often painless or 'indigestion'; fever, tachycardia and hypertension from pain, catecholamines and withheld beta-blocker/ACE-I).
