Differentials kept in parallel: PE, intra-abdominal complication (bile leak/collection), pneumonia, atelectasis excluded by the normal chest. Discriminating behaviour: refusing the reflex atelectasis label when the respiratory findings are normal, and moving to ECG + serial troponin + monitoring + medical team in the room.
plan: Stability statement · intro · open question · concern statement (as MED-50)
Fever block, then the post-op review block including pain and analgesia

Chest questions — nothing much. ★ Cardiac: 'any chest pain or tightness, even briefly? heart racing? previous heart trouble? family history?' → 'tightness across my chest last night, twenty minutes, thought it was indigestion; heart thumping; Dad had a heart attack at fifty' · ★ 'Which of your usual tablets were stopped for the operation?' → BP tablets withheld
Urine, wound, legs/VTE, travel, cannula + date, reaction history; PMH, meds, allergies
Examination in the fixed order; findings: chest entirely normal, abdomen soft, wound clean, calves soft

★ To the examiner: 'With a normal respiratory rate, normal saturations and no chest findings I can't call this atelectasis. My working diagnosis is a cardiac event until proven otherwise — 12-lead ECG now, serial troponin, cardiac monitoring, medical team; and I want to know which cardiac and antihypertensive medicines were withheld. PE and an intra-abdominal complication stay on the list.'

To the patient in plain English: 'I'm concerned the operation may have put strain on your heart. I want to rule out a heart attack first because that's the one that can't wait — heart tracing and blood test now, and the medical team to see you.' Differentials named.

Management: monitored bed, ECG, troponin now and repeat, aspirin if no surgical contraindication after discussion with surgeon VERIFY, analgesia and antipyretic, restart withheld antihypertensives when safe, CXR/bloods/urine as baseline, medical registrar + cardiology, safety net, summary
ask: ★ 'Any chest pain or tightness, even briefly? Have you noticed your heart racing? Any previous heart trouble, and does anyone in the family have heart disease?'
★ 'Which of your regular medicines were stopped for the operation, and have they been restarted?'
★ 'With a normal respiratory rate, normal saturations and no chest findings, I can't call this atelectasis. My working diagnosis is a cardiac event until proven otherwise.'
'I'd like a 12-lead ECG now, serial troponin, cardiac monitoring, and I'd involve the medical team.'

'I'm concerned the operation may have put strain on your heart. I want to rule out a heart attack first, because that's the one that can't wait — so I'm doing a heart tracing and a blood test right now.'
'I've also thought about a clot in the lung, a problem inside the tummy from the operation, and a chest infection — nothing points to those, but I'm checking.'
Safety net: 'Tell the nurses immediately if the tightness comes back, you feel your heart racing, you feel faint or short of breath.'
pefe: Given: T 38.4, HR 112, BP 168/96, RR 16, SpO2 97%. Chest examination entirely normal. Abdomen soft, wound clean, calves soft.

Request the same fixed sequence as MED-50 — general, vitals, respiratory in full with vocal resonance, CVS, abdomen with the four asks + drain, cannula, calves, dipstick — the normal chest is the point.

Investigations: 12-lead ECG now and repeat; troponin now and at 3–6 h (high-sensitivity) VERIFY; FBE, UEC, CRP, LFT, glucose; CXR; blood cultures if rigors; CTPA only if the ECG/troponin do not explain it and PE is suspected

Peri-operative MI: often silent or atypical; risk peaks day 1–3; withheld beta-blocker/ACE-I and catecholamine surge contribute; management is with cardiology and the surgeon — antiplatelet/anticoagulant decisions weigh surgical bleeding risk VERIFY
SA: medical registrar / cardiology; rural — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to a PCI-capable centre (RAH/FMC/LMH) if STEMI or high-risk NSTEACS VERIFY
fails: Calling atelectasis with a normal RR, normal SpO2 and a normal chest ★
Never asking the cardiac questions — the tightness is only volunteered on direct questioning ★
Not ordering an ECG and troponin in the room; sending him for physio ★
Not asking which medicines were withheld peri-operatively
Dropping PE and intra-abdominal complication from the differential
Jargon to the patient ('ACS', 'troponin') without translation; no safety net
numbers: Version B obs: T 38.4 · HR 112 · BP 168/96 · RR 16 · SpO2 97%
Changed answers: 20 min chest tightness overnight 'indigestion' · heart thumping · father MI at 50 · BP tablets withheld for surgery
hs-troponin at 0 and 3–6 h; ECG repeat with any symptoms; monitored bed VERIFY
Post-op MI peak day 1–3 · fever + tachycardia + hypertension ≠ atelectasis

setting: General practice. You are the GP. The patient's relative (cousin) gives the history; the patient is beside her, awake but not really talking.
stem: A 40-year-old woman has been brought to the clinic feeling unwell. Her relative is with her and will speak to you.
Vital signs: BP 85/55 · pulse 122 · respiratory rate 18 · SpO2 93% on room air · temperature 36.8°C.
tasks: Take a history from the relative
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials
time: 8 minutes. Stability + flat positioning 0:00 · consent gate · unpack 'unwell' · timing · 'what was she doing just before?' (the sting) → treatment sentence and keep going · four anaphylaxis systems · mimic sweep · background · examination airway-first · diagnosis with three reasons + six lay differentials + after-care.

back.dx: Anaphylaxis to an insect sting (Marie Whitcombe, 40; history from cousin Dawn): sudden onset within minutes of a sting, hypotension with tachycardia (warm shock, CRT 3 s), widespread expiratory wheeze, flushing/pruritus, presyncope, nausea — no upper airway involvement, no stridor, no retained sting, glucose 6.2, ECG sinus tachycardia. Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis; adrenaline IM outer mid-thigh now, flat, ambulance. Differentials swept and named in lay terms with a reason each: septicaemia/meningococcaemia (no fever, blanching rash), cardiac event/arrhythmia (no chest pain, ECG sinus tach), stroke/SAH (normal neuro), ruptured ectopic/AAA/GI bleed (no pain, no bleeding, abdomen soft), hypoglycaemia (6.2), drug reaction (no medicines). Discriminating behaviours: the consent gate before disclosure, asking tongue/throat/voice by name, and airway + sting FIRST in the examination.
plan: Gel; ★ to examiner: 'treatment room, lie her flat, continuous monitoring, a colleague stays with her while I take the history'; intro; 'I can see you're both worried — what has happened?'; concern statement; ★ consent gate: 'has she agreed to my discussing her condition with you?'
Unpack 'unwell' (confused/sleepy, weak, feverish, struggling to breathe) · onset · worsening · ever before · ★ 'what was she doing just before this started?' → sting on the neck
★ Treatment sentence, then keep going: 'I want her lying flat, I'm giving adrenaline into her thigh now, and I'm calling an ambulance.'

Four systems: skin (rash/hives/welts, itch, lip/face/eye swelling) · lower airway (noisy breathing — what sound, SOB, cough) · ★ upper airway by name (tongue swollen? throat tight? voice changed?) · CVS (dizzy, faint, collapse) · GI (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain)

Mimic sweep, signposted: fever/chills, rash blanches?, headache/neck stiffness/photophobia, recent flu-like illness · chest pain/palpitations · weakness/numbness/slurred speech/gait/thunderclap headache · abdominal/back pain, bleeding, ★ LMP · asthma, allergies, EpiPen, medicines (diabetes, BP)

Examination airway-first: general (distress, cyanosis, rash, conscious state) → ★ lip/tongue swelling, ★ stridor, ★ visible sting — may I remove it? → chest (air entry, added sounds) → CVS (S1 S2, murmurs, CRT, peripheral temperature) → abdomen incl. expansile pulsatile mass → neuro (cranial nerves, fundoscopy, limbs) → bedside ★ glucose, dipstick, 12-lead ECG. Read the findings back before interpreting.

Diagnosis with three reasons (minutes after the sting; low BP + fast heart = circulation; wheeze = tightened airways); adrenaline given, repeatable; ambulance; ≥4 h observation in hospital because of biphasic reactions; six differentials in lay language with why each is less likely

Replies: 'is she going to be alright?' · 'never allergic before' (sensitisation) · after-care: two autoinjectors, action plan, training, allergy referral, venom immunotherapy; 'can she go home?' → not before 4 h; 'any questions or concerns?' (hidden agenda: cousin's guilt — reassure, no delay caused harm); summary
ask: ★ 'With those observations I'd take her to the treatment room, lie her flat and put her on continuous monitoring.'

★ 'Has she agreed to my discussing her condition with you?' (if 'only her cousin': 'she isn't well enough to consent right now, so I'll share what I need to in order to treat her, and speak to her directly as soon as she's able')
'Can you describe what you mean by unwell — confused, weak, feverish, or struggling to breathe?' / ★ 'What was she doing just before this started?'
★ 'That changes what I think is going on. I want her lying flat and not standing up, I'm giving adrenaline into the muscle of her thigh now, and I'm calling an ambulance.'
★ 'Is her tongue swollen? Does she say her throat feels tight? Has her voice changed?'
'I'm confident this is an allergic reaction, but I want to be sure I'm not missing an infection, a cardiac problem or a bleed.' / 'Does the rash fade when you press on it?'

★ To examiner: 'Before the systems — is there swelling of the lips or tongue? Is there stridor? Do I see a sting — if so, may I remove it?' / 'Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis — I'm not waiting for a test.'

'It's a severe allergic reaction — the sting has made her blood vessels open up and her airways tighten. The treatment is adrenaline into the thigh muscle, which I've given; it works within minutes and we can repeat it.'

'She needs at least four hours of observation, because occasionally these reactions come back.' / 'She'll go home with two adrenaline pens, a written action plan and training, and a specialist referral — venom immunotherapy can substantially reduce the risk.'
'Should I walk her through?' → ★ 'No — please keep her lying flat; standing up can drop her blood pressure further.'
Summary: sudden collapse ten minutes after an insect sting with low BP, fast heart and wheeze — anaphylaxis; adrenaline given, flat, ambulance, hospital observation, specialist follow-up
pefe: Given: pale, distressed, no cyanosis, mild chest flushing, alert. No lip/tongue swelling, no stridor. Insect bite on the neck, no retained sting. Air entry equal, widespread expiratory wheeze. Heart sounds dual, no murmur, CRT 3 s, peripheries warm. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses. Neuro normal. BSL 6.2. Dipstick negative. ECG sinus tachycardia.

Variant — airway (stridor, tongue swelling, croaky voice, 'throat closing'): highest-risk anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline now, repeat at 5 min, nebulised adrenaline, high-flow O2, 000 + anaesthetic support, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 early; do NOT examine the throat; sit with legs out if flat worsens breathing VERIFY

Variant — mimic (fever, shivering, non-blanching purpura, headache, photophobia, no sting): meningococcaemia until proven otherwise — adrenaline is NOT the treatment; immediate IM/IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone before transfer, cultures if no delay, fluids, ambulance/retrieval; notifiable — public health for contact prophylaxis VERIFY

Variant — drug trigger (amoxicillin this morning; card says penicillin allergy, nobody looked): stop the drug, adrenaline IM, flat, O2, fluids, ambulance; then ★ open disclosure — apologise for the event, state known facts, no blame or speculation, commit to incident report, allergy flag, and to coming back ADDED

Variant — teaching the autoinjector: 'blue to the sky, orange to the thigh' — pull blue cap, orange end firmly into outer thigh until it clicks (through clothing), hold 3 s (EpiPen; Anapen 10 s — CORRECTION to the teaching source's 5 s; check the device), rub 10 s, call 000 and say 'anaphylaxis', keep flat, second pen at 5 min if no better VERIFY

Post-event: tryptase 15 min–3 h + later baseline; ≥4 h observation (longer if severe, required repeat adrenaline, or asthma); discharge with 2 autoinjectors, ASCIA action plan, allergy referral, venom immunotherapy; TIS 131 450; healthdirect 1800 022 222
fails: Disclosing to the relative without the consent gate ★
Not asking 'what was she doing just before this started?' — the sting is volunteered only on that question ★
Not naming adrenaline with dose, IM route and outer thigh, or not keeping her flat / letting the cousin stand her up ★
Asking only about wheeze — omitting tongue swelling, throat tightness and voice change ★
Examining in textbook order and never reaching the airway/stridor/sting first
Racing to the diagnosis on 'stung' and dropping the mimic sweep and bedside glucose
Diagnosis without differentials, or no after-care (4 h observation, two pens, action plan, referral)
numbers: Stem obs: BP 85/55 · HR 122 · RR 18 · SpO2 93% · T 36.8°C
Adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 IM outer mid-thigh, max 0.5 mg (adult 0.5 mg = 0.5 mL), repeat every 5 min if no improvement
Autoinjectors: 150 mcg (7.5–20 kg) · 300 mcg (>20 kg / adult) · 500 mcg Anapen (>50 kg where supplied) · EpiPen hold 3 s · Anapen hold 10 s VERIFY
Fluid bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline if hypotensive · high-flow O2 · observation minimum 4 h · tryptase 15 min–3 h + baseline
Six lay differentials: blood infection · heart · stroke · bleed inside (ectopic/AAA) · low sugar · medicine reaction

stem: Your next patient is Sarah Whitlock, 50, complaining of tiredness.
Practice nurse observations: T 36.6 °C · pulse 88 · BP 118/74 · RR 14 · SpO2 99% · BMI 24.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Tell the patient your most likely diagnosis with your reasons, and give your differential diagnoses (2 minutes)
Investigations and management are not your task
time: 8 minutes. 0:35 open + concern · 1:45 four questions on the complaint · 5:30 HEMI-AD-COP in one burst, 1–2 questions per letter · 5:50 closure (expendable) · 6:00 hard stop → answer.

back.dx: Two things together: menopause transition (irregular cycle — two months apart, sometimes twice a month; hot flushes day and night; drenching night waking) AND iron-deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding (flooding, clots bigger than a coin, six or seven pads on the worst day, ibuprofen for the pain) → exertional palpitations and breathlessness on the stairs. Three months, low energy not sleepiness, sleeps fine, rest helps a bit, dropped two shifts. Everything else negative; mum had 'thyroid trouble'; no intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding (asked — the endometrial safety question). The three positives — heavy periods, exertional palpitations/dyspnoea, flushes with an irregular cycle — are the whole case, and candidates who ask periods only inside SADMA at 7:30 never find them. Hidden agenda: a colleague had bowel cancer after 'just feeling tired'.
plan: Intro, name, open question → she says she's worried → ONE sentence, then the set line, then work; 'lots of short questions, some won't seem related, yes or no is fine'
Four questions: ★ 'what do you mean by tiredness — sleepy, low in energy, or feverish?' · how long / every day / worse · better or worse with anything · how is it affecting your life

H: tanning, jaundice, dark urine/pale stools, itch · E: weather preference, polyuria, polydipsia · M: weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats, cancer in you/family · I: fever/chills, flu-like/sore throat, 'have you EVER been sexually active', condoms, travel · ★ A: palpitations/exertional SOB, blood loss (heavy periods, PR blood, surgery) → POSITIVE → probe (pads, clots, flooding, previous anaemia/iron, red meat, intermenstrual/post-coital bleeding)

AD: shoulder/hip stiffness, headaches, joints, rash · D: drugs, medicines incl. OTC, mood, anhedonia, stress · C: greasy stools, PR blood, chest pain, leg swelling, cough/haemoptysis, smoking · O: snoring/gasping, occupation/nights · ★ P: LMP, hot flushes → POSITIVE → note 'is that the change?' and keep moving
Closure if time: smoking, alcohol, allergies, PMHx, FHx (mum — thyroid)

Answer: name both → plain explanation → three reasons → three differentials excluded by one finding each (thyroid, depression, diabetes) → rapid-fire the rest until the bell (coeliac, bowel cancer, lymphoma/leukaemia, CKD, liver disease/haemochromatosis, glandular fever/long COVID, HIV, sleep apnoea, heart failure, medication side effects) → 'is it cancer?' in one honest sentence, keep listing
ask: 'Good morning, I'm Dr —. Am I speaking with Sarah Whitlock? How can I help you today?' → 'I'm sorry to hear that, Sarah, and I understand your concern. Let me ask you some questions, then examine you, so I can find the cause and make the best plan for you. Some of my questions will seem unrelated — I'm checking off causes one by one. Yes or no is fine.'

★ Can you tell me what you mean by tiredness — are you sleepy all the time, low in energy, or feeling feverish and unwell? How long? Every day or comes and goes? Getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse? How is it affecting your life?

Any tanning or bronzing of the skin? Yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, itching? Weather preference — cold or heat? Passing more urine? More thirsty? Weight loss without trying? Appetite? Lumps or bumps? Night sweats? Cancer in you or the family? Fevers or chills? Flu-like illness or sore throat recently? Have you ever been sexually active — condoms? Travel?

★ Any racing of the heart, or shortness of breath on exertion? Any recent blood loss — heavy periods, blood in the bowel motions, surgery? → 'How many pads on your heaviest day? Clots larger than a fifty-cent piece? Flooding through onto clothes or bedding? Ever told you were anaemic or given iron? Do you eat red meat? Any bleeding between periods or after intercourse? Any vaginal dryness?'

Shoulder or hip stiffness, new headaches, joint pains, rashes? Drugs? Medicines, including over the counter? Mood — still enjoying the things you used to? Stress at home or work? Greasy stools, blood in the stool? Chest pain, leg swelling? Cough — ever coughed up blood? Smoke? Has anyone told you that you snore or gasp in your sleep? What's your job — nights?
★ When was your last menstrual period? Have you had any hot flushes? → 'It may well be part of it — let me put it all together'

★ 'Sarah, I think there are two things happening together. First, you are going through the menopause transition — your ovaries are winding down, which explains the irregular periods, the hot flushes and the broken sleep. Second, because those periods have been so heavy, I think you have become iron deficient and anaemic — low in the iron your blood needs to carry oxygen around the body, which is why you are so flat. One, your periods have become irregular and very heavy over the last year; two, hot flushes and night sweats at fifty; three, your heart races and you get breathless on the stairs, which is what anaemia does.'

'I did also think about an underactive thyroid — less likely, no weather preference and no weight change. Depression — less likely, your mood is good and you still enjoy things. Diabetes — not passing more urine or thirsty.' → 'I don't have long, so let me tell you the rest I've been checking: coeliac disease, bowel cancer, lymphoma and leukaemia, chronic kidney disease, liver disease and haemochromatosis, glandular fever and long COVID, HIV and other infections, sleep apnoea, heart failure, and medication side effects.' 'So it's not cancer?' → 'I can't rule it out today, and that is exactly why I asked about weight, lumps, night sweats and bleeding. Nothing points that way, and the tests will cover it.'
pefe: No examination task in Version A (obs in the stem). If an examination request is needed (Version B, 2-min hard stop): general — pallor, jaundice, rash, cachexia · vitals, temperature first · thyroid — goitre/nodule · full lymph node examination · CVS — S1 S2, murmur, added sounds · respiratory — air entry, added sounds · abdomen — hepatosplenomegaly · office tests BSL, dipstick (+ BMI, neck circumference, Mallampati for OSA)

HEMI-AD-COP: Hepatic/Haemochromatosis · Endocrine (thyroid, diabetes) · Malignancy · Infection · Anaemia · Autoimmune/Drugs · Depression/Drugs · Coeliac/Cardiac/Chest · OSA/Occupation · Pregnancy/Periods — the letters are a memory aid; what's scored is that each system was actively excluded. If challenged: 'a nine-letter checklist so my questioning covers every system rather than being symptom-led.' The old F (chronic fatigue syndrome) was dropped — a diagnosis of exclusion, IOM 2015/NICE criteria, unreachable in 8 min
Umbrella words ('infections, cancers, psychological') score nothing — name each. No investigations, no iron tablets, no management: every second there is a differential you didn't say

Harder moments: 'just do a blood test' at 2 min → 'I will — the test I order depends on these answers, let me finish' · tearful → 'take your time, I can see this has been hard' then resume the letter · late agenda ('my sister had leukaemia') → thank, name lymphoma/leukaemia in the list, FBE · 'I don't know' to everything → offer options (more, less, about the same)

If asked afterwards: FBE, ferritin/iron studies, TFT, UEC/LFT, BSL/HbA1c, coeliac serology, B12/folate; pelvic ultrasound + endometrial assessment if intermenstrual/post-coital bleeding or persistent HMB at 50; menopause symptom management; SA — Country Health Connect; TIS 131 450
fails: Never asking about periods/LMP/hot flushes inside the differential block — reaching the end without them ★
Accepting 'tired' without defining sleepy vs low energy vs feverish ★
Not started the answer by 6:00 ★
Cruising past her opening worry; or spending forty seconds exploring the fear
Umbrella words; no reasons for the diagnosis; launching into investigations/iron
Three or four questions on a negative topic (she says 'no, definitely not'); 'don't worry, you're in good hands'
numbers: 8 min = 6 + 2 (or 4 + 2 + 2) · 1–2 screening questions per letter · 2:00 hard stop in PEFE · 60–90 s for diagnosis + differentials · ~6 s per differential · 3 reasons · 2–3 excluded individually then ≥8 rapid-fire

HMB: ≥7 pads/day, clots > 50-cent piece, flooding, >7 days · iron deficiency: ferritin <30 microg/L; anaemia Hb <120 g/L (women) VERIFY · menopause transition: cycle variability ≥7 days, then ≥60 days between cycles; menopause = 12 months amenorrhoea VERIFY
Endometrial red flags at 50: intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, HMB not responding, risk factors → ultrasound/endometrial sampling VERIFY
Red flags across the cluster: weight loss · lumps · night sweats · fever · bleeding · sleepiness with a commercial licence
Version B (James Corrigan OSA, truck driver) → MED-54 · Version C (Amy Deng pregnancy) → MED-55

stem: James Corrigan, 46, presents with six weeks of tiredness.
Observations: T 36.7 °C · pulse 84 · BP 138/86 · RR 16 · SpO2 96% · BMI 34.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings (2 minutes, hard stop)
Give your diagnosis with reasons and your differential diagnoses (2 minutes)
time: 8 minutes: 4 + 2 + 2. The occupation question is where the station lives.

back.dx: Obstructive sleep apnoea — sleepiness (not low energy) in a man with BMI 34, neck 44 cm, Mallampati III, BP 138/86, snoring/gasping/witnessed apnoeas and unrefreshing sleep; he is a LONG-HAUL TRUCK DRIVER, revealed only when you ask the occupation question. Sleepiness plus a commercial licence is a single-item fail if the driving line is omitted. Run HEMI-AD-COP in four minutes at one question per letter, keep the O block intact, examination request in region-plus-target closed form with BMI, neck circumference and Mallampati added, then diagnosis with three reasons and the differentials.
plan: Intro, open, one-sentence acknowledgement, set line
★ Define it: sleepy vs low energy vs feverish → SLEEPY → duration, daily, worse, modifiers, impact (dozing at the wheel? falling asleep watching TV?)

Compressed sweep, one question per letter: H · E (weather, urine, thirst — also asks diabetes at BMI 34) · M · I · A · AD · D (medicines, alcohol, mood) · C · ★ O: 'has anyone told you that you snore or gasp during sleep — do you stop breathing? wake unrefreshed, morning headaches, dry mouth? what's your job — and do you drive for a living?' → truck driver → ★ 'have you ever felt sleepy or nodded off at the wheel?'
'James, give me a moment — I'll speak with my examiner' → region + target, closed-ended, in order; add BMI, neck circumference, Mallampati; turn back

Diagnosis with three reasons (sleepiness with snoring/gasping; BMI 34, neck 44 cm, Mallampati III; blood pressure creeping up) → ★ the driving line → differentials: hypothyroidism, depression, diabetes, anaemia, narcolepsy/shift work, medication/alcohol, heart failure, chronic infection; sleep study referral if asked
ask: ★ What do you mean by tired — sleepy all the time, low in energy, or feverish and unwell? How long, every day, getting worse? What makes it better or worse? How is it affecting your life — do you find yourself dozing off?
★ Has anyone told you that you snore, or gasp, or stop breathing in your sleep? Do you wake unrefreshed? Morning headaches or a dry mouth? How many hours do you sleep, and are they regular?
★ What's your job? → 'long-haul truck driver' → 'How many hours a day are you driving? Have you ever felt sleepy, or nodded off, at the wheel? Any near-misses?'

Compressed letters: tanning/jaundice? weather preference, urine, thirst? weight change, lumps, sweats? fever, sore throat, sexual history, travel? palpitations, breathless on exertion, blood loss? stiffness, joints, rash? medicines, alcohol — how much, mood? bowels, chest pain, pillows, cough, smoking? (partner, children, stress — brief)

★ Examiner: 'On general appearance: any pallor, jaundice, rash or cachexia? Vital signs — temperature first, then BP, pulse, RR, saturations. Thyroid: any goitre or nodule? Full lymph node examination: any lymphadenopathy? Cardiovascular: S1 and S2 normal, any murmur or added sounds? Respiratory: air entry equal, added sounds? Abdomen: hepatosplenomegaly? Office tests — BSL and urine dipstick. For this patient I'd also like his BMI, neck circumference and Mallampati score.' → 'Thank you, James, I'm back with you'

★ 'James, the most likely explanation is obstructive sleep apnoea — during sleep the soft tissues at the back of your throat collapse and block the airway, you briefly stop breathing, and your brain wakes you just enough to start again, dozens of times an hour, so you never get refreshing sleep. Three reasons: you're sleepy rather than just low in energy, and you snore and gasp; your build — the weight and the size of your neck — makes the airway more likely to close; and your blood pressure is creeping up, which sleep apnoea does.'

★ 'I have to be direct about one thing because it matters for your safety and other people's: with this level of sleepiness and a heavy-vehicle licence, you must not drive until this has been assessed and treated. I know what that means for your income and I'll help you with that — a sleep study can be arranged quickly. I'm also obliged to tell you that you must inform the licensing authority, and if you don't, I have to.'

'I also thought about an underactive thyroid — less likely, no weather preference; depression — mood is alright and you still enjoy things; diabetes — worth a blood test at your weight but no thirst or urine changes; anaemia; heart failure; medications and alcohol; narcolepsy; and chronic infection.' 'Is it cancer?' → honest one sentence.
pefe: Findings: no pallor/jaundice/rash/cachexia · T 36.7, BP 138/86, P 80, RR 16, SpO2 96% · thyroid normal · no lymphadenopathy · heart normal · chest clear · no hepatosplenomegaly · BSL 6.4 · dipstick normal · BMI 34, neck circumference 44 cm, Mallampati III

Traps: 'I'd like to examine the respiratory system' → 'what are you looking for?' costs 15 s each time; forgetting to turn back to the patient; not asking BMI/neck/Mallampati; asking the occupation but not the driving question

If asked next steps: Epworth Sleepiness Scale, STOP-Bang, sleep study (level 1 in-lab or home level 2), CPAP if moderate–severe, weight loss, alcohol reduction, positional therapy; FBE, TFT, HbA1c, lipids, UEC; BP follow-up; fitness-to-drive assessment — Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive: commercial licence with sleepiness → non-driving until treated and reviewed; SA — notify Service SA/DPTI; sleep service via Country Health Connect/PATS VERIFY
Version A (Sarah Whitlock) → MED-53 · Version C (Amy Deng) → MED-55

Not defining sleepy vs low energy ★
Open examination requests; no BMI/neck/Mallampati; not turning back to the patient ★
Exceeding the 2-minute PEFE; not started the answer by 6:00
Diagnosis without three reasons; umbrella-word differentials
False reassurance; going into CPAP/management detail at the expense of differentials

STOP-Bang: Snoring, Tired, Observed apnoea, Pressure, BMI >35, Age >50, Neck >40 cm, male Gender — ≥3 intermediate, ≥5 high · Epworth ≥11 excessive sleepiness · AHI 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe VERIFY

Austroads commercial standard: OSA with excessive sleepiness → unfit until treated; conditional licence on specialist review; patient obliged to notify; doctor may notify in SA if the patient won't and risk is serious VERIFY
Sleep study: level 1 laboratory PSG or level 2 home study; CPAP first-line for moderate–severe; mandibular advancement splint for mild VERIFY

ask: What do you mean by tiredness — sleepy, low in energy, or feverish? How long, every day, worse? Better or worse with anything? How is it affecting your life?

Tanning, yellowing, dark urine? Weather preference, urine, thirst? Weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats? Fever, sore throat, flu-like illness? Have you ever been sexually active — what contraception, condoms? Travel? Palpitations, breathless on exertion, heavy periods, other bleeding? Stiffness, joints, rash? Medicines, drugs, mood, stress? Bowels, chest pain, cough, smoking? Snoring, job, shifts?

★ When was your last menstrual period? → 'about eight weeks ago — I've never been regular' → 'Any nausea, particularly in the mornings? Breast tenderness? Passing urine more often? What contraception are you using — any missed pills? Is there any chance you could be pregnant? Any bleeding or tummy pain?'
'Would a pregnancy be something you'd hoped for, or not?' — asked neutrally, before the diagnosis

★ 'Amy, the most likely explanation for your tiredness is that you are pregnant. I'm saying that because, one, your last period was around eight weeks ago; two, you have some morning nausea and breast tenderness; and three, everything else in my questioning has been normal. I'd like to do a pregnancy test today to confirm it.'

'I also thought about an underactive thyroid — less likely, no weather preference or weight change; low iron or anaemia — no heavy periods or palpitations; depression — mood is fine. And the rest I've been checking: glandular fever, diabetes, coeliac disease, liver problems, lymphoma and leukaemia, HIV, sleep problems, and medication effects.'

'Why?' when asked LMP → 'Tiredness is one of the earliest symptoms of pregnancy, so I ask everyone your age.' If she's upset or pleased — acknowledge, one sentence; the options conversation is a separate consultation
Summary and invite questions
pefe: No examination task. If asked: general, vitals, thyroid, nodes, CVS, resp, abdomen; office tests — urine β-hCG, dipstick, BSL

If the test is positive and time allows: dating by LMP is unreliable (irregular) → early ultrasound; folic acid/iodine; ectopic red flags (pain, bleeding, shoulder-tip pain) → ED; options discussion at a dedicated visit — all options, non-directive; SA — Pregnancy Advisory Centre, MSI, Country Health Connect midwives; TIS 131 450 VERIFY
Traps: asking periods only in SADMA; not probing once LMP is 8 weeks; assuming the pregnancy is welcome (or not); going into antenatal management instead of finishing the differential list
Version A → MED-53 · Version B → MED-54
fails: Not asking LMP/pregnancy inside the differential block — the only positive missed ★
Not probing once the LMP is eight weeks (nausea, breasts, contraception, chance of pregnancy) ★
Not started the answer by 6:00; diagnosis without three reasons ★
Assuming her feelings about a pregnancy; jumping to antenatal advice instead of differentials
Umbrella words for the rest of the list
Not naming the pregnancy test today
numbers: Tiredness is an early pregnancy symptom (from ~4–6 weeks) · urine β-hCG positive from around the missed period · irregular cycles → date by ultrasound VERIFY
Ectopic red flags: unilateral pain, bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness → ED
Folic acid 400–500 microg (5 mg if high risk) · iodine 150 microg VERIFY
6 + 2 · P letter inside the block · three reasons
Pregnancy Advisory Centre SA · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450
All other HEMI-AD-COP letters negative — say the list anyway

setting: Regional general practice, Wallaroo, South Australia.
stem: Jane Sotiris, a 35-year-old woman, presents to your general practice complaining of tiredness. Nothing else is given in the stem.
Version A (online): history 6 minutes, then examination findings appear on screen. Version B (face to face): history 4 minutes, then physical examination from the examiner.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
You will then be given the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Exploration is five questions, not a conversation; the marks are in the M probe, the four node words, the word cancer, one feelings check, and excision biopsy.

back.dx: Lymphoma — four months of constant, worsening lack of energy (not sleepiness); 5 kg unintentional weight loss over a few months, appetite fine; two lumps in the LEFT axilla for two months, slightly bigger, painless; drenching night sweats (changes her nightie); no fever, no itch, no alcohol-induced pain; no breast lumps; no family cancer; screening two years ago; one cat, no scratches; safe sex; no travel. Examination: two 2 cm HARD, FIXED, NON-TENDER left axillary nodes, no other chain, breasts normal, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness, afebrile, office tests and pregnancy test normal. Hidden agenda: a friend had lumps that were cancer. Must say 'lymphoma, which is a type of cancer of the lymph glands'; excision of a whole node, not a needle. Automatic fails: never saying cancer/lymphoma · never characterising the nodes · no malignancy screen · prognosis or cure rate · FNA as the test · false reassurance.
plan: Intro, open, ★ acknowledge the worry she volunteers, contract, 'some questions will sound unrelated'
Five questions: lack of energy vs sleepy vs feverish · how long · constant · worse · better/worse · impact
H and E in ten seconds each (all no)

★ M: weight → YES 5 kg → PROBE, do not move on: appetite, lumps → two in the armpit → how long, bigger, painful; night sweats — change the sheets?; fevers; itching without rash; alcohol pain; breast lumps/dimpling/discharge; cancer in you/family; last cervical screen
I: fever/chills, sore throat/flu-like, sexually active + safe sex (HIV can present exactly like this — ask everyone), travel, pets — cat scratches on that arm, TB contact
A, AD, D, C, O, P in one run; alcohol/allergies/PMHx/FHx; ★ 'was there anything you were worried this might be?' → friend → 'thank you — I'll examine you and be straight with you'

Examination: general (pallor, jaundice, cachexia, bruising/petechiae, scratch marks) · temperature · thyroid · ★ full lymph node examination by chain → 'two enlarged in the left axilla' → ★ immediately: size, stony hard or rubbery, fixed or mobile, tender → breasts + axillary tail, skin of the arm → CVS, resp → abdomen hepatosplenomegaly → bone tenderness sternum/spine → BSL, dipstick, urine pregnancy test

Name it → ★ one feelings check → three reasons from her findings → differentials reasoned (breast cancer; infections incl. HIV — offer the test; pregnancy excluded) then rapid list → plan: bloods today, CXR, urgent haematology referral in Adelaide for excision biopsy, phoned today; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 + travel → safety-net → support person → questions → 'is it curable?' → no numbers before type/stage
ask: 'Good morning, my name is Dr —, one of the doctors here. What has brought you in today?' → 'I am sorry to hear that, and I can understand why it is worrying you. Let me ask a number of questions to find the cause, then examine you and explain what I think. Some questions will sound unrelated; I ask everyone.'

Can you describe what you mean by tired — a lack of energy, feeling sleepy, or feeling feverish? How long? Constant or coming and going? Getting worse? Anything making it better or worse? How is it affecting your life?

★ Have you lost weight recently? → 'That is important, let me ask more. Has your appetite changed? Have you noticed any lumps or bumps anywhere in your body? How long have they been there, are they getting bigger, are they painful? Any night sweats — do you have to change the sheets or your nightclothes? Any fevers? Any itching all over without a rash? Do the lumps ache after alcohol? Any breast lumps, skin dimpling or nipple discharge? Any cancer in you or your family? When did you last have a cervical screening test?'

Any fevers or chills, sore throat or flu-like illness? Are you sexually active — do you practise safe sex? Any recent travel? Any pets — any cat scratches or bites on that arm? Anyone around you with tuberculosis?

Short of breath or heart racing on exertion? Stiffness in your shoulders or hips? Headaches, joint pains, rashes? Any medicines at all? Mood — still enjoying things, any stress? Greasy stools or blood in the stool? Chest pain? How many pillows? Ankle swelling? Cough, do you smoke? Has anyone said you snore or gasp? Occupation? Last period — regular, heavy, any chance of pregnancy? Alcohol, allergies, other medical problems, family history? ★ Was there anything you were worried this might be?

★ Examiner: 'On general appearance — pallor, jaundice, cachexia, bruising or petechiae, scratch marks? Vital signs, the temperature particularly. A thyroid examination. Then a full lymph node examination of every chain: occipital, pre- and post-auricular, submental, submandibular, anterior and posterior cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal and popliteal.' → ★ 'How large are they? Stony hard, or rubbery? Fixed or mobile? Tender? I would also like to examine both breasts and the axillary tail and inspect the skin of that arm. Cardiovascular — heart sounds and murmurs. Respiratory — air entry and added sounds. Abdomen — hepatomegaly or splenomegaly? Bone tenderness over the sternum or spine? Office tests — blood sugar, urine dipstick, and a urine pregnancy test.'

★ 'Jane, tiredness can have many different causes. In your case, I am concerned about the possibility of lymphoma, which is a type of cancer of the lymph glands. I am not certain yet — a biopsy is what confirms it — but I would not be honest if I said anything less. How are you feeling about what I have just said?' [one check-in, then continue] 'The reasons I am concerned: you have lost about five kilograms without trying; the two lumps in your armpit are hard and not moving when I examine them; and you have drenching night sweats. Those three things together point that way.'

'Because the lumps are in your armpit and you are 35, I also have to think about other cancers, particularly breast cancer — your examination was normal, but I will still arrange imaging. Then infections: glandular fever, HIV, toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis and cat-scratch disease — less likely because you have no fever, no travel and no unsafe sexual practice, but I would like to include an HIV test. Then pregnancy — excluded today. Beyond those: underactive thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, hepatitis, haemochromatosis, coeliac disease, autoimmune conditions such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, medications, depression, sleep apnoea and heart failure.' → 'Which do you think?' → 'The lymphoma is the one I am acting on today.' ★ 'Blood tests today, a chest x-ray, and an urgent referral to a blood specialist in Adelaide for a small operation to remove one gland whole and look at it under the microscope — a needle sample is not enough. I will phone the referral through today. Cancer Council SA on 13 11 20 can help with information and the travel. Come straight back or to hospital if you get a fever, your face or neck swells, you become breathless lying flat, or you start bruising or bleeding. Is there someone who can come with you? What questions do you have?' → 'Is it curable?' → 'I cannot give you numbers before we know which type this is, and many lymphomas respond very well to treatment. Let me get the biopsy done.'
pefe: Findings: well, no pallor/jaundice/cachexia/rash/bruising · afebrile, P and BP normal · thyroid normal · two enlarged left axillary nodes ~2 cm, hard, fixed, non-tender; no other group · breasts and arm skin normal · heart and chest normal · no hepatosplenomegaly · no bone tenderness · BSL, dipstick, pregnancy test normal

Summary to the examiner: 35 F, four months progressive fatigue, 5 kg unintentional loss, two painless left axillary lumps, drenching night sweats; two hard fixed non-tender left axillary nodes, no other lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bruising or scratch marks, afebrile, breasts normal, office tests normal → most likely lymphoma, leukaemia alongside, metastatic breast carcinoma not excluded; EBV, CMV, HIV, toxoplasmosis, TB; then the general causes. Plan: FBE with film, LDH, ESR, HIV and EBV serology, CXR, urgent referral for excision biopsy

Variants: 4-minute face-to-face → one question per block, keep the M probe intact, move on the prompt mid-sentence · 'is it cancer?' at 90 s → one of the things I need to rule out; three more minutes · rubbery and mobile → more typical of lymphoma than of spread — still biopsy · left supraclavicular node → Virchow's — look for an abdominal/chest primary (stomach, pancreas, lung, ovary) → CT chest/abdomen/pelvis · bruising and bleeding gums → leukaemia equally — FBE and film today, phone the haematology registrar · facial swelling + breathless lying flat → SVC obstruction — hospital today · declines Adelaide (children) → PATS covers travel/accommodation, Cancer Council SA can arrange; find a date
Never say to the patient: lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, FNA, excisional biopsy unexplained, 'probably nothing'
SA: urgent haematology at RAH/FMC; PATS (>100 km); Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if SVC obstruction; TIS 131 450
fails: Never saying cancer or lymphoma ('swollen glands') ★
Never characterising the nodes — accepting 'two enlarged nodes' and going to the diagnosis ★
No malignancy screen; hearing 'weight loss' and moving to the next letter ★
Giving a prognosis or cure rate; offering fine-needle aspiration as the diagnostic test; false reassurance ★
Skipping the sexual history because she 'sounds married'; being reassured by a negative family history (most lymphoma is sporadic)
Not eliciting the hidden concern; waiting in silence >5 s after naming cancer; more than a minute on the exploration; no breast examination request
numbers: 5 kg unintentional · 2 nodes · left axilla · 2 cm · hard, fixed, non-tender · four months · night sweats changing nightclothes
B symptoms: fever >38 °C · drenching night sweats · weight loss >10% in 6 months · node >1 cm persisting >4 weeks without explanation → biopsy VERIFY local criteria

Four characterising words: size · consistency · mobility · tenderness (+ overlying skin, matting) · excision biopsy of a whole node — NOT FNA (architecture needed) · FBE/film, LDH, ESR, EBV/CMV/HIV/toxo serology, CXR, then staging CT/PET after diagnosis VERIFY

Lymph node chains: occipital, pre/post-auricular, submental, submandibular, anterior/posterior cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal, popliteal · Virchow's = left supraclavicular
Axillary node differentials: lymphoma · leukaemia · breast cancer (metastatic) · melanoma/skin cancer of the arm · cat-scratch · EBV/CMV/HIV/toxo · TB · reactive
Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · PATS >100 km · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450

setting: General practice. You are the GP. The patient attends alone and yawns repeatedly throughout — scripted behaviour.
stem: Lily, 22, a university student, presents with tiredness. She is worried because it is not getting better.
Examination findings (given on screen after the history): entirely normal — afebrile, no lymphadenopathy, ENT, cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination normal, office tests normal.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6–7 minutes)
Physical examination findings will be provided
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Open and address the concern · 'low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?' decides the station · timing and impact in 40 s · sleep history in three phases (bedtime AND sleep-onset time separately; quantify caffeine AND time the last dose; weekend/holiday pattern) · mood, narcolepsy, pregnancy, ★ driving · rapid general sweep · interpret the normal examination out loud · sleep restriction with BOTH reasons · prioritised, specific differentials · sleep hygiene, diary, caffeine taper, driving advice; no hypnotic.

back.dx: Chronic sleep restriction (sleep deprivation) with behavioural sleep-onset insomnia: sleepy — not low-energy — for months; bed at 10 pm but asleep at 3 am (five hours lying awake on her phone in a noisy share house), ~5 h/night, unrefreshing, 4–5 coffees plus energy drinks with the last at 9 pm, feels better after sleeping in to midday at weekends; no snoring/gasping, no cataplexy or sleep paralysis, mood normal now, not pregnant; entirely normal examination, BMI 22. Two reasons: the sleep history, and the completely normal remainder of history and examination. Prioritised differentials: other sleep disorders — OSA (no snoring/gasping), narcolepsy (no cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hallucinations), delayed sleep–wake phase disorder (holiday pattern doesn't fully fit); psychological — major depression, adjustment disorder, GAD (onset with exams, mood normal now); pregnancy (excluded); anaemia (periods not heavy, no exertional symptoms); then thyroid, diabetes, EBV/infection, leukaemia/lymphoma, coeliac, autoimmune, medications. Discriminating behaviour: asking sleep-onset time separately from bedtime, and asking about driving.
plan: Intro, name, 'how can I help?'; acknowledge the worry ('especially when the exams are over and it hasn't settled'); contract
★ 'Do you feel low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?' → sleepy · duration, constant, worsening, modifiers, impact (concentration, falling behind, stopped going out) — 40 s only
★ 'I've noticed you've been yawning — can you tell me more about your sleep?' Phase 1: bedtime → ★ 'and what time do you actually fall asleep?' → 3 am · phone/TV in bed · room quiet and dark · pets

Phase 2–3: hours per night · refreshing? · initiation vs maintenance · nightmares · snoring/gasping · restless legs · hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations · drugs, medications, alcohol · ★ caffeine quantified AND timing of last · ★ weekend/holiday pattern (longer? better?)

Mood: 'started around exams — how has your mood been? still enjoying things? appetite? stressors?' · narcolepsy: ★ 'ever woken unable to move or speak? sudden weakness with strong emotion?' · LMP, pregnancy risk, heavy periods · ★ 'Do you drive? Ever felt sleepy at the wheel?' → near-miss → 'I'm glad you told me, we'll come back to that'

Rapid HEMI-AD-COP sweep with red flags: tanning/jaundice, polyuria/thirst, heat/cold intolerance, weight/appetite/lumps/night sweats, fever/sore throat/travel, exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, bowel symptoms, joints/rash, PMH/meds/allergies/smoking
Examination: read it back and ★ interpret it aloud as a positive finding; confirm no pallor, no goitre, normal BMI

★ Diagnosis with both reasons · 'there is something wrong — you're about three hours short every night, and it's fixable without a tablet' · hidden agenda (friend's glandular fever) answered honestly · prioritised, named differentials each with the excluding finding · plan: 2-week sleep diary, fixed bed/wake time 7 days, no phone for an hour before bed, caffeine taper with none after ~2 pm, daytime exercise, earplugs, CBT-i if still not falling asleep, Sleep Health Foundation, uni counselling; ★ driving advice; baseline bloods; review 3–4 weeks; red flags; summary
ask: ★ 'Do you feel low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?'
★ 'I've noticed you've been yawning — can you tell me more about your sleep?' / ★ 'What time do you go to bed? And what time do you actually fall asleep?'

'How many hours do you get on an average night? Is your sleep refreshing?' / 'Has anyone told you that you snore or gasp during sleep?' / 'Any pain or restlessness in your legs at night? Ever seen anything frightening as you fell asleep or woke up?'
★ 'How many caffeinated drinks a day — and how late is the last one?' / ★ 'On weekends or holidays, do you sleep longer, and do you feel better?'
★ 'Have you ever had sudden weakness with a strong emotion? Have you ever woken unable to move or speak?'
★ 'Do you drive? Have you ever felt sleepy at the wheel?'

★ 'Most likely you have sleep restriction — you're not getting enough good-quality sleep. Two reasons: your sleep history — bed at ten, asleep at three, five hours, phone in bed, four or five caffeinated drinks with the last at nine at night; and, just as important, the rest of your history and your whole examination are completely normal.'

'So there's nothing actually wrong with me?' → ★ 'There is something wrong — you're running about three hours short every night, and that has real effects on concentration, mood and driving safety. The difference is it's completely fixable, and it doesn't need a tablet.'

Driving: 'Do not drive when you feel sleepy. If it happens, pull over somewhere safe and have a fifteen-minute nap. Opening the window or turning up the music does not work. Drowsy driving causes as many crashes as drink driving.'
'Is a sleeping tablet safe? Will I get hooked?' → don't offer one: schedule and caffeine first, then CBT-i, which works better than tablets
Three phrases that lose marks: 'there's nothing wrong with you' · 'psychological problems' (name them) · 'I'll refer you for a sleep study' (not without snoring, apnoeas or narcolepsy features)
pefe: Given: entirely normal — afebrile, no lymphadenopathy, ENT/CVS/respiratory/abdomen normal, office tests normal; confirm no pallor, no goitre, BMI 22. Say aloud that the normal examination is half the justification.

Variant — cataplexy or sleep paralysis: narcolepsy → explain ('the brain's control of sleep and wakefulness isn't working, so sleep intrudes into the day'); polysomnography + multiple sleep latency test via sleep physician; ★ do not drive until assessed VERIFY

Variant — holidays restore her completely (sleeps 1–10 am, nine hours, fully refreshed): delayed sleep–wake phase disorder — sleep itself normal, clock running late; treat by shifting the clock: morning light, consistent wake time, timed melatonin under specialist advice ADDED VERIFY
Variant — low mood, anhedonia, early waking, weight loss: major depressive disorder — the sleep problem may be part of it, not the cause; ★ never omit 'have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?'

Sleep history in three phases (15 questions): environment/behaviour (bedtime, sleep-onset, screens, room, pets) · sleep itself (hours, refreshing, initiation vs maintenance, nightmares, snoring/gasping, restless legs, hallucinations) · substances and pattern (drugs, medications, alcohol, caffeine amount and timing, weekend/holiday)
SA/AU: Sleep Health Foundation fact sheets · university counselling · Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636 · Lifeline 13 11 14 · TIS 131 450
fails: Never asking sleepy vs low energy vs feverish and running the general mnemonic for six minutes ★
Asking bedtime only and never sleep-onset time — the 10 pm/3 am gap is the station ★
Never asking about driving — the near-miss only comes out if asked ★
'There's nothing wrong with you' ★ / offering a hypnotic ★
Ignoring the yawning, or reading it as a bored role-player
'Do you drink coffee?' → 'yes' accepted — not quantified, not timed
'Psychological problems' or 'other sleep disorders' without naming each and its excluding finding; treating the normal examination as an empty result; referring for a sleep study without indications
numbers: Bed 10 pm · asleep 3 am · ~5 h/night · 4–5 coffees + energy drinks · last caffeine 9 pm · BMI 22
Adult sleep need ~7–9 h VERIFY · caffeine half-life ~5–6 h VERIFY · Epworth >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness VERIFY
Sleep diary 2 weeks · review 3–4 weeks · no caffeine after ~2 pm, taper to avoid withdrawal headache · no screens 1 h before bed
Narcolepsy tetrad: sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations
Driving: pull over, 15-minute nap; drowsy driving ≈ drink driving for crash risk
Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636 · Lifeline 13 11 14 · Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800 · TIS 131 450

setting: General practice, 90 minutes from Adelaide. You are the GP; a colleague saw her last week and arranged bloods.
stem: Margaret Hollis, 50, attended a week ago with tiredness. She looked pale; your colleague arranged blood tests. She has returned to discuss the results.
Results: haemoglobin low · MCV low · MCH low · MCHC low · ferritin low · anisocytosis and poikilocytosis on film.
tasks: Explain the results
Take a focused, relevant history
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
Outline your management
time: 8 minutes, four tasks. Budget 1:30 results · 3:00 history (six questions) · 1:30 diagnosis and differentials · 1:30 management · 0:30 close. Open before you read out numbers. Cause first, iron last. Both scopes. No FOBT.

back.dx: Iron deficiency anaemia (low Hb, low MCV/MCH/MCHC, low ferritin, aniso- and poikilocytosis) in a post-menopausal woman with two red flags found only on specific questioning: three months of darker stools and 6 kg unintentional weight loss in two months, plus daily over-the-counter ibuprofen, some indigestion, an undone bowel screening kit, and melaena on rectal examination. Concern: gastrointestinal malignancy (colorectal or gastric). Differentials, specific: NSAID-related peptic ulcer (bleeding); low dietary intake (e.g. vegetarian diet without red meat — not her); blood loss from heavy periods, surgery, bleeding episode, frequent donation (not her); malabsorption — coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease. Rule: iron deficiency in any man or any post-menopausal woman without an obvious cause → endoscopy AND colonoscopy. The first management sentence is the one that passes: find the cause and treat the cause — refer for both scopes; then stop the NSAID, coeliac serology, iron replacement alongside with the priority stated, recheck, safety net, PATS.
plan: Intro, confirm name, ★ 'how can I help you today?' before any numbers; 'I have them in front of me — let's go through them together'

Six lines, no more: red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, made of iron · 1 total Hb low · 2 cell size decreased · 3 haemoglobin per cell and its concentration low · 4 ferritin (iron store) low · 5 anisocytosis = different sizes · 6 poikilocytosis = abnormal shapes → 'together these confirm iron deficiency anaemia'. No white cells, no platelets.

Permission; tiredness briefly (low energy, 4–5 months, worse). ★ Six questions: 1 'do you eat red meat?' · 2 surgery, bleeding episodes, donations, LMP and heavy/irregular before stopping · 3 ★ 'any blood in the stools, or dark or black stools?' → darker for 3 months → say it back: 'you may be losing blood in the stomach or bowel' · 4 ★ 'anti-inflammatories — ibuprofen, Nurofen, Voltaren, anything you buy yourself?' + indigestion/heartburn/pain/vomiting · 5 ★ weight loss quantified, appetite, lumps, bowel habit, bowel screening kit, family history · 6 chronic diarrhoea, greasy floating stools, mouth ulcers, joints, shin rash

Examination request: conjunctival pallor, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis; pulse and postural BP; flow murmur; abdominal masses, epigastric tenderness, organomegaly; lymph nodes incl. left supraclavicular; ★ rectal examination with consent and chaperone

★ 'Iron deficiency can have several causes. In your case I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer in the bowel or the stomach. My reasons: you've been losing weight, and you have dark stools, which means you are bleeding somewhere in your stomach or bowel.' → sit with the five-second silence · peptic ulcer named (NSAID) · the other causes specifically · 'the weight loss and dark stools are the two things I cannot ignore'

★ 'The first and most important step is to find the cause and treat the cause — I'm referring you to a gastroenterologist for both an endoscopy and a colonoscopy' (explain both in lay terms, samples if growth or ulcer) · stop the Nurofen, safer analgesia for the back · further bloods incl. coeliac serology · iron replacement (tablets or infusion) once cause found — may start alongside with priority stated · recheck in a few weeks · urgent referral, PATS for travel · safety net: haematemesis, black tarry stools, chest pain/breathlessness/dizziness at rest → ED
Teach-back: 'what will you tell your husband tonight?' → 'low in iron, bleeding somewhere, two camera tests to find out why'
ask: ★ 'How can I help you today?' — even in a results station

'Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, and haemoglobin is made of iron.' / 'Your ferritin — your body's iron store — is low.' / 'Anisocytosis means the red cells are of different sizes; poikilocytosis means some have abnormal shapes.' / 'All of these confirm iron deficiency anaemia.'

'Is it all right if I ask you a few questions to work out why?' / ★ 'Do you eat red meat?' / ★ 'Have you had any dark or black stools?' / ★ 'How much weight, over what period?' / ★ 'Anything you buy yourself for pain or your joints?'
★ 'In your case, I am concerned about the possibility of…' then the reasons

'Cancer? I only came about being tired.' → 'I know, and I'm sorry to raise it. I'm not certain — that is exactly why I want the tests. It could also be an ulcer in the stomach, which bleeds, and the Nurofen makes that more likely.'

★ 'The first and most important step is to find the cause and treat the cause. That means both an endoscopy and a colonoscopy.' / 'Once we have treated the cause, replacing the iron is straightforward.'

'Can you just give me iron tablets?' → 'We will absolutely replace your iron — but not first. If I top up the iron without finding where it's going, I might make the blood test look better while missing the reason. Find the cause, treat the cause, then replace the iron.'

Examiner: 'Could you just give her iron instead?' → 'No. A trial of iron in place of investigation would be wrong here, and so would deferring the scopes until her haemoglobin responded. I'm happy to start oral iron at the same time, but the priority is to exclude a gastrointestinal cancer.'
Variant — multiple findings (vegetarian, heavy periods, ibuprofen, dark stools, weight loss): name them all, then choose the one you will not leave untested and justify it by the red flag

Variant — 62-year-old man, no cause: 'everything you've told me is normal, and that is precisely why I want to look — in a man there is no monthly blood loss, so unexplained low iron means we look inside the gut at both ends, even when you feel well'
pefe: Examiner: pale with conjunctival pallor; pulse 96, no postural drop; soft ejection systolic (flow) murmur; mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy; ★ rectal examination shows melaena

Investigations: repeat FBE + film if needed, iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation — ferritin is an acute phase reactant; normal ferritin with TSAT <~16% is still iron deficiency VERIFY), CRP, UEC, LFT, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA), ± B12/folate; then gastroscopy AND colonoscopy — urgent referral; no FOBT in a symptomatic patient; no transfusion in a stable outpatient
Ulcer pathway: gastric ulcer → biopsy and repeat gastroscopy to confirm healing; duodenal ulcer → no biopsy, does not become malignant; H. pylori testing and eradication; stop NSAID, PPI VERIFY

Iron replacement: oral ferrous sulfate ~100 mg elemental daily or alternate days (alternate-day dosing improves absorption/tolerance) VERIFY; IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) if intolerant, malabsorption, rapid replacement needed or pregnancy; recheck FBE/ferritin ~4 weeks; continue ~3 months after Hb normalises VERIFY
National Bowel Cancer Screening Program 45–74, two-yearly VERIFY — but a symptomatic patient bypasses screening and goes straight to colonoscopy
SA: urgent GI referral (RAH/QEH/FMC/LMH) · PATS for >100 km VERIFY · Country Health Connect · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · TIS 131 450 · healthdirect 1800 022 222

setting: General practice. You are the GP. Version B of the iron-deficiency station — the same results in a pregnant patient whose pregnancy has been uneventful.
stem: Amy Kaur, 24, is pregnant and attended a week ago with tiredness. She looked pale and bloods were arranged. She has returned for the results.
Results: haemoglobin low · MCV low · MCH low · MCHC low · ferritin low · anisocytosis and poikilocytosis on film. Her pregnancy has been uneventful.
tasks: Explain the results
Take a focused, relevant history
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
Outline your management
time: 8 minutes, four tasks, same budget as MED-58 (1:30 · 3:00 · 1:30 · 1:30 · 0:30). Same six-line result explanation and the same six questions — plus obstetric interval, number of pregnancies and dietary iron. Do NOT take a full obstetric history: the stem says the pregnancy is uneventful.

back.dx: Iron deficiency anaemia of pregnancy from increased demand: three pregnancies in two years (short inter-pregnancy intervals — stores never rebuilt), on top of the physiological iron cost of each pregnancy; possibly low dietary intake. Same six questions exclude blood loss (no dark stools, no NSAIDs, no bleeding), malabsorption (no coeliac/IBD symptoms) and weight loss red flags. Differentials stated specifically: low dietary iron (e.g. vegetarian diet without red meat), blood loss (previous heavy periods, GI bleeding — dark stools, NSAIDs), malabsorption (coeliac disease, IBD), and — if any red flag or male/post-menopausal — GI malignancy needing both scopes (not indicated here). Management: treat the cause (spacing pregnancies, diet) and replace iron — IV iron is usually preferred in pregnancy when replacement must be rapid; recheck; antenatal team informed.
plan: Intro, confirm name, 'how can I help you today?'; 'I have the results — let's go through them together'

Six lines: red cells/haemoglobin/iron · total Hb low · cells smaller · haemoglobin per cell and concentration low · ferritin (store) low · anisocytosis = sizes · poikilocytosis = shapes → 'together these confirm iron deficiency anaemia'

Permission; tiredness briefly. Six questions: ★ red meat/dietary iron · surgery, bleeding, donations, ★ 'how many pregnancies, and how far apart?' → three in two years · ★ dark/black stools, blood in stool · anti-inflammatories/OTC, indigestion, vomiting (hyperemesis?) · weight change, appetite, lumps, bowel habit, family history · chronic diarrhoea, greasy stools, mouth ulcers, joints, shin rash; antenatal supplements taken?
Examination: conjunctival pallor, koilonychia, cheilitis, glossitis; pulse, postural BP; flow murmur; abdomen (fundal height appropriate, no tenderness); no rectal examination unless GI symptoms

★ 'Amy, the most likely cause is the three pregnancies you've had in the last two years. In each pregnancy your body has to build extra blood, and the baby needs a large amount of iron. We usually suggest waiting a while after a delivery so your stores can rebuild — if the next pregnancy starts soon after, you begin it already low.' Then the specific differentials and why they don't fit.

Management: ★ 'because we can't wait for tablets to work slowly in pregnancy, an iron infusion is usually preferred, and I'll recheck your blood afterwards' · dietary iron and vitamin C, avoid tea/coffee with meals · continue antenatal folate/iodine · inform the antenatal team; delivery planning if Hb low near term · postnatal contraception/spacing conversation · safety net: breathlessness at rest, palpitations, chest pain, bleeding · review after infusion
Teach-back and summary
ask: ★ 'How can I help you today?' / 'Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, and haemoglobin is made of iron.' / 'All of these confirm iron deficiency anaemia.'
★ 'How many pregnancies have you had, and how far apart?' / ★ 'Do you eat red meat?' / ★ 'Any dark or black stools?' / 'Anything you buy yourself for pain?'
★ 'The most likely cause is the three pregnancies in two years — each one costs a large amount of iron, and the stores didn't have time to rebuild.'
★ 'In pregnancy an iron infusion is usually preferred because we can't wait for tablets to work slowly, and I'll recheck your blood afterwards.'

'Is the infusion safe for the baby?' → 'Yes — intravenous iron is used routinely in the second and third trimesters; the main risk is a reaction during the infusion, which we monitor for, and it avoids the stomach upset of tablets.' VERIFY
'Will this happen again?' → 'It can — so we'll check your iron after this baby, top it up before you're pregnant again, and talk about spacing.'

Investigations: iron studies (ferritin, TSAT), CRP, ± B12/folate, coeliac serology if symptoms or poor response; no scopes in a young woman with an obvious cause and no red flags VERIFY

setting: General practice, country town. You are the GP. Online: 6-minute history, findings on screen, then diagnosis and differentials. Face to face: 4 + 2 + 2.
stem: Your next patient is John Brennan, 45, complaining of tiredness. He told the receptionist he has been tired for about three weeks and it is getting worse.
His record notes that he was told as a child that he had a heart murmur. He has no regular medications and has not attended the practice for several years.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Tiredness in 60 s · the murmur — three 'I don't remember's, then CHANGE TACK (long-course antibiotics, sore throats, follow-up) · screen until 'feverish' → take it as fever · the two endocarditis probes (dental work, marks on the hands) · say the timing match aloud · cardiac failure questions · examination requested by name incl. Osler/Janeway/splinters · 40-second explanation, four reasons · grouped differentials with reasons for the top two · hospital TODAY.

back.dx: Subacute infective endocarditis on a rheumatic mitral valve (mitral stenosis): childhood murmur with years of antibiotics/injections and constant sore throats and no follow-up (rheumatic fever → RHD), three weeks of worsening fatigue starting at the time of a root canal with no prophylaxis, feverish, splinter haemorrhages; T 38.5, mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the apex, dipstick blood 1+. Four reasons to the patient: murmur as a child and a murmur today; fever; dental work three weeks ago matching the three weeks of tiredness; marks under the nails. Differentials, grouped with reasons: heart failure on the stenotic valve (less likely — no chest pain, oedema, orthopnoea, PND); blood cancers — leukaemia/lymphoma (no weight loss, lumps, night sweats); other infections — TB, EBV, HIV, hepatitis; thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, autoimmune, medications and mood, coeliac/IBD, OSA. Plan: three sets of blood cultures before any antibiotic, bloods, urine, ECG, CXR, hospital today for echocardiography and IV antibiotics. Discriminating behaviours: changing tack on the murmur, asking about dental work, naming the peripheral stigmata to the examiner.
plan: Intro, consent, 'tell me about the tiredness' → low energy, 3 weeks, constant, worse, nothing helps, can't get out of bed — 60 s

★ 'Before I go further, I want to ask about that heart murmur — it may be important': when, what, treatment → three 'I don't remember's → ★ CHANGE TACK: 'antibiotics for a long time as a child — months or years, injections? lots of sore throats? any follow-up for your heart?' → yes, yes, none
Screen: 'a checklist — most will be no' — liver, endocrine, malignancy… ★ 'any fever or chills?' → 'feverish, hot and cold' → 'have you measured it?' → 'I'll take that as a fever'

★ The two probes: 'any dental work recently — filling, extraction, root canal? other procedures?' → root canal 3 weeks ago → ★ say the timing match aloud · 'antibiotics before it?' → no · ★ 'any rashes, spots or marks on your hands or fingers?' → marks under the nails

Finish the screen in groups: ★ cardiac failure (chest pain, ankle swelling, pillows, PND), exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, joints/headache/rash, cough/snoring, bowels, medications and drugs (injecting), mood, occupation (truck driver), alcohol, smoking; 'what were you worried this might be?' (brother's bowel cancer)

Examination by name: general (pale, jaundiced, rash, unwell) · ★ temperature, HR, BP, RR, SpO2 · thyroid, lymph nodes · CVS: apex visible/displaced, JVP, murmurs, S3, opening snap — timing, site, radiation, character · chest · abdomen (hepatosplenomegaly) · urine dipstick · ★ 'specifically, the hands — Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages?' → photograph
★ 40-second explanation: 'infective endocarditis — a valve narrowed since childhood, bacteria from the mouth after the root canal settled on it'; four reasons; no anatomy lecture

Differentials grouped, reasons for the top two (heart failure, blood cancers), then list · ★ plan: three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, bloods, urine, ECG, CXR, hospital TODAY for echo and IV antibiotics; who can drive you, who to call; respond to the cancer fear
ask: ★ 'Before I go further, I want to ask about that heart murmur you were told about as a child — it may be important.' → ★ 'Do you remember being on antibiotics for a long time as a child — months or years, maybe injections? Did you get a lot of sore throats? Any follow-up for your heart since?'
'Have you measured your temperature?' → ★ 'I'll take that as a fever.'

★ 'Have you had any dental work recently — a filling, an extraction, a root canal? Any other procedures?' → 'Three weeks — the same time your tiredness started. Were you given any antibiotics before it?'
★ 'Have you noticed any rashes, spots or marks on your hands or fingers?'
★ To examiner: 'May I look at the hands — Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, clubbing, or splinter haemorrhages?' (never 'any skin changes?')

'I believe you have infective endocarditis. One of your heart valves is narrowed — that's the murmur from childhood. When you had the root canal, bacteria from the mouth got into the bloodstream and settled on that damaged valve. Four reasons: the murmur then and now; a fever; dental work three weeks ago, the same three weeks you've been tired; and the marks under your fingernails.'

'The main alternative is heart failure from the long-standing valve problem — less likely because no chest pain, no leg swelling, one pillow, not waking breathless. I also thought about blood cancers like leukaemia and lymphoma — less likely, no weight loss, lumps or night sweats; other infections such as TB, glandular fever, HIV and hepatitis; thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, autoimmune conditions, medications and mood, coeliac and bowel disease, and sleep apnoea.'

★ 'Three separate sets of blood cultures before any antibiotic, other bloods, a urine test, an ECG and a chest X-ray — then hospital today, because this needs an ultrasound of the heart and antibiotics through a drip.'

'Is this because of the dentist? Can I sue?' → 'I can hear you're angry. This isn't about anyone doing anything wrong — mouth bacteria enter the bloodstream briefly in all of us. The problem is a valve that was damaged and never followed up. Right now my focus is treating the infection.'

'I can't go — I'm driving to Adelaide Monday. Give me tablets.' → 'I can't make you go, but this infection sits on a heart valve; untreated it can destroy the valve or throw clots to the brain. Tablets are not enough. Can we ring your wife and sort the driving? If you still decline, I'll do the tests today and see you tomorrow — but I'd be failing you if I didn't say how serious this is.'
'It's not cancer, is it? My brother…' → honest, one sentence: asked the questions, nothing points that way, bloods will cover it
pefe: Examiner: unwell-looking, not pale/jaundiced, no rash · T 38.5, HR 96 regular, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 97% · thyroid and nodes normal · JVP not raised, apex not displaced, mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the mitral area, no S3 · chest clear · no hepatosplenomegaly · no Osler nodes, no Janeway lesions · photograph of splinter haemorrhages ONLY if asked by name · dipstick blood 1+

Variant — T 37.4 (2018 face-to-face version): 'a low-grade temperature rather than a frank fever, but subacute endocarditis characteristically runs low-grade; in a symptomatic patient with valve disease I regard it as supportive, not reassuring' — do not say 'afebrile' and abandon infection

Variant — Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient: RHD far commoner; the follow-up gap is a system failure — involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer/ACCHS, notify to the SA RHD register, lifelong secondary prophylaxis and echo follow-up
Variant — injecting drug use, murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo's sign): right-sided/tricuspid endocarditis, Staphylococcus aureus; look for septic pulmonary emboli on CXR

Investigations: ★ blood cultures ×3 sets, three sites, before antibiotics; FBE, ESR/CRP, UEC, LFT, urine MCS (microscopic haematuria), ECG (PR prolongation = abscess), CXR; TTE then TOE; Duke criteria — 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor VERIFY; IV antibiotics 4–6 weeks; surgical referral for heart failure, abscess, embolism, uncontrolled infection VERIFY

RHD secondary prophylaxis: benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21–28 days VERIFY; dental/procedural prophylaxis for high-risk valve lesions per Therapeutic Guidelines VERIFY; SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · RFDS · PATS · TIS 131 450 · SA RHD register
fails: Never asking about a portal of entry (dental work/procedures) ★
Never naming Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and splinter haemorrhages to the examiner — 'any skin changes?' leaves the photograph under the papers ★
Sending him home with oral antibiotics and a review — hospital TODAY ★
Running out of time before the differentials ★
Abandoning the murmur after three 'I don't remember's without changing tack
Discounting 'feverish' because there is no number; saying 'afebrile' at 37.4 and dropping infection
Skipping the heart failure questions; explaining four chambers of the heart; naming every cancer separately
numbers: Tiredness 3 weeks · root canal 3 weeks — say the match · T 38.5°C (older version 37.4) · Duke minor criterion >38°C
Murmur: mid-diastolic, rumbling, mitral area — 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
Blood cultures ×3 sets, three sites, BEFORE antibiotics · Duke: 2 major / 1 major + 3 minor / 5 minor VERIFY · IV antibiotics 4–6 weeks
RHD prophylaxis: benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21–28 days VERIFY
