setting: Rural general practice clinic with limited facilities. You are the GP. Face to face 4 + 2 + 2; online 6-minute history then findings on screen.
stem: Your next patient is Alex Wooten, 17, who presents complaining of tiredness and feeling unwell. He works on his family's farm and has been complaining that he is not able to keep up with his work.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the concern in the stem within 30 s · tiredness in 60 s · screen until thirst and urine turn positive — record them as symptoms, never argue with his explanation · probe: polyphagia, recurrent infections, vision, feet, ★ abdominal pain/nausea/vomiting, weight · finish the whole differential screen anyway (incl. farm animal contact) · examination incl. dehydration, breathing pattern, BSL and dipstick — 'glucose and ketones' · diagnosis in 25 seconds, two layers · differentials · hospital today.

back.dx: Diabetic ketoacidosis (ketosis; acidosis still to be confirmed) complicating undiagnosed type 1 diabetes in a lean 17-year-old: months of worsening low energy, polydipsia and polyuria explained away as farm work in the sun, polyphagia, two slow-healing skin infections, weight loss (belt tighter), nausea; aunt with T1DM. Examination: tired, mildly dehydrated, observations normal, breathing not deep or sighing; BSL mid-high teens; dipstick glucose 4+, ketones 3+. Two-layer diagnosis to the patient in 25 seconds: 'diabetic ketoacidosis, a complication of diabetes you didn't know you had — sugar goes up, the body makes chemicals called ketones, which I found in your urine'; reasons: tired for months, passing more urine, drinking more, hungrier, high sugar with sugar and ketones in the urine. Differentials reasoned for two, listed for the rest: leukaemia/lymphoma (no lumps, night sweats, that kind of weight loss); infections — EBV, HIV, Q fever from the animals (no fever/flu-like illness); then hepatitis, thyroid, anaemia, autoimmune, drugs, depression/stress, coeliac/IBD, cardiorespiratory, OSA. Disposition: hospital today — IV access, fluids started, bloods, specialist team phoned. Discriminating behaviours: recording the explained-away thirst/urine as symptoms, 'glucose and ketones' on the dipstick, and a 25-second explanation that leaves time for the differentials.
plan: Intro; ★ 'not being able to keep up with the work must be really frustrating, and I can hear it's weighing on you'; consent; tiredness: low energy vs sleepy, months, constant, worse, nothing helps, impact — 60 s

Checklist — liver, thyroid (weather) … ★ 'passing more urine? more thirsty or drinking more?' → 'only because I work in the sun — that's normal, isn't it?' → 'That does make sense, and I'll still note it.'
★ Probe: hungrier/eating more · recurrent infections (skin, thrush, urine) · blurred vision · numb/tingling feet · ★ tummy pain, nausea, vomiting · weight loss without trying

★ Finish the screen anyway, in groups: malignancy (weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, family cancer) · infection (fever, chills, sore throat, sexual activity, travel, ★ animal contact on the farm — Q fever) · anaemia · autoimmune · drugs/alcohol/smoking · mood, stress at home/school, bullying, brief HEADSS (a bit down — parents think he's lazy; no self-harm) · bowels · cardiorespiratory, snoring · family history (aunt T1DM)

Examination: unwell? ★ dehydration (dry mucosa, turgor, sunken eyes), pale, jaundiced, wasted · T, HR, BP incl. postural, RR, SpO2 · thyroid, nodes · CVS · respiratory — ★ 'is his breathing deep and sighing?' · abdomen (tenderness, organomegaly) · ★ 'blood sugar level and urine dipstick' → 'what are you looking for?' → ★ 'glucose and ketones'; say the observations are normal — ketosis, acidosis needs blood ketone + venous gas

★ Diagnosis in 25 s, two layers, five reasons; no pancreas/insulin/fat metabolism/acidosis. Physiology questions → 'I'll come back to that — let me first tell you what else I've considered and what happens next.'

Differentials: reason two, list the rest · ★ 'You need to go to hospital today — I'll put a drip in, start fluid, take bloods and ring the specialist team now. Very treatable; once controlled there's no reason you can't do the farm work. Who can drive you? Would you like me to call your parents?' · close on the hidden agenda: 'I'll tell Mum it's not because you've been slacking off.'
ask: ★ 'Not being able to keep up with the work must be really frustrating.'
★ 'Are you passing more urine than usual? Are you more thirsty, or drinking more?' → ★ 'That does make sense, and I'll still note it.' (never argue)
'Are you hungrier than usual? Any infections that keep coming back?' / ★ 'Any tummy pain, nausea or vomiting?' / 'Any contact with animals on the farm?'
★ 'Could I have a blood sugar level and a urine dipstick?' → 'Glucose and ketones.'

★ 'Alex, I think you have diabetic ketoacidosis, which is a complication of diabetes you didn't know you had. In diabetes the sugar in your blood goes up; when that happens your body starts producing chemicals called ketones — that's what I've found in your urine today. The reasons: tired for months, passing more urine, drinking more, hungrier than usual, and your blood sugar is high with sugar and ketones in your urine.'
'Diabetes? But I'm not overweight.' → 'This is the type that isn't about weight — the body stops making its own insulin. It can happen to fit people.'

'Can I still drive the ute and the tractor?' → 'Once you're on insulin there are national driving rules because of the risk of a hypo at the wheel — it doesn't mean you can't drive, it means checking your sugar before you drive and carrying something sugary. Same for machinery. We'll go through it once you're stable.'

'Do my parents have to know?' → 'What you tell me is confidential, and at 17 you can make your own decisions if you understand what's involved. But this is serious and you'll need help — and knowing you've been unwell will change how they see the last few months. Would you like me to be there when you tell them?' ADDED
★ 'You need to go to hospital today — but once this is under control there's no reason you can't do your work.'
pefe: Examiner: tired, mildly dehydrated, not pale/jaundiced · T 36.5, HR 82, BP 110/70, RR 12, SpO2 normal · thyroid, nodes, CVS, chest, abdomen normal; breathing not deep or sighing · ★ BSL high (mid–high teens mmol/L) · dipstick glucose 4+, ketones 3+

Variant — frankly acidotic (Kussmaul RR 28, HR 124, abdominal tenderness, drowsy): 'clinical ketoacidosis — large-bore cannula, 0.9% sodium chloride, bloods for glucose, ketones, gas, electrolytes, call retrieval immediately — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33'
Variant — 5-year-old known T1DM, vomiting with ketones (online paediatric version): DKA until proven otherwise; cautious fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion without a bolus — cerebral oedema risk

Variant — glucose 9 with ketones 3+ and eating very little: starvation/dehydration ketosis possible — blood ketone and venous gas before calling it DKA; euglycaemic DKA only if on an SGLT2 inhibitor ADDED

Management order if asked: fluid → potassium → insulin infusion (0.05–0.1 units/kg/h), no insulin bolus in children; monitor glucose hourly, ketones/gas/K 2-hourly; find the precipitant; specialist team; then education, NDSS registration, sick-day rules, driving rules VERIFY

SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · RFDS · PATS · NDSS · Diabetes SA; adolescent confidentiality and Gillick/mature-minor competence at 17 under SA Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (16+ may consent) VERIFY
fails: Accepting his explanation for the thirst and urine and moving on ★
Generic dipstick answer ('leucocytes, nitrites, protein, blood') — the answer is glucose and ketones ★
Explaining ketogenesis and acidosis beautifully and the bell going during the second differential ★
Treating him in the clinic with fluids and reviewing tomorrow — same-day referral ★

Stopping at polyuria/polydipsia — missing polyphagia, infections, complication questions and the DKA questions (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting)
Insulin bolus / insulin before fluids if asked for management; not asking farm animal contact

Dipstick here: glucose 4+, ketones 3+ · DKA triad: hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia (blood ketones ≥3.0) + acidosis (venous pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15) VERIFY

Timing: diagnosis and mechanism 25 s · reasons 15 s · differentials the rest · watch the clock — ≥60 s left at the start of Task 3

setting: Regional general practice, Wallaroo, South Australia. You are the GP. Version A online: 6-minute history then findings on screen. Version B face to face: 4-minute history then examination from the examiner.
stem: Jane Ellery, a 45-year-old woman, presents to your general practice complaining of tiredness. There is nothing else in the stem.
tasks: Take a focused history
You will then be given the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis AND your differentials to the patient — two marked items
time: 8 minutes. Open, acknowledge, contract · define 'tired' and explore (ask even though she volunteered some) · H, then E — cold intolerance is where it turns → switch from screening to PROBING (five key-point questions) · keep sweeping M, I, A, D, C, O, P anyway · menstrual questions exclude the closest mimic · thyroid examination requested by name, pulse, reflex relaxation phase · name it, reason it from her own answers and findings · reason three differentials incl. menopause · TSH, plan, safety net, certificate.

back.dx: Primary hypothyroidism, probably Hashimoto thyroiditis: months of progressive lack of energy affecting work; cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, weight gain, hair loss with outer-eyebrow thinning, morning periorbital puffiness; examination — dressed warmly, dry coarse skin, pulse 60, diffuse non-nodular goitre moving on swallowing, no retrosternal extension, no lymphadenopathy, delayed relaxation phase of the ankle reflexes, normal power, office tests normal. Reasons given from her own answers and findings. Differentials reasoned: menopause (regular periods, no hot flushes — the single closest mimic at 45), anaemia (no exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, periods not heavy — still check), depression (mood reasonable, still enjoys things); malignancy — lymphoma/leukaemia (no weight loss, lumps, night sweats); infection — EBV, hepatitis, HIV; then diabetes, coeliac, haemochromatosis, autoimmune (SLE, RA), medications, OSA, heart failure. Plan: TSH (free T4 if abnormal, TPO antibodies for cause) plus FBE, ferritin, HbA1c, coeliac serology, UEC, LFT; levothyroxine once confirmed; recheck TSH 6–8 weeks; certificate. Automatic fails: diagnosing off the single weather-preference answer without probing; never requesting a thyroid examination; abandoning the malignancy/infection screen; omitting the differentials; describing the reflexes as brisk.
plan: Intro, open question; ★ acknowledge ('I understand that can be concerning') and contract ('questions, then examine, then a plan together')
Define: lack of energy / sleepy / feverish · duration · constant · worse · modifiers · impact (sick leave, boss unhappy — 'we'll come back to the work side')

H: tanning, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools · E: polyuria, thirst, ★ 'any weather preference — intolerant of cold or heat?' → 'always cold' → ★ SWITCH TO PROBING: dry skin · constipation · weight gain · hair loss incl. outer third of eyebrows · puffiness of eyelids/face/legs · hoarse voice · neck swelling or dysphagia

★ Keep sweeping: M (weight loss, appetite, lumps, night sweats, cancer history) · I (fever, sore throat, sexual history/safe sex, travel) · A (exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, stiffness, headache, joints, rash) · D (medicines, mood, anhedonia, stress)

C (greasy stools, blood, chest pain, pillows, ankles, cough, smoking) · O (snoring, occupation) · ★ P: LMP, regular, heavy, hot flushes · alcohol, allergies, PMH, FHx · 'anything you were worried this might be?'

Examination: general — dressed for the weather? dry skin? pallor/jaundice/rash · temperature, ★ pulse rate, BP · ★ thyroid examination with consent to expose the neck, chaperone: inspection (swelling, moves on swallowing), palpation (diffuse vs nodular, size, consistency, tenderness), percussion over the manubrium · lymph nodes · CVS · respiratory · abdomen · ★ relaxation phase of the ankle reflexes · proximal power (rise from a chair) · Pemberton's sign · office tests, ★ 'random or fasting glucose?'

★ Name it in one plain line ('the gland in the front of your neck is underactive, not making enough of its hormone — that hormone sets the pace for everything, which is why everything feels like an effort'); ★ reasons from her answers (cold, dry skin, constipation, weight gain, hair loss) and findings (dry skin, slow pulse, enlarged gland, slow-relaxing reflexes)

★ Differentials: menopause, anaemia, depression reasoned; malignancy and infection reasoned; the rest listed · plan: TSH today ('measures how hard your body is pushing the gland') + anaemia, diabetes, coeliac, liver tests; levothyroxine once confirmed, empty stomach, recheck 6–8 weeks; certificate; safety net (neck swelling, dysphagia, chest pain); questions; summary on request
ask: 'I understand that can be concerning. Let me ask you a number of questions, then examine you, and we will make a plan together.' / 'Is it a lack of energy, feeling sleepy, or feeling feverish?'
★ 'Do you have any weather preference — are you intolerant of cold or of heat?' → 'Thank you, that is helpful. Let me ask a few more about that.'

★ 'Has your skin been dry?' / ★ 'Have you been constipated?' / ★ 'Have you had any weight gain?' / ★ 'Any hair loss — and have you noticed the outer part of your eyebrows thinning?' / ★ 'Any puffiness of your eyelids, face or legs?' / 'Has your voice become hoarse? Any swelling in your neck or difficulty swallowing?'
★ 'When was your last period? Are they regular? Any hot flushes?'

★ 'I would like to perform a thyroid examination — asking her permission to expose the neck and remove any scarf, and offering a chaperone.' / ★ 'What is the relaxation phase of the ankle reflex?' / 'Can she rise from a chair without using her arms?' / 'Pemberton's sign, given the goitre' / 'Is that sugar random or fasting?'

★ 'Most likely you have hypothyroidism. The gland in the front of your neck is underactive and is not making enough of its hormone.' / ★ 'The reasons I have come to this today are your own answers and what I found when I examined you…'

★ 'I considered menopause — it can cause exactly this at your age, but it is less likely in you because your periods are regular and you have no hot flushes.' / 'Anaemia — less likely, no breathlessness or palpitations on exertion, periods not heavy, but I will still check.' / 'Depression — less likely, your mood is reasonable and you still enjoy things.'

'The main test is called TSH, which measures how hard your body is having to push the gland.' / 'Will I be on tablets forever?' → 'Usually yes — one tablet a day, inexpensive, and most people feel like themselves again.' / 'Will the weight come off?' → 'Some usually does — a lot is fluid — but treating the thyroid does not usually take off all the weight on its own; it should give you back the energy to be active.'
Never say to the patient: TSH unexplained, euthyroid, myxoedema, Woltman sign, or 'your metabolism is slow' without the plain-English version
pefe: Examiner: dressed warmly; dry, coarse skin; no pallor/jaundice/rash · T normal, ★ pulse 60 regular, BP 110/70 · ★ diffusely enlarged thyroid, moves on swallowing, no nodules, non-tender, percussion resonant (no retrosternal extension) · no lymphadenopathy · HS normal, chest clear · no hepatosplenomegaly · ★ reflexes present with delayed relaxation phase · power normal · Pemberton negative · random BSL normal, dipstick normal

If asked what you are looking for mid-thyroid exam: 'a swelling that moves upwards on swallowing — thyroid rather than node or cyst; diffuse vs nodular — a discrete nodule changes the pathway to ultrasound; percussion for retrosternal extension'
Variant — single firm nodule: thyroid ultrasound ± FNA by sonographic features and size; still TSH first (suppressed TSH → functioning nodule) VERIFY
Variant — periods stopped 8 months ago with hot flushes: menopause moves to the top, but they overlap and coexist — still check TSH before attributing everything to menopause
Variant — lithium or amiodarone: both cause hypothyroidism; check TSH (lithium: renal function and level too); discuss with the prescriber rather than stopping it
Variant — pregnant or planning: requirement rises, targets tighter — urgent TSH, start/increase early, obstetric team, monitor more often VERIFY

Bloods: TSH first → free T4 if abnormal → TPO antibodies for cause; high TSH + low fT4 = primary; high TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical · plus FBE, ferritin, HbA1c, coeliac serology, UEC, LFT · levothyroxine ~1.6 µg/kg/day full replacement, start 25–50 µg if older or cardiac VERIFY · empty stomach, separate from calcium/iron by ~4 h · recheck TSH 6–8 weeks · SA: TIS 131 450 · PATS >100 km VERIFY

setting: General practice. You are the GP. The patient attends alone. Version 1 — she stopped the prednisolone abruptly.
stem: Samantha (Sam) Doyle, 60, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica four months ago (some versions: giant cell arteritis; Version 3: sarcoidosis). She attends today concerned about tiredness and, separately, loss of weight.
tasks: Take a relevant history (7 minutes)
Give your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses (1 minute)
time: 8 minutes — 7 + 1, the longest history and shortest close in the cluster. Acknowledge the concern · both complaints explored, weight loss quantified (how much, over how long) · the steroid block and the hinge question 'abruptly, or reduced gradually?' · follow the dog into the mood · adrenal features (nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, postural dizziness, salt craving) and steroid-diabetes questions · malignancy red flags and the THREE screening programs · rest of the mnemonic, postmenopausal bleeding, geriatric screen · 60-second answer: name, two-sentence explanation, reasons, then the list fast.

back.dx: Secondary adrenal insufficiency (not crisis — stable, talking) after abrupt cessation of prednisolone four months into PMR treatment: six weeks of profound fatigue, 5–6 kg unintentional weight loss, poor appetite, nausea, abdominal pain, loose bowels, postural light-headedness; stopped the tablet abruptly six weeks ago after her dog died, nobody told her to taper, missed follow-up; no PMR/GCA relapse features; mood flat since the bereavement (grief; screen, not diagnose). Reasons: tired, weight loss, abrupt cessation after four months, GI features. Differentials (the list is the mark): malignancy — leukaemia, lymphoma, breast, bowel (no lumps, screening up to date); depression/adjustment disorder after the loss; relapse of PMR/GCA; steroid-induced diabetes; thyroid, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac, other autoimmune, medications, heart failure, OSA. Plan: morning cortisol today (short Synacthen if needed), restart prednisolone with a proper taper, steroid card, sick-day rules, emergency advice, mood review next week. Handle 'is it my fault?' without blame.
plan: Intro, 'how would you like me to address you?'; ★ acknowledge the concern in one line; permission to proceed

Tired: feverish / low energy / sleepy → no energy · 6 weeks · constant · worse · nothing helps · can't do housework · ★ weight: 'how many kilograms, and over what period?' → 5–6 kg in 6 weeks, not trying

★ Steroid block: when diagnosed · what treatment · 'are you taking it regularly?' → stopped · why? → the dog · ★ 'did you stop it abruptly, or reduce the dose gradually?' → just stopped · side effects (weight gain) · follow-up (missed) · relapse: shoulder/hip stiffness; GCA: headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual change
★ 'I'm so sorry about your dog — how are you coping?' · mood · anhedonia (three questions, twenty seconds)
★ Adrenal features: nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, postural dizziness, salt craving · steroid-diabetes: polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent infections
Malignancy: appetite, lumps, night sweats, family cancer · ★ three screening programs: mammogram, cervical screening test, bowel cancer kit

Rest of the mnemonic briskly: tanning/jaundice, heat/cold, exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, joints/rash, fever/travel, bowel change/blood, cough, smoking, snoring, occupation, other meds/OTC, allergies · ★ 'when did your periods stop — any bleeding since?' · geriatric screen: memory, who do you live with, support, falls, who cooks (lives alone, husband died 3 years ago, son in Perth, 'toast mostly') · 'what are you worried about?' (sister — cancer)

★ 60 s: 'adrenal insufficiency — on long-term steroids the adrenal gland stops working; stop suddenly and it can't restart straight away'; reasons; ★ the list, read fast; 'bloods today incl. morning cortisol, restart the steroid with a plan to reduce slowly, a card, sick-day rules; vomiting, very dizzy or confused = ambulance; see you next week about your mood'
ask: 'When you say tired — feverish, low in energy, or sleepy?' / ★ 'How many kilograms, and over what period?'
'When were you diagnosed? What treatment? Are you taking it regularly?' → 'Can I ask why you stopped?' → ★ 'Did you stop it abruptly, or did you reduce the dose gradually?'
'Any shoulder or hip stiffness? Any headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, or change in your vision?'
★ 'I'm so sorry about your dog. How are you coping with that?' → 'How has your mood been? Still enjoying the things you used to?'
★ 'Any nausea or vomiting? Tummy pain? Diarrhoea? Dizziness when you stand? Craving salty food?' / 'Because you've been on steroids — more urine, thirstier, recurrent infections?'
★ 'Are you up to date with your mammogram, cervical screening test and bowel kit?' / ★ 'When did your periods stop — have you had any bleeding since?'
'How's your memory? Who do you live with? Enough support? Any falls? Who does the cooking?'

★ 'When you take steroids for a long time the adrenal gland stops working; if you stop suddenly it can't restart straight away.' / 'My reasons are that you're tired, you've lost weight, you stopped your prednisolone abruptly after four months, and you've had nausea, tummy pain and loose bowels.'

'So it's my fault for stopping the tablets?' → ★ 'No — nobody explained that these tablets have to be reduced slowly rather than stopped, and that's something we should have made much clearer. It's very treatable.'
★ 'If you start vomiting, become very dizzy or confused — that's an emergency, call an ambulance.'
Three phrases that lose marks: 'steroid cessation syndrome' (not a diagnosis) · 'you're in adrenal crisis' (she is stable) · 'it's just the grief' (premature closure with unexplained weight loss)
pefe: No examination task. If invited: postural BP, pigmentation (absent in secondary insufficiency), weight, temporal arteries, thyroid, lymph nodes, breasts, abdomen; BSL.

Investigations (if asked): 8 am cortisol, ± short Synacthen test VERIFY; UEC (secondary: normal potassium, ± low sodium), BSL/HbA1c, FBE, ESR/CRP (PMR relapse), TSH, LFT, ferritin, coeliac serology; CXR; screening as due

Management: restart prednisolone at the previous or a physiological dose, then taper per PMR plan; steroid alert card; ★ sick-day rule — double the dose when ill; vomiting/unable to take tablets → ED/ambulance; crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM + fluids VERIFY; specialist/GP follow-up re-established; mood review next week; bereavement support
Version 3 — sarcoidosis instead of PMR: only the complication questions change (cough, breathlessness, rashes, red or painful eyes); diagnosis, reasons and list identical

setting: General practice. You are the GP. Version 2 of the steroid station — she is still taking the prednisolone. Stem reconstructed from the variant section.
stem: Samantha (Sam) Doyle, 60, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica four months ago and remains on prednisolone. She attends today concerned about tiredness and loss of weight.
tasks: Take a relevant history (7 minutes)
Give your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses (1 minute)
time: 8 minutes, 7 + 1. Identical spine to MED-63 — the steroid block comes back clean (compliant, followed up, no relapse, no side effects). Say nothing about the recall; work down the mnemonic until you reach mood, then complete the depression criteria and the safety question. Do NOT do a full psychiatric history — plan the case from the complaint, not the outcome.

back.dx: Major depressive disorder presenting as tiredness and weight loss in a bereaved 60-year-old widow living alone: low mood, anhedonia, middle-of-the-night waking, poor appetite with weight loss, poor concentration, guilt/worthlessness, fatigue — five or more of nine features over more than two weeks; no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. Steroid history clean (taking it, tapering as planned, follow-up kept, no relapse). Differentials — the same broad list: malignancy (leukaemia, lymphoma, breast, bowel — no lumps, screening up to date), adrenal insufficiency (excluded — never stopped), PMR/GCA relapse, steroid-induced diabetes, thyroid, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications (steroid-induced mood change), heart failure, OSA. The one exception to 'no full psychiatric history' is the safety question — never omit it. If challenged: 'I approached this as undifferentiated tiredness and screened organic causes first; having reached a mood disorder I would complete a full mental state assessment at a dedicated follow-up.'
plan: Intro, name preference, ★ acknowledge the concern, permission
Tired defined, explored; ★ weight loss quantified (amount, period)
Steroid block: diagnosed 4 months ago, prednisolone, taking it regularly (yes), tapering per plan, follow-up kept, side effects, relapse (girdle stiffness) and GCA features — all clean

Adrenal/GI and steroid-diabetes questions (negative) · malignancy red flags · ★ three screening programs · rest of the mnemonic · ★ postmenopausal bleeding · geriatric screen (lives alone, husband died, son in Perth, toast mostly)

★ Mood reached in the sweep: 'how has your mood been? still enjoying things? sleep — trouble getting off, or waking and not getting back? appetite? concentration? feeling guilty or worthless?' → ★ 'have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?'
Brief context only: the loss (dog/husband), isolation, alcohol; no mania screen, psychosis, insight or full risk assessment here

★ 'Most likely you have major depressive disorder — an intense low mood and sadness that affects how you function and commonly causes tiredness and weight loss. My reasons are the features you described: low mood, no longer enjoying things, waking in the night, poor appetite, poor concentration, feeling guilty, and the tiredness itself — five or more features over more than two weeks.' Then the list fast; bloods today to exclude organic causes; dedicated follow-up for a full assessment and treatment plan; safety net.
ask: 'When you say tired — feverish, low in energy, or sleepy?' / 'How many kilograms, over what period?'
'Are you taking the prednisolone regularly? Reducing it as planned? Still under follow-up? Any shoulder or hip stiffness back? Headache, jaw pain, vision change?'

★ 'How has your mood been? Are you still enjoying the things you used to enjoy? How's your sleep — trouble getting off, or waking in the night and not getting back? Appetite? Concentration? Have you been feeling guilty or worthless?'
★ 'And have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?'
★ 'Most likely you have major depressive disorder. That is an intense low mood and sadness that affects how you function and commonly causes tiredness and weight loss.'

'I did consider other things — because of the weight loss, cancers such as leukaemia, lymphoma, breast and bowel, but no lumps and your screening is up to date; a relapse of the polymyalgia; the steroid affecting your mood or your sugar; thyroid disease, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac disease, other autoimmune conditions, heart failure and sleep apnoea.'

If challenged on the brief psychiatric history: 'I approached this as undifferentiated tiredness and screened for organic causes first. Having reached a mood disorder I would complete a full mental state assessment at a dedicated follow-up.' ADDED
'Is it just the grief?' → 'Grief is part of it, but what you're describing has gone on longer and deeper than grief alone, and it's treatable — I don't want to leave it.'

Steroids can themselves cause mood disturbance — usually early and at higher doses; note it as a differential, do not stop the prednisolone
